lessons.title: Solutions
Opening, reading and writing files
lessons.body:
open(path, mode, encoding=...) returns a **file object**. Always use it in a with block so the file is closed even if an exception occurs (Chapter 11.8); an unclosed file can lose buffered data and leaks a limited OS resource (a **file handle**).

```code
with open("run1.log", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("12:00:01 INFO boot start\n")
    f.write("12:00:05 ERROR nvme0 timeout\n")
    print("written chars:", f.write("12:00:06 INFO retry\n"))
with open("run1.log", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    content = f.read()
print(repr(content[:26]))
print(len(content.splitlines()), "lines")
```

Output:

```output
written chars: 20
'12:00:01 INFO boot start\n1'
3 lines
```

- "w" opens for writing, **creating or truncating** the file. write() does not add a newline; you add \n. It returns the number of characters written.

- Opening with no mode means "r" (read text).

- f.read() returns the **whole file** as one string. Fine for small files; dangerous for a 5 GB log (12.9). **Always pass encoding="utf-8".** Without it, Python uses the platform default, which historically differed (often cp1252 on Windows), so a script that works on Linux breaks on Windows. Python 3.15 makes UTF-8 the default (PEP 686), but explicit is still clearer and works on every version.

**Reading line by line:**

```code
from pathlib import Path
Path("run1.log").write_text("line 1\nline 2\nline 3\n", encoding="utf-
8")
with open("run1.log", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    first = f.readline()
    rest = f.readlines()
print(repr(first), rest)
with open("run1.log", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for n, line in enumerate(f, 1):
        print(n, line.rstrip("\n"))
```

Output:

```output
'line 1\n' ['line 2\n', 'line 3\n']
1 line 1
2 line 2
3 line 3
```

readline() reads one line (including \n; returns "" at end of file); readlines() reads all remaining lines into a list. **Iterating the file object** (line 7) is the best way: lazy, one line at a time.

lessons.title: File modes
lessons.body:
| Mode | Meaning | If file exists | If missing |
| read text (default) | read from start | "r" | FileNotFoundErro |

```code
r
```

| "w" | write text | truncated to empty | created |
| append text | writes go to the end | created | "a" |
| exclusive create | created | "x" | FileExistsError |
| read and write | read/write from start | "r+" | FileNotFoundErro |

```code
r
```

| add "b" | binary: "rb", "wb", | bytes instead of text |

```code
                  "ab"
from pathlib import Path
p = Path("history.log")
p.write_text("run 1 PASS\n", encoding="utf-8")
with open(p, "a", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("run 2 FAIL\n")
print(p.read_text(encoding="utf-8"), end="")
with open(p, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("overwritten\n")
print(p.read_text(encoding="utf-8"), end="")
```

Output:

```output
run 1 PASS
run 2 FAIL
overwritten
```

The classic data-loss bug: opening an existing results file with "w" when you meant "a". Use "x" when overwriting would be a mistake:

```code
from pathlib import Path
Path("report.json").write_text("{}", encoding="utf-8")
try:
    with open("report.json", "x", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        f.write("{}")
except FileExistsError as e:
    print("refusing to overwrite:", e.filename)
Output: refusing to overwrite: report.json.
```

**Writing several lines:**

```code
lines = ["ssd0 PASS", "ssd1 FAIL"]
with open("summary.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.writelines(line + "\n" for line in lines)
    print("third line", file=f)
print(open("summary.txt", encoding="utf-8").read(), end="")
```

Output:

```output
ssd0 PASS
ssd1 FAIL
third line
```

writelines does **not** add newlines despite its name. print(..., file=f) writes to a file with print’s formatting and newline. (Line 5 opens a file without with, acceptable only in a throwaway example.) **pathlib shortcuts** for whole-file operations: Path.read_text(), Path.write_text(), Path.read_bytes(), Path.write_bytes(). They open, transfer and close in one call; use them for small files.

lessons.title: Text encodings
lessons.body:
Files store **bytes**. A **text encoding** maps characters to bytes. UTF-8 handles every language and is the standard; older tools and some vendor logs use Latin-1 or Windows code pages. Decoding bytes with the wrong encoding either fails or produces garbage.

```code
from pathlib import Path
Path("latin.log").write_bytes("Température: 41°C\n".encode("latin-1"))
try:
    Path("latin.log").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
except UnicodeDecodeError as e:
    print("UnicodeDecodeError:", e.reason, "at byte", e.start)
print(Path("latin.log").read_text(encoding="latin-1"), end="")
print(Path("latin.log").read_text(encoding="utf-8", errors="replace"),
end="")
print("°C".encode("utf-8"), "°C".encode("latin-1"))
```

Output:

```output
UnicodeDecodeError: invalid continuation byte at byte 4
Température: 41°C
Tempfrature: 41fC
b'\xc2\xb0C' b'\xb0C'
```

- The same ° is two bytes in UTF-8 and one byte in Latin-1 (line 9), which is why decoding one as the other fails.

- errors="replace" substitutes f for undecodable bytes so processing can continue. For UART captures and device logs that contain random binary noise, errors="replace" (or "backslashreplace", which shows the byte value) prevents a parser from crashing on one corrupt byte.

- Never use errors="ignore" on data you need to trust: it silently deletes bytes.

lessons.title: Binary files: firmware images and checksums
lessons.body:
Binary mode ("rb", "wb") reads and writes bytes objects with no encoding and no newline translation. Use it for firmware images, register dumps, packet captures and anything that is not text.

```code
import hashlib
from pathlib import Path
image = bytes(range(256)) * 4096
Path("fw_v2.bin").write_bytes(image)
data = Path("fw_v2.bin").read_bytes()
print(type(data).__name__, len(data), data[:4], data[:4].hex())
sha = hashlib.sha256()
with open("fw_v2.bin", "rb") as f:
    while chunk := f.read(64 * 1024):
        sha.update(chunk)
print(sha.hexdigest())
print(hashlib.sha256(data).hexdigest() == sha.hexdigest())
```

Output:

```output
bytes 1048576 b'\x00\x01\x02\x03' 00010203
fbbab289f7f94b25736c58be46a994c441fd02552cc6022352e3d86d2fab7c83
True
```

Line by line:

- Line 3: builds a 1 MiB test “image” (bytes 0–255 repeated).

- Line 6: indexing or slicing bytes gives byte values; .hex() shows them as hex text.

- Lines 7–10: computes a SHA-256 checksum **in 64 KiB chunks**, so a 2 GB image never sits in memory. while chunk := f.read(...) uses the walrus operator (Chapter 19): read a chunk, stop when it is empty (end of file).

- Line 12: the chunked hash equals the whole-file hash. **Real use:** before flashing, verify the image’s checksum against the release manifest; after a firmware dump, compare checksums to confirm what is on the device. A mismatch should abort the flash. **Parsing a binary header** with struct:

```code
import struct
from pathlib import Path
header = struct.pack("<4sHHI", b"FWIM", 2, 14, 1048576)
Path("img.bin").write_bytes(header + b"\x00" * 16)
with open("img.bin", "rb") as f:
    magic, major, minor, size = struct.unpack("<4sHHI", f.read(12))
print(magic, major, minor, size)
Output: b'FWIM' 2 14 1048576.
```

The format string "<4sHHI" means: little-endian (<), a 4-byte string, two unsigned 16-bit integers, one unsigned 32-bit integer (12 bytes in total). This is how you read a vendor image header, an EEPROM FRU record or a binary log entry. The layout here is invented for the example; real layouts come from the vendor specification.

lessons.title: Paths with pathlib
lessons.body:
pathlib.Path represents a filesystem path as an object, with operators and methods instead of string manipulation. It works the same on Windows and Linux.

```code
from pathlib import Path
logs = Path("lab") / "logs" / "2026-10-10"
report = logs / "run_42.json"
print(report)
print(report.name, report.stem, report.suffix, report.parent.name)
print(report.with_suffix(".html").name)
print(report.parts)
print(Path("/var/log/syslog").is_absolute(), report.is_absolute())
print(Path.cwd().is_dir(), Path.home().exists())
```

Windows paths behave the same way (shown with PureWindowsPath, which manipulates Windows paths on any OS):

```code
from pathlib import PureWindowsPath, PurePosixPath
w = PureWindowsPath(r"C:\lab\logs\run1.log")
print(w.name, w.parent, w.drive)
print(PurePosixPath("/lab/logs") / "run1.log")
```

Output:

```output
run1.log C:\lab\logs C:
/lab/logs/run1.log
```

**Relative paths are relative to the current working directory**, not to the script’s folder. A script that opens "configs/lab.yaml" works when run from the project root and fails from anywhere else (classic in Jenkins). To find files next to the script, use `Path(__file__).resolve().parent / "configs" / "lab.yaml".`

lessons.title: Creating directories and traversing trees
lessons.body:
```code
from pathlib import Path
base = Path("lab")
for day in ["2026-10-09", "2026-10-10"]:
    d = base / "logs" / day
    d.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    for i in range(1, 3):
        (d / f"run_{i}.log").write_text(f"day {day} run {i}\n",
encoding="utf-8")
(base / "logs" / "2026-10-10" / "notes.txt").write_text("x",
encoding="utf-8")
print(sorted(p.name for p in (base / "logs").iterdir()))
print(sorted(str(p) for p in base.glob("logs/*/run_*.log")))
print(len(list(base.rglob("*.log"))), "log files")
print([p.name for p in sorted(base.rglob("*")) if p.is_file() and
p.suffix != ".log"])
```

Output:

```output
['2026-10-09', '2026-10-10']
['lab/logs/2026-10-09/run_1.log', 'lab/logs/2026-10-09/run_2.log',
'lab/logs/2026-10-10/run_1.log', 'lab/logs/2026-10-10/run_2.log']
4 log files
['notes.txt']
```

- mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) creates all missing parent folders and does not fail if the folder exists: the idempotent “make sure it exists” call.

- iterdir() lists one level, in **arbitrary order**; sort for predictable output.

- glob(pattern) matches within the given path: * matches any characters in one path component, ? one character, [0-9] a range.

- rglob(pattern) searches recursively through all subfolders (same as `glob("**/pattern")).` os.walk is the older recursive walker, still useful when you want each folder with its files:

```code
import os
for root, dirs, files in os.walk("lab"):
    dirs.sort()
    print(root, sorted(files))
```

Output (with the same tree):

```output
lab []
lab/logs []
lab/logs/2026-10-09 ['run_1.log', 'run_2.log']
lab/logs/2026-10-10 ['run_1.log', 'run_2.log']
```

Sorting dirs **in place** controls the walk order; removing names from dirs prunes those subtrees (for example, skipping .git).

lessons.title: File metadata
lessons.body:
```code
import time
from pathlib import Path
p = Path("stat_demo.log")
p.write_text("x" * 1500, encoding="utf-8")
st = p.stat()
print(st.st_size, "bytes")
age_s = time.time() - st.st_mtime
print("modified recently:", age_s < 60)
print(oct(st.st_mode & 0o777))
```

Output:

```output
1500 bytes
modified recently: True
0o644
```

st_size is the size in bytes; st_mtime the last-modification time as seconds since 1970 (a **Unix timestamp**); st_mode & 0o777 the permission bits (0o644 = owner read/write, others read). Permissions are a Linux concept (Chapter 28); Windows reports a simplified mode. **Finding files older than N days**, the core of every log-cleanup job:

```code
import os, time
from pathlib import Path
d = Path("old_logs"); d.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
now = time.time()
for name, days_old in [("a.log", 1), ("b.log", 10), ("c.log", 40)]:
    p = d / name
    p.write_text(name, encoding="utf-8")
    os.utime(p, (now - days_old * 86400, now - days_old * 86400))
cutoff = now - 7 * 86400
old = sorted(p.name for p in d.glob("*.log") if p.stat().st_mtime <
cutoff)
print("older than 7 days:", old)
```

Output: older than 7 days: ['b.log', 'c.log']. Line 7 (os.utime) back-dates the files so the example is reproducible; 86,400 is the number of seconds in a day.

**Safe deletion.** A bug in a cleanup script that computes the wrong path can delete a home directory or a lab share. Guard every recursive delete:

```code
import shutil
from pathlib import Path
ALLOWED_ROOT = Path("workspace").resolve()
def safe_rmtree(target):
    target = Path(target).resolve()
    if target == ALLOWED_ROOT or ALLOWED_ROOT not in target.parents:
        raise ValueError(f"refusing to delete {target}: outside
{ALLOWED_ROOT}")
    shutil.rmtree(target)
    return target.name
Path("workspace/run_7").mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
print("deleted", safe_rmtree("workspace/run_7"))
for bad in ["workspace", "workspace/../etc", "/"]:
    try:
        safe_rmtree(bad)
    except ValueError as e:
        print("blocked:", bad)
```

Output:

```output
deleted run_7
blocked: workspace
blocked: workspace/../etc
blocked: /
```

resolve() turns workspace/../etc into its real absolute location, so .. tricks cannot escape the allowed root. Add a dry-run mode that only prints what would be deleted, and log every deletion.

lessons.title: Large-file processing
lessons.body:
Rule: **never call read() or readlines() on a file whose size you do not control.** Iterate line by line (text) or read fixed-size chunks (binary).

```code
from pathlib import Path
with open("big.log", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for i in range(200_000):
        level = "ERROR" if i % 5000 == 0 else "INFO"
        f.write(f"{i:06d} {level} event {i}\n")
size_mb = Path("big.log").stat().st_size / 1e6
errors = 0
with open("big.log", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for line in f:
        if " ERROR " in line:
            errors += 1
print(f"{size_mb:.1f} MB, {errors} errors")
```

Output: 4.9 MB, 40 errors. Memory use stays constant whether the file is 5 MB or 50 GB. **The last N lines** (like tail -n 3), with a deque that keeps only the newest items:

```code
from collections import deque
with open("big.log", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    last = deque(f, maxlen=3)
print("".join(last), end="")
```

Output (for a 200,000-line log of INFO events):

```output
199997 INFO event 199997
199998 INFO event 199998
199999 INFO event 199999
```

This still reads the whole file once but holds only three lines. For huge files, seeking from the end in binary mode is faster; that is an optimisation to measure first (Chapter 20). **Line endings.** Windows files and UART output use \r\n. Text mode translates them to \n by default (“universal newlines”); newline="" keeps them, which matters when you must reproduce exact bytes:

```code
from pathlib import Path
Path("crlf.log").write_bytes(b"login: \r\nPassword: \r\n")
print(Path("crlf.log").read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines())
with open("crlf.log", encoding="utf-8", newline="") as f:
    print([line for line in f])
```

Output:

```output
['login: ', 'Password: ']
['login: \r\n', 'Password: \r\n']
```

lessons.title: Temporary files and atomic writes
lessons.body:
**Temporary files** (tempfile module) get a unique name in the system temp folder and are cleaned up automatically. Use them for intermediate dumps, generated configs and test fixtures, so parallel runs never collide on the same filename.

```code
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory(prefix="fwtest_") as tmp:
    tmp = Path(tmp)
    (tmp / "dump.bin").write_bytes(b"\x00" * 10)
    print(tmp.name.startswith("fwtest_"), [p.name for p in
tmp.iterdir()])
    saved = tmp
print("exists after block:", saved.exists())
with tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile("w", suffix=".cfg", delete=False,
encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("timeout=30\n")
    cfg_path = Path(f.name)
print(cfg_path.suffix, cfg_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8").strip())
cfg_path.unlink()
```

Output:

```output
True ['dump.bin']
exists after block: False
.cfg timeout=30
```

TemporaryDirectory deletes the whole folder when the block ends. NamedTemporaryFile(delete=False) keeps the file so another program (or a reopen) can use it; you delete it yourself. In pytest, the tmp_path fixture does this for you (Chapter 25). **Atomic writes.** If a process crashes halfway through writing status.json, readers find a half-written, corrupt file. Write to a temporary file in the same folder, then rename it over the target with os.replace, which is atomic on the same filesystem: readers see either the old file or the new one, never a partial one.

```code
import os, tempfile, json
from pathlib import Path
def write_atomic(path, text):
    path = Path(path)
    fd, tmp = tempfile.mkstemp(dir=path.parent, prefix=path.name +
".")
    try:
        with os.fdopen(fd, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
            f.write(text)
            f.flush()
            os.fsync(f.fileno())
        os.replace(tmp, path)
    except BaseException:
        Path(tmp).unlink(missing_ok=True)
        raise
write_atomic("status.json", json.dumps({"state": "flashing",
"progress": 40}))
print(Path("status.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
Output: {"state": "flashing", "progress": 40}.
```

mkstemp creates a unique temp file and returns an OS-level file descriptor plus its path; os.fsync forces the data to disk before the rename; except BaseException cleans up even on Ctrl+C, then re-raises. Use this for state files, result databases and anything a dashboard or another job reads while you write.

lessons.title: Permissions and common errors
lessons.body:
```code
from pathlib import Path
import os
p = Path("locked.txt"); p.write_text("secret", encoding="utf-8")
p.chmod(0o000)
print("running as root:", os.geteuid() == 0)
try:
    p.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    print("read succeeded (root ignores file permissions)")
except PermissionError as e:
    print("PermissionError:", e.strerror)
p.chmod(0o644)
```

Output when run as root (as on this build machine):

```code
running as root: True
read succeeded (root ignores file permissions)
```

As a normal user the same code prints PermissionError: Permission denied. This difference is itself a lesson: a test that passes in a root-run container can fail on a developer laptop, and running automation as root hides permission bugs (least privilege, Chapter 34). os.geteuid exists only on Unix-like systems.

lessons.title: Practical tool: collecting results into a report
lessons.body:
Each DUT writes results/<dut>/result.json. Collect them, detect DUTs that produced nothing, and write a summary:

```code
import json
from pathlib import Path
root = Path("results")
for dut, status, secs in [("ssd0", "PASS", 12.1), ("ssd1", "FAIL",
3.4), ("ssd2", "PASS", 11.8)]:
    d = root / dut; d.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    (d / "result.json").write_text(json.dumps({"dut": dut, "status":
status, "secs": secs}), encoding="utf-8")
(root / "ssd3").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
results = []
for path in sorted(root.glob("*/result.json")):
    results.append(json.loads(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")))
missing = sorted(d.name for d in root.iterdir() if d.is_dir() and not
(d / "result.json").exists())
passed = sum(r["status"] == "PASS" for r in results)
lines = [f"{r['dut']:<6}{r['status']:<6}{r['secs']:>6.1f}" for r in
results]
report = Path("summary.txt")
report.write_text("\n".join(lines) + f"\n{passed}/{len(results)}
passed; missing: {missing}\n", encoding="utf-8")
print(report.read_text(encoding="utf-8"), end="")
```

Output:

```output
ssd0  PASS    12.1
ssd1  FAIL     3.4
ssd2  PASS    11.8
2/3 passed; missing: ['ssd3']
```

Lines 3–7 simulate the per-DUT outputs (ssd3 crashed before writing). Line 11 detects the missing result; **a DUT with no result must be reported, never silently ignored**. sum(r["status"] == "PASS" ...) counts True values as 1. JSON is covered in Chapter 13; Project P5 turns this into a reporting system.

lessons.title: Best practices
lessons.body:
- with for every file; encoding="utf-8" for every text file.

- pathlib for paths; never build paths by string concatenation.

- Stream big files line by line or in chunks.

- "x" mode or atomic writes for files that must not be clobbered or half-written.

- Guard recursive deletes with an allowed root and a dry-run option.

- Temp files via tempfile (or pytest tmp_path), never fixed names like `/tmp/out.txt.`

- Checksums before flashing and after dumping firmware.

lessons.title: Exercises
lessons.body:
1. Write count_levels(path) that returns a dict of how many lines contain INFO, WARN and ERROR, reading line by line.

2. Append a timestamped line to history.log each time a script runs, without losing earlier lines.

3. Write sha256_file(path, chunk_size=1 << 20) and use it to compare two files.

4. List every .log file under a folder, recursively, sorted by size (largest first), printing size in KB.

5. Write cleanup_old_logs(folder, days, dry_run=True) that prints (or deletes when dry_run=False) .log files older than days.

6. Read a file that may be Latin-1 or UTF-8: try UTF-8 first, fall back to Latin-1 on `UnicodeDecodeError.`

7. Write the bytes DE AD BE EF to pattern.bin and read them back, printing `deadbeef.`

8. Build the path to configs/lab.yaml relative to the script’s own folder, so it works from any working directory.

9. Explain why opening an existing results file with "w" is dangerous and give two safer alternatives.

lessons.title: Solutions
JSON
lessons.body:
JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is the standard format for REST APIs including Redfish, and a good format for result files. It maps closely to Python types:

| JSON | Python |
| object {...} | dict (keys are always strings) |
| array [...] | list (tuples become arrays on output) |
| string | str |
| number | int or float |

```code
 true / false               True / False
 null                          None
import json
inventory = {
    "dut": "BMC-02",
    "firmware": {"bmc": "2.14.1", "bios": "1.07"},
    "fans": [7200, 7150, None],
    "healthy": True,
}
text = json.dumps(inventory)
print(text)
print(type(text).__name__)
back = json.loads(text)
print(back["firmware"]["bmc"], back["fans"][2], back == inventory)
```

Output:

```output
{"dut": "BMC-02", "firmware": {"bmc": "2.14.1", "bios": "1.07"},
"fans": [7200, 7150, null], "healthy": true}
str
2.14.1 None True
```

**Name trick:** the functions ending in **s** work with **s**trings (dumps, loads); the others work with files (dump, load). **Readable output** for humans and Git diffs:

```code
import json
data = {"dut": "BMC-02", "tags": ["smoke", "nightly"], "limits":
{"temp_max": 85}}
print(json.dumps(data, indent=2, sort_keys=True))
```

Output:

```output
{
  "dut": "BMC-02",
  "limits": {
    "temp_max": 85
  },
  "tags": [
    "smoke",
    "nightly"
  ]
}
```

**Type conversion surprises:**

```code
import json
print(json.dumps({"a": (1, 2), 1: "int key", "t": True, "n": None,
"f": 3.0}))
print(json.loads('{"1": "x"}'))
try:
    json.dumps({"s": {1, 2}})
except TypeError as e:
    print("TypeError:", e)
```

Output:

```output
{"a": [1, 2], "1": "int key", "t": true, "n": null, "f": 3.0}
{'1': 'x'}
TypeError: Object of type set is not JSON serializable
```

The integer key 1 became the string "1" and does **not** come back as an integer, so a round trip changes the data. Tuples come back as lists. Sets, datetimes, Path objects and your own classes cannot be serialized directly. **Serializing custom types** with a default function, which json calls for every object it cannot handle:

```code
import json
from datetime import datetime
from pathlib import Path
record = {"started": datetime(2026, 10, 10, 12, 0, 1), "log":
Path("logs/run1.log"), "codes": {3, 1}}
def to_jsonable(obj):
    if isinstance(obj, datetime):
        return obj.isoformat()
    if isinstance(obj, Path):
        return str(obj)
    if isinstance(obj, set):
        return sorted(obj)
    raise TypeError(f"cannot serialise {type(obj).__name__}")
print(json.dumps(record, default=to_jsonable))
```

Output:

```output
{"started": "2026-10-10T12:00:01", "log": "logs/run1.log", "codes":
[1, 3]}
```

ISO 8601 timestamps (2026-10-10T12:00:01) are the standard text form for dates; datetime.fromisoformat() reads them back. Always raise TypeError for unknown types so mistakes are not hidden.

**Files:**

```code
import json
from pathlib import Path
results = [{"test": "boot", "status": "PASS", "secs": 12.0}, {"test":
"fw", "status": "FAIL", "secs": 0.4}]
with open("results.json", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    json.dump({"run_id": 42, "results": results}, f, indent=2)
with open("results.json", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    loaded = json.load(f)
print(loaded["run_id"], [r["status"] for r in loaded["results"]])
print(Path("results.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines()
[:3])
```

Output:

```output
42 ['PASS', 'FAIL']
['{', '  "run_id": 42,', '  "results": [']
```

**Malformed JSON:**

```code
import json
for bad in ['{"dut": "BMC-01",}', "{'dut': 'BMC-01'}", '{"temp":
NaN}', ""]:
    try:
        print("parsed:", json.loads(bad))
    except json.JSONDecodeError as e:
        print(f"{bad!r:24} -> {e.msg} (line {e.lineno}, col
{e.colno})")
```

Output:

```output
'{"dut": "BMC-01",}'     -> Illegal trailing comma before end of
object (line 1, col 17)
"{'dut': 'BMC-01'}"      -> Expecting property name enclosed in double
quotes (line 1, col 2)
parsed: {'temp': nan}
''                       -> Expecting value (line 1, col 1)
```

- Trailing commas and single quotes are not JSON (they are Python). JSONDecodeError gives the line and column to look at.

- NaN is **not** valid standard JSON, but Python accepts and produces it by default. Other parsers (JavaScript, Go) reject it. Use json.dumps(..., allow_nan=False) to fail fast if a reading is NaN.

- An **empty response body** gives Expecting value (line 1, col 1): the most common JSON error in API testing. It usually means the server returned an error page or nothing at all; check the HTTP status and content type before parsing (Chapter 27). **JSON Lines** (.jsonl) stores one JSON object per line. It suits event logs and long-running results because you can append one record at a time and read the file as a stream:

```code
import json
from pathlib import Path
events = [{"t": 1, "msg": "boot"}, {"t": 5, "msg": "nvme timeout"}]
Path("events.jsonl").write_text("".join(json.dumps(e) + "\n" for e in
events), encoding="utf-8")
with open("events.jsonl", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for line in f:
        print(json.loads(line)["msg"])
```

Output:

```output
boot
nvme timeout
```

If a test run crashes, every line already written is still valid, unlike a single big JSON document that needs its closing bracket.

lessons.title: Parsing nested API responses
lessons.body:
This is a trimmed response shaped like a Redfish Thermal resource. Real BMCs differ: some omit thresholds, mark absent sensors with null readings, or use the newer ThermalSubsystem resources. Code must tolerate that variation.

```code
import json
response_text = """
{
  "@odata.id": "/redfish/v1/Chassis/1/Thermal",
  "Temperatures": [
    {"Name": "CPU1 Temp", "ReadingCelsius": 64,
"UpperThresholdCritical": 95, "Status": {"State": "Enabled", "Health":
"OK"}},
    {"Name": "Inlet Temp", "ReadingCelsius": 24,
"UpperThresholdCritical": 45, "Status": {"State": "Enabled", "Health":
"OK"}},
    {"Name": "PCH Temp", "ReadingCelsius": null, "Status": {"State":
"Absent"}}
  ],
  "Fans": [
    {"Name": "Fan1", "Reading": 7200, "ReadingUnits": "RPM", "Status":
{"Health": "OK"}},
    {"Name": "Fan2", "Reading": 0, "ReadingUnits": "RPM", "Status":
{"Health": "Critical"}}
  ]
}
"""
thermal = json.loads(response_text)
for sensor in thermal["Temperatures"]:
    reading = sensor.get("ReadingCelsius")
    state = sensor.get("Status", {}).get("State", "Unknown")
    if state != "Enabled" or reading is None:
        print(f"{sensor['Name']:<11} skipped ({state})")
        continue
    limit = sensor.get("UpperThresholdCritical")
    verdict = "PASS" if limit is None or reading < limit else "FAIL"
    print(f"{sensor['Name']:<11} {reading:>3} C  limit {limit}
{verdict}")
unhealthy = [f["Name"] for f in thermal["Fans"] if f.get("Status",
{}).get("Health") != "OK"]
print("unhealthy fans:", unhealthy)
```

Output:

```output
CPU1 Temp    64 C  limit 95  PASS
Inlet Temp   24 C  limit 45  PASS
PCH Temp    skipped (Absent)
unhealthy fans: ['Fan2']
```

Patterns to reuse:

- sensor["Name"] with [] for fields that must exist: a missing name is a real problem worth a KeyError.

- .get() with a default for optional fields; .get("Status", {}) before going deeper.

- Check **state before value**: an absent sensor’s null is not a failure, but an enabled sensor with null might be. Decide and document your rule.

- limit is None or reading < limit handles a missing threshold explicitly instead of crashing on 64 < None.

**A reusable safe-access helper:**

```code
def dig(data, *path, default=None):
    current = data
    for key in path:
        try:
            current = current[key]
        except (KeyError, IndexError, TypeError):
            return default
    return current
system = {"Status": {"Health": "OK"}, "Links": {"Chassis":
[{"@odata.id": "/redfish/v1/Chassis/1"}]}}
print(dig(system, "Status", "Health"))
print(dig(system, "Links", "Chassis", 0, "@odata.id"))
print(dig(system, "Links", "Chassis", 5, "@odata.id", default="none"))
print(dig(system, "MemorySummary", "TotalSystemMemoryGiB",
default="unknown"))
```

Output:

```output
OK
/redfish/v1/Chassis/1
none
unknown
```

*path collects any number of keys and list indexes (Chapter 8.6). TypeError covers indexing into None or a string. Use dig for **optional** data only; required data should fail loudly.

lessons.title: CSV
lessons.body:
CSV (comma-separated values) is the common language of spreadsheets, power-meter exports, oscilloscope captures and simple result tables. It looks trivial, but fields can contain commas, quotes and newlines, so **always use the csv module** instead of split(",").

```code
import csv
from pathlib import Path
Path("sensors.csv").write_text(
    "sensor,value,unit,low,high\n"
    "P3V3,3.31,V,3.135,3.465\n"
    "P12V,12.9,V,11.4,12.6\n"
    '"CPU Temp, die",64.5,C,,95\n',
    encoding="utf-8")
with open("sensors.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for row in csv.DictReader(f):
        value = float(row["value"])
        low = float(row["low"]) if row["low"] else float("-inf")
        high = float(row["high"])
        verdict = "PASS" if low <= value <= high else "FAIL"
        print(f"{row['sensor']:<15} {value:>6} {row['unit']}
{verdict}")
```

Output:

```output
P3V3              3.31 V PASS
P12V              12.9 V FAIL
CPU Temp, die     64.5 C PASS
```

- newline="" is required when opening CSV files: the csv module handles line endings itself, and omitting it can produce blank lines on Windows.

- csv.DictReader uses the header row as keys, so each row is a dict.

- **Every CSV value is a string.** Convert explicitly; empty fields are "", not None (line 12 treats a missing low limit as minus infinity).

- The quoted field "CPU Temp, die" stays one value. A naive split breaks it:

```code
import csv
from pathlib import Path
Path("sensors.csv").write_text('sensor,value\nP3V3,3.31\n"CPU Temp,
die",64.5\n', encoding="utf-8")
with open("sensors.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    reader = csv.reader(f)
    header = next(reader)
    rows = list(reader)
print(header, rows)
print("naive split:", 'CPU Temp, die",64.5'.split(","))
```

Output:

```output
['sensor', 'value'] [['P3V3', '3.31'], ['CPU Temp, die', '64.5']]
naive split: ['CPU Temp', ' die"', '64.5']
```

csv.reader yields plain lists; next(reader) takes the header row off first.

**Writing CSV:**

```code
import csv
results = [
    {"test": "boot", "dut": "ssd0", "status": "PASS", "secs": 12.0},
    {"test": "fw_version", "dut": "ssd0", "status": "FAIL", "secs":
0.4, "note": "expected 2.14"},
]
fields = ["test", "dut", "status", "secs"]
with open("results.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    writer = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=fields,
extrasaction="ignore")
    writer.writeheader()
    writer.writerows(results)
print(open("results.csv", encoding="utf-8").read(), end="")
```

Output:

```output
test,dut,status,secs
boot,ssd0,PASS,12.0
fw_version,ssd0,FAIL,0.4
```

fieldnames fixes the column order. A dict with an extra key (note) raises ValueError unless you pass extrasaction="ignore"; missing keys are written as empty fields. The writer quotes values containing commas automatically. **Other delimiters** (tab-separated output from tools):

```code
import csv, io
text = "name\tvalue\nfan1\t7200\n"
print(list(csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(text), delimiter="\t")))
```

Output:

```output
[{'name': 'fan1', 'value': '7200'}]
```

io.StringIO wraps a string so it behaves like a file, which is handy for parsing command output with the csv module. Excel note: Excel reliably opens UTF-8 CSV only when it starts with a byte-order mark; write with encoding="utf-8-sig" when the audience uses Excel.

lessons.title: XML
lessons.body:
XML appears in JUnit test reports (what Jenkins reads), some BMC and switch configurations, tool exports and older vendor APIs. An XML document is a tree of **elements** (<testcase>), each with **attributes** (name="..."), optional **text**, and **children**. Python’s xml.etree.ElementTree (imported as ET) parses and builds it.

**Reading a JUnit report:**

```code
import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET
xml_text = """<?xml version="1.0"?>
<testsuites>
  <testsuite name="smoke" tests="3" failures="1" skipped="1"
time="13.2">
    <testcase classname="tests.test_boot" name="test_boot"
time="12.0"/>
    <testcase classname="tests.test_fw" name="test_fw_version"
time="0.4">
      <failure message="expected 2.14.1, got
2.13.0">AssertionError</failure>
    </testcase>
    <testcase classname="tests.test_fan" name="test_fan_curve"
time="0.8">
      <skipped message="no fan controller on this SKU"/>
    </testcase>
  </testsuite>
</testsuites>"""
root = ET.fromstring(xml_text)
print(root.tag, len(root))
suite = root.find("testsuite")
print(suite.get("name"), suite.attrib["tests"], suite.get("errors",
"0"))
for case in suite.iter("testcase"):
    failure = case.find("failure")
    skipped = case.find("skipped")
    if failure is not None:
        status = f"FAIL: {failure.get('message')}"
    elif skipped is not None:
        status = f"SKIP: {skipped.get('message')}"
    else:
        status = "PASS"
    print(f"{case.get('name'):<16} {float(case.get('time')):>5.1f}s
{status}")
print([c.get("name") for c in root.findall(".//testcase[failure]")])
```

Output:

```output
testsuites 1
smoke 3 0
test_boot         12.0s  PASS
test_fw_version    0.4s  FAIL: expected 2.14.1, got 2.13.0
test_fan_curve     0.8s  SKIP: no fan controller on this SKU
['test_fw_version']
```

| Call | Returns |
| ET.fromstring(text) / | root element |

```code
ET.parse(path).getroot()
```

| el.tag, el.attrib, el.text | name, attribute dict, text content one attribute (string) or default el.get("name", default) first matching direct child, or None el.find("child") list of matching direct children el.findall("child") |
| el.iter("tag") | every matching element at any depth |
| el.findall(".//tag[child]") | XPath subset: any depth, having a child text of a child el.findtext("child", default) |

Two traps: **attributes are always strings** (convert time), and an element with no children is **falsy**, so always test if failure is not None:, never if failure: (Python 3.12+ warns about this).

**Writing XML:**

```code
import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET
suite = ET.Element("testsuite", name="hw", tests="2", failures="1")
ET.SubElement(suite, "testcase", name="test_psu", time="1.5")
tc = ET.SubElement(suite, "testcase", name="test_fan", time="0.2")
fail = ET.SubElement(tc, "failure", message="Fan2 0 RPM")
fail.text = "Fan2 reading 0 RPM below 1000"
ET.indent(suite)
print(ET.tostring(suite, encoding="unicode"))
```

Output:

```output
<testsuite name="hw" tests="2" failures="1">
  <testcase name="test_psu" time="1.5" />
  <testcase name="test_fan" time="0.2">
    <failure message="Fan2 0 RPM">Fan2 reading 0 RPM below
1000</failure>
  </testcase>
</testsuite>
```

ET.indent (Python 3.9+) adds readable indentation. To save:

```code
ET.ElementTree(suite).write("report.xml", encoding="utf-8",
```

xml_declaration=True). pytest writes JUnit XML for you (--junitxml, Chapter 25); this skill is for custom tools and for reading reports. **Namespaces** are the most common XML confusion:

```code
import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET
doc = """<Inventory xmlns="urn:example:inventory">
  <Device id="1"><Model>X710</Model></Device>
  <Device id="2"><Model>E810</Model></Device>
</Inventory>"""
root = ET.fromstring(doc)
print(root.tag)
print(root.findall("Device"))
ns = {"inv": "urn:example:inventory"}
print([d.findtext("inv:Model", namespaces=ns) for d in
root.findall("inv:Device", ns)])
```

Output:

```output
{urn:example:inventory}Inventory
[]
['X710', 'E810']
```

With a default namespace, every tag’s real name includes the URI in braces, so findall("Device") finds **nothing**, silently. Map a prefix to the URI and use it in every search. **Security:** the standard library’s XML parsers are not hardened against maliciously crafted XML (“billion laughs” entity expansion and similar attacks). Parsing reports your own tools produced is fine; for XML from untrusted sources, use the defusedxml package, which wraps the same API safely.

lessons.title: YAML
lessons.body:
YAML is the most readable format for **configuration written by people**: lab inventories, test parameters, CI settings. It is not in the standard library; install **PyYAML** (python -m pip install pyyaml, imported as yaml). This handbook used PyYAML 6.0.3.

```code
import yaml
config_text = """
lab: lab-a
bmc:
  host: 10.0.0.5
  port: 443
  verify_tls: true
duts:
  - name: SSD-01
    slot: 3
  - name: SSD-02
    slot: 4
thresholds: {temp_max_c: 85, fan_min_rpm: 1000}
timeout_s: 30
"""
cfg = yaml.safe_load(config_text)
print(cfg["bmc"]["host"], type(cfg["bmc"]["port"]).__name__,
cfg["bmc"]["verify_tls"])
print([d["name"] for d in cfg["duts"]], cfg["thresholds"]
["temp_max_c"])
```

Output:

```output
10.0.0.5 int True
['SSD-01', 'SSD-02'] 85
```

Indentation means nesting (spaces only, never tabs); - starts a list item; key: value makes a mapping; {...} and [...] are inline forms. Unlike CSV, YAML infers types: 443 is an int, true a bool.

**That type inference is YAML’s biggest trap:**

```code
import yaml
print(yaml.safe_load("""
country: NO
version: 1.10
octal: 0755
time: 12:30
password: ""
empty:
fw: "2.14.1"
"""))
```

Output:

```output
{'country': False, 'version': 1.1, 'octal': 493, 'time': 750,
'password': '', 'empty': None, 'fw': '2.14.1'}
```

- NO (Norway) became False: PyYAML follows YAML 1.1, where yes/no/on/off are booleans.

- Firmware version 1.10 became the float 1.1, so two different versions collapse into one.

- 0755 became the octal number 493; 12:30 became 750 (base-60 notation).

- An empty value is None.

- **Quote every value that must stay text**: versions, serial numbers, part numbers, hex strings, passwords. fw: "2.14.1" is correct. Then validate types after loading (13.6).

**Writing YAML:**

```code
import yaml
print(yaml.safe_dump({"dut": "SSD-01", "slots": [3, 4], "retries": 3},
sort_keys=False), end="")
```

Output:

```output
dut: SSD-01
slots:
- 3
- 4
retries: 3
```

**Always use safe_load; never use yaml.load with the full loader on untrusted input.** Full YAML can construct arbitrary Python objects, including ones that run commands:

```code
import yaml
try:
    yaml.safe_load("!!python/object/apply:os.system ['echo pwned']")
except yaml.constructor.ConstructorError as e:
    print("blocked:", e.problem)
```

Output:

```output
blocked: could not determine a constructor for the tag
'tag:yaml.org,2002:python/object/apply:os.system'
```

safe_load only builds plain dicts, lists, strings, numbers, booleans and None. Never put secrets in YAML files committed to Git (Chapter 34).

lessons.title: Data validation
lessons.body:
Parsing proves data is **well-formed** (correct syntax). Validation proves it is **valid** (the right fields, types and ranges). Validate at the boundary, as soon as config or an API response is loaded, so errors appear with a clear message instead of a KeyError deep inside a test hours later.

**Manual validation** that collects every problem, not just the first:

```code
def validate_dut(entry):
    errors = []
    name = entry.get("name")
    if not isinstance(name, str) or not name:
        errors.append("name: required non-empty string")
    slot = entry.get("slot")
    if not isinstance(slot, int) or isinstance(slot, bool) or not 0 <=
slot <= 15:
        errors.append(f"slot: integer 0-15 required, got {slot!r}")
    fw = entry.get("expected_fw")
    if fw is not None and not isinstance(fw, str):
        errors.append(f"expected_fw: must be a string, got
{type(fw).__name__}")
    return errors
for entry in [{"name": "SSD-01", "slot": 3}, {"name": "", "slot":
"3"}, {"name": "SSD-03", "slot": 22, "expected_fw": 2.14}]:
    print(entry.get("name") or "<blank>", "->", validate_dut(entry) or
"OK")
```

Output:

```output
SSD-01 -> OK
<blank> -> ['name: required non-empty string', "slot: integer 0-15
required, got '3'"]
SSD-03 -> ['slot: integer 0-15 required, got 22', 'expected_fw: must
be a string, got float']
```

The third entry shows the YAML trap being caught: an unquoted 2.14 arrived as a float.

**Schema validation concepts.** For larger data, describe the shape declaratively in a **schema** and let a library check it. **JSON Schema** is a standard schema language; it validates any dict/list data, including loaded YAML. Install jsonschema (this handbook used 4.26.0):

```code
import jsonschema
schema = {
    "type": "object",
    "required": ["name", "slot"],
    "properties": {
        "name": {"type": "string", "minLength": 1},
        "slot": {"type": "integer", "minimum": 0, "maximum": 15},
        "expected_fw": {"type": "string", "pattern": r"^\d+\.\d+(\.\
d+)?$"},
    },
    "additionalProperties": False,
}
validator = jsonschema.Draft202012Validator(schema)
for entry in [{"name": "SSD-01", "slot": 3, "expected_fw": "2.14.1"},
              {"name": "SSD-02", "slot": 22, "expected_fw": "v2"},
              {"slot": 1, "colour": "red"}]:
    errors = sorted(validator.iter_errors(entry), key=lambda e:
list(e.path))
    if not errors:
        print("valid:", entry["name"])
    for e in errors:
        where = "/".join(map(str, e.path)) or "(root)"
        print(f"  {where}: {e.message}")
```

Output:

```output
valid: SSD-01
  expected_fw: 'v2' does not match '^\\d+\\.\\d+(\\.\\d+)?$'
  slot: 22 is greater than the maximum of 15
  (root): 'name' is a required property
  (root): Additional properties are not allowed ('colour' was
unexpected)
```

- required, type, minimum/maximum, pattern (a regular expression, Chapter 17) and additionalProperties: false (which catches typos such as colour) cover most config validation.

- iter_errors reports **all** problems; jsonschema.validate(data, schema) raises on the first.

- The DMTF publishes JSON Schemas for Redfish resources, so API responses can be checked against the official definitions (Chapter 27). Other approaches: **dataclasses** with checks in __post_init__ (Chapter 14), and the third-party **Pydantic** library, which converts and validates data into typed objects (Chapter 22). JSON Schema is the language-neutral option.

lessons.title: Handling missing and malformed fields: a policy
lessons.body:
| Situation | Policy |
| Required field missing in config | Fail at startup with a validation error listing all problems |
| Required field missing in a device response | Mark the test FAIL (or ERROR) with the field path; it may be a firmware bug |
| Optional field missing | Use a documented default or skip that check; log at DEBUG/INFO |
| Value has the wrong type ("64" for 64) | Convert at the boundary if the spec allows it; otherwise report |
| Value out of range | Validation error (config) or test FAIL (device data) |
| Unparseable file / body | Raise with context (file name, URL, first 200 characters) chained to the parse error |
| Unknown extra fields | Ignore in device data (vendors add OEM properties); reject in your own config (typos) |

source.section: 13.7 Handling missing and malformed fields: a policy

lessons.title: Choosing a format
lessons.body:
| Format | Strengths | Weaknesses | Use for |
| JSON | universal, typed | no comments, no | API payloads, |
| basics, API standard | dates, strict syntax | machine-written results, fixtures |
| JSON Lines | streamable, append- | one object per line | event logs, long- |
| safe | only | running result streams |
| CSV | spreadsheets, | everything is a string, | sensor logs, power- |
| compact tables | flat only | meter data, simple tables |
| XML | schemas, | verbose, parsing | JUnit reports, legacy |
| namespaces, tool | quirks | vendor formats ecosystem |
| YAML | comments, readable, | type surprises, needs | human-edited |
| nested | PyYAML | configs, lab inventories |
| TOML | readable, | less common for data | pyproject.toml, |
| unambiguous types, | tool settings tomllib in stdlib (read-only) |
| INI | very simple | flat, strings only | legacy tool configs |

```code
(configparser)
```

Rule of thumb for this handbook’s framework: **YAML for configuration humans edit,**

**JSON/JSONL for data machines write, JUnit XML for CI, CSV for data people open in a**

**spreadsheet.**

lessons.body:
| Mistake | Symptom | Fix |

```code
double quotes
```

| tripped | string keys |

lessons.title: Exercises
lessons.body:
1. Write save_results(path, results) and load_results(path) using JSON with indent=2, and show that a round trip preserves the data.

2. Serialize a result containing a datetime start time and a set of failing DUT names.

3. Given the Thermal response from 13.2, return a list of (name, reading, limit) for every **enabled** temperature sensor at or above 90% of its critical threshold.

4. Read a CSV of timestamp,psu,watts rows and print the average and maximum watts per PSU.

5. Convert a JSON results list into a CSV file with columns test,status,secs.

6. Parse a JUnit XML file and print the total, failed and skipped counts, plus the names of failed tests.

7. Write a YAML lab config with two BMCs (host, port, and a credentials **reference** rather than a password) and load it; quote every value that must remain a string.

8. Write a JSON Schema for that config and validate it; introduce two errors and print both.

9. Explain what happens to fw: 1.10 and country: NO in YAML and how to prevent it.

lessons.title: Solutions
lessons.body:
```code
import json
from pathlib import Path
def save_results(path, results):
    Path(path).write_text(json.dumps(results, indent=2),
encoding="utf-8")
def load_results(path):
    return json.loads(Path(path).read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
data = [{"test": "boot", "status": "PASS"}]
save_results("r.json", data)
assert load_results("r.json") == data
```

2. Use the to_jsonable default function from 13.1: json.dumps(record,

```code
     default=to_jsonable).
def near_limit(thermal, ratio=0.9):
    hits = []
    for s in thermal.get("Temperatures", []):
        reading = s.get("ReadingCelsius")
        limit = s.get("UpperThresholdCritical")
        if s.get("Status", {}).get("State") != "Enabled" or reading is
None or limit is None:
            continue
        if reading >= ratio * limit:
            hits.append((s["Name"], reading, limit))
    return hits
```

With the sample data it returns [] (64 < 85.5 and 24 < 40.5).

```code
import csv
from collections import defaultdict
from pathlib import Path
Path("psu.csv").write_text("timestamp,psu,watts\n1,PSU1,410\
n2,PSU1,430\n1,PSU2,395\n", encoding="utf-8")
watts = defaultdict(list)
```

lessons.title: Classes and objects
lessons.body:
A **class** is a blueprint that defines what data an object holds and what it can do. An **object** (or **instance**) is one concrete thing built from that blueprint. int, str and list are classes you have used all along; "SSD-01" is an instance of str.

```code
class Device:
    def __init__(self, name, ip):
        self.name = name
        self.ip = ip
        self.connected = False
    def connect(self):
        self.connected = True
        return f"connected to {self.name} at {self.ip}"
bmc = Device("BMC-01", "10.0.0.5")
ssd_host = Device("HOST-07", "10.0.0.17")
print(bmc.connect())
print(bmc.connected, ssd_host.connected)
print(type(bmc).__name__, isinstance(bmc, Device))
```

Output:

```output
connected to BMC-01 at 10.0.0.5
True False
Device True
```

Line by line:

- Line 1: class Device: defines a new type. Class names use CapWords.

- Line 2: __init__ is the **initialiser** (often called the constructor). Python calls it automatically when you create an object, after allocating it.

- Line 2: self is the object being initialised. Python passes it automatically; you never pass it yourself.

- Lines 3–5: self.name = name creates an **instance attribute**: data stored on this particular object.

- Lines 7–9: connect is a **method**: a function defined in a class that receives the object as `self.`

- Line 11: Device("BMC-01", "10.0.0.5") creates a new object and calls `__init__(new_object, "BMC-01", "10.0.0.5").`

- Line 13: bmc.connect() is translated by Python into Device.connect(bmc). That is the whole secret of self.

- Line 14: each object has its **own** attributes; connecting bmc did not change ssd_host.

**Why not just dictionaries and functions?** You could store devices as dicts and write connect(device_dict). Classes add: one place that defines the shape of a device, methods that travel with the data, type checks (isinstance), and the ability to create specialised device types that share code (14.5).

lessons.title: Attributes, methods and the object’s namespace
lessons.body:
```code
class Device:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
d = Device("SSD-01")
d.slot = 3
print(vars(d))
print(hasattr(d, "slot"), getattr(d, "fw", "unknown"))
try:
    print(d.serial)
except AttributeError as e:
    print("AttributeError:", e)
```

Output:

```output
{'name': 'SSD-01', 'slot': 3}
True unknown
AttributeError: 'Device' object has no attribute 'serial'
```

Instance attributes live in a per-object dictionary (vars(d) or d.__dict__). Python lets you add attributes from outside (line 6), but that makes objects inconsistent; **create every attribute in __init__**, even if its initial value is None. getattr(obj, name, default) reads an attribute by name with a fallback.

lessons.title: Instance, class and static methods
lessons.body:
| Kind | Decorator | First parameter | Use for |
| Instance method | (none) | self (the object) | behaviour that uses one object’s data |
| Class method | cls (the class) | alternative | @classmethod constructors, class-wide state |
| Static method | none | helper logically | @staticmethod related to the class but needing neither |

```code
class Bmc:
    default_port = 443
    def __init__(self, host, port=None):
        self.host = host
        self.port = port or Bmc.default_port
    def base_url(self):
        return f"https://{self.host}:{self.port}"
    @classmethod
    def from_config(cls, cfg):
        return cls(cfg["host"], cfg.get("port"))
    @staticmethod
    def is_valid_host(text):
        return bool(text) and " " not in text
bmc = Bmc.from_config({"host": "10.0.0.5"})
print(bmc.base_url())
print(Bmc.is_valid_host("10.0.0.5"), Bmc.is_valid_host("bad host"))
```

Output:

```output
https://10.0.0.5:443
True False
```

- from_config is an **alternative constructor**: it builds an object from a config dict. Using cls(...) instead of Bmc(...) means subclasses inherit a constructor that builds the subclass.

- is_valid_host needs no object and no class; it is a plain function grouped with the class for discoverability. A module-level function is often just as good.

- @ before classmethod is **decorator** syntax (Chapter 16): it modifies the function defined below it.

lessons.title: Class variables versus instance variables
lessons.body:
A **class variable** is defined in the class body and shared by all instances; an **instance variable** is set on self and belongs to one object.

```code
class TestCase:
    created = 0
    tags = []
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        TestCase.created += 1
a = TestCase("boot")
b = TestCase("fans")
a.tags.append("smoke")
print(TestCase.created, b.tags)
b.priority = 1
print(hasattr(a, "priority"))
```

Output:

```output
2 ['smoke']
False
```

- created is a shared counter: correct use of a class variable.

- tags = [] is the **mutable class variable bug**, the class-level twin of the mutable default argument (Chapter 8.3). a.tags.append changed the one list shared by every test, so b is now tagged smoke too. Create mutable per-object data in __init__:

```code
self.tags = [].
```

- Reading self.x looks on the object first, then the class. **Assigning** self.x = ... always creates an instance attribute, which then hides the class variable for that object.

lessons.title: Encapsulation and properties
Inheritance, overriding and super()
lessons.body:
**Inheritance** creates a new class (the **subclass** or child) from an existing one (the **base class** or parent). The child gets all the parent’s methods and can **override** (replace) or extend them.

```code
class Device:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
    def health(self):
        return "UNKNOWN"
    def describe(self):
        return f"{self.name}: {self.health()}"
class Ssd(Device):
    def __init__(self, name, media_errors=0):
        super().__init__(name)
        self.media_errors = media_errors
    def health(self):
        return "OK" if self.media_errors == 0 else "DEGRADED"
class Bmc(Device):
    def health(self):
        return "OK"
for dev in [Device("generic"), Ssd("SSD-01"), Ssd("SSD-02",
media_errors=3), Bmc("BMC-01")]:
    print(dev.describe())
print(issubclass(Ssd, Device), isinstance(Ssd("x"), Device))
```

Output:

```output
generic: UNKNOWN
SSD-01: OK
SSD-02: DEGRADED
BMC-01: OK
True True
```

- class Ssd(Device): means Ssd is a Device.

- super().__init__(name) calls the parent’s initialiser so self.name is set; then the child adds its own attribute. Forgetting it is a common bug: the object then lacks the parent’s attributes and fails later with AttributeError.

- Ssd.health **overrides** Device.health. describe is inherited unchanged, yet when it calls self.health(), Python looks up health on the actual object’s class first, so each device reports correctly. This lookup order is the **method resolution order** (MRO, Chapter 19).

- Bmc inherits __init__ because it does not define its own.

lessons.title: Polymorphism
lessons.body:
**Polymorphism** means code can work with objects of different classes through the same interface. The loop in 14.6 calls describe() on four different types without checking which type each is. Adding a new PowerSupply(Device) class requires **no change** to that loop. Compare the non-polymorphic version:

```code
def health(dev):
    if dev["type"] == "ssd":
        return "OK" if dev["media_errors"] == 0 else "DEGRADED"
    elif dev["type"] == "bmc":
        return "OK"
    else:
        return "UNKNOWN"
print(health({"type": "ssd", "media_errors": 2}), health({"type":
"psu"}))
```

Output:

```output
DEGRADED UNKNOWN
```

Every new device type means editing this function and every other function with the same if/elif chain. With polymorphism, each class carries its own behaviour.

Python’s polymorphism is also **duck typing**: “if it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it is a duck”. A function that calls obj.health() works with any object that has a health method, related by inheritance or not. Protocols (14.12) let you describe such interfaces for type checkers.

lessons.title: Abstraction and abstract base classes
Composition versus inheritance
Dunder methods: making objects behave like built-ins
lessons.body:
**Dunder** (“double underscore”) methods, also called special or magic methods, let your objects work with Python syntax and built-ins. Python calls them for you: len(x) calls

```code
x.__len__(), a == b calls a.__eq__(b).
class TestSuite:
    def __init__(self, name, tests=None):
        self.name = name
        self.tests = list(tests or [])
    def __repr__(self):
        return f"TestSuite({self.name!r}, tests={self.tests!r})"
    def __str__(self):
        return f"{self.name} ({len(self)} tests)"
    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.tests)
    def __iter__(self):
        return iter(self.tests)
    def __contains__(self, test_name):
        return test_name in self.tests
    def __add__(self, other):
        return TestSuite(f"{self.name}+{other.name}", self.tests +
other.tests)
    def __eq__(self, other):
        if not isinstance(other, TestSuite):
            return NotImplemented
        return self.name == other.name and self.tests == other.tests
smoke = TestSuite("smoke", ["boot", "fw_version"])
power = TestSuite("power", ["ac_cycle"])
print(repr(smoke))
print(smoke)
print(len(smoke), "boot" in smoke, [t.upper() for t in smoke])
print(smoke + power)
print(smoke == TestSuite("smoke", ["boot", "fw_version"]), smoke ==
"smoke")
```

Output:

```output
TestSuite('smoke', tests=['boot', 'fw_version'])
smoke (2 tests)
2 True ['BOOT', 'FW_VERSION']
smoke+power (3 tests)
True False
```

| Method | Triggered by | Notes |
| __init__ | Cls(...) | initialise |
| __repr__ | repr(x), REPL, debugger, | unambiguous, ideally valid |
| containers | Python; always define it |
| str(x), print(x), f-strings | human-friendly; falls back to | __str__ |

```code
__repr__
```

return NotImplemented for __eq__ == unknown types

| __lt__, __le__, … | <, <=, sorting | functools.total_order ing fills the rest |
| __len__, __iter__, | len, for, in, x[i] | container behaviour |

```code
__contains__,
__getitem__
```

| __add__, __sub__, … | +, - | operator overloading |
| __bool__ | if x: | truthiness |
| __hash__ | sets, dict keys | needed with __eq__ for hashable objects |
| __enter__, __exit__ | context managers (Chapters | with 11, 15) callable objects __call__ x(...) |

A good __repr__ pays for itself the first time you debug: without it, a failing assertion shows `<__main__.TestSuite object at 0x7f...>. Defining __eq__ without __hash__` makes instances unhashable, which is correct for mutable objects.

lessons.title: Dataclasses
lessons.body:
Classes that mainly hold data need a lot of boilerplate: __init__, __repr__, __eq__. The dataclasses module generates them from **type-annotated** class attributes (annotations were introduced in Chapter 8.11).

```code
from dataclasses import dataclass, field, asdict
from datetime import datetime
@dataclass
class TestResult:
    name: str
    status: str
    duration_s: float = 0.0
    messages: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    def __post_init__(self):
        allowed = {"PASS", "FAIL", "SKIP", "ERROR"}
        if self.status not in allowed:
            raise ValueError(f"status must be one of
{sorted(allowed)}, got {self.status!r}")
    @property
    def passed(self):
        return self.status == "PASS"
r1 = TestResult("boot", "PASS", 12.0)
r2 = TestResult("fw_version", "FAIL", 0.4)
r2.messages.append("expected 2.14.1, got 2.13.0")
print(r1)
print(r2.passed, r2.messages, r1.messages)
print(r1 == TestResult("boot", "PASS", 12.0))
print(asdict(r2))
try:
    TestResult("fans", "PASSED")
except ValueError as e:
    print(e)
```

Output:

```output
TestResult(name='boot', status='PASS', duration_s=12.0, messages=[])
False ['expected 2.14.1, got 2.13.0'] []
True
{'name': 'fw_version', 'status': 'FAIL', 'duration_s': 0.4,
'messages': ['expected 2.14.1, got 2.13.0']}
status must be one of ['ERROR', 'FAIL', 'PASS', 'SKIP'], got 'PASSED'
```

- The annotations (name: str) declare the fields, in order; fields with defaults come after those without.

- field(default_factory=list) creates a **new** list per object. Writing messages: list[str] = [] is rejected by dataclasses with ValueError: mutable default ... is not allowed, which protects you from the shared-default bug.

- __post_init__ runs after the generated __init__: the place for validation.

- asdict converts to a plain dict, ready for json.dumps (Chapter 13). Useful options:

```code
from dataclasses import dataclass, replace
@dataclass(frozen=True, order=True)
class FwVersion:
    major: int
    minor: int
    patch: int = 0
    @classmethod
    def parse(cls, text):
        return cls(*(int(p) for p in text.lstrip("v").split(".")))
    def __str__(self):
        return f"{self.major}.{self.minor}.{self.patch}"
versions = [FwVersion.parse(t) for t in ["2.14.1", "2.9.7", "v2.15"]]
print([str(v) for v in sorted(versions)])
print(max(versions), FwVersion(2, 14) < FwVersion(2, 14, 1))
v = versions[0]
try:
    v.patch = 9
except AttributeError as e:
    print(type(e).__name__, "-", e)
print(replace(v, patch=9), {v: "current"})
```

Output:

```output
['2.9.7', '2.14.1', '2.15.0']
2.15.0 True
FrozenInstanceError - cannot assign to field 'patch'
2.14.9 {FwVersion(major=2, minor=14, patch=1): 'current'}
```

- order=True generates <, <=, >, >= comparing fields in order, so versions sort numerically: the complete fix for the string-version bug from Chapter 3.

- frozen=True makes instances immutable (and hashable, so they can be dict keys). replace builds a modified copy.

- @dataclass(slots=True) (3.10+) uses less memory and blocks accidental new attributes; kw_only=True forces keyword arguments. **When to use what:** dataclass for records with behaviour or validation; namedtuple for lightweight immutable tuples; dict for truly dynamic data such as raw JSON; a normal class when behaviour dominates and the data is internal.

lessons.title: SOLID principles (introductory)
lessons.body:
SOLID is a set of five design guidelines; interviewers for framework roles often ask about them.

| Principle | Meaning | Example in this chapter |
| Single responsibility | A class has one reason to | TestResult holds data; |
| change | Runner runs; SimulatedBmc simulates |
| Open/closed | Open for extension, closed for | Add a test class without |
| modification | editing Runner |
| Liskov substitution | A subclass must work | Every TestCase can be |
| anywhere its parent does | passed to Runner; every PowerController supports |

```code
power_cycle
```

| Interface segregation | Prefer small, focused | SupportsReboot asks only |
| interfaces | for reboot |
| Dependency inversion | Depend on abstractions, not | Tests depend on “a DUT with |
| concrete classes | firmware_version()”, not on a specific BMC client |

They are guidelines, not laws: apply them when they reduce the cost of change, not as a checklist that multiplies classes.

lessons.title: When not to use OOP
lessons.body:
- **A pure transformation** (parse a line, compute a pass rate): a function is simpler. A class with one method and no state is a function in disguise.

- **Plain data passed through** (a JSON response you read once): a dict is fine; a dataclass if you access it in many places.

- **Deep inheritance trees** (four or more levels) or inheritance for code reuse between unrelated things: prefer composition or helper functions.

- **“Manager”, “Helper”, “Util” classes** full of static methods: use a module of functions.

- **Getter/setter boilerplate** for every attribute: use plain attributes and add properties when needed. Python is multi-paradigm: the best automation codebases mix modules of functions, a few well-chosen classes for devices and framework components, and dataclasses for records.
