lessons.title: Virtual environments
lessons.body:
A **virtual environment** (venv) is a self-contained folder with its own Python interpreter link and its own site-packages directory. Packages installed in it do not affect the system Python or other projects. **Why:** project A needs requests 2.31, project B needs 2.34; the OS uses its own Python packages; Jenkins agents must reproduce your environment exactly. One venv per project avoids all of these conflicts.

**Linux / macOS:**

```code
$ cd ~/fwcheck
$ python3 -m venv .venv
$ source .venv/bin/activate
(.venv) $ which python; python --version
~/fwcheck/.venv/bin/python
Python 3.14.6
(.venv) $ deactivate
```

**Windows (PowerShell):**

```code
> cd C:\work\fwcheck
> py -3.14 -m venv .venv
> .venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
(.venv) > Get-Command python | Select-Object Source
(.venv) > python --version
(.venv) > deactivate
```

Windows Command Prompt uses .venv\Scripts\activate.bat. If PowerShell blocks the `script, run once: Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser RemoteSigned.`

What **activation** does: it puts .venv/bin (or .venv\Scripts) at the front of PATH, so python and pip mean the venv’s copies, and shows (.venv) in the prompt. Activation is a convenience; you can always call the interpreter directly: .venv/bin/python -m pytest (Linux) or .venv\Scripts\python -m pytest (Windows). CI scripts often do exactly that. Rules:

- One venv per project, inside the project (.venv), listed in .gitignore. Never commit it: it contains platform-specific binaries and absolute paths.

- A venv is **disposable**: if it breaks, delete the folder and recreate it from your dependency files.

- Never sudo pip install into the system Python. Modern Linux distributions block it (“externally-managed-environment”, PEP 668).

- Point your IDE at the venv interpreter (Chapter 1.4).

lessons.title: pip: installing and inspecting packages
lessons.body:
```code
(.venv) $ python -m pip install "requests>=2.32,<3"
(.venv) $ python -m pip list
Package            Version
------------------ ---------
certifi            2026.7.22
charset-normalizer 3.5.2
idna               3.20
pip                26.1.2
requests           2.34.2
urllib3            2.8.0
```

One requested package brought four **transitive dependencies** (dependencies of dependencies).

| Task | Command |
| Install / with version range | python -m pip install |

```code
"pkg>=2.0,<3"
```

| Upgrade | python -m pip install --upgrade |

```code
pkg
```

| Uninstall | python -m pip uninstall pkg |
| Show details and dependencies | python -m pip show pkg |
| List / outdated | python -m pip list, python -m pip |

```code
list --outdated
```

| Check installed set is consistent | python -m pip check |
| Install from a file | python -m pip install -r |

```code
requirements.txt
```

| Install from a private index | python -m pip install --index-url |

```code
https://pypi.example.lab/simple
pkg
```

Always use python -m pip (Chapter 1.5) so packages go into the interpreter you will run. Quote version specifiers in the shell (">=" would otherwise be a redirection). **Version specifiers** (PEP 440):

| Specifier | Meaning |
| ==2.34.2 | exactly this version (pin) at least 2.32, below 3 (allow fixes and >=2.32,<3 features, block breaking major versions) |
| ~=2.32.0 | compatible release: >=2.32.0,<2.33 |
| !=2.33.0 | exclude a known-bad version |

lessons.title: Dependency pinning and requirements.txt
lessons.body:
Two different needs are often confused:

- **Declare** what your code needs, as ranges, so it can be installed alongside other things:

```code
requests>=2.32,<3. This belongs in pyproject.toml.
```

- **Pin** an exact, tested set of every package, including transitive ones, so every machine gets identical versions: a **lock file**. pip freeze records the exact versions currently installed:

```code
(.venv) $ python -m pip freeze > requirements.txt
(.venv) $ cat requirements.txt
certifi==2026.7.22
charset-normalizer==3.5.2
idna==3.20
requests==2.34.2
urllib3==2.8.0
```

requirements.txt files work everywhere and are fine for simple projects. Limitations: freeze captures everything in the venv (including tools you installed by hand), has no hashes by default, does not distinguish direct from transitive dependencies, and is easy to forget to update. Tools such as pip-tools (pip-compile) and uv (23.6) generate proper lock files from your declared dependencies. **Why pin in test automation:** an unpinned requests or pytest release can change behaviour overnight, making last night’s regression run fail for reasons unrelated to the firmware. When a test result changes, you need to know whether the **firmware** changed or the **tooling** did. Pin, then upgrade deliberately (on a branch, with a full test run). `23.4 pyproject.toml` pyproject.toml is the standard single file for a Python project’s build configuration, metadata, dependencies and tool settings (PEP 517, 518, 621). The src layout from Chapter 10.11:

```code
fwcheck/
├── pyproject.toml
├── README.md
├── src/
│   └── fwcheck/
│       ├── __init__.py
│       └── cli.py
└── tests/
pyproject.toml:
[build-system]
requires = ["setuptools>=77", "wheel"]
build-backend = "setuptools.build_meta"
[project]
name = "fwcheck"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "Firmware version checks for lab DUTs (learning
project)"
readme = "README.md"
requires-python = ">=3.12"
license = "MIT"
authors = [{ name = "Your Name" }]
dependencies = [
    "requests>=2.32,<3",
    "PyYAML>=6.0",
]
[project.optional-dependencies]
dev = ["pytest>=8", "mypy>=1.10", "ruff>=0.6"]
[project.scripts]
fwcheck = "fwcheck.cli:main"
[tool.setuptools.packages.find]
where = ["src"]
```

| Section | Purpose |
| [build-system] | which tool builds the package (setuptools here; hatchling, flit-core, uv_build and poetry-core are alternatives) |
| [project] | metadata: name, version, Python requirement, runtime dependencies as ranges |
| [project.optional-dependencies] | “extras”: groups installed on request, e.g. pip |

```code
install ".[dev]"
```

| [project.scripts] | console commands: fwcheck runs |

```code
fwcheck.cli:main
```

| [tool.*] | settings for tools: |

```code
                                 [tool.pytest.ini_options],
                                 [tool.mypy], [tool.ruff],
                                    [tool.coverage.run]
src/fwcheck/cli.py:
import argparse
from fwcheck import __version__
def main(argv=None):
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="fwcheck")
    parser.add_argument("--version", action="version",
version=f"fwcheck {__version__}")
    parser.add_argument("dut")
    args = parser.parse_args(argv)
    print(f"checking {args.dut} with fwcheck {__version__}")
    return 0
if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())
```

lessons.title: Editable installs
lessons.body:
An **editable install** (pip install -e .) installs your project so that Python imports it **from your source folder**: edits take effect immediately without reinstalling. Console scripts are created too.

```code
(.venv) $ python -m pip install -e ".[dev]"
(.venv) $ fwcheck --version
fwcheck 0.1.0
(.venv) $ fwcheck BMC-01
checking BMC-01 with fwcheck 0.1.0
(.venv) $ python -c "import fwcheck; print(fwcheck.__file__)"
~/fwcheck/src/fwcheck/__init__.py
(.venv) $ python -m pip show fwcheck
Name: fwcheck
Version: 0.1.0
Summary: Firmware version checks for lab DUTs (learning project)
...
Location: ~/fwcheck/.venv/lib/python3.14/site-packages
Editable project location: ~/fwcheck
Requires: PyYAML, requests
```

- ".[dev]" installs the project plus the dev extra (pytest, mypy, ruff).

- fwcheck.__file__ points into src/, proving the editable install.

- This is the fix for the “it imports in my IDE but not in pytest/Jenkins” problems from Chapter 10.4: tests import the installed package, not a path hack.

lessons.title: Lock files and uv
lessons.body:
**uv** is a fast Python package and project manager (Astral, the makers of Ruff). It can install Python versions, create venvs, resolve and lock dependencies, and run commands in the project environment. pip and venv remain fully valid; uv is increasingly common because it is fast and produces cross-platform lock files.

```code
$ uv init --package labtool --python 3.14
Initialized project `labtool` at `~/labtool`
$ cd labtool
$ uv add requests pyyaml
Resolved 7 packages in 1.03s
Installed 7 packages in 7ms
 + pyyaml==6.0.3
 + requests==2.34.2
$ uv add --dev pytest
Resolved 13 packages in 150ms
 + pytest==9.1.1
$ uv run labtool
Hello from labtool!
$ ls
README.md  pyproject.toml  src  uv.lock
```

- uv add records a **range** in pyproject.toml ("requests>=2.34.2") and the **exact resolution** of every package, with hashes, in uv.lock.

- uv run CMD makes sure the venv (.venv) matches the lock file, then runs the command inside it.

- uv sync installs exactly what uv.lock specifies; uv sync --locked fails if the lock file is out of date (use it in CI).

- uv lock --upgrade-package requests upgrades one dependency deliberately.

- **Commit uv.lock** for applications and test frameworks, so every developer and CI agent gets byte-identical dependencies. A lock file excerpt:

```code
version = 1
revision = 3
requires-python = ">=3.14"
[[package]]
name = "certifi"
version = "2026.7.22"
source = { registry = "https://pypi.org/simple" }
```

Other tools in the same space: pip-tools, Poetry, PDM, Hatch. Whichever your team uses, the principles are the same: ranges in pyproject.toml, exact pins in a committed lock file, deliberate upgrades.

lessons.title: Dependency conflicts
lessons.body:
A **conflict** occurs when requirements cannot all be satisfied at once:

```code
(.venv) $ python -m pip install "requests==2.34.2" "urllib3<1.21"
ERROR: Cannot install requests==2.34.2 and urllib3<1.21 because these
package versions have conflicting dependencies.
The conflict is caused by:
    The user requested urllib3<1.21
    requests 2.34.2 depends on urllib3<3 and >=1.26
```

Diagnosis and resolution:

1. Read the “caused by” lines: they name the packages and ranges involved.

2. Find who requires what: python -m pip show <pkg> (Requires / Required-by), uv tree, or pipdeptree (third-party).

3. Loosen **your** pins where possible; avoid exact pins in pyproject.toml.

4. Upgrade or downgrade the package that imposes the strict constraint.

5. Isolate conflicting tools: install CLI tools that need different versions (e.g. a vendor tool requiring an old library) with pipx or uv tool install, each in its own environment.

6. Check an existing environment for inconsistencies with python -m pip check (ideally “No broken requirements found.”).

lessons.title: Environment variables
lessons.body:
An **environment variable** is a named string the operating system passes to every process. They are the standard way to give programs **deployment-specific** settings (which lab, which BMC) and **secrets** (Jenkins injects credentials this way) without changing code.

| Action | Linux / macOS (bash) | Windows PowerShell |
| Set for this shell | export LAB_NAME=lab-a | $env:LAB_NAME = "lab- |

```code
a"
```

| Set for one command | LAB_NAME=lab-a python | (set, run, then remove) |

```code
run.py
```

| Read | echo $LAB_NAME | $env:LAB_NAME |
| Unset | unset LAB_NAME | Remove-Item |

```code
Env:LAB_NAME
```

| Persist for user | add to ~/.bashrc | [Environment]::SetEnv |

```code
ironmentVariable("LAB
_NAME","lab-
a","User")
```

Reading them in Python, with required versus optional handling and type conversion:

```code
import os
os.environ["FWCHECK_TIMEOUT_S"] = "45"
os.environ["FWCHECK_VERIFY_TLS"] = "false"
def env_str(name, default=None, required=False):
    value = os.environ.get(name, default)
    if required and not value:
        raise RuntimeError(f"environment variable {name} is required
but not set")
    return value
def env_bool(name, default=False):
    raw = os.environ.get(name)
    if raw is None:
        return default
    return raw.strip().lower() in ("1", "true", "yes", "on")
timeout_s = float(env_str("FWCHECK_TIMEOUT_S", "30"))
verify_tls = env_bool("FWCHECK_VERIFY_TLS", True)
print(timeout_s, verify_tls, env_str("FWCHECK_LAB", "lab-a"))
try:
    env_str("FWCHECK_BMC_PASSWORD", required=True)
except RuntimeError as e:
    print(e)
```

Output:

```output
45.0 False lab-a
environment variable FWCHECK_BMC_PASSWORD is required but not set
```

Prefix your variables (FWCHECK_) to avoid clashes; convert types explicitly (all values are strings, and bool("false") is True, Chapter 2.5); fail early with a clear message when something required is missing, without printing secret **values**.

lessons.title: Configuration management
lessons.body:
A test framework needs settings from several sources. Use one clear **precedence order**, from lowest to highest:

1. **Defaults in code** (sensible values for everything optional).

2. **Config file in the repository** (e.g. configs/lab-a.yaml: hosts, slots, thresholds, no secrets).

3. **Environment variables** (CI and per-machine overrides, secrets).

4. **Command-line options** (this one run).

```code
import os
from collections import ChainMap
from dataclasses import dataclass
DEFAULTS = {"timeout_s": "30", "retries": "2", "lab": "simulator",
"verify_tls": "true"}
def from_env(prefix="FWCHECK_"):
    return {k[len(prefix):].lower(): v for k, v in os.environ.items()
if k.startswith(prefix)}
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Settings:
    lab: str
    timeout_s: float
    retries: int
    verify_tls: bool
def load_settings(file_cfg, cli_args):
    merged = ChainMap({k: v for k, v in cli_args.items() if v is not
None}, from_env(), file_cfg, DEFAULTS)
    return Settings(
        lab=merged["lab"],
        timeout_s=float(merged["timeout_s"]),
        retries=int(merged["retries"]),
        verify_tls=str(merged["verify_tls"]).lower() in ("1", "true",
"yes", "on"),
    )
os.environ["FWCHECK_TIMEOUT_S"] = "60"
file_cfg = {"lab": "lab-a", "timeout_s": 45, "retries": 3}
print(load_settings(file_cfg, {"retries": 5, "lab": None}))
```

Output:

```output
Settings(lab='lab-a', timeout_s=60.0, retries=5, verify_tls=True)
```

lab came from the file, timeout_s from the environment (overriding the file’s 45), retries from the command line, verify_tls from defaults. ChainMap (Chapter 18.9) implements the precedence without copying; a frozen dataclass makes the result typed and immutable. Validate the merged result (Chapter 13.6 or Pydantic, Chapter 22.7). **Log the effective configuration at start-up** (with secrets masked): it answers “what settings did that failed nightly run actually use?”

lessons.title: Secret handling
lessons.body:
Credentials (BMC passwords, API tokens, SSH keys) must never appear in source code, config files in Git, command lines, logs, test reports or screenshots. Chapter 34 covers security in depth; the essentials:

| Do | Don’t |
| Inject via environment variables from the CI | Hard-code password="admin123" |

credential store (Jenkins withCredentials, Chapter 32)

| Use a secret manager or OS keyring | Commit .env files |

(keyring package) for local runs

| Keep a .env.example with variable names | Put secrets in YAML configs |

only

| Mask secrets in logs (*, Chapter 17.9) | Log request headers or full URLs with tokens |
| Rotate any secret that was ever committed | Assume deleting the line removes it |

(Git history keeps it)

| Use per-lab, least-privilege accounts | Share the admin account across all automation |

.gitignore entries every project needs:

```code
.venv/
__pycache__/
*.pyc
.env
dist/
build/
*.egg-info/
.pytest_cache/
.mypy_cache/
.ruff_cache/
reports/
```

For local development, python-dotenv (third-party) can load a git-ignored .env file into environment variables; the code still reads only os.environ, so CI and laptops behave the same.

lessons.title: Building and distributing packages
lessons.body:
A **wheel** (.whl) is a ready-to-install built package; an **sdist** (.tar.gz) is a source archive. python -m build (package build) creates both:

```code
(.venv) $ python -m pip install build
(.venv) $ python -m build
...
Successfully built fwcheck-0.1.0.tar.gz and fwcheck-0.1.0-py3-none-
any.whl
(.venv) $ ls dist
fwcheck-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl
fwcheck-0.1.0.tar.gz
```

py3-none-any means pure Python, any OS, any CPU. Distribution options for lab tooling:

- **Install the wheel directly** on agents: python -m pip install dist/fwcheck- `0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl.`

- Install from Git: python -m pip install "fwcheck @ `git+https://git.example.lab/team/fwcheck.git@v0.1.0" (pin to a tag).`

- **Private package index** (Artifactory, Nexus, devpi, GitLab/GitHub package registries):

```code
upload with twine upload --repository-url ... dist/* or uv publish,
```

install with --index-url.

- **Public PyPI**: only for code you are allowed to open-source; check with your employer first. **Versioning:** follow semantic versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH): increment MAJOR for breaking changes to the framework’s API, MINOR for features, PATCH for fixes. Tag releases in Git (Chapter 24).

lessons.title: The mental model
lessons.body:
Git stores **snapshots**, not differences. Each **commit** is a full picture of every tracked file at one moment, plus metadata: author, date, message and a pointer to its **parent** commit(s). A commit is named by a SHA-1 hash of its content, for example 1e83f8f. Change one byte and the hash changes, which is why history cannot be silently edited.

There are three places a file can live:

Command that moves

| Area | What it is | files into it |
| Working tree | The files you edit on | (you edit them) disk |
| Staging area (index) | The draft of your next | git add commit |
| Repository (.git | All committed snapshots | git commit |

folder)

A **branch** is only a movable label that points at one commit. HEAD is the label “where I am now”, normally pointing at a branch. When you commit, the current branch label moves forward to the new commit. That is all a branch is, which is why creating one is instant. **Analogy:** commits are photographs in an album, each one noting which photograph came before it. Branches are sticky notes on photographs. HEAD is your finger showing which sticky note you are working from.

lessons.title: First-time setup
lessons.body:
Run once per machine:

```code
$ git config --global user.name "Asha Rao"
$ git config --global user.email "asha@example.com"
$ git config --global init.defaultBranch main
$ git config --global pull.rebase false
$ git config --list --show-origin      # check what is set and where
```

On Windows, install Git for Windows; it gives you Git Bash plus git in PowerShell. Set line endings once so Windows and Linux colleagues do not fight over \r\n:

```code
> git config --global core.autocrlf true      # Windows
$ git config --global core.autocrlf input     # Linux / macOS
```

For a team, a .gitattributes file in the repository is stronger than personal settings. A line * text=auto eol=lf makes every text file use LF in the repository. Add *.bin binary for firmware images so Git never tries to “fix” them.

lessons.title: Creating a repository and the first commit
lessons.body:
We start a tiny project with one function:

```code
def parse_version(text):
    """Turn '2.14.3' into (2, 14, 3)."""
    return tuple(int(p) for p in text.split("."))
print(parse_version("2.14.3"))
```

Output:

```output
(2, 14, 3)
```

The repository file version.py contains only the function (no print). A .gitignore holds three lines: __pycache__/, *.log and .venv/.

```code
$ git init
$ git status --short
?? .gitignore
?? version.py
$ git add .
$ git commit -m "Add firmware version parser"
[main (root-commit) 1e83f8f] Add firmware version parser
 2 files changed, 6 insertions(+)
 create mode 100644 .gitignore
 create mode 100644 version.py
$ git log --oneline
1e83f8f Add firmware version parser
```

Line by line:

- git init creates the hidden .git folder. Nothing is tracked yet.

- git status --short shows two columns. ?? means untracked: Git sees the file but has never stored it.

- git add . copies the current content of every changed file into the staging area.

- git commit -m turns the staging area into a commit. root-commit means it has no parent. 1e83f8f is the short hash.

- “6 insertions” is 3 lines in each file. Other status codes you will see: M modified, A added (staged new file), D deleted, R renamed, UU both modified during a conflict. The left column is the staging area and the right column is the working tree. So M (space then M) means “modified but not staged” and M means “staged”. **Stage selectively.** git add -p shows each changed hunk and asks whether to stage it. Use it to split one messy editing session into two clean commits. Avoid git add . in a folder full of logs and captures until .gitignore is correct.

lessons.title: Branches
lessons.body:
A feature branch lets you work without disturbing main:

```code
$ git switch -c feature/strip-v-prefix
Switched to a new branch 'feature/strip-v-prefix'
```

Firmware tools often report versions as v2.14.3. We change the parser on this branch and look at the diff before committing:

```code
$ git diff
diff --git a/version.py b/version.py
index da2105c..3ca6aec 100644
--- a/version.py
+++ b/version.py
@@ -1,3 +1,3 @@
 def parse_version(text):
     """Turn '2.14.3' into (2, 14, 3)."""
-    return tuple(int(p) for p in text.split("."))
+    return tuple(int(p) for p in text.strip().lstrip("v").split("."))
$ git commit -am "Accept versions with a leading v"
```

Reading a diff: lines starting with - were removed, + were added, and a space means unchanged context. @@ -1,3 +1,3 @@ means “3 lines starting at line 1 in the old file became 3 lines starting at line 1 in the new file”. commit -am stages all tracked modified files and commits them in one step. It never adds new untracked files. Useful branch commands:

```code
$ git branch                    # list local branches, * marks the
current one
$ git branch -a                 # include remote branches
$ git switch main               # move to an existing branch
$ git branch -d feature/old     # delete a merged branch
$ git branch -D feature/old     # force delete an unmerged branch
(careful)
```

Older tutorials use git checkout for both switching branches and restoring files. Modern Git split that into git switch and git restore, which are clearer. Both styles work.

lessons.title: Merging and a real conflict
lessons.body:
Meanwhile, a colleague changed the same line on main to split into at most three parts, so 2.14.3-rc1.5 keeps its suffix in the last part:

```code
$ git switch main
$ (edit: text.split(".") -> text.split(".", 2))
$ git commit -am "Limit version split to three parts"
$ git merge feature/strip-v-prefix
Auto-merging version.py
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in version.py
Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.
$ git status --short
UU version.py
```

Both branches changed the same line in different ways, so Git cannot choose. It writes **conflict markers** into the file:

```code
def parse_version(text):
    """Turn '2.14.3' into (2, 14, 3)."""
<<<<<<< HEAD
    return tuple(int(p) for p in text.split(".", 2))
=======
    return tuple(int(p) for p in text.strip().lstrip("v").split("."))
>>>>>>> feature/strip-v-prefix
```

- Between <<<<<<< HEAD and ======= is the version on your current branch (main).

- Between ======= and >>>>>>> is the incoming version from the feature branch. Resolving means **deciding what the code should be**, not picking a side blindly. Here we want both behaviours: strip the v and limit to three parts. Edit the file so it contains no markers:

```code
def parse_version(text):
    """Turn '2.14.3' into (2, 14, 3)."""
    return tuple(int(p) for p in text.strip().lstrip("v").split(".",
2))
```

Then **test it** before you finish the merge:

```code
def parse_version(text):
    """Turn '2.14.3' into (2, 14, 3)."""
    return tuple(int(p) for p in text.strip().lstrip("v").split(".",
2))
for s in ["2.14.3", " v2.14.3\n", "v1.0.12"]:
    print(repr(s), "->", parse_version(s))
```

Output:

```output
'2.14.3' -> (2, 14, 3)
' v2.14.3\n' -> (2, 14, 3)
'v1.0.12' -> (1, 0, 12)
```

Now mark it resolved and commit:

```code
$ git add version.py
$ git commit --no-edit
$ git log --oneline --graph
*   371ed41 Merge branch 'feature/strip-v-prefix'
|\
| * 58da072 Accept versions with a leading v
* | 4e81702 Limit version split to three parts
|/
* 1e83f8f Add firmware version parser
```

The graph shows the two lines of work separating after 1e83f8f and joining in the **merge commit** 371ed41, which has two parents. Conflict rules that save hours:

1. Run git status first. It lists every conflicted file.

2. Search for <<<<<<< in all files before committing. A marker left in a Python file is a SyntaxError, and in a YAML or JSON config it silently breaks the pipeline.

3. Run the tests after resolving. A clean text merge can still be a broken program.

4. If you are lost, git merge --abort returns to the state before the merge.

5. Avoid conflicts by merging main into your branch (or rebasing) often, and by keeping branches short-lived. A **fast-forward** merge happens when main has not moved since you branched: Git simply moves the main label forward and creates no merge commit. git merge --no-ff forces a merge commit if your team wants every feature to appear as one unit in history.

lessons.title: Rebase (Intermediate)
lessons.body:
git rebase main (run on your feature branch) replays your commits on top of the latest main, giving a straight history without a merge commit. The replayed commits get **new hashes**.

```code
$ git switch feature/retry-logic
$ git fetch origin
$ git rebase origin/main
# fix any conflict, then: git add <file>; git rebase --continue
# give up:                git rebase --abort
$ git push --force-with-lease
```

**The golden rule:** rebase only commits that nobody else has based work on, normally your own feature branch. Rewriting main breaks every colleague’s clone. Use --force-with-lease instead of --force: it refuses to overwrite the remote if someone pushed there since you last fetched. Interactive rebase (git rebase -i HEAD~4) lets you squash “fix typo” commits into the main commit before review. Many teams instead use “Squash and merge” in the pull-request page, which does the same at merge time.

lessons.title: Undoing things safely
lessons.body:
| Situation | Command | Rewrites history? |
| Discard unstaged edits to a | No | git restore file.py |

file

| Unstage a file but keep the | No | git restore --staged |
| edits | file.py |
| Fix the last commit’s message | git commit --amend | Yes (last commit only) |

or add a forgotten file (not yet pushed)

| Undo a commit that is | git revert <hash> | No, adds a new commit |

already pushed

| Put work aside to switch | No | git stash push -m |
| branches | "msg" |
| Move the branch back, keep | git reset --soft | Yes |
| changes in files | HEAD~1 |
| Throw away commits and | Yes, dangerous | git reset --hard |
| changes completely | <hash> |

A real stash and revert from the demo repository:

```code
$ git stash push -m "debug print"
Saved working directory and index state On main: debug print
$ git stash list
stash@{0}: On main: debug print
$ git commit -qm "Set retries to zero"        # a bad change, already
shared
$ git revert --no-edit HEAD
[main 4770f3a] Revert "Set retries to zero"
 Date: Sat Oct 10 11:00:00 2026 +0530
 1 file changed, 1 deletion(-)
 delete mode 100644 config.py
$ git log --oneline -3
4770f3a Revert "Set retries to zero"
0eec246 Set retries to zero
371ed41 Merge branch 'feature/strip-v-prefix'
```

revert keeps the bad commit in history and adds its opposite. That is safe for shared branches and leaves an audit trail, which matters when you must explain why a nightly regression changed. **Safety net:** git reflog lists every position HEAD has had in the last 90 days (default). If a reset --hard or a rebase went wrong, find the old hash there and git switch -c

```code
rescue <hash>.
24.9 .gitignore
```

.gitignore tells Git which untracked files to ignore. It does **not** affect files already committed. A good .gitignore for a Python test-automation repository:

```code
# Python
__pycache__/
*.py[cod]
.venv/
*.egg-info/
build/
dist/
# Tools
.pytest_cache/
.mypy_cache/
.ruff_cache/
.coverage
htmlcov/
# Test outputs (published by CI as artifacts, never committed)
reports/
allure-results/
*.log
*.pcap
captures/
# Local configuration and secrets
.env
*.local.toml
secrets/
# Editors and OS
.vscode/*
!.vscode/extensions.json
.idea/
.DS_Store
Thumbs.db
```

Pattern rules: name/ matches only folders; * matches anything except /; **/ matches any depth; a leading ! re-includes something an earlier rule excluded; a leading / anchors to the repository root. Check why a file is ignored:

```code
$ git check-ignore -v run.log
.gitignore:2:*.log  run.log
```

The answer is “line 2 of .gitignore, pattern *.log”.

If you committed a file by mistake and now want it ignored, add it to .gitignore and remove it from the index only: git rm --cached secrets.env. **If that file held a password or token, it is still in history and on the server: rotate the secret immediately.** Rewriting history (git filter-repo) does not help copies that are already cloned.

lessons.title: Writing good commit messages
lessons.body:
A commit message is for the engineer who runs git log or git blame in six months, probably you.

```code
Retry Redfish GET on HTTP 503 during BMC reboot
The BMC web server returns 503 for up to 40 s after a cold reset,
which made test_power_cycle fail about one run in five on rack R12.
Retry GET up to 5 times with 2^n second backoff (max 30 s total).
Other 5xx codes still fail immediately.
Refs: AUTO-1423
```

Rules:

1. Subject line in the imperative (“Add”, “Fix”, “Retry”), up to about 50 characters, no full stop.

2. Blank line, then a body wrapped at about 72 characters explaining **why** and any trade-off. The diff already shows what.

3. Reference the ticket.

4. One logical change per commit. “Fix timeout and rename module and update README” should be three commits. Some teams use **Conventional Commits** (fix: retry Redfish GET on 503, feat:, test:, ci:, docs:), which tools can turn into changelogs and version numbers. Follow whatever your team uses. A **commit-msg hook** can enforce the rules locally. Git runs .git/hooks/commit-msg <file> before accepting the commit; a non-zero exit code rejects it. The checking logic is plain Python, so test it like any other function:

```code
import re
TYPES = ("feat", "fix", "test", "ci", "docs", "refactor", "chore")
PATTERN = re.compile(rf"^({'|'.join(TYPES)})(\([\w-]+\))?: \S.{{0,60}}
$")
def check_subject(message: str) -> list[str]:
    subject = message.splitlines()[0] if message.strip() else ""
    problems = []
    if not PATTERN.match(subject):
        problems.append("subject must look like 'fix(redfish): retry
on 503'")
    if subject.endswith("."):
        problems.append("subject must not end with a full stop")
    lines = message.splitlines()
    if len(lines) > 1 and lines[1].strip():
        problems.append("second line must be blank")
    return problems
for msg in ["fix(redfish): retry GET on 503",
            "Fixed stuff.",
            "test: add NVMe smart-log checks\nmissing blank line"]:
    print(repr(msg.splitlines()[0]), check_subject(msg) or "OK")
```

Output:

```output
'fix(redfish): retry GET on 503' OK
'Fixed stuff.' ["subject must look like 'fix(redfish): retry on 503'",
'subject must not end with a full stop']
'test: add NVMe smart-log checks' ['second line must be blank']
```

Line by line: the f-string builds the pattern ^(feat|fix|...)(\([\w-]+\))?: \S. {0,60}$ (the doubled braces {{0,60}} produce literal {0,60} inside an f-string); the optional group allows a scope such as (redfish); every rule appends a message rather than stopping at the first, so the author sees all problems at once. To install it, save a script that reads sys.argv[1], calls check_subject, prints problems and exits with 1 if there are any, as .git/hooks/commit-msg, and make it executable. Hooks are not cloned with the repository, so teams usually share them through the pre-commit framework (Chapter 22) and repeat the important checks in CI.

lessons.title: Remotes: clone, fetch, pull, push
lessons.body:
A **remote** is another copy of the repository, usually on GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket or a company Gerrit server. origin is the default name for the one you cloned from.

```code
$ git clone git@github.com:example-org/fwcheck.git
$ git remote -v
$ git fetch origin                 # download new commits, change
nothing locally
$ git pull                         # fetch + merge into the current
branch
$ git push -u origin feature/x     # first push of a new branch, sets
upstream
$ git push                         # later pushes
```

origin/main is your local, read-only record of where main was on the server at the last fetch. git status saying “Your branch is behind ‘origin/main’ by 3 commits” compares against that record, so run git fetch first if the answer matters. **Authentication:** use SSH keys or a personal access token stored in the OS credential manager, never a password in a URL such as https://user:token@host/..., because that URL ends up in shell history, Jenkins logs and .git/config. **Tags** mark releases of your test framework so a test report can name exactly what ran:

```code
$ git tag -a v0.1.0 -m "First tagged release"
$ git push origin v0.1.0
$ git describe --tags            # e.g. v0.1.0-3-g4770f3a: 3 commits
after v0.1.0
```

Write git describe --tags --always --dirty into every test report. -dirty reveals that someone ran tests with uncommitted local edits.

lessons.title: Pull requests
lessons.body:
A **pull request** (PR; GitLab calls it a merge request) asks for a branch to be reviewed and merged. A typical flow:

1. git switch -c fix/redfish-503-retry from an up-to-date main.

2. Make small, focused commits. Run tests and linters locally.

3. git push -u origin fix/redfish-503-retry and open the PR.

4. CI runs automatically: lint, type check, unit tests, perhaps a simulator smoke test.

5. Reviewers comment. You push more commits to the same branch; the PR updates.

6. When approved and green, merge (merge commit, squash or rebase, per team rules). Delete the branch. A useful PR description:

```code
## What
Retry Redfish GET on HTTP 503 for up to 30 s.
## Why
BMC returns 503 for ~40 s after cold reset; test_power_cycle failed
1 run in 5 on rack R12 (AUTO-1423).
## How tested
- Unit tests with a fake session returning 503, 503, 200
- 20 runs of test_power_cycle against the Redfish mock: 20 passed
- Not yet run on hardware rack R12 (needs lab slot)
## Risk
Real 503 faults now take 30 s longer to report.
```

The “How tested” section is the most important for automation code. State plainly what was **not** tested, such as a hardware rack you could not book. **Small PRs get better reviews.** A 150-line PR gets careful comments; a 3,000-line PR gets “LGTM”. Split refactoring from behaviour changes.

lessons.title: Code review
lessons.body:
As a reviewer, look in this order:

1. **Correctness:** does the test actually check the requirement? Can it pass when the product is broken (no assert, assert on the wrong field, caught-and-ignored exception)?

2. **Reliability:** fixed sleep() calls instead of polling with a timeout; dependence on test order; shared state; real time and randomness without seeds.

3. **Safety:** passwords in code or logs; destructive operations (firmware flash, secure erase, power off) without guards for the right device; missing cleanup.

4. **Readability:** names, size of functions, duplicated logic that belongs in a fixture or helper.

5. **Style:** let Ruff and the formatter handle it; do not spend human time on spacing. Write comments that can be acted on, and label how strongly you mean them:

| Weak comment | Useful comment |
| “This is wrong.” | “If get_temp() returns None when the sensor is absent, line 42 raises TypeError. Should absent sensors be skipped or failed?” |
| “Use a fixture.” | “nit: the same BMC login appears in 4 tests; a module-scoped fixture would cut ~30 lines. Fine to do in a follow-up.” |
| “Why sleep?” | “blocking: sleep(60) waits even when the BMC is up in 15 s, and fails if it takes 70 s. Could this poll /redfish/v1 with a 120 s timeout?” |

As an author: reply to every comment, say “done in abc123” or explain why not, and do not take review personally. The review is of the code.

lessons.title: Branching workflows
lessons.body:
| Workflow | How it works | Fits |
| GitHub flow / trunk-based | Short-lived branches from | Most test-framework |
| main, merged by PR within | repositories; teams with good |
| days; main is always | CI releasable |
| Release branches | main plus | Test suites that must match a |
| release/2026.10 | product release, such as an |
| branches that only receive | OpenBMC or SSD firmware |
| fixes; tags mark releases | drop |
| Git Flow | main, develop, feature/*, | Large scheduled releases; |
| release/*, hotfix/* | more ceremony than most teams need now |

For embedded test automation, a common and practical setup: trunk-based development on main for the framework, plus **release branches or tags that pin the test suite to each firmware release**. When firmware 2.14 is in the field and 2.16 is in development, a bug report against 2.14 is re-tested with the tag that validated 2.14, not with today’s main, whose tests may expect 2.16 behaviour.

**Branch protection** on main (a server setting): require a PR, at least one approval, passing CI checks and an up-to-date branch; disallow force pushes. This turns the review and CI process into a rule rather than a habit. Branch naming conventions keep the branch list readable: feature/nvme-smart-log, `fix/redfish-503-retry, test/pldm-fw-update, ci/jenkins-parallel-stages,` optionally with the ticket: fix/AUTO-1423-redfish-retry.

lessons.title: Organising a GitHub (or GitLab) project
lessons.body:
- **README** with purpose, quick start, how to run tests against the simulator and against hardware, and who to contact.

- **Issues** with labels (bug, flaky-test, lab-blocked, good-first-issue) and templates asking for firmware version, rack, logs.

- **CODEOWNERS** file so changes to, for example, src/fwcheck/redfish/ automatically request review from the Redfish owners.

- **PR template** (.github/pull_request_template.md) containing the What/Why/How tested/Risk sections above.

- **Releases** created from tags, with a changelog.

- **Secrets** stored in the CI system’s secret store (GitHub Actions secrets, Jenkins credentials), never in the repository.

- **Large binaries** (firmware images, packet captures) kept out of Git, in an artifact store, or tracked with Git LFS if they must be versioned.

lessons.title: A sample automation repository
lessons.body:
This is the layout used by the portfolio projects in Part V. It combines Chapters 22, 23 and this one.

```code
fwcheck/
├── .github/
│   ├── workflows/ci.yml
│   ├── pull_request_template.md
│   └── CODEOWNERS
├── .gitattributes
├── .gitignore
├── .pre-commit-config.yaml
├── Jenkinsfile
├── README.md
├── pyproject.toml
├── uv.lock
├── src/fwcheck/
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── version.py
│   ├── redfish/client.py
│   └── cli.py
├── tests/
│   ├── conftest.py
│   ├── unit/test_version.py
│   └── integration/test_redfish_mock.py
├── configs/
│   ├── lab-r12.toml           # no secrets: they come from the
environment
│   └── simulator.toml
└── docs/
    └── running-on-hardware.md
```

Choices worth explaining in an interview:

- src/ layout so tests run against the installed package, not loose files (Chapter 23).

- unit/ tests run everywhere in seconds; integration/ tests need the mock server or hardware and are selected with pytest markers (Chapter 25).

- Configuration per lab or rack in configs/, credentials from environment variables injected by CI.

- The lock file is committed so CI and laptops install identical versions. A minimal GitHub Actions workflow, .github/workflows/ci.yml:

```code
name: ci
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      matrix:
        python-version: ["3.13", "3.14"]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: ${{ matrix.python-version }}
      - run: python -m pip install -e ".[dev]"
      - run: ruff check .
      - run: mypy src
      - run: pytest -m "not hardware" --junitxml=reports/junit.xml
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        if: always()
        with:
          name: reports-${{ matrix.python-version }}
          path: reports/
```

The equivalent Jenkins pipeline, the full form of which is in Chapter 32:

```code
pipeline {
  agent { label 'linux' }
  stages {
    stage('Setup') { steps { sh 'python3.14 -m venv .venv &&
.venv/bin/pip install -e ".[dev]"' } }
    stage('Lint')  { steps { sh '.venv/bin/ruff check . &&
.venv/bin/mypy src' } }
    stage('Test')  { steps { sh '.venv/bin/pytest -m "not hardware" --
junitxml=reports/junit.xml' } }
  }
  post { always { junit 'reports/junit.xml' } }
}
```

Action versions such as actions/checkout@v4 change over time. Check the current major versions in the GitHub Actions documentation before copying. Many teams pin actions to a full commit hash for supply-chain safety.

lessons.title: Real-world automation examples
lessons.body:
- **Finding when a test started failing:** git bisect performs a binary search over `commits. git bisect start; git bisect bad HEAD; git bisect good` v0.1.0, then Git checks out the middle commit; you run the test and type git bisect good or bad. Automate it with git bisect run pytest tests/unit/test_version.py. It finds the first bad commit among 1,000 in about 10 steps (because 2^10 = 1024).

- **Traceability:** every Jenkins build records the test-framework commit (git rev-parse HEAD) and the firmware version under test. A failure report then says exactly which test code and which firmware produced it.

- **Lab configuration in Git:** rack and device inventories as TOML or YAML files reviewed by PR give an audit trail of who changed which IP address and when.

lessons.title: Common mistakes
lessons.body:
| Mistake | Effect | Fix |

| captures | -r --cached .venv |
| Committing a password or | Secret leaked to everyone | Rotate the secret now; then |
| token | with access, forever in | remove the file; use CI secret |
| history | stores |
| Working directly on main | Unreviewed changes, painful | Branch protection; always |
| pulls | branch |
| Long-lived branches | Large, risky conflicts | Merge or rebase from main daily; small PRs |
| Leaving conflict markers | SyntaxError or broken YAML | Search for <<<<<<<; run tests before committing the merge |
| git push --force on a | Colleagues lose commits | Never on shared branches; |
| shared branch | use --force-with-lease on your own |
| git reset --hard with | Edits lost (not in reflog, since | git stash first; commit |
| uncommitted work | never committed) | often |
| Mistake | Effect | Fix |

| “changes”) | debugging |
| Mixing formatting and logic | Review misses the real | Separate commits or PRs |

lessons.title: Debugging Git problems
lessons.body:
- **“Your local changes would be overwritten”** when switching branches: commit, stash or restore the changes first.

- **“refusing to merge unrelated histories”:** you created a repository locally and on the server separately. Usually you should clone the server repository and copy your files in instead.

- **“rejected … (fetch first)” on push:** the remote has commits you do not. git pull (or git pull --rebase), resolve, then push.

- **Detached HEAD:** you checked out a commit or tag rather than a branch. New commits there belong to no branch; create one with git switch -c my-branch before leaving.

- **“I don’t know what state I’m in”:** git status (it names the operation in progress and how to continue or abort), then git log --oneline --graph --all -15.

lessons.title: Exercises
lessons.body:
1. (Essential) Create a repository with version.py and .gitignore. Make three commits with good messages. Show git log --oneline.

2. (Essential) Create a branch that adds compare_versions(a, b) returning -1, 0 or 1. Merge it into main. Was it a fast-forward? Why?

3. (Essential) Create a conflict deliberately: change the same docstring line differently on two branches, merge, and resolve keeping parts of both. Show the markers you saw.

4. (Essential) Write a .gitignore for a project that produces reports/junit.xml, `run_2026-10-10.log, uart_capture.bin and .env, but must keep configs/example.env. Verify with git check-ignore -v.`

5. (Intermediate) A teammate pushed a commit that set TIMEOUT_S = 1. Undo it on the shared main without rewriting history.

6. (Intermediate) Extend check_subject so the subject (without the type prefix) must not start with a capital letter, and so Merge ... and Revert ... messages generated by Git are always accepted.

7. (Intermediate) Write a PR description for adding NVMe SMART log checks that were tested only against a simulated device.

8. (Advanced) Use git bisect run on a repository where a test started failing somewhere in the last 20 commits (create the history with a script).

lessons.title: Solutions
lessons.body:
**1.**

```code
$ git init fwcheck && cd fwcheck
$ (create version.py and .gitignore)
$ git add .gitignore && git commit -m "Ignore caches, logs and venv"
$ git add version.py && git commit -m "Add firmware version parser"
$ (add the v-prefix handling)
$ git commit -am "Accept versions with a leading v"
$ git log --oneline
```

Expect three lines, newest first. Your hashes will differ.

**2.** The function:

```code
def parse_version(text):
    return tuple(int(p) for p in text.strip().lstrip("v").split(".",
2))
def compare_versions(a: str, b: str) -> int:
    va, vb = parse_version(a), parse_version(b)
    return (va > vb) - (va < vb)
print(compare_versions("2.14.3", "2.9.10"), compare_versions("v1.0.0",
"1.0.0"),
      compare_versions("1.2.3", "1.10.0"))
```

Output:

```output
1 0 -1
```

Tuples compare element by element, so (2, 14, 3) > (2, 9, 10) because 14 > 9; comparing the strings would give the wrong answer since "2.14" < "2.9" as text. (va > vb) - (va < vb) turns two booleans into -1, 0 or 1. If main received no commits while you worked on the branch, the merge is a fast-forward: main simply moves to the branch’s commit and no merge commit is created.

**3.** You will see markers like those in 24.6. Edit to the combined text, delete all three marker lines, run the code, then git add and git commit.

**4.**

```code
reports/
*.log
*.bin
.env
*.env
!configs/example.env
```

Checked:

```code
$ git check-ignore -v reports/junit.xml
.gitignore:1:reports/   reports/junit.xml
$ git check-ignore -v .env
.gitignore:5:*.env  .env
$ git check-ignore -v configs/example.env
.gitignore:6:!configs/example.env   configs/example.env
$ git check-ignore configs/example.env; echo "exit=$?"
exit=1
```

With -v, Git shows the rule that decided, even when it is the ! rule that re-includes the file. Without -v, a file that is not ignored prints nothing and the exit code is 1. Note that ! cannot re-include a file if its parent **folder** is ignored; that is why we did not ignore configs/.

```code
5. git log -S "TIMEOUT_S = 1" --oneline to find the commit, then git revert
```

<hash> and push. Reset plus force push would rewrite shared history.

**6.**

```code
import re
TYPES = ("feat", "fix", "test", "ci", "docs", "refactor", "chore")
PATTERN = re.compile(rf"^({'|'.join(TYPES)})(\([\w-]+\))?: (?P<text>\
S.{{0,60}})$")
def check_subject(message: str) -> list[str]:
    subject = message.splitlines()[0] if message.strip() else ""
    if subject.startswith(("Merge ", "Revert ")):
        return []
    problems = []
    m = PATTERN.match(subject)
    if not m:
        problems.append("subject must look like 'fix(redfish): retry
on 503'")
    elif m["text"][0].isupper():
        problems.append("text after the type must start in lower
case")
    if subject.endswith("."):
        problems.append("subject must not end with a full stop")
    return problems
for msg in ["fix: Retry on 503", "fix: retry on 503",
            "Merge branch 'feature/strip-v-prefix'", 'Revert "Set
retries to zero"']:
    print(repr(msg), check_subject(msg) or "OK")
```

Output:

```output
'fix: Retry on 503' ['text after the type must start in lower case']
'fix: retry on 503' OK
"Merge branch 'feature/strip-v-prefix'" OK
'Revert "Set retries to zero"' OK
```

The named group (?P<text>...) captures the description so it can be checked separately. str.startswith accepts a tuple of prefixes.

**7.** What: add test_smart_log.py checking critical warning bits, temperature and percentage used. Why: requirement FW-REQ-88. How tested: 12 tests pass against the simulated NVMe device from Chapter 33 (fake nvme smart-log JSON outputs, including one with critical warning set); **not run on real drives**. Risk: field names in the JSON are those of nvme-cli 2.x and may differ on older versions.

**8.** A script that creates 20 commits, where commit 13 breaks the test, then runs bisect. build.py changes in every commit so that every commit has something to record:

```code
$ for i in $(seq 1 20); do
>   echo "BUILD = $i" > build.py
>   if [ $i -ge 13 ]; then echo "LIMIT = 1" > limit.py; else echo
"LIMIT = 5" > limit.py; fi
>   printf 'from limit import LIMIT\ndef test_limit(): assert LIMIT >=
5\n' > test_limit.py
>   git add . && git commit -qm "Commit $i"
> done
$ export PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1
$ git bisect start HEAD HEAD~19
$ git bisect run python -m pytest -q -p no:cacheprovider test_limit.py
Bisecting: 9 revisions left to test after this (roughly 3 steps)
[f05026c...] Commit 10
1 passed in 0.01s
Bisecting: 4 revisions left to test after this (roughly 2 steps)
[8d7df86...] Commit 15
1 failed in 0.02s
Bisecting: 2 revisions left to test after this (roughly 1 step)
[6975383...] Commit 12
1 passed in 0.00s
Bisecting: 0 revisions left to test after this (roughly 1 step)
[ba587e9...] Commit 14
1 failed in 0.02s
Bisecting: 0 revisions left to test after this (roughly 0 steps)
[33fed59...] Commit 13
1 failed in 0.02s
33fed592221bf3e353ad2e8d6234c3618a90d677 is the first bad commit
    Commit 13
$ git bisect reset
```

(Output shortened: pytest’s failure details and long hashes are trimmed.) Five test runs found the culprit among 19 candidates. git bisect run treats exit code 0 as good and 1 to 127 (except 125, meaning “skip”) as bad, which matches pytest’s exit codes for pass and fail. **A real trap found while preparing this solution:** the first attempt, without PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1, wrongly reported commit 20 as the first bad one. LIMIT = 5 and LIMIT = 1 have the same file size, and bisect checked out the files within the same second, so Python reused the stale cached bytecode in __pycache__/limit.cpython- 314.pyc (the cache is validated by source modification time and size). When bisecting Python code, disable bytecode writing or delete __pycache__ in the test command.

lessons.title: Installing pytest and the example project
lessons.body:
```code
$ python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate        #
Windows: .venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
(.venv) $ python -m pip install pytest
(.venv) $ pytest --version
pytest 9.1.1
```

The example project, bmccheck, uses the src layout from Chapter 23:

```code
bmccheck/
├── pyproject.toml
├── src/bmccheck/
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── sensors.py        # parsing, classification, HTTP fetch,
report saving
│   └── fakebmc.py        # in-memory BMC simulator
└── tests/
    ├── conftest.py       # shared fixtures
    ├── test_parse.py
    ├── test_classify.py
    ├── test_power.py
    └── test_io.py
```

The code under test:

```code
# file: src/bmccheck/sensors.py
"""Sensor helpers for a (simulated) BMC."""
import json
import os
from dataclasses import dataclass
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Reading:
    name: str
    value: float | None
    unit: str
    status: str
def parse_sdr_line(line: str) -> Reading:
    """Parse one line of `ipmitool sdr` style output.
    'CPU0_Temp        | 45 degrees C      | ok'  ->
Reading('CPU0_Temp', 45.0, 'degrees C', 'ok')
    """
    parts = [p.strip() for p in line.split("|")]
    if len(parts) != 3:
        raise ValueError(f"expected 3 fields, got {len(parts)}: {line!
r}")
    name, raw, status = parts
    if raw in ("no reading", "disabled"):
        return Reading(name, None, "", status)
    number, _, unit = raw.partition(" ")
    return Reading(name, float(number), unit, status)
def classify(temp_c: float, warn: float = 80.0, crit: float = 95.0) ->
str:
    if warn >= crit:
        raise ValueError("warn must be below crit")
    if temp_c >= crit:
        return "critical"
    if temp_c >= warn:
        return "warning"
    return "normal"
def bmc_host() -> str:
    """BMC address comes from the environment, never from code."""
    host = os.environ.get("BMC_HOST")
    if not host:
        raise RuntimeError("BMC_HOST is not set")
    return host
def fetch_temperature(session, host: str, sensor: str) -> float:
    """Read one temperature through a Redfish-like HTTP session."""
    url = f"https://{host}/redfish/v1/Chassis/1/Sensors/{sensor}"
    response = session.get(url, timeout=10)
    response.raise_for_status()
    return float(response.json()["Reading"])
def save_report(readings: list[Reading], path) -> int:
    rows = [r.__dict__ for r in readings]
    with open(path, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        json.dump(rows, f, indent=2)
    return len(rows)
# file: src/bmccheck/fakebmc.py
"""A tiny in-memory BMC simulator used by the tests."""
class FakeBmc:
    def __init__(self):
        self.power = "Off"
        self.sensors = {"CPU0_Temp": 45.0, "Inlet_Temp": 24.0}
        self.logged_in = False
        self.log: list[str] = []
    def login(self, user: str, password: str) -> None:
        if password != "simulated":
            raise PermissionError("bad credentials")
        self.logged_in = True
        self.log.append(f"login {user}")
    def logout(self) -> None:
        self.logged_in = False
        self.log.append("logout")
    def set_power(self, state: str) -> None:
        if not self.logged_in:
            raise PermissionError("not logged in")
        if state not in ("On", "Off"):
            raise ValueError(f"bad power state {state!r}")
        self.power = state
        self.log.append(f"power {state}")
```

pytest’s settings live in pyproject.toml:

```code
[tool.pytest.ini_options]
testpaths = ["tests"]
pythonpath = ["src"]
addopts = "-ra --strict-markers"
markers = [
    "slow: takes more than a few seconds",
    "hardware: needs a real BMC (deselect with -m 'not hardware')",
]
```

- testpaths: where to look for tests when you just type pytest.

- pythonpath = ["src"]: adds src to sys.path so import bmccheck works without installing. In a real project you would normally pip install -e . instead (Chapter 23); both work.

- addopts: options added to every run. -ra prints a short summary of everything that did not simply pass. --strict-markers turns a misspelt marker into an error (25.8).

- markers: registers custom markers with a description.
