lessons.title: Debugging command automation
lessons.body:
1. Print the exact command with shlex.join(cmd) and run it by hand in a terminal as the **same user** (sudo -u jenkins -i).

2. Compare environments: env in the terminal versus os.environ in the script (PATH, LANG, HOME, proxy variables).

3. Capture both streams and the exit code every time; stderr usually explains the failure.

4. For hangs, check what the process is doing: ps -ef --forest, cat /proc/<pid>/wchan, strace -p <pid>. A command waiting for input (password prompt, “Are you sure?”) is the most common cause; stdin=subprocess.DEVNULL makes it fail fast instead.

5. For SSH problems, run ssh -vvv with the same options. Exit code 255 means the problem is SSH itself, not the remote command.

lessons.title: Exercises
lessons.body:
1. (Essential) Write free_space_mb(path) using df -Pm <path> via subprocess.run and parse the “Available” column. Then write it again with shutil.disk_usage and compare.

2. (Essential) Write a function that runs ping -c 1 -W 1 <host> and returns True or False, treating a missing ping program as an error, not as “host down”.

3. (Essential) Rewrite cat /etc/passwd | cut -d: -f1,7 | grep bash in Python without any subprocess.

4. (Intermediate) Write run_streaming(cmd, timeout) that prints each output line with a timestamp, kills the process group on timeout, and returns the exit code (or raises on timeout).

5. (Intermediate) Use the SSH helper from 28.9 to collect uname -r and fwinfo from a list of hosts and write a CSV report with one row per host, including unreachable ones.

6. (Advanced) Add a --dry-run flag and an inventory file (TOML) to the fwcheck CLI so that a future --flash option could only act on listed hosts.

lessons.title: Solutions
lessons.body:
**1.**

```code
import shutil
import subprocess
def free_space_mb(path: str) -> int:
    out = subprocess.run(["df", "-Pm", path], capture_output=True,
text=True,
                         check=True, timeout=10).stdout
    header, data = out.splitlines()[:2]
    columns = dict(zip(header.split(), data.split()))
    return int(columns["Available"])
via_df = free_space_mb("/")
via_python = shutil.disk_usage("/").free // (1024 * 1024)
print(abs(via_df - via_python) <= 1, "(df and shutil agree within 1
MB)")
```

Output:

```output
True (df and shutil agree within 1 MB)
```

-P asks for the POSIX output format, which never wraps long device names onto two lines, so the parsing stays reliable. shutil.disk_usage needs no external program at all and is the better choice in Python; the df version shows the parsing technique for tools that have no Python equivalent.

**2.**

```code
import shutil
import subprocess
def is_reachable(host: str) -> bool:
    if shutil.which("ping") is None:
        raise RuntimeError("ping is not installed on this machine")
    r = subprocess.run(["ping", "-c", "1", "-W", "1", host],
                       stdout=subprocess.DEVNULL,
stderr=subprocess.DEVNULL, timeout=5)
    return r.returncode == 0
try:
    print(is_reachable("127.0.0.1"))
except RuntimeError as e:
    print("RuntimeError:", e)
```

Output (on this machine):

```output
RuntimeError: ping is not installed on this machine
```

This container has no ping installed, and the function correctly reports that as an error instead of “host unreachable”. On a machine with ping, it prints True. Confusing “tool missing” with “device down” is a classic source of misleading lab reports.

**3.**

```code
from pathlib import Path
for line in Path("/etc/passwd").read_text().splitlines():
    fields = line.split(":")
    if "bash" in fields[6]:
        print(f"{fields[0]}:{fields[6]}")
```

Output (on this machine):

```output
root:/bin/bash
ubuntu:/bin/bash
postgres:/bin/bash
claude:/bin/bash
tester:/bin/bash
```

**4.**

```code
import datetime
import os
import signal
import subprocess
import threading
def run_streaming(cmd: list[str], timeout: float) -> int:
    proc = subprocess.Popen(cmd, stdout=subprocess.PIPE,
stderr=subprocess.STDOUT, text=True,
                            bufsize=1, start_new_session=True)
    timed_out = threading.Event()
    def watchdog():
        timed_out.set()
        os.killpg(proc.pid, signal.SIGTERM)
    timer = threading.Timer(timeout, watchdog)
    timer.start()
    try:
        for line in proc.stdout:
            print(datetime.datetime.now().strftime("%H:%M:%S.%f")[:-
3], line.rstrip())
        returncode = proc.wait()
    finally:
        timer.cancel()
    if timed_out.is_set():
        raise TimeoutError(f"{cmd[0]} exceeded {timeout} s and was
terminated")
    return returncode
print("exit:", run_streaming(["bash", "-c", "echo a; sleep 0.1; echo
b; exit 3"], timeout=5))
try:
    run_streaming(["bash", "-c", "echo start; sleep 30; echo never"],
timeout=0.5)
except TimeoutError as e:
    print("TimeoutError:", e)
```

Output (one run printed):

```output
16:11:31.835 a
16:11:31.938 b
exit: 3
16:11:31.942 start
TimeoutError: bash exceeded 0.5 s and was terminated
```

The important design choice is the **watchdog timer**. In the second command the child printed start and then went silent for 30 seconds, so the for loop was blocked waiting for the next line. A deadline check inside the loop (as in 28.6) would only run when another line arrived, 30 seconds later. The threading.Timer fires after 0.5 s regardless, kills the whole process group, the pipe closes, the loop ends, and the function raises. timer.cancel() in finally stops the watchdog when the command finishes in time. A production version would follow SIGTERM with SIGKILL after a grace period.

lessons.title: When to automate the browser
lessons.body:
Browser tests are the slowest and most fragile layer of the test pyramid. A single UI test may take seconds, depends on page layout, and can fail because of timing. Use them for what only a browser can check:

- critical user journeys end to end (log in, view health, power on, log out);

- that the UI shows the same data as the API (a sensor reading in the web page matches Redfish);

- client-side behaviour: form validation, error banners, redirects after session expiry;

- web tasks with no API, such as exporting a report from an old lab portal. Test business logic and data through the API (Chapter 27) instead: it is faster, more precise and more stable. A healthy suite has many unit tests, fewer API tests, and a small set of browser tests for the critical flows.

**Playwright vs Selenium**

| Playwright | Selenium WebDriver |
| Browsers | Chromium, Firefox, WebKit | Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Safari |
| (bundled builds) | via drivers |
| Waiting | Auto-waits for elements to be | Explicit waits |
| actionable; web-first | (WebDriverWait) needed assertions retry |
| Speed | Fast; browser contexts give | Slower; usually one browser |
| isolated sessions cheaply | per session |
| Extras | Network interception, | Huge ecosystem, Selenium |
| tracing, codegen, API | Grid, W3C standard protocol requests |
| Languages | Python, JS/TS, Java, .NET | Almost every language |

Both are good tools. Selenium is common in existing suites and required by some enterprise grids; Playwright needs less waiting code and is usually the better choice for new Python projects. The concepts in this chapter (locators, waits, page objects) apply to both.

lessons.title: Installing Playwright
lessons.body:

$ python -m pip install playwright pytest-playwright
$ python -m playwright install chromium          # downloads the
matching browser build
$ python -m playwright install --with-deps chromium   # Linux CI: also

lessons.title: The simulated BMC web interface
A first script
lessons.body:
```code
from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright
from bmc_webui import start
server, base = start()
with sync_playwright() as p:
    browser = p.chromium.launch()                # headless by default
    page = browser.new_page()
    page.goto(f"{base}/login.html")
    print("title:", page.title())
    page.get_by_label("Username").fill("admin")
    page.get_by_label("Password").fill("simulated")
    page.get_by_role("button", name="Log in").click()
    page.wait_for_url("**/dashboard.html")
    print("now at:", page.url.removeprefix(base))
    print("heading:", page.get_by_role("heading",
level=1).inner_text())
    page.screenshot(path="overview.png")
    browser.close()
server.shutdown()
```

Output:

```output
title: Mock BMC - Login
now at: /dashboard.html
heading: Server overview
```

Line by line:

- sync_playwright() starts the Playwright driver; the with block stops it. There is also an async_playwright API for asyncio code; the synchronous API is simpler for tests and scripts.

- p.chromium.launch() starts a headless browser. Pass headless=False (and optionally slow_mo=500, milliseconds between actions) to watch it while developing.

- new_page() opens a tab in a fresh, isolated **browser context** (its own cookies and storage, like a private window).

- get_by_label("Username") finds the input linked to the <label for="user">. fill clears it and types the text.

- get_by_role("button", name="Log in") finds a button by its accessible role and visible name, the way a user or a screen reader sees it.

- wait_for_url waits until the JavaScript redirect has happened. screenshot saves an image for reports and debugging.

lessons.title: Locators
lessons.body:
A **locator** describes how to find an element. It does not search immediately; it searches each time you act on it, so it keeps working when the page re-renders.

| Locator | Finds | Use when |
| Element by ARIA role and | First choice for buttons, | page.get_by_role("but |
| ton", name="Power | accessible name | links, headings, checkboxes |

```code
on")
```

| Form field by its label | Inputs | page.get_by_label("Pa |

```code
ssword")
```

| Element by visible text | Messages, non-interactive | page.get_by_text("Sen |
| sor data | text |

```code
unavailable")
```

| Element with data- | Stable hooks added by | page.get_by_test_id(" |
| power-state") | testid="power-state" | developers for tests |
| CSS selector | Structure (tables), when | page.locator("#sensor |
| s tbody tr") | nothing better exists |
| page.locator("xpath=/ | XPath | Rarely; brittle and hard to read /td[text()='FAN2']") |

Prefer locators that reflect what the **user** sees (role, label, text) or explicit test IDs. CSS classes and long XPath expressions change whenever a developer restyles the page, and then many tests break at once. If you work with the product team, ask them to add data-testid attributes to important elements; it is the cheapest way to stable UI tests. Locators are **strict**: an action on a locator that matches more than one element raises an error instead of silently picking the first:

```code
from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright, Error
from bmc_webui import start
server, base = start()
with sync_playwright() as p:
    browser = p.chromium.launch()
    page = browser.new_page()
    page.goto(f"{base}/login.html")
    page.evaluate("sessionStorage.setItem('auth', '1')")       #
shortcut: pretend we logged in
    page.goto(f"{base}/dashboard.html")
    buttons = page.get_by_role("button", name="Power")
    print("buttons matching 'Power':", buttons.count())
    try:
        buttons.click(timeout=2000)
    except Error as e:
        print(e.message.splitlines()[0])
    page.get_by_role("button", name="Power on", exact=True).click()
    print("clicked the exact one")
    browser.close()
server.shutdown()
```

Output:

```output
buttons matching 'Power': 2
Locator.click: Error: strict mode violation: get_by_role("button",
name="Power") resolved to 2 elements:
clicked the exact one
```

name="Power" matches by substring by default, so it found both power buttons. Narrow the locator (exact=True, a longer name, or chaining such as `page.locator("#controls").get_by_role(...)) rather than using .first, which` hides the ambiguity. The sessionStorage shortcut skips the login form; tests of other pages commonly log in through an API or stored session state instead of typing credentials every time.

lessons.title: Auto-waiting and web-first assertions
lessons.body:
The power button changes the state to “Powering on…” and then, 0.8 s later, to “On”. A naive script reads the text immediately:

```code
from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright, expect
from bmc_webui import start
import time
server, base = start()
with sync_playwright() as p:
    browser = p.chromium.launch()
    page = browser.new_page()
    page.goto(f"{base}/login.html")
    page.evaluate("sessionStorage.setItem('auth', '1')")
    page.goto(f"{base}/dashboard.html")
    state = page.get_by_test_id("power-state")
    page.get_by_role("button", name="Power on").click()
    print("read immediately:", state.inner_text())
    t0 = time.monotonic()
    expect(state).to_have_text("On", timeout=5000)
    print(f"expect() passed after about {time.monotonic() - t0:.1f}
s")
    page.get_by_role("button", name="Power off").click()
    try:
        expect(state).to_have_text("On", timeout=1500)       # wrong
expectation on purpose
    except AssertionError as e:
        print(str(e).splitlines()[0])
    browser.close()
server.shutdown()
```

Output (one run printed; the timing varies slightly):

```output
read immediately: Powering on...
expect() passed after about 0.9 s
Locator expected to have text 'On'
```

- Actions such as click and fill **auto-wait**: before acting, Playwright waits until the element is attached, visible, stable (not animating), enabled and able to receive events. That removes most of the sleep calls that Selenium scripts used to need.

- Reading text (inner_text) does **not** wait for a particular value; it returns what is there now (“Powering on…”).

- expect(locator).to_have_text("On") is a **web-first assertion**: it re-checks repeatedly until the condition is true or the timeout expires (5 s default). It passed as soon as the page showed “On”, after about 0.8 s.

- When it times out, the AssertionError message shows the locator, the expected value and what it actually found, which is exactly what you need in a CI log. Other useful assertions: to_be_visible(), to_be_hidden(), to_be_enabled(), `to_have_value(), to_contain_text(), to_have_count(n), to_have_url(),` to_have_title(). For page-level conditions there are page.wait_for_url, `page.wait_for_load_state("networkidle") and page.expect_response(...).`

**Never use time.sleep() to wait for the UI.** A sleep is too long on a fast day and too short on a slow one. Wait for the condition that matters: a text, an element, a URL, a network response.

lessons.title: Reading data from the page
lessons.body:
Comparing UI data with the API is a common BMC test: the web page must show the same sensor readings as Redfish.

```code
from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright, expect
from bmc_webui import start, SENSORS
server, base = start()
with sync_playwright() as p:
    browser = p.chromium.launch()
    page = browser.new_page()
    page.goto(f"{base}/login.html")
    page.evaluate("sessionStorage.setItem('auth', '1')")
    page.goto(f"{base}/dashboard.html")
    rows = page.locator("#sensors tbody tr")
    expect(rows).to_have_count(3)                        # waits for
the fetch to fill the table
    table = [[cell.strip() for cell in
row.locator("td").all_inner_texts()] for row in rows.all()]
    for name, reading, status in table:
        print(f"{name:<11} {reading:>8}  {status}")
    from_api = [[s["name"], s["reading"], s["status"]] for s in
SENSORS]
    print("UI matches API data:", table == from_api)
    warnings = rows.filter(has_text="Warning")
    print("rows with warnings:",
warnings.locator("td").first.inner_text())
    browser.close()
server.shutdown()
```

Output:

```output
CPU0_Temp       45 C  OK
Inlet_Temp      24 C  OK
FAN2         900 RPM  Warning
UI matches API data: True
rows with warnings: FAN2
```

- to_have_count(3) waits for the asynchronous fetch to replace the “Loading…” row. Reading the rows before that would have returned the placeholder.

- rows.all() returns one locator per row; all_inner_texts() returns the text of every matching cell.

- filter(has_text=...) narrows a set of locators, here to the row whose status is “Warning”.

- In a real test, from_api would come from a Redfish request made in the same test (Chapter 27), not from a constant.

lessons.title: The Page Object Model
Tests with pytest-playwright
lessons.body:
The pytest-playwright plugin provides fixtures: page (a new page in a new context for each test), context, browser, browser_name, and command-line options such as --headed, --

```code
browser firefox, --slowmo 200, --tracing retain-on-failure, --screenshot
only-on-failure and --base-url.
# file: conftest.py
import pytest
from bmc_webui import start
@pytest.fixture(scope="session")
def base_url():
    server, url = start()
    yield url
    server.shutdown()
# file: test_webui.py
import pytest
from playwright.sync_api import expect
from pages import LoginPage
@pytest.fixture
def overview(page, base_url):
    return LoginPage(page, base_url).open().login("admin",
"simulated")
def test_login_shows_overview(overview):
    expect(overview.page).to_have_title("Mock BMC - Overview")
@pytest.mark.parametrize("user, password", [("admin", "wrong"), ("",
""), ("ADMIN", "simulated")])
def test_bad_login_shows_error(page, base_url, user, password):
    login = LoginPage(page, base_url).open()
    login.login(user, password)
    expect(login.error).to_be_visible()
    expect(page).to_have_url(f"{base_url}/login.html")
def test_power_on_then_off(overview):
    overview.power("On")
    overview.power("Off")
def test_fan_warning_is_shown(overview):
    assert overview.sensors()["FAN2"] == "Warning"
def test_logout_requires_login_again(overview, base_url):
    login = overview.logout()
    expect(login.username).to_be_visible()
    overview.page.goto(f"{base_url}/dashboard.html")
    expect(overview.page).to_have_url(f"{base_url}/login.html")
$ pytest -q test_webui.py
.......
[100%]
7 passed in 5.42s
```

Seven tests (the bad-login test runs three times), about 0.8 s each, most of it browser start-up and the deliberate 0.8 s power delays.

- base_url is a session fixture that starts the server once. pytest-playwright also defines a base_url fixture fed by --base-url; overriding it in conftest.py, as here, is the documented way to supply your own.

- Each test gets a **fresh browser context**, so cookies and session storage never leak between tests. That is why test_logout_requires_login_again cannot affect the others.

- The tests read like a test plan; all selectors live in pages.py.

- The last test is a real security check: after logout, the protected page must redirect to login. (In this mock the protection is client-side JavaScript only; a real web UI must also reject the API calls, which an API test should verify.)

lessons.title: Intercepting the network
lessons.body:
page.route lets a test intercept requests and answer them itself. Use it to test error handling that is hard to trigger on a real device:

```code
from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright, expect
from bmc_webui import start
server, base = start()
with sync_playwright() as p:
    browser = p.chromium.launch()
    page = browser.new_page()
    page.route("**/api/sensors.json", lambda route:
route.fulfill(status=503, body="BMC busy"))
    page.goto(f"{base}/login.html")
    page.evaluate("sessionStorage.setItem('auth', '1')")
    page.goto(f"{base}/dashboard.html")
    expect(page.get_by_text("Sensor data
unavailable")).to_be_visible()
    print("503 handled: error row shown")
    page.unroute("**/api/sensors.json")
    page.route("**/api/sensors.json", lambda route: route.fulfill(
        json=[{"name": "CPU0_Temp", "reading": "101 C", "status":
"Critical"}]))
    page.reload()
    expect(page.locator("#sensors tbody
tr")).to_have_text(["CPU0_Temp101 CCritical"])
    print("fake critical reading rendered")
    with page.expect_response("**/api/sensors.json") as info:
        page.reload()
    print("response status seen by the page:", info.value.status)
    browser.close()
server.shutdown()
```

Output:

```output
503 handled: error row shown
fake critical reading rendered
response status seen by the page: 200
```

- route.fulfill returns a fake response; the real server never sees the request. route.abort() simulates a network failure; route.continue_() lets it through, optionally modified.

- The first case revealed a real weakness in the mock UI: on a 503 its JavaScript tried to parse “BMC busy” as JSON, failed, and fell into the catch that shows “Sensor data unavailable”. The behaviour happens to be acceptable, but only by accident; a test like this documents the intended behaviour.

- expect_response waits for a specific response, which is the correct way to wait for “the data has loaded”. It reports 200 here because the fake route from the second case is still installed and fulfill defaults to status 200.

- to_have_text on a multi-row locator compares the list of row texts. The cells’ texts are joined without spaces because <td> elements have no whitespace between them in this page.

The trace viewer is the most useful tool for CI failures: archive test-results/ as a build artifact and open the trace of the failed test locally. Codegen is a good way to discover locators, but rewrite its output into page objects; recorded scripts are not maintainable tests. A trace can also be recorded manually:

```code
from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright
from bmc_webui import start
import zipfile
server, base = start()
with sync_playwright() as p:
    browser = p.chromium.launch()
    context = browser.new_context()
    context.tracing.start(screenshots=True, snapshots=True)
    page = context.new_page()
    errors = []
    page.on("pageerror", lambda exc: errors.append(str(exc)))
    page.goto(f"{base}/login.html")
    page.get_by_label("Username").fill("admin")
    page.get_by_label("Password").fill("wrong")
    page.get_by_role("button", name="Log in").click()
    context.tracing.stop(path="trace.zip")
    browser.close()
server.shutdown()
with zipfile.ZipFile("trace.zip") as z:
    names = z.namelist()
print("trace files:", len(names) > 0, "| has trace.trace:",
"trace.trace" in names)
print("JavaScript errors on page:", errors)
```

Output:

```output
trace files: True | has trace.trace: True
JavaScript errors on page: []
```

lessons.title: Browser tests in CI
lessons.body:
- Run headless (the default). Install browsers in the pipeline with python -m playwright install --with-deps chromium, or use Microsoft’s official Playwright Docker image, whose tag must match your Playwright version.

- Publish JUnit XML (--junitxml), and archive screenshots, videos and traces of failures as artifacts.

- Run tests in parallel with pytest-xdist (-n auto); browser contexts keep them isolated. Do not parallelise tests that change shared state on the same real BMC (power, settings).

- Use a dedicated test account on the BMC with only the privileges the tests need. Store its password in the CI credential store and pass it through an environment variable.

- Lab BMCs often use self-signed TLS certificates. `browser.new_context(ignore_https_errors=True) accepts them; limit it to` lab configuration, as with verify=False in Chapter 27.

lessons.title: Selenium for comparison
lessons.body:
The same login in Selenium 4, for reading existing suites (shown for comparison; not run here):

```code
# file: selenium_login.py
from selenium import webdriver
from selenium.webdriver.common.by import By
from selenium.webdriver.support import expected_conditions as EC
from selenium.webdriver.support.ui import WebDriverWait
driver = webdriver.Chrome()          # Selenium Manager finds a
matching driver automatically
try:
    driver.get("http://127.0.0.1:8000/login.html")
    driver.find_element(By.ID, "user").send_keys("admin")
    driver.find_element(By.ID, "pw").send_keys("simulated")
    driver.find_element(By.CSS_SELECTOR,
"button[type=submit]").click()
    WebDriverWait(driver, 10).until(EC.url_contains("dashboard.html"))
    state = driver.find_element(By.CSS_SELECTOR, "[data-testid=power-
state]")
    driver.find_element(By.ID, "power-on").click()
    WebDriverWait(driver, 10).until(EC.text_to_be_present_in_element(
        (By.CSS_SELECTOR, "[data-testid=power-state]"), "On"))
finally:
    driver.quit()
```

The structure is the same; the differences are explicit WebDriverWait calls where Playwright auto-waits, and driver.quit() in finally to avoid leaving browser processes behind.

lessons.title: Common mistakes
lessons.body:
| Mistake | Effect | Fix |
| time.sleep() to wait for | Slow and still flaky | Auto-waiting actions, |
| the UI | expect, expect_response |
| Long CSS/XPath selectors | Break on every redesign | Role, label, text and data-testid locators |
| .first / .nth(0) to | Clicks the wrong element | Make the locator unique |
| silence strictness errors | later |
| Reading text and asserting | Race with page updates | expect(locator).to_ha |
| with assert immediately | ve_text(...) |
| Logging in through the UI in | Slow suites | Log in once; reuse storage |
| every test | state or set up through the API |
| Testing business logic | Slow, fragile, imprecise | Move it to API or unit tests |

through the UI

| Sharing one page between | State leaks, order dependence | Fresh context per test |
| tests | (pytest-playwright default) |
| Credentials hard-coded in | Leaked secrets | Environment variables, CI |
| page objects | credentials |
| Not archiving | CI failures impossible to | --tracing retain-on-failure, artifacts traces/screenshots analyse |

lessons.title: Exercises
lessons.body:
1. (Essential) Write a script that logs in with a wrong password and prints the error message text.

2. (Essential) Add a method wait_for_sensors(count) to OverviewPage and use it in a test.

3. (Essential) Write a test that the “Power on” button changes the state to “Powering on…” before it reaches “On”.

4. (Intermediate) Use page.route with route.abort() to simulate a network failure for the sensor API and check the UI message.

5. (Intermediate) Save the logged-in state once with context.storage_state(path=...) and reuse it in a second context to open the overview without logging in. Explain why this mock needs a different approach.

6. (Advanced) Write a test that compares every sensor shown in the UI with the mock Redfish data from Chapter 27, reporting all differences at once.

lessons.body:
**1.**
