**Known protocol weakness — awareness only.** The RAKP design in IPMI v2.0 lets a party that can start a session handshake obtain data derived from a user’s password (publicly documented, e.g. CVE-2013-4786). The specification cannot be fixed, so the mitigations are operational: strong unique passwords, restricting IPMI LAN access to trusted management networks, or disabling IPMI over LAN in favour of Redfish.

lessons.title: Troubleshooting authentication and transport failures — lab
lessons.body:
Using the fake ipmitool (Chapter 10), reproduce and classify:

```code
wrong password   -> rc=1 'mc info' failed: Error: Unable to establish IPMI
v2 / RMCP+ session
unreachable BMC  -> rc=None 'mc info' timed out after 1s
```

Questions: Which of these would you retry? What extra evidence would you collect on a real system?

**Answer.** Neither should be retried blindly. A fast session failure is usually deterministic (credentials, cipher suite, IPMI disabled): retrying risks account lockout and wastes time. A timeout might be a transient BMC reboot, so one retry after a readiness check is reasonable. Evidence: ipmitool -vv output (no secrets), a capture of UDP 623 on the test host, the BMC’s network IPMI service logs, lan print output (cipher suites, enabled state), and whether HTTPS on the same BMC works at that moment.

source.section: 11.9 Troubleshooting authentication and transport failures — lab

lessons.title: Common mistakes
lessons.body:
- Using cipher suite 0 or 1 “because it works”.

- Running all automation as Administrator.

- Interpreting every session failure as a wrong password.

- Repeated failed logins from a script locking out a shared account.

- Leaving IPMI over LAN enabled on systems where only Redfish is required.

lessons.title: Exercises
lessons.body:
1. Write a pytest check (for an authorised lab BMC) asserting that cipher suite 0 is not offered, using ipmitool lan print 1 output.

2. Explain the effective privilege when a user has Administrator limit, the session requests Operator, and the cipher suite max is User.

3. Why is UDP harder to troubleshoot than TCP?

**Solutions.**

1.

```code
import re
def offered_cipher_suites(lan_print: str) -> set[int]:
    for line in lan_print.splitlines():
        if line.strip().startswith("RMCP+ Cipher Suites"):
            values = line.split(":", 1)[1]
            return {int(v) for v in re.findall(r"\d+", values)}
    raise AssertionError("RMCP+ Cipher Suites line not found; check ipmitool
version")
def test_cipher_suite_zero_disabled(ipmitool):
    assert 0 not in offered_cipher_suites(ipmitool.run("lan", "print", "1"))
```

(The label text is how ipmitool prints it in common versions; confirm on yours.) 2. User — the minimum of the three limits. 3. UDP has no handshake and no RST-based refusal; lost requests or replies produce only silence, so “blocked”, “service down” and “wrong address” look the same until you capture packets or check from the BMC side.

lessons.title: Summary
lessons.body:
- IPMI LAN = RMCP over UDP 623; IPMI v2.0 adds RMCP+ with RAKP and negotiated algorithms.

- Cipher suite selects authentication/integrity/encryption; prefer 17, never 0.

- Effective privilege is the minimum of user, session and cipher limits.

- UDP failures are silent; troubleshoot systematically and from both sides.

- Validate secure configuration; prefer Redfish; keep IPMI on isolated networks.

lessons.title: Purpose of Platform Level Data Model
lessons.body:
**PLDM (Platform Level Data Model)** is a family of DMTF specifications, produced by the **PMCI** (Platform Management Components Intercommunication) working group, that define how a management controller (usually the BMC) and the components inside a platform (NICs, GPUs, storage controllers, CPUs, power supplies, the host firmware) exchange management data.

The problem PLDM solves: every component vendor used to define its own management commands over I²C or proprietary channels, so BMC firmware needed custom code per device. PLDM defines **common data models and commands** for recurring needs — discovery, sensors, inventory, firmware update, BIOS settings — so a BMC can manage devices from many vendors with one implementation.

PLDM is **transport-independent**: the messages are defined separately from how they travel. In practice PLDM almost always travels over **MCTP** (binding defined in DSP0241), and MCTP in turn runs over SMBus/I²C, PCIe VDM, I3C, serial and others. OpenBMC also uses PLDM between the BMC and host firmware on some platforms.

source.section: 12.1 Purpose of Platform Level Data Model

lessons.title: The specification family
lessons.body:
| Spec | Title (abridged) | PLDM type |
| DSP0240 | PLDM Base Specification — | — message format, base commands, timing |
| DSP0245 | PLDM IDs and Codes — | — type numbers, codes |
| DSP0241 | PLDM over MCTP Binding | — |
| DSP0240 (type 0) | Messaging Control and Dis‐ | 0 covery |
| DSP0246 | PLDM for SMBIOS Transfer | 1 |
| DSP0248 | PLDM for Platform Monitor‐ | 2 ing and Control |
| DSP0247 | PLDM for BIOS Control and | 3 Configuration |
| DSP0257 | PLDM for FRU Data | 4 |
| DSP0267 | PLDM for Firmware Update | 5 |
| DSP0218 | PLDM for Redfish Device | 6 Enablement (RDE) |

(Type numbers are defined in DSP0245. Check the DMTF PMCI page for current versions.)

lessons.title: PLDM message structure and terminology
lessons.body:
Every PLDM message starts with a 3-byte header **[Spec: DSP0240]**:

```code
 byte 0:  bit 7  Rq        1 = request, 0 = response
          bit 6  D         datagram bit (1 = unacknowledged request, no
response)
          bit 5  reserved
          bits 4..0  Instance ID (0..31)
 byte 1:  bits 7..6  Hdr Ver   header version, 00b for current spec
          bits 5..0  PLDM Type (0..63)
 byte 2:  PLDM Command Code
 byte 3+: payload. In a response, the FIRST payload byte is the Completion
Code.
```

Terminology:

- **Requester / responder** — the sender and answerer of a request.

- **Instance ID** — a 5-bit number the requester puts in each request; the responder copies it into the response so the requester can match them. A requester should not reuse an instance ID for a new request while one is outstanding.

- **PLDM terminus** — a PLDM-capable endpoint (a device or a firmware component). Each has a **TID** (Terminus ID) used to identify it in PLDM data such as PDRs and events. TID 0x00 and 0xFF have special meanings (unassigned / reserved).

- **PDR (Platform Descriptor Record)** — records describing sensors, effecters, entities and their relationships (DSP0248), analogous to IPMI SDRs.

Encoding and decoding is a few lines of Python. Project 3’s module:

```code
fwval/fwval/protocols/pldm.py
 """PLDM message header encoding and base (Type 0) command helpers.
 Based on DMTF DSP0240 (PLDM Base Specification) and DSP0245 (PLDM IDs and
 Codes). Header layout:
     byte 0 : [7] Rq, [6] D (datagram), [5] reserved, [4:0] Instance ID
     byte 1 : [7:6] header version (0b00), [5:0] PLDM type
     byte 2 : PLDM command code
 Responses carry a completion code as the first payload byte.
 When PLDM is carried over MCTP (DSP0241), the MCTP message-type byte 0x01
 precedes this header; that byte belongs to MCTP, not to PLDM.
 """
 from __future__ import annotations
 from dataclasses import dataclass
 # PLDM types (DSP0245), subset
 TYPE_BASE = 0x00          # messaging control and discovery
 TYPE_SMBIOS = 0x01
 TYPE_PLATFORM = 0x02      # platform monitoring and control (DSP0248)
 TYPE_BIOS = 0x03
 TYPE_FRU = 0x04           # FRU data (DSP0257)
 TYPE_FW_UPDATE = 0x05     # firmware update (DSP0267)
 TYPE_RDE = 0x06           # Redfish device enablement (DSP0218)
 TYPE_NAMES = {0: "base", 1: "smbios", 2: "platform", 3: "bios", 4: "fru",
               5: "fw_update", 6: "rde"}
# Base (type 0) commands (DSP0240)
CMD_SET_TID = 0x01
CMD_GET_TID = 0x02
CMD_GET_PLDM_VERSION = 0x03
CMD_GET_PLDM_TYPES = 0x04
CMD_GET_PLDM_COMMANDS = 0x05
# Generic completion codes (DSP0240)
CC_SUCCESS = 0x00
CC_ERROR = 0x01
CC_ERROR_INVALID_DATA = 0x02
CC_ERROR_INVALID_LENGTH = 0x03
CC_ERROR_NOT_READY = 0x04
CC_ERROR_UNSUPPORTED_PLDM_CMD = 0x05
CC_ERROR_INVALID_PLDM_TYPE = 0x20
CC_NAMES = {
    0x00: "SUCCESS", 0x01: "ERROR", 0x02: "ERROR_INVALID_DATA",
    0x03: "ERROR_INVALID_LENGTH", 0x04: "ERROR_NOT_READY",
    0x05: "ERROR_UNSUPPORTED_PLDM_CMD", 0x20: "ERROR_INVALID_PLDM_TYPE",
}
class PldmError(Exception):
    pass
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class PldmMessage:
    request: bool
    instance_id: int
    pldm_type: int
    command: int
    payload: bytes = b""
    datagram: bool = False
    header_version: int = 0
    def encode(self) -> bytes:
        if not 0 <= self.instance_id <= 0x1F:
            raise PldmError("instance id must be 0..31")
        if not 0 <= self.pldm_type <= 0x3F:
            raise PldmError("PLDM type must be 0..63")
        b0 = (0x80 if self.request else 0) | (0x40 if self.datagram else 0) |
self.instance_id
        b1 = ((self.header_version & 0x3) << 6) | self.pldm_type
        return bytes([b0, b1, self.command & 0xFF]) + self.payload
    @classmethod
    def decode(cls, raw: bytes) -> "PldmMessage":
        if len(raw) < 3:
            raise PldmError(f"PLDM message too short ({len(raw)} bytes)")
        hdr_ver = raw[1] >> 6
        if hdr_ver != 0:
            raise PldmError(f"unsupported PLDM header version {hdr_ver}")
        return cls(
            request=bool(raw[0] & 0x80), datagram=bool(raw[0] & 0x40),
            instance_id=raw[0] & 0x1F, pldm_type=raw[1] & 0x3F,
            command=raw[2], payload=bytes(raw[3:]), header_version=hdr_ver,
        )
    @property
    def completion_code(self) -> int:
        if self.request:
            raise PldmError("requests have no completion code")
        if not self.payload:
            raise PldmError("response has no completion code byte")
        return self.payload[0]
def request(instance_id: int, pldm_type: int, command: int, payload: bytes = b
"") -> PldmMessage:
    return PldmMessage(True, instance_id, pldm_type, command, payload)
def check_response(req: PldmMessage, resp: PldmMessage) -> None:
    """Validate that resp really answers req (the checks a test should
make)."""
    if resp.request:
        raise PldmError("got a request where a response was expected")
    if resp.instance_id != req.instance_id:
        raise PldmError(f"instance id mismatch: sent {req.instance_id}, got {r
esp.instance_id}")
    if (resp.pldm_type, resp.command) != (req.pldm_type, req.command):
        raise PldmError(
            f"type/command mismatch: sent {req.pldm_type}/{req.command:#04x},
"
            f"got {resp.pldm_type}/{resp.command:#04x}")
def bitfield_to_set(data: bytes) -> set[int]:
    """Byte 0 bit 0 = item 0, byte 0 bit 7 = item 7, byte 1 bit 0 = item
8 ..."""
    return {i * 8 + bit for i, byte in enumerate(data) for bit in range(8) if
byte >> bit & 1}
def set_to_bitfield(items: set[int], length: int) -> bytes:
    out = bytearray(length)
    for item in items:
        if not 0 <= item < length * 8:
            raise PldmError(f"item {item} does not fit in {length} bytes")
        out[item // 8] |= 1 << (item % 8)
    return bytes(out)
def parse_get_tid(resp: PldmMessage) -> int:
    if resp.completion_code != CC_SUCCESS:
        raise PldmError(f"GetTID failed: {CC_NAMES.get(resp.completion_code, h
ex(resp.completion_code))}")
    if len(resp.payload) != 2:
        raise PldmError(f"GetTID response length {len(resp.payload)} != 2")
    return resp.payload[1]
def parse_get_pldm_types(resp: PldmMessage) -> set[int]:
    if resp.completion_code != CC_SUCCESS:
        raise PldmError(f"GetPLDMTypes failed: {CC_NAMES.get(resp.completion_c
ode, hex(resp.completion_code))}")
    if len(resp.payload) != 1 + 8:
        raise PldmError(f"GetPLDMTypes response length {len(resp.payload)} !=
9")
    return bitfield_to_set(resp.payload[1:])
```

lessons.title: Message types and command–response interactions
lessons.body:
A **PLDM type** selects the command set. Within type 0 (Messaging Control and Discovery), the **base commands** are **[Spec: DSP0240]**:

| Code | Command | Purpose |
| 0x01 | SetTID | Assign the terminus ID |
| 0x02 | GetTID | Read the terminus ID |
| 0x03 | GetPLDMVersion | Versions of a given PLDM type the terminus supports (multipart transfer) |
| 0x04 | GetPLDMTypes | Bitfield of supported PLDM types |
| 0x05 | GetPLDMCommands | Bitfield of supported commands for a given type and version |

A typical discovery conversation when the BMC finds a new endpoint:

```code
BMC (requester)                         Device (responder)
  GetTID ───────────────────────────────▶
  ◀──────────────────────── CC=SUCCESS, TID
  GetPLDMTypes ─────────────────────────▶
  ◀────────── CC=SUCCESS, 8-byte bitfield (e.g. types 0,2,4,5)
  GetPLDMVersion(type 2) ───────────────▶
  ◀────────── CC, version(s) of DSP0248 supported
  GetPLDMCommands(type 2, version) ─────▶
  ◀────────── CC, 32-byte bitfield of supported type-2 commands
  GetPDR (type 2) ... repeatedly ───────▶   read all PDRs: sensors, effecters
   ◀──────────────────────────── PDR records
   GetSensorReading / GetStateSensorReadings (periodic polling)
```

Representative commands of other types (codes from the respective specs; confirm against the version you implement):

| Type | Commands (code) |
| 2 Platform M&C (DSP0248) | PlatformEventMessage (0x0A), GetSensor‐ Reading (0x11), GetStateSensorReadings (0x21), SetNumericEffecterValue (0x31), SetStateEffecterStates (0x39), GetPDR (0x51) |
| 4 FRU (DSP0257) | GetFRURecordTableMetadata (0x01), Get‐ FRURecordTable (0x02) |
| 5 Firmware update (DSP0267) | QueryDeviceIdentifiers (0x01), GetFirmwareParameters (0x02), RequestUpdate (0x10), PassComponentTable (0x13), UpdateComponent (0x14), RequestFirmwareData (0x15), TransferComplete (0x16), VerifyComplete (0x17), Apply‐ Complete (0x18), ActivateFirmware (0x1A), GetStatus (0x1B), CancelUpdate (0x1D) |

lessons.title: Request and response formats
lessons.body:
Example: **GetPLDMTypes**. Request: header only, no payload. Response payload: one completion-code byte followed by 8 bytes (64 bits); bit n set means type n is supported, with byte 0 bit 0 = type 0.

Encoding, wrapping and decoding with the book’s code (all bytes produced by our encoder from the field definitions — **not** captured traffic):

```code
examples/ch12_pldm_bytes.py
 """Chapters 12-15: build PLDM and MCTP messages byte by byte and watch them
 travel
 through the simulated MCTP network from Project 3.
 All bytes shown are produced by our encoder from the DSP0236/DSP0240 field
 layouts. They are NOT captured traffic from real hardware.
 """
 from __future__ import annotations
 import sys
from pathlib import Path
sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1] / "projects" / "fwv
al"))
from fwval.adapters.mctp_sim import SimEndpoint, SimMctpNetwork  # noqa: E402
from fwval.protocols import mctp, pldm  # noqa: E402
def hx(b: bytes) -> str:
    return " ".join(f"{x:02x}" for x in b)
# 1. A PLDM GetPLDMTypes request, header bits explained
req = pldm.request(instance_id=3, pldm_type=pldm.TYPE_BASE, command=pldm.CMD_G
ET_PLDM_TYPES)
raw = req.encode()
print("PLDM GetPLDMTypes request :", hx(raw))
print(f"  byte0 {raw[0]:08b} -> Rq={raw[0] >> 7} D={(raw[0] >> 6) & 1}
InstanceID={raw[0] & 0x1F}")
print(f"  byte1 {raw[1]:08b} -> HdrVer={raw[1] >> 6} PLDMType={raw[1] &
0x3F}")
print(f"  byte2 {raw[2]:#04x}     -> command GetPLDMTypes")
# 2. Wrapped for MCTP: the MCTP message-type byte 0x01 goes first
msg = bytes([mctp.MSG_TYPE_PLDM]) + raw
pkts = mctp.fragment(msg, dest=9, src=8, tag=2, tag_owner=True)
print("\nMCTP packet (binding-independent part):", hx(pkts[0].encode()))
h = pkts[0].encode()
print(f"  hdr ver={h[0] & 0xF} dest EID={h[1]} src EID={h[2]} "
      f"flags={h[3]:08b} (SOM={h[3] >> 7} EOM={(h[3] >> 6) & 1} seq={(h[3] >>
4) & 3} "
      f"TO={(h[3] >> 3) & 1} tag={h[3] & 7})")
# 3. A long message split into several packets
big = bytes([mctp.MSG_TYPE_PLDM]) + bytes(150)
for p in mctp.fragment(big, 9, 8, tag=5, tag_owner=True, mtu=64):
    print(f"  packet seq={p.seq} SOM={int(p.som)} EOM={int(p.eom)} payload={le
n(p.payload)} bytes")
# 4. Full exchange through the simulated network
net = SimMctpNetwork(local_eid=8)
net.add(SimEndpoint(eid=9, tid=7))
answer = net.exchange(9, msg)
resp = pldm.PldmMessage.decode(answer[1:])
print("\nResponse bytes           :", hx(answer))
print("  completion code        :", pldm.CC_NAMES[resp.completion_code])
print("  supported PLDM types   :", sorted(pldm.parse_get_pldm_types(resp)),
      "->", [pldm.TYPE_NAMES[t] for t in sorted(pldm.parse_get_pldm_types(resp
))])
print("\nWire trace:")
for direction, wire in net.trace:
    print(f"  {direction} {hx(wire)}")
# 5. Error path: an unsupported command
bad = pldm.request(4, pldm.TYPE_BASE, 0x7E)
answer = net.exchange(9, bytes([mctp.MSG_TYPE_PLDM]) + bad.encode())
code = pldm.PldmMessage.decode(answer[1:]).completion_code
print("\nUnsupported command 0x7e ->", f"{code:#04x}", pldm.CC_NAMES[code])
```

**Output [Run]:**

```code
PLDM GetPLDMTypes request : 83 00 04
  byte0 10000011 -> Rq=1 D=0 InstanceID=3
  byte1 00000000 -> HdrVer=0 PLDMType=0
  byte2 0x04     -> command GetPLDMTypes
MCTP packet (binding-independent part): 01 09 08 ca 01 83 00 04
  hdr ver=1 dest EID=9 src EID=8 flags=11001010 (SOM=1 EOM=1 seq=0 TO=1 tag=2)
  packet seq=0 SOM=1 EOM=0 payload=64 bytes
  packet seq=1 SOM=0 EOM=0 payload=64 bytes
  packet seq=2 SOM=0 EOM=1 payload=23 bytes
Response bytes           : 01 03 00 04 00 35 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
  completion code        : SUCCESS
  supported PLDM types   : [0, 2, 4, 5] -> ['base', 'platform', 'fru',
'fw_update']
Wire trace:
  tx 01 09 08 c8 01 83 00 04
  rx 01 08 09 c0 01 03 00 04 00 35 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
Unsupported command 0x7e -> 0x05 ERROR_UNSUPPORTED_PLDM_CMD
```

Reading the output:

- 83 00 04 is the request: 0x83 = 1000 0011 → Rq=1, D=0, instance ID 3; 0x00 → header version 0, type 0 (base); 0x04 = GetPLDMTypes.

- The response 00 04 00 35 00 ... (after the MCTP type byte and with instance 3) has Rq=0, same type and command, completion code 00 and bitfield byte 0x35 = 0011 0101 → bits 0, 2, 4, 5 → types base, platform, FRU and firmware update.

- The wire trace shows MCTP tag 0, while the manually fragmented packet in section 2 used tag 2: the simulated network allocates its own tags per exchange. Tags are a transport concern; PLDM matching uses the instance ID.

lessons.title: Completion codes
lessons.body:
Generic completion codes defined by DSP0240 **[Spec]**:

| Code | Name | Meaning |
| 0x00 | SUCCESS | Command completed |
| 0x01 | ERROR | Generic failure |
| 0x02 | ERROR_INVALID_DATA | A field value is invalid |
| 0x03 | ERROR_INVALID_LENGTH | Request has the wrong length |
| 0x04 | ERROR_NOT_READY | Responder temporarily unable; requester may retry |
| 0x05 | ER‐ | Command not supported ROR_UNSUPPOR‐ TED_PLDM_CMD |
| 0x20 | ER‐ | Invalid/unsupported PLDM |
| ROR_INVALID_PLDM_TYPE | type (used by base commands that take a type parameter) |

Each type specification adds command-specific codes in the 0x80+ range (for example firmware update defines codes such as NOT_IN_UP‐ DATE_MODE and INVALID_STATE_FOR_COMMAND). A response with a non-SUCCESS completion code usually carries no other payload fields — parsers must check the code before reading data.

lessons.title: Discovery and endpoint concepts
lessons.body:
Discovery happens at two levels:

1. **MCTP level** — find endpoints and assign EIDs (Chapter 14).

2. **PLDM level** — for each MCTP endpoint that supports message type 1 (PLDM), ask GetTID/GetPLDMTypes/GetPLDMVersion/GetPLDMCommands, then read PDRs to learn its sensors, effecters and entities.

On OpenBMC, pldmd performs this discovery for configured or discovered endpoints and publishes resulting sensors and inventory on D-Bus, where bmcweb can expose them through Redfish **[Impl]**.

lessons.title: Firmware update concepts
lessons.body:
PLDM for Firmware Update (DSP0267) defines how an **Update Agent (UA)** — typically the BMC — updates a **Firmware Device (FD)**:

- Firmware is delivered in a **PLDM firmware update package**: a header describing which devices it applies to (by descriptors such as PCI vendor/device IDs) and one or more **component images**.

- The FD **pulls** image data: after the UA starts a component update, the FD sends RequestFirmwareData requests for chunks at offsets it chooses.

- The FD reports progress with TransferComplete, VerifyComplete and ApplyComplete; the UA finally sends ActivateFirmware. Activation may need a device reset or a platform reset.

- The FD follows a state machine: IDLE → LEARN COMPONENTS → READY XFER → DOWNLOAD → VERIFY → APPLY → (READY XFER for further components) → ACTIVATE. CancelUpdate returns to IDLE. Commands sent in the wrong state get specific completion codes.

```code
UA (BMC)                                              FD (e.g. NIC)
 QueryDeviceIdentifiers / GetFirmwareParameters ───▶  (identify, current
versions)
 RequestUpdate ────────────────────────────────────▶  IDLE -> LEARN COMPONENTS
 PassComponentTable (for each component) ──────────▶  -> READY XFER
 UpdateComponent ──────────────────────────────────▶  -> DOWNLOAD
             ◀──────────────────── RequestFirmwareData(offset, length)
(repeated)
 (data) ───────────────────────────────────────────▶
             ◀──────────────────── TransferComplete   -> VERIFY
             ◀──────────────────── VerifyComplete     -> APPLY
             ◀──────────────────── ApplyComplete      -> READY XFER
 ActivateFirmware ─────────────────────────────────▶  -> ACTIVATE (then
device-specific)
```

In Redfish terms on OpenBMC, a PLDM device update may be started through UpdateService and tracked as a task, while pldmd runs the PLDM flow underneath **[Impl]**.

lessons.title: Monitoring and platform management use cases
lessons.body:
PLDM type 2 (DSP0248) provides:

- **Numeric sensors** (temperature, voltage, power) read with Get‐ SensorReading.

- **State sensors** (presence, health) read with GetStateSensorReadings.

- **Effecters** — controls the BMC can set (numeric or state effecters), e.g. a fan speed or a power state.

- **Events** — devices send PlatformEventMessage to report sensor threshold crossings or state changes; alternatively the BMC polls.

- **PDRs** describe all of the above, including units and conversion.

source.section: 12.9 Monitoring and platform management use cases

lessons.title: PLDM versus IPMI and Redfish
lessons.body:
| Aspect | IPMI | PLDM | Redfish |
| Primary direction | Remote admin and | BMC ↔ components | Remote admin/soft‐ |
| host OS ↔ BMC | inside the platform | ware ↔ BMC |
| Encoding | Binary | Binary | JSON |
| Typical transport | RMCP+/UDP, KCS, | MCTP over SMBus/ | HTTPS |
| IPMB | PCIe/I3C |
| Records | SDR, SEL, FRU | PDRs, FRU records, | Resources/schem‐ |
| event messages | as, LogServices |
| Firmware update | Mostly OEM | Standard | UpdateService |
| (DSP0267) | (may drive PLDM underneath) |
| Who defines | IPMI promoters | DMTF PMCI | DMTF Redfish Forum |

PLDM for RDE (type 6) even lets a device expose Redfish-style data to the BMC, which the BMC then publishes in its Redfish tree.

lessons.title: Standards and implementation dependencies
lessons.body:
What the standard fixes: header bits, base command formats, generic completion codes, type-specific data structures, state machines (firmware update), timing parameters.

What depends on the implementation:

- Which types, versions and commands a device supports (discover them!).

- Which optional commands exist; PDR contents and numbering.

- Exact choice among allowed error codes in some error situations.

- Performance: how long a device takes to answer, how many outstanding requests it accepts.

- BMC software behaviour: polling intervals, retries, how PLDM data maps to Redfish.

DSP0240 specifies timing parameters (such as maximum responder time and requester retry behaviour). Look up the values in the version you implement rather than assuming numbers you have seen elsewhere.

lessons.title: Common mistakes
lessons.body:
- Reading payload fields without checking the completion code first.

- Forgetting that the response instance ID must match the request’s.

- Confusing the MCTP message-type byte (0x01) with part of the PLDM header.

- Assuming every device supports every type or command — use Get‐ PLDMTypes and GetPLDMCommands.

- Treating ERROR_NOT_READY as a failure instead of a retryable condition.

- Bit-order mistakes in bitfields (byte 0 bit 0 is item 0).

lessons.title: Exercises
lessons.body:
1. Encode a GetTID request with instance ID 17.

2. Decode the header 0x1F 0x05 0x15.

3. A GetPLDMTypes response has bitfield bytes 07 00 00 00 00 00 00 00. Which types?

**Solutions.**

1. Byte 0 = 0x80 | 17 = 0x91; byte 1 = 0x00 (version 0, type 0); byte 2 = 0x02 → 91 00 02.

2. 0x1F → Rq=0 (response), D=0, instance 31; 0x05 → version 0, type 5 (firmware update); 0x15 → RequestFirmwareData. So: a response to RequestFirmwareData with instance 31. (Remember the FD sends RequestFirmwareData, so here the UA is the responder.)

3. 0x07 = bits 0, 1, 2 → types 0 (base), 1 (SMBIOS), 2 (platform M&C).

lessons.title: Summary
lessons.body:
- PLDM standardises management data between the BMC and platform components.

- Header: Rq/D/instance ID, header version/type, command; responses start with a completion code.

- Base commands discover TID, types, versions and commands.

- Firmware update is a pull-based, state-machine-driven protocol.

- Discover capabilities; never assume them.

lessons.title: PLDM command testing methodology
lessons.body:
For each supported command, cover five dimensions:

| Dimension | Questions |
| Format | Does the response have the right header (Rq=0, same type/command/instance ID) and length? |
| Semantics | Are the field values valid and consistent with other sources? |
| Errors | Does each invalid input produce the specified completion code and no side effect? |
| State | Is the command accepted only in valid states? |
| Robustness | Does the responder survive malformed, truncated, repeated, concurrent and late messages? |

Derive the command list from the device itself (GetPLDMTypes/GetPLD‐ MCommands) and compare with the expected list from the product specification — an extra or missing command is itself a finding.

lessons.title: Request–response validation
lessons.body:
The PldmRequester in Project 3 centralises the checks every PLDM exchange needs:

```code
fwval/fwval/pldm_requester.py
 """Transport-independent PLDM requester logic.
 Responsibilities that every PLDM requester has, regardless of transport:
 * rotate the 5-bit instance ID so responses can be matched to requests,
 * validate that a response really belongs to the request,
 * retry a bounded number of times on timeout or ERROR_NOT_READY.
 Retry counts and delays here are configurable test policy; DSP0240 defines
 timing parameters you should consult for your device's requirements.
 """
 from __future__ import annotations
 import itertools
 import logging
 import time
 from collections.abc import Callable
 from .interfaces import InterfaceTimeout
 from .protocols import mctp, pldm
 log = logging.getLogger("fwval.pldm")
 # exchange(eid, mctp_message_bytes) -> mctp_message_bytes ; raises on timeout
 Exchange = Callable[[int, bytes], bytes]
 class PldmRequester:
     def __init__(self, exchange: Exchange, timeout_exc: type[Exception],
                  retries: int = 2, retry_delay_s: float = 0.0):
         self._exchange = exchange
         self._timeout_exc = timeout_exc
         self.retries = retries
         self.retry_delay_s = retry_delay_s
         self._iids = itertools.cycle(range(32))
     def send(self, eid: int, pldm_type: int, command: int, payload: bytes = b"
 ") -> pldm.PldmMessage:
         last_error: Exception | None = None
         for attempt in range(self.retries + 1):
             req = pldm.request(next(self._iids), pldm_type, command, payload)
             wire = bytes([mctp.MSG_TYPE_PLDM]) + req.encode()
             try:
                 answer = self._exchange(eid, wire)
             except self._timeout_exc as exc:
                 last_error = exc
                 log.warning("PLDM eid=%d type=%d cmd=%#x attempt %d: timeout",
                            eid, pldm_type, command, attempt + 1)
                time.sleep(self.retry_delay_s)
                continue
            if not answer or answer[0] & 0x7F != mctp.MSG_TYPE_PLDM:
                raise pldm.PldmError("response is not an MCTP PLDM message")
            resp = pldm.PldmMessage.decode(answer[1:])
            pldm.check_response(req, resp)
            if resp.completion_code == pldm.CC_ERROR_NOT_READY and attempt < s
elf.retries:
                log.info("PLDM eid=%d not ready; retrying", eid)
                time.sleep(self.retry_delay_s)
                continue
            return resp
        raise InterfaceTimeout(f"PLDM eid={eid} cmd={command:#x}: no response
after "
                               f"{self.retries + 1} attempts: {last_error}")
    def get_tid(self, eid: int) -> int:
        return pldm.parse_get_tid(self.send(eid, pldm.TYPE_BASE,
pldm.CMD_GET_TID))
    def get_types(self, eid: int) -> set[int]:
        return pldm.parse_get_pldm_types(self.send(eid, pldm.TYPE_BASE,
pldm.CMD_GET_PLDM_TYPES))
```

And the response checks themselves (check_response in pldm.py, shown in Chapter 12) verify: it is a response (Rq=0), instance ID matches, type and command match. Command-specific parsers then check the **length** of the payload for the success case (parse_get_pldm_types requires exactly 1 + 8 bytes) before reading fields.

A response validation checklist:

1. Transport delivered a complete message (MCTP reassembly succeeded).

2. MCTP message type is PLDM (0x01).

3. PLDM header: Rq=0, header version 0, type and command equal to the request, instance ID equal to the request.

4. Completion code present; if not SUCCESS, the payload is typically just the code.

5. On SUCCESS, payload length is exactly what the command defines (or within the defined variable-length rules).

6. Field values valid (enums, ranges, reserved bits zero).

7. Values consistent with other observations (e.g. TID stable across calls; types include base type 0).

lessons.title: Invalid field and unsupported-command testing
lessons.body:
| Test | How | Expected (check spec wording for your type) |
| Unsupported command | Valid type, undefined com‐ | ER‐ |
| mand code | ROR_UNSUPPOR‐ TED_PLDM_CMD |
| Unsupported type | Header type the device | An error completion code |
| does not support | (check DSP0240 for the required code) or no response |
| Extra payload | GetTID with one extra byte | ERROR_INVALID_LENGTH typical |
| Truncated payload | GetPLDMCommands | ERROR_INVALID_LENGTH without the version field |
| Invalid field value | GetPLDMCommands with | ER‐ |
| type not supported | ROR_INVALID_PLDM_TYPE |
| Wrong header version | Hdr Ver = 01b | Ignored or error — implementation-dependent |
| Response sent as request | Rq=0 to responder | Ignored |
| Reserved bits set | Reserved header bit = 1 | Ignored per spec rules / no crash |

Project 3’s simulator responds to some of these; tests:

```code
fwval/tests/test_negative_and_faults.py
 def test_pldm_unsupported_type_reports_invalid_type(world):
     from fwval.adapters.sim import SimPldm
     p = SimPldm(world)
     resp = p.requester.send(10, pldm_proto.TYPE_FRU, 0x01)  # EID 10 lacks FRU
     assert resp.completion_code == pldm_proto.CC_ERROR_INVALID_PLDM_TYPE
 def test_pldm_endpoint_types_differ(pldm, world):
     assert pldm.get_types(9) == {0, 2, 4, 5}
     assert pldm.get_types(10) == {0, 2}
```

**[Sim]** The simulator returns ERROR_INVALID_PLDM_TYPE for a request whose header type the endpoint does not support. Real devices may answer differently or not at all; confirm the required behaviour in DSP0240 for the version you test and against the device’s documentation before turning this into a pass/fail rule on hardware.

To send malformed messages on real hardware you need a tool that allows raw bytes. OpenBMC’s pldmtool raw subcommand can send arbitrary PLDM bytes to an endpoint (check pldmtool raw --help on your build for its exact options).

lessons.title: Completion-code handling
lessons.body:
Rules for requesters and tests:

- **SUCCESS** → parse fields.

- **ERROR_NOT_READY** → retry after a delay, a bounded number of times (the requester above does this); a device that is always not ready is a failure.

- **ERROR_INVALID_DATA / INVALID_LENGTH** in a positive test → your request is wrong or the device is non-conformant: inspect the bytes.

- **ERROR_UNSUPPORTED_PLDM_CMD** → command missing; compare with GetPLDMCommands.

- **Type-specific codes** → interpret with the type spec (e.g. firmware update codes reveal the device’s state).

- **Unknown codes** → log them in hex; never crash on them.

Test for the retry behaviour:

```code
fwval/tests/test_negative_and_faults.py
 def test_pldm_not_ready_is_retried(pldm, world):
     world.mctp.endpoints[9].not_ready_count = 2
     assert pldm.get_tid(9) == 1  # two NOT_READY answers, then success
 def test_pldm_absent_endpoint_times_out(pldm, world):
     with pytest.raises(InterfaceTimeout):
         pldm.get_tid(0x42)
```

lessons.title: State transitions and timeout scenarios
lessons.body:
Firmware update is the richest PLDM state machine. The book provides a **deliberately simplified model** of the firmware-device state machine to practise state-based test design:

```code
examples/ch13_fwupdate_model.py
 """Chapter 13: a SIMPLIFIED model of the PLDM firmware-device (FD) state
 machine.
 Based on the state names and command flow in DMTF DSP0267 (PLDM for Firmware
 Update), heavily simplified for teaching state-based testing:
   * one component at a time, no package data / metadata commands,
   * no timing rules, no background busy states, no self-contained activation,
   * completion codes are referred to by NAME; numeric values are in DSP0267.
 Never treat this model as a reference implementation of DSP0267.
 """
 from __future__ import annotations
 from enum import Enum
 class State(Enum):
     IDLE = "IDLE"
     LEARN_COMPONENTS = "LEARN COMPONENTS"
     READY_XFER = "READY XFER"
     DOWNLOAD = "DOWNLOAD"
     VERIFY = "VERIFY"
     APPLY = "APPLY"
     ACTIVATE = "ACTIVATE"
 SUCCESS = "SUCCESS"
 NOT_IN_UPDATE_MODE = "NOT_IN_UPDATE_MODE"
 ALREADY_IN_UPDATE_MODE = "ALREADY_IN_UPDATE_MODE"
 INVALID_STATE_FOR_COMMAND = "INVALID_STATE_FOR_COMMAND"
 COMMAND_NOT_EXPECTED = "COMMAND_NOT_EXPECTED"
 class FirmwareDevice:
     def __init__(self) -> None:
         self.state = State.IDLE
         self.history: list[tuple[str, State, str]] = []
     def _move(self, cmd: str, allowed: set[State], new: State | None) -> str:
         if self.state not in allowed:
             code = NOT_IN_UPDATE_MODE if self.state is State.IDLE else
 INVALID_STATE_FOR_COMMAND
             self.history.append((cmd, self.state, code))
             return code
        old = self.state
        if new is not None:
            self.state = new
        self.history.append((cmd, old, SUCCESS))
        return SUCCESS
    # --- commands sent by the update agent (UA), e.g. the BMC ---
    def request_update(self) -> str:
        if self.state is not State.IDLE:
            self.history.append(("RequestUpdate", self.state,
ALREADY_IN_UPDATE_MODE))
            return ALREADY_IN_UPDATE_MODE
        return self._move("RequestUpdate", {State.IDLE},
State.LEARN_COMPONENTS)
    def pass_component_table(self, last: bool) -> str:
        return self._move("PassComponentTable", {State.LEARN_COMPONENTS},
                          State.READY_XFER if last else None)
    def update_component(self) -> str:
        return self._move("UpdateComponent", {State.READY_XFER},
State.DOWNLOAD)
    def activate_firmware(self) -> str:
        return self._move("ActivateFirmware", {State.READY_XFER},
State.ACTIVATE)
    def cancel_update(self) -> str:
        allowed = set(State) - {State.IDLE}
        return self._move("CancelUpdate", allowed, State.IDLE)
    # --- notifications the FD sends to the UA (modelled as FD-side steps) ---
    def transfer_complete(self) -> str:
        return self._move("TransferComplete", {State.DOWNLOAD}, State.VERIFY)
    def verify_complete(self) -> str:
        return self._move("VerifyComplete", {State.VERIFY}, State.APPLY)
    def apply_complete(self) -> str:
        return self._move("ApplyComplete", {State.APPLY}, State.READY_XFER)
    def activation_done(self) -> None:
        """Device finished activating (e.g. after its own reset)."""
        if self.state is State.ACTIVATE:
            self.state = State.IDLE
HAPPY_PATH = [
    ("request_update", (), State.LEARN_COMPONENTS),
    ("pass_component_table", (True,), State.READY_XFER),
    ("update_component", (), State.DOWNLOAD),
    ("transfer_complete", (), State.VERIFY),
    ("verify_complete", (), State.APPLY),
    ("apply_complete", (), State.READY_XFER),
     ("activate_firmware", (), State.ACTIVATE),
 ]
 if __name__ == "__main__":
     fd = FirmwareDevice()
     for method, args, _expected in HAPPY_PATH:
         code = getattr(fd, method)(*args)
         print(f"{method:<22} -> {code:<26} state={fd.state.value}")
     fd.activation_done()
     print(f"{'(device activates)':<22}    {'':<26} state={fd.state.value}")
     print("\nOut-of-state commands:")
     for method, args in [("update_component", ()), ("activate_firmware", ()),
                          ("cancel_update", ())]:
         print(f"{method:<22} -> {getattr(fd, method)(*args)}")
     fd.request_update()
     print(f"{'request_update (again)':<22} -> {fd.request_update()}")
```

**Output [Run]:**

```code
request_update         -> SUCCESS                    state=LEARN COMPONENTS
pass_component_table   -> SUCCESS                    state=READY XFER
update_component       -> SUCCESS                    state=DOWNLOAD
transfer_complete      -> SUCCESS                    state=VERIFY
verify_complete        -> SUCCESS                    state=APPLY
apply_complete         -> SUCCESS                    state=READY XFER
activate_firmware      -> SUCCESS                    state=ACTIVATE
(device activates)                                   state=IDLE
Out-of-state commands:
update_component       -> NOT_IN_UPDATE_MODE
activate_firmware      -> NOT_IN_UPDATE_MODE
cancel_update          -> NOT_IN_UPDATE_MODE
request_update (again) -> ALREADY_IN_UPDATE_MODE
```

State-based tests: every state reachable, every UA command in every state, rejected commands do not change state, cancel from every state returns to IDLE and a new update can start:

```code
examples/test_ch13_fwupdate_states.py
 """Chapter 13: state-based tests for the simplified firmware-update model.
 The same test design (every state reachable, every valid transition, every
 invalid command in every state, cancel from every state) applies to a real
 firmware device; only the driver underneath changes.
 """
 import pytest
 from ch13_fwupdate_model import (ALREADY_IN_UPDATE_MODE, HAPPY_PATH,
 INVALID_STATE_FOR_COMMAND,
                                 NOT_IN_UPDATE_MODE, SUCCESS, FirmwareDevice,
State)
UA_COMMANDS = {
    "request_update": (), "pass_component_table": (True,),
"update_component": (),
    "activate_firmware": (), "cancel_update": (),
}
# Which UA commands are valid in which state (from the simplified model).
VALID = {
    State.IDLE: {"request_update"},
    State.LEARN_COMPONENTS: {"pass_component_table", "cancel_update"},
    State.READY_XFER: {"update_component", "activate_firmware", "cancel_update
"},
    State.DOWNLOAD: {"cancel_update"},
    State.VERIFY: {"cancel_update"},
    State.APPLY: {"cancel_update"},
    State.ACTIVATE: {"cancel_update"},
}
def drive_to(target: State) -> FirmwareDevice:
    fd = FirmwareDevice()
    for method, args, _reached in HAPPY_PATH:
        if fd.state is target:
            break
        assert getattr(fd, method)(*args) == SUCCESS
    assert fd.state is target
    return fd
def test_happy_path_visits_every_state():
    fd = FirmwareDevice()
    visited = {fd.state}
    for method, args, expected in HAPPY_PATH:
        assert getattr(fd, method)(*args) == SUCCESS
        assert fd.state is expected
        visited.add(fd.state)
    assert visited == set(State)
@pytest.mark.parametrize("state", list(State), ids=lambda s: s.name)
@pytest.mark.parametrize("command", list(UA_COMMANDS))
def test_every_command_in_every_state(state, command):
    fd = drive_to(state)
    code = getattr(fd, command)(*UA_COMMANDS[command])
    if command in VALID[state]:
        assert code == SUCCESS
    elif command == "request_update":
        assert code == ALREADY_IN_UPDATE_MODE
    elif state is State.IDLE:
        assert code == NOT_IN_UPDATE_MODE
        assert fd.state is State.IDLE
    else:
        assert code == INVALID_STATE_FOR_COMMAND
        assert fd.state is state            # a rejected command must not
change state
@pytest.mark.parametrize("state", [s for s in State if s is not State.IDLE],
ids=lambda s: s.name)
def test_cancel_returns_to_idle_and_update_can_restart(state):
    fd = drive_to(state)
    assert fd.cancel_update() == SUCCESS
    assert fd.state is State.IDLE
    assert fd.request_update() == SUCCESS   # recovery: a new update can start
def test_multi_entry_component_table_stays_in_learn():
    fd = drive_to(State.LEARN_COMPONENTS)
    assert fd.pass_component_table(last=False) == SUCCESS
    assert fd.state is State.LEARN_COMPONENTS
    assert fd.pass_component_table(last=True) == SUCCESS
    assert fd.state is State.READY_XFER
```

**Output [Run]:**

```code
...........................................
[100%]
43 passed in 0.05s
```

The test_every_command_in_every_state test generates 35 cases (7 states × 5 commands) from two tables. On a real device, the same table-driven approach applies: a driver function moves the device to each state (via real PLDM commands), then each command is sent and its completion code compared with the table derived from DSP0267.

Timeout scenarios to test:

- The FD stops requesting data mid-download → the UA must time out according to the spec’s timing rules and cancel/clean up.

- The UA stops answering RequestFirmwareData → the FD must time out and return to a safe state.

- A response arrives after the requester gave up → it must be discarded (instance ID no longer outstanding), not mistaken for the answer to a newer request.

- The device resets during APPLY → after recovery, the old (or new, depending on design) firmware must be running and the FD must be in IDLE.

lessons.title: Firmware-update validation concepts
lessons.body:
A firmware-update test plan for a PLDM device should cover:

| Area | Checks |
| Identification | QueryDeviceIdentifiers descriptors match the package; GetFirmwareParameters shows active/pending versions |
| Package validation | Package for a different device is rejected; corrupted image fails verification; wrong component classification rejected |
| Happy path | Update, activate, version changes, device functional |
| Same version / downgrade | Behaviour per policy (allowed, refused, needs force flag) |
| Cancel | CancelUpdate in each state; device stays on old firmware; new update possible |
| Interruption | BMC reboot, device reset, bus error during DOWNLOAD/VERIFY/APPLY; recovery |
| Concurrency | Second RequestUpdate during an update rejected (ALREADY_IN_UPDATE_MODE-type code) |
| Redfish integration | UpdateService task reflects progress and final state; FirmwareInventory shows new version |
| Repeatability | 20+ consecutive updates without failure or degradation |

**Warning.** Firmware-update interruption tests can brick devices. Run them only on hardware set aside for destructive testing, with a known recovery procedure.

lessons.title: Negative testing and recovery scenarios
lessons.body:
- Send each command with every invalid length from 0 to expected+2.

- Flip reserved bits; set the datagram bit on commands that expect a response.

- Reuse an outstanding instance ID.

- Send requests faster than the device’s documented capability.

- Restart pldmd on the BMC during polling; verify sensors recover.

- Disconnect/reconnect the device’s bus segment (hardware lab), verify rediscovery.

The recovery criterion: after the fault is removed, the system returns to correct operation within a defined time **without manual action**, and the fault was logged.

lessons.title: Logging and diagnostic evidence
lessons.body:
For each PLDM exchange, log: timestamp (monotonic and wall-clock), EID, instance ID, type, command, request bytes, response bytes, completion code, latency, retry count. Project 3’s simulated network keeps a trace of every packet; on a real BMC:

- OpenBMC pldmtool has a verbose option that prints the request and response bytes (check pldmtool --help).

- pldmd logs go to the journal: journalctl -u pldmd.

- MCTP-level capture on Linux: the kernel MCTP stack can be observed with packet capture tools on MCTP interfaces where supported (for example Wireshark has an MCTP dissector); a bus analyser (Chapter 18) can capture SMBus/I²C-level traffic.

Never present such logs in reports as “captured” unless they truly were; label simulator traces as simulated.

lessons.title: Python test architecture
lessons.body:
```code
tests/               -> express intent; use the PldmPort interface
fwval/interfaces.py  -> PldmPort: get_tid(), get_types()
fwval/pldm_requester -> instance IDs, response checks, NOT_READY retries
fwval/protocols/     -> pure encode/decode (unit tested)
adapters/
  sim.py + mctp_sim  -> simulated endpoints over a simulated MCTP network
  real.py            -> pldmtool over SSH (unverified on hardware)
```

The key property: **byte-level logic is identical** in simulation and on hardware when a byte-level transport exists (for instance, a future adapter using Linux AF_MCTP sockets would reuse PldmRequester unchanged; Python’s standard socket module does not currently provide AF_MCTP constants, so such an adapter needs extra work or a helper library).

lessons.title: Simulators and hardware-dependent tests
lessons.body:
| Test kind | Simulator | Hardware |
| Codec correctness | ✔ (unit tests) | Not needed |
| Requester logic (matching, retries) | ✔ | Confirms timings |
| Device conformance | ✘ (simulator is not the device) | ✔ |
| Firmware update | Logic/state tables only | ✔ required |
| Performance | ✘ | ✔ |

Mark hardware tests clearly, skip them when hardware is absent, and never report a simulated pass as device validation.

lessons.title: Exercises
lessons.body:
1. Write a test that sends GetTID twice and asserts that the TID is stable and the instance IDs differ.

2. Extend the firmware-device model with a GetStatus command valid in every state that returns the current state name; add it to the state table tests.

3. Design a test for “late response after timeout is discarded”.

**Solutions.**

1.

```code
def test_tid_stable_and_instance_ids_rotate(world):
    from fwval.adapters.sim import SimPldm
    p = SimPldm(world)
    r1 = p.requester.send(9, 0, 0x02)
    r2 = p.requester.send(9, 0, 0x02)
    assert r1.payload == r2.payload            # same CC and TID
    assert r1.instance_id != r2.instance_id
```

1. Add def get_status(self): self.history.append(("GetStatus", self.state, SUCCESS)); return self.state.value; in the tests, add a separate parametrised test asserting it never changes state.

2. In a simulator, make the endpoint answer request N only after the requester’s timeout, then send request N+1; assert the requester returns N+1’s response, not N’s, by checking instance IDs (the requester must drop the stale one).

lessons.title: Summary
lessons.body:
- Validate format, semantics, errors, state and robustness for each command.

- Check instance ID/type/command echo and payload length before reading fields.

- Retry ERROR_NOT_READY with limits; log unknown codes.

- Use table-driven state tests for firmware update; interruption tests need sacrificial hardware.

- Separate pure logic, requester logic and transports; label simulated evidence.

lessons.title: Purpose of Management Component Transport Protocol

source.section: 14.1 Purpose of Management Component Transport Protocol

lessons.title: The specification family
lessons.body:
| Spec | Content |
| DSP0236 | MCTP Base Specification: packets, messages, control commands, EIDs, routing |
| DSP0239 | MCTP IDs and Codes: message type numbers and other codes |
| DSP0237 | MCTP SMBus/I²C Transport Binding |
| DSP0238 | MCTP PCIe VDM Transport Binding |
| DSP0233 | MCTP I3C Transport Binding |
| DSP0253 | MCTP Serial Transport Binding |
| DSP0241 | PLDM over MCTP Binding |

(Other bindings and companion specs exist, e.g. for KCS and the host interface; see the DMTF PMCI page for the current list and versions.)

lessons.title: Endpoints, EIDs, messages and transport bindings
lessons.body:
- **Endpoint** — an MCTP-capable function that sends/receives MCTP messages.

- **EID (Endpoint ID)** — an 8-bit logical address. **[Spec]** 0x00 is the null EID (used before an EID is assigned / for physical addressing), 0xFF is the broadcast EID, 0x01–0x07 are reserved, so **0x08–0xFE** are assignable.

- **Bus owner** — the endpoint responsible for assigning EIDs on a bus (often the BMC).

- **Bridge** — an endpoint that routes MCTP packets between buses; it maintains a routing table.

- **Transport binding** — the specification for carrying MCTP packets over one physical medium: it defines physical addressing, framing, the maximum transmission unit and medium-specific discovery.

- **Message** vs **packet** — a message is the unit an application sends (a PLDM request); a packet is what one bus transfer carries. Large messages are split into several packets.

lessons.title: Message headers and packet concepts
lessons.body:
The binding-independent part of every MCTP packet **[Spec: DSP0236]**:

```code
 byte 0:  bits 7..4 reserved      bits 3..0 header version (0001b)
 byte 1:  destination EID
 byte 2:  source EID
 byte 3:  bit 7 SOM   start of message
          bit 6 EOM   end of message
          bits 5..4   packet sequence number (0..3, increments per packet)
          bit 3 TO    tag owner (1 = the source allocated this tag, i.e. a
request
                      or unsolicited message; responses carry TO = 0)
          bits 2..0   message tag (0..7) - identifies the message among others
in flight
 byte 4+: packet payload. In the FIRST packet of a message (SOM = 1) the
payload
          starts with the message header byte:
          bit 7 IC    integrity check present (message-type specific)
          bits 6..0   message type (0x00 control, 0x01 PLDM, 0x02 NC-SI, 0x03
Ethernet,
                      0x04 NVMe-MI, 0x05 SPDM, 0x7E vendor PCI, 0x7F vendor
IANA)
```

The **baseline transmission unit** is 64 bytes of packet payload; bindings may negotiate larger units. The complete codec from Project 3:

```code
fwval/fwval/protocols/mctp.py
 """MCTP transport-header encoding, packetisation and reassembly.
 Based on the DMTF MCTP Base Specification (DSP0236). This module models the
 *binding-independent* MCTP packet (the 4-byte transport header plus payload).
 Each physical binding wraps this in its own framing - for example the
 SMBus/I2C binding (DSP0237) adds a destination address, command code 0x0F,
 byte count, source address and PEC; the PCIe VDM binding (DSP0238) uses a PCIe
 vendor-defined message header. Those binding layers are NOT modelled here.
 Transport header layout (DSP0236):
     byte 0 : [7:4] reserved, [3:0] header version (0b0001)
     byte 1 : destination endpoint ID (EID)
     byte 2 : source endpoint ID
     byte 3 : [7] SOM, [6] EOM, [5:4] packet sequence, [3] TO, [2:0] message
 tag
 The first payload byte of the first packet (SOM=1) is the message header:
     [7] IC (integrity check present), [6:0] message type
 """
 from __future__ import annotations
 from dataclasses import dataclass
HEADER_VERSION = 0x1
BASELINE_TRANSMISSION_UNIT = 64  # bytes of packet payload (DSP0236 baseline)
NULL_EID = 0x00
BROADCAST_EID = 0xFF
# Message types (DSP0239 "MCTP IDs and Codes"); only common ones listed.
MSG_TYPE_CONTROL = 0x00
MSG_TYPE_PLDM = 0x01
MSG_TYPE_NCSI = 0x02
MSG_TYPE_ETHERNET = 0x03
MSG_TYPE_NVME_MI = 0x04
MSG_TYPE_SPDM = 0x05
MSG_TYPE_VENDOR_PCI = 0x7E
MSG_TYPE_VENDOR_IANA = 0x7F
# MCTP control command codes (DSP0236), subset.
CTRL_SET_ENDPOINT_ID = 0x01
CTRL_GET_ENDPOINT_ID = 0x02
CTRL_GET_ENDPOINT_UUID = 0x03
CTRL_GET_VERSION_SUPPORT = 0x04
CTRL_GET_MESSAGE_TYPE_SUPPORT = 0x05
# MCTP control completion codes (DSP0236), subset.
CC_SUCCESS = 0x00
CC_ERROR = 0x01
CC_ERROR_INVALID_DATA = 0x02
CC_ERROR_INVALID_LENGTH = 0x03
CC_ERROR_NOT_READY = 0x04
CC_ERROR_UNSUPPORTED_CMD = 0x05
class MctpError(Exception):
    """Malformed packet or reassembly failure."""
def is_valid_endpoint_eid(eid: int) -> bool:
    """EIDs 0x00 (null) and 0xFF (broadcast) are special and 0x01-0x07 are
    reserved by DSP0236, so 0x08-0xFE are the assignable endpoint IDs."""
    return 0x08 <= eid <= 0xFE
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class MctpPacket:
    dest: int
    src: int
    som: bool
    eom: bool
    seq: int
    tag_owner: bool
    tag: int
    payload: bytes
    version: int = HEADER_VERSION
    def encode(self) -> bytes:
        for name, value, hi in (("dest", self.dest, 0xFF), ("src", self.src, 0
xFF),
                                ("seq", self.seq, 3), ("tag", self.tag, 7)):
            if not 0 <= value <= hi:
                raise MctpError(f"{name}={value} out of range 0..{hi}")
        flags = (
            (0x80 if self.som else 0)
            | (0x40 if self.eom else 0)
            | (self.seq << 4)
            | (0x08 if self.tag_owner else 0)
            | self.tag
        )
        return bytes([self.version & 0x0F, self.dest, self.src, flags]) +
self.payload
    @classmethod
    def decode(cls, raw: bytes) -> "MctpPacket":
        if len(raw) < 5:  # 4-byte header + at least one payload byte
            raise MctpError(f"packet too short ({len(raw)} bytes)")
        version = raw[0] & 0x0F
        if version != HEADER_VERSION:
            raise MctpError(f"unsupported header version {version}")
        flags = raw[3]
        return cls(
            dest=raw[1], src=raw[2],
            som=bool(flags & 0x80), eom=bool(flags & 0x40),
            seq=(flags >> 4) & 0x3, tag_owner=bool(flags & 0x08), tag=flags &
0x7,
            payload=bytes(raw[4:]), version=version,
        )
def fragment(message: bytes, dest: int, src: int, tag: int, tag_owner: bool,
             mtu: int = BASELINE_TRANSMISSION_UNIT, first_seq: int = 0) -> lis
t[MctpPacket]:
    """Split a message (message-type byte + body) into MCTP packets."""
    if not message:
        raise MctpError("empty message")
    if mtu < 1:
        raise MctpError("mtu must be positive")
    chunks = [message[i:i + mtu] for i in range(0, len(message), mtu)]
    packets = []
    for i, chunk in enumerate(chunks):
        packets.append(MctpPacket(
            dest=dest, src=src, som=(i == 0), eom=(i == len(chunks) - 1),
            seq=(first_seq + i) % 4, tag_owner=tag_owner, tag=tag, payload=chu
nk,
        ))
    return packets
def reassemble(packets: list[MctpPacket]) -> bytes:
    """Rebuild a message, enforcing SOM/EOM, sequence and tag consistency."""
    if not packets:
        raise MctpError("no packets")
    first = packets[0]
    if not first.som:
        raise MctpError("first packet does not have SOM set")
    if not packets[-1].eom:
        raise MctpError("last packet does not have EOM set")
    expected_seq = first.seq
    body = bytearray()
    for i, pkt in enumerate(packets):
        if i > 0 and pkt.som:
            raise MctpError(f"unexpected SOM in packet {i}")
        if i < len(packets) - 1 and pkt.eom:
            raise MctpError(f"unexpected EOM in packet {i}")
        if pkt.seq != expected_seq:
            raise MctpError(f"sequence error at packet {i}: got {pkt.seq},
expected {expected_seq}")
        if (pkt.src, pkt.tag, pkt.tag_owner) != (first.src, first.tag,
first.tag_owner):
            raise MctpError(f"packet {i} belongs to a different message (src/
tag/TO mismatch)")
        if 0 < i < len(packets) - 1 and len(pkt.payload) != len(first.payload)
:
            # Middle packets are expected to be full-sized; a short middle
            # packet usually means a lost or truncated fragment.
            raise MctpError(f"packet {i} payload size {len(pkt.payload)} != {l
en(first.payload)}")
        body += pkt.payload
        expected_seq = (expected_seq + 1) % 4
    return bytes(body)
def message_type(message: bytes) -> tuple[bool, int]:
    """Return (integrity_check_flag, message_type) from the first byte."""
    if not message:
        raise MctpError("empty message")
    return bool(message[0] & 0x80), message[0] & 0x7F
# ----------------------------------------------------------- control messages
def control_request(instance_id: int, command: int, data: bytes = b"") -> byte
s:
    """MCTP control request: msg type, [Rq|D|rsvd|InstanceID], command,
data."""
    if not 0 <= instance_id <= 0x1F:
        raise MctpError("instance id must be 0..31")
    return bytes([MSG_TYPE_CONTROL, 0x80 | instance_id, command]) + data
def control_response(instance_id: int, command: int, cc: int, data: bytes = b"
") -> bytes:
    return bytes([MSG_TYPE_CONTROL, instance_id & 0x1F, command, cc]) + data
 @dataclass(frozen=True)
 class ControlResponse:
     instance_id: int
     command: int
     completion_code: int
     data: bytes
 def parse_control_response(message: bytes) -> ControlResponse:
     if len(message) < 4:
         raise MctpError("control response too short")
     _, mtype = message_type(message)
     if mtype != MSG_TYPE_CONTROL:
         raise MctpError(f"not a control message (type {mtype:#x})")
     if message[1] & 0x80:
         raise MctpError("Rq bit set: this is a request, not a response")
     return ControlResponse(message[1] & 0x1F, message[2], message[3], bytes(me
 ssage[4:]))
```

Unit tests pin the bit layout and edge cases:

```code
fwval/tests/test_protocol_codecs.py
 def test_mctp_header_encoding_matches_bit_layout():
     pkt = mctp.MctpPacket(dest=0x09, src=0x08, som=True, eom=True, seq=2,
                           tag_owner=True, tag=5, payload=b"\x01")
     raw = pkt.encode()
     assert raw[:4] == bytes([0x01, 0x09, 0x08, 0b1110_1101])
     assert mctp.MctpPacket.decode(raw) == pkt
 @pytest.mark.parametrize("length", [1, 63, 64, 65, 128, 200])
 def test_fragment_and_reassemble_round_trip(length):
     msg = bytes([mctp.MSG_TYPE_PLDM]) + bytes(range(256))[: length - 1]
     pkts = mctp.fragment(msg, dest=9, src=8, tag=3, tag_owner=True, mtu=64,
 first_seq=3)
     assert len(pkts) == -(-length // 64)
     assert pkts[0].som and pkts[-1].eom
     assert [p.seq for p in pkts] == [(3 + i) % 4 for i in range(len(pkts))]
     assert mctp.reassemble(pkts) == msg
 def test_reassembly_rejects_out_of_order_packets():
     pkts = mctp.fragment(bytes(150), 9, 8, 1, True, mtu=64)
     with pytest.raises(mctp.MctpError, match="sequence|SOM|EOM"):
         mctp.reassemble([pkts[0], pkts[2], pkts[1]])
 @pytest.mark.parametrize("eid, valid", [(0x00, False), (0x07, False), (0x08, T
 rue),
                                         (0xFE, True), (0xFF, False)])
def test_eid_ranges(eid, valid):
    assert mctp.is_valid_endpoint_eid(eid) is valid
```

lessons.title: Message types and message exchange
lessons.body:
- A **request** is sent with TO=1 and a tag chosen by the requester.

- The **response** uses the same tag with TO=0, sent back from the responder’s EID to the requester’s EID.

- The tag together with source EID and TO identifies which message a packet belongs to, so a requester can have several messages in flight to different endpoints.

- **MCTP control messages** (type 0x00) have their own header byte: Rq bit, D bit and a 5-bit instance ID, then a command code; responses add a completion code.

Common control commands **[Spec: DSP0236]**:

| Code | Command | Use |
| 0x01 | Set Endpoint ID | Bus owner assigns an EID |
| 0x02 | Get Endpoint ID | Read EID and endpoint type |
| 0x03 | Get Endpoint UUID | Stable identity of the endpoint |
| 0x04 | Get MCTP Version Support | Versions of the base spec or a message type supported |
| 0x05 | Get Message Type Support | Which message types (PLDM, NVMe-MI, …) the endpoint supports |
| 0x06 | Get Vendor Defined Mes‐ | Vendor message capabilit‐ |
| sage Support | ies |
| 0x07 | Resolve Endpoint ID | Find the physical address/ route for an EID |
| 0x08 | Allocate Endpoint IDs | Give a bridge a pool of EIDs for its downstream bus |
| 0x09/0x0A | Routing Information Up‐ | Routing management date / Get Routing Table Entries |
| Code | Command | Use |
| 0x0B–0x0D | Prepare for Endpoint Dis‐ | Discovery on buses that |
| covery / Endpoint Discov‐ | support it (e.g. PCIe) ery / Discovery Notify |

Control completion codes: 0x00 SUCCESS, 0x01 ERROR, 0x02 ER‐ ROR_INVALID_DATA, 0x03 ERROR_INVALID_LENGTH, 0x04 ER‐ ROR_NOT_READY, 0x05 ERROR_UNSUPPORTED_CMD.

lessons.title: Endpoint discovery and addressing concepts
lessons.body:
How endpoints get EIDs depends on the bus:

- **SMBus/I²C** — devices have fixed or configurable 7-bit addresses. The bus owner knows (from platform configuration) or probes which addresses host MCTP endpoints, sends Get Endpoint ID to the physical address with the null destination EID, then Set Endpoint ID to assign one. Some systems use static EIDs configured on both sides.

- **PCIe VDM** — endpoints announce themselves with Discovery Notify; the bus owner (typically reached via the PCIe root complex) runs the discovery flow and assigns EIDs.

- **Bridges** receive EID pools (Allocate Endpoint IDs) and assign them downstream.

After assignment, the bus owner queries Get Message Type Support and UUID, and upper layers (PLDM, NVMe-MI) do their own discovery.

On Linux (and therefore OpenBMC), MCTP is implemented in the **kernel** (since 5.15) with AF_MCTP sockets. User-space tools from the mctp project manage it: the mctp command (mctp link, mctp addr, mctp route, mctp neigh) configures interfaces, addresses and routes, and the mctpd daemon performs discovery and EID assignment and publishes endpoints on D-Bus **[Impl]**. Older OpenBMC builds used a user-space libmctp/mctp-demux-daemon stack instead.

lessons.title: MCTP over SMBus/I²C and other supported transports
lessons.body:
**SMBus/I²C binding (DSP0237)** wraps an MCTP packet in an SMBus Block Write:

```code
 [dest slave addr (7 bit) + W] [command code 0x0F = MCTP] [byte count]
 [source slave addr (7 bit) + 1] [ MCTP transport header (4 bytes) ]
[ payload ... ] [PEC]
```

- Each packet is a separate SMBus transaction, written by the sender to the receiver’s address (both sides act as SMBus masters/controllers when sending).

- The byte count limits the packet size; the baseline is 64 bytes of MCTP payload.

- **PEC** (Packet Error Code, a CRC-8) protects the transaction.

- Multi-master arbitration, clock stretching and NACKs on a busy target are real sources of failure.

**PCIe VDM binding (DSP0238)** carries MCTP packets in PCIe Vendor- Defined Messages (Type 0) with the DMTF vendor ID, routed by ID, to the root complex, or broadcast. It offers much higher bandwidth and larger transmission units, useful for firmware update.

**I3C binding** uses the faster I3C bus with in-band interrupts; the **serial binding** frames packets with byte stuffing and a CRC over a UART.

**Do not assume identical framing across bindings.** Only the 4-byte transport header and payload are common. Physical addressing, packet size limits, error detection and discovery are binding-specific. Project 3’s simulator models only the binding-independent part and is documented as such.

lessons.title: Relationship between MCTP, PLDM and the physical transport
lessons.body:
```code
  PLDM message:          [Rq|D|IID][Ver|Type][Cmd][payload...]
       ▲ carried as MCTP message type 0x01
  MCTP message:          [IC|MsgType=0x01][PLDM message ...]
       ▲ split into packets (≤ transmission unit)
  MCTP packet(s):        [Ver][DestEID][SrcEID][SOM|EOM|Seq|TO|Tag][payload
chunk]
       ▲ framed by the binding
  SMBus/I²C:             [Addr][0x0F][Count][SrcAddr][MCTP packet][PEC]
  or PCIe VDM:           [TLP header + VDM header][MCTP packet]
```

A PLDM timeout at the top can be caused by any layer below: a missing route for the EID, a wrong physical address, an I²C NACK, a reassembly error from a lost packet, or a responder that never answered.

lessons.title: Message boundaries, fragmentation and reassembly
lessons.body:
Rules enforced by the reassembler (from DSP0236 behaviour):

- The first packet has SOM=1; the last has EOM=1; a single-packet message has both.

- Sequence numbers increment by one (mod 4) for each packet of a message.

- All packets of a message have the same source EID, tag and TO.

- A packet with an unexpected sequence number, a new SOM in the middle, or a missing EOM means the message is corrupt and is dropped.

- Middle packets are full-size; a short middle packet indicates a problem. (DSP0236 constrains packet sizes within a message — confirm the exact rule in the version you work with.)

The 2-bit sequence number detects a lost packet only if fewer than four consecutive packets are lost; combined with message-level checks (lengths, integrity check where used) the upper layer still catches most corruption.

Example **[Run]** from Chapter 12’s program: a 151-byte message split into packets of 64, 64 and 23 bytes with sequence 0, 1, 2 and SOM/EOM on the first and last.

lessons.title: Common communication failures
lessons.body:
| Symptom | Possible causes |
| No response to Get Endpoint ID on SMBus | Wrong physical address; device not powered; device does not implement MCTP over SMBus; bus stuck (SDA held low); wrong bus |
| Endpoint answers but upper-layer mes‐ | Endpoint does not support that message |
| sages time out | type (check Get Message Type Support); EID not routed |
| Sporadic reassembly errors | Bus noise, arbitration loss, clock-stretching timeouts, firmware bugs in sequence handling |
| EID conflicts | Static EID configuration overlapping dynamically assigned EIDs |
| Works after BMC boot, fails after device re‐ | Device lost its EID and must be re-as‐ |
| set | signed; discovery not re-triggered |
| Large messages fail, small succeed | Transmission-unit mismatch; fragmentation bugs |

lessons.title: Common mistakes
lessons.body:
- Treating the MCTP message type byte as part of the PLDM header.

- Using EIDs 0x01–0x07.

- Forgetting TO=0 and the same tag on responses.

- Assuming SMBus framing applies to PCIe VDM.

- Ignoring that an endpoint can lose its EID on reset.

lessons.title: Exercises
lessons.body:
1. Decode the transport header 01 0A 08 D3.

2. How many packets does a 200-byte message need with a 64-byte transmission unit, and what are the SOM/EOM flags?

3. Why can’t a responder use TO=1 in its response?

**Solutions.**

1. Version 1; destination EID 0x0A (10); source EID 8; 0xD3 = 1101 0011 → SOM=1, EOM=1, seq=01b=1, TO=0, tag=3: a single-packet response (TO=0) with tag 3.

2. ⌈200/64⌉ = 4 packets (64, 64, 64, 8 bytes): SOM on the first, EOM on the last, neither on the middle two; sequence numbers incrementing mod 4.

3. TO=1 means “I allocated this tag” — it marks requests/unsolicited messages. The response must reuse the requester’s tag with TO=0 so the requester can match it.

lessons.title: Summary
lessons.body:
- MCTP: EID-addressed, routable, packetised transport for management messages.

- 4-byte transport header: version, dest/src EID, SOM/EOM/seq/TO/tag.

- Message type byte selects PLDM, NVMe-MI, SPDM, control, …

- Bindings (SMBus, PCIe VDM, I3C, serial) differ in framing and discovery.

- Reassembly rules detect lost or out-of-order packets.

lessons.title: The simulated MCTP network
Endpoint discovery testing
Request–response validation
lessons.body: Covered by the PLDM requester (Chapter 13) and control-response parser (Chapter 14). For MCTP control messages also check: response comes from the addressed EID, tag matches with TO=0, instance ID matches, completion code SUCCESS, data length correct for the command (e.g. Get Endpoint ID returns EID, endpoint type and medium-specific byte).

lessons.title: Unsupported message handling
lessons.body:
An endpoint that receives a message type it does not support typically drops it silently; the requester sees a timeout. Tests:

- Send each message type the endpoint does not list in Get Message Type Support — expect no response (timeout) and no side effects.

- Send an unsupported MCTP control command — expect ER‐ ROR_UNSUPPORTED_CMD.

- Send an unsupported PLDM command — expect ER‐ ROR_UNSUPPORTED_PLDM_CMD.

Example **[Run]** from Chapter 12: Unsupported command 0x7e -> 0x05 `ERROR_UNSUPPORTED_PLDM_CMD.`

lessons.title: Timeout and recovery testing
lessons.body:
```code
 fwval/tests/test_negative_and_faults.py
  def test_silent_endpoint_is_reported_not_hung(world):
      world.mctp.add(SimEndpoint(eid=11, silent=True))
      try:
          with pytest.raises(MctpTimeout):
              world.mctp.exchange(11, mctp.control_request(0,
  mctp.CTRL_GET_ENDPOINT_ID))
    finally:
        del world.mctp.endpoints[11]
def test_mctp_lost_packet_detected_on_reassembly(world):
    world.mctp.mtu = 4   # 6-byte response -> 2 packets
    world.mctp.drop_next_response_packet = True
    msg = mctp.control_request(1, mctp.CTRL_GET_MESSAGE_TYPE_SUPPORT)
    try:
        with pytest.raises(mctp.MctpError, match="EOM"):
            world.mctp.exchange(9, msg)
    finally:
        world.mctp.mtu = mctp.BASELINE_TRANSMISSION_UNIT
```

Points:

- A silent endpoint must produce a clear, bounded failure — never a hang.

- A lost middle/last packet must be detected by reassembly; the requester then retries or reports.

- try/finally restores shared simulated state (MTU, endpoint table) so later tests are unaffected.

Hardware recovery tests (lab): power-cycle a device and verify rediscovery; restart mctpd/pldmd; hold the bus in reset briefly with a bus fault injector; each with a recovery-time criterion.

lessons.title: Sequence and state validation
lessons.body:
- **Sequence numbers**: unit tests feed out-of-order and mixed-tag packets into the reassembler (Chapter 14) — they must be rejected.

- **Instance IDs**: the requester rotates 0..31; tests assert consecutive requests use different IDs and stale responses are rejected.

- **Protocol state**: firmware-update state tables (Chapter 13); EID state (before and after Set Endpoint ID).

lessons.title: Packet or message logging
lessons.body:
The simulated network records every packet in trace (direction + raw bytes), as seen in Chapter 12’s output. In a real framework, log at two levels:

1. **Message level** (always): EID, message type, PLDM type/command/instance ID, completion code, latency, retries.

2. **Packet level** (on demand or on failure): raw packet bytes with direction and timestamps.

Use the same JSON-lines format as the Redfish client so logs from all interfaces can be merged (Chapter 20).

lessons.body:

- Interface fixtures skip cleanly if PLDM is disabled in the target config.

- A world fixture exposes simulated state for fault injection and skips on real targets.

- Codecs have their own fast unit tests (marker unit).

```code
$ pytest -v -k "pldm or mctp"
```

lessons.title: Hardware and firmware dependencies
Exercises: practical debugging
lessons.body:
**Exercise 1 — endpoint not discovered.** Symptoms: mctpd logs no endpoint on bus 3; PLDM sensors for a NIC missing in Redfish. Plan an investigation.

Solution. (1) Confirm the device is powered and present (FRU, presence GPIO). (2) On the BMC: i2cdetect -y 3 (only if probing that bus is approved) — does the NIC ACK its address? (3) Check mctp link/mctp addr that the MCTP interface for bus 3 exists. (4) Check device-tree/config for the MCTP binding on that bus. (5) Look for kernel I²C errors (dmesg | grep -i i2c). (6) Check the NIC firmware supports MCTP over SMBus (some ship with it disabled). (7) Use a bus analyser to see whether Get Endpoint ID is sent and answered.

**Exercise 2 — intermittent PLDM timeouts.** 1 in 200 GetSensorReading requests times out.

Solution. Correlate timeouts with other bus activity (another poller on the same bus? firmware update traffic?). Check for NACKs/arbitration lost in kernel logs. Measure response latency distribution: are successful responses close to the timeout (device slow → timeout too tight)? Verify instance IDs on late responses. Test with polling disabled for other devices. Capture with an analyser around a failure.

**Exercise 3 — reassembly errors on large messages only.** GetPDR for large PDRs fails; small commands work.

Solution. Suspect transmission-unit mismatch or fragmentation bugs. Compare the negotiated/configured MTU on both sides; capture packets and check sequence numbers and SOM/EOM; reproduce in the simulator with the observed MTU; check whether middle packets have unexpected sizes.

lessons.title: Summary
lessons.body:
- A byte-accurate simulator lets you test codecs, requesters and fault handling deterministically.

- Discovery, unsupported-message, timeout, recovery and sequence tests form the core.

- Log at message level always and packet level on failure.

- List hardware/firmware dependencies explicitly; never claim simulated results as hardware validation.

lessons.title: UART fundamentals
lessons.body:
A **UART** (Universal Asynchronous Receiver/Transmitter) sends bytes one bit at a time over a single wire per direction, without a shared clock. Both sides agree in advance on the bit rate; the receiver re-synchronises on every byte using a start bit.

```code
 idle (high) ─┐  start ┌ b0 ┬ b1 ┬ b2 ┬ b3 ┬ b4 ┬ b5 ┬ b6 ┬ b7 ┬(parity)┬ stop
┌─ idle
              └────────┘    data bits, least-significant first
└──────┘
```

- **Idle** is logic high. A **start bit** (low) marks the beginning of a frame.

- **Data bits** (usually 8) follow, least-significant bit first.

- An optional **parity bit** (even/odd) allows single-bit error detection.

- One or two **stop bits** (high) end the frame.

A typical BMC console uses **115200 8N1**: 115200 bits per second, 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit. Each byte costs 10 bit times, so the maximum throughput is 11,520 bytes per second — fast enough for a console, slow enough that a burst of kernel logging can take seconds.

Physical layer facts that cause real lab problems:

- **TX connects to RX** and **RX to TX**, plus **ground**. Without a common ground, you get garbage or nothing.

- **Voltage levels**: board UART headers are usually 3.3 V (sometimes 1.8 V) logic (“TTL”); a PC’s DB9 serial port uses RS-232 levels (roughly ±3 to ±15 V). Connecting RS-232 directly to a 3.3 V pin can damage the board. Use the correct USB-to-serial adapter.

- **Flow control**: hardware (RTS/CTS) or software (XON/XOFF) flow control is usually off for BMC consoles. If one side expects it and the other does not, output stalls.

lessons.title: Baud rate, data bits, parity and stop bits
lessons.body:
| Setting | Common value | What happens if mis‐ matched |
| Baud rate | 115200 | Garbage characters, framing errors, or nothing readable |
| Data bits | 8 | Corrupted characters (7-bit loses the top bit) |
| Parity | None | Parity errors or corrupted bytes |
| Stop bits | 1 | Usually still works at low load; framing errors at high load |
| Flow control | None | Output stops when the buffer “fills” waiting for CTS |

**Note.** The console baud rate is configured in firmware (U-Boot environment, kernel command line console=ttyS4,115200n8). Different consoles on the same board (BMC console vs host console) can use different settings.

lessons.title: pySerial
lessons.body:
**pySerial** is the standard Python library for serial ports on Linux, Windows and macOS.

```code
$ pip install pyserial
$ python -m serial.tools.list_ports -v          # list available ports
$ python -m serial.tools.miniterm /dev/ttyUSB0 115200   # interactive terminal
```

Port names: Linux /dev/ttyUSB0, /dev/ttyACM0 (user must be in the dialout group or equivalent); Windows COM3; macOS /dev/cu.usbserial-XXXX. Prefer stable names on Linux: /dev/serial/by-id/usb-... survives re-plugging; / dev/ttyUSB0 may become ttyUSB1.

Core API:

| Call | Purpose |
| serial.Serial(port, baudrate=115200, | Open the port |

```code
timeout=0.1)
```

```code

```

| ser.write(data) / ser.flush() | Send bytes; wait until sent |
| Call | Purpose |
| ser.reset_input_buffer() | Discard unread input In-memory loopback for tests serial.serial_for_url("loop://") |
