6. **Distinguishing causes.** recv without timeout → missing timeout; SSH read pattern → window deadlock; input() or prompt → interactive.

7. **Corrective actions.** Explicit timeouts everywhere; drain SSH streams together; BatchMode; pipeline-level timeout(); pytest-timeout.

8. **Interview-ready explanation.** “A hang is always a missing timeout somewhere. I take a stack dump to find the blocking call, fix that call’s timeout, and add defence in depth: pytest-timeout and a pipeline timeout, so one bug can’t block the lab for a night.”

source.section: 26.20 Scenario 20 — A Jenkins job hangs forever

lessons.title: Scenario 21 — A PATCH is accepted but the value reverts after reboot
lessons.body:
1. **Symptoms.** AssetTag set, reads back correctly, lost after BMC reboot.

2. **Plausible causes.** Setting stored only in volatile memory; persistence service failure; configuration restored from defaults by an update or factory-reset flag; two sources of truth (e.g. FRU vs settings DB).

3. **Investigation sequence.** Repeat with logs; inspect where the setting persists; check journal at shutdown/startup for persistence errors.

4. **Commands/code.**

```code
# journalctl -b -1 | grep -i -E "persist|save|settings"   (previous boot)
# df -h                                                   (writable
partition full?)
```

5. **Expected observations.** Write errors, full partition, or the property not implemented as persistent.

6. **Distinguishing causes.** Errors in log → persistence failure; no errors → design issue/defaults restored.

7. **Corrective actions.** Bug report with reproduction; persistence tests across reboot, AC cycle and update.

8. **Interview-ready explanation.** “Read-after-write proves the API, not persistence. I always add a reboot step to settings tests; when values revert, I check the previous boot’s logs and storage health to find whether saving failed or the value was never meant to persist.”

source.section: 26.21 Scenario 21 — A PATCH is accepted but the value reverts after reboot

lessons.title: Scenario 22 — BMC reboots randomly during a long soak test
lessons.body:
1. **Symptoms.** Every few hours BMC uptime resets; tests see connection resets.

2. **Plausible causes.** Watchdog timeout due to CPU starvation; out-of-memory kills of critical services; kernel panic; hardware reset (power/ brown-out).

3. **Investigation sequence.** Console capture across the event; journal from previous boot (if persistent); watchdog/OOM messages; correlate with test load; memory trend.

4. **Commands/code.**

```code
# journalctl -b -1 -p warning | tail -100
# dmesg | grep -i -E "watchdog|oom|panic"
# cat /proc/meminfo
```

**Expected observations.** OOM killer messages and rising memory, 5. watchdog pre-timeout, or a panic trace on the console.

6. **Distinguishing causes.** OOM + growth → leak; watchdog + load → starvation; panic → kernel/driver; nothing logged + console shows sudden U-Boot → hardware reset.

7. **Corrective actions.** Bug with evidence; memory trend monitoring in soak tests; evidence collection hooks.

8. **Interview-ready explanation.** “Unexplained reboots during soak are usually memory leaks, watchdog starvation or crashes. Console capture plus previous-boot logs and memory trends tell them apart, and the soak test becomes the reproducer.”

source.section: 26.22 Scenario 22 — BMC reboots randomly during a long soak test

lessons.title: Scenario 23 — Logging stops / SEL full
lessons.body:
1. **Symptoms.** No new event log entries; SEL shows “full” or oldest entries remain.

2. **Plausible causes.** Log capacity reached with no-overwrite policy; logging service crashed; storage full.

3. **Investigation sequence.** Check log service capacity/policy (Redfish LogService MaxNumberOfRecords, OverWritePolicy), service status, storage.

4. **Commands/code.** `$ ipmitool ... sel info # systemctl status xyz.openbmc_project.Logging*     (unit names vary)`

5. **Expected observations.** Entries = max with policy NeverOver‐ Writes; or logging service failed.

6. **Distinguishing causes.** Policy-based → configuration/test hygiene; crashed service → defect.

7. **Corrective actions.** Save and clear logs in test setup (on dedicated systems); verify overwrite policy behaviour as a test.

8. **Interview-ready explanation.** “When events vanish, I first check whether the log is simply full under a no-overwrite policy — a test-environment issue — before chasing a logging-service defect.”

lessons.title: Scenario 24 — pldmtool works manually but pldmd shows sensors unavailable
lessons.body:
1. **Symptoms.** pldmtool platform GetSensorReading returns values; Redfish shows the sensor as unavailable.

2. **Plausible causes.** pldmd failed PDR parsing for that sensor; sensor association wrong; pldmd polling disabled/backed off after errors; D- Bus publication failure.

3. **Investigation sequence.** pldmd journal; D-Bus sensor objects; compare PDR data via pldmtool with what pldmd published.

4. **Commands/code.**

```code
# journalctl -u pldmd -b | grep -i -E "sensor|pdr|error"
# busctl tree xyz.openbmc_project.PLDM
```

5. **Expected observations.** Parse errors, missing D-Bus object, or Available=false with errors logged.

6. **Distinguishing causes.** No D-Bus object → discovery/PDR parsing; object but stale → polling; object fine but Redfish wrong → bmcweb.

7. **Corrective actions.** Bug to the right component with PDR dump; test comparing pldmtool readings to D-Bus/Redfish.

8. **Interview-ready explanation.** “pldmtool proves the device and transport work, which isolates the problem to pldmd’s processing or publication. D-Bus tells me which.”

source.section: 26.24 Scenario 24 — pldmtool works manually but pldmd shows sensors unavailable

lessons.title: Scenario 25 — SSH host-key verification fails in CI after a factory reset
lessons.body:
1. Symptoms. REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED in CI.

2. **Plausible causes.** Expected regeneration after reset; unexpected change (possible interception, or a different device answering on that IP).

3. **Investigation sequence.** Confirm reset occurred; verify new fingerprint via console (ssh-keygen -lf /etc/ssh/ssh_host_*.pub or Dropbear equivalent); confirm MAC/IP mapping.

4. **Commands/code.**

```code
$ ssh-keyscan -t ed25519 bmc.example.test | ssh-keygen -lf -
```

5. **Expected observations.** Fingerprint matches the console-reported key → legitimate.

6. **Distinguishing causes.** Matches → update known_hosts; doesn’t → investigate network.

7. **Corrective actions.** Update managed known_hosts through a reviewed change; never disable checking.

8. **Interview-ready explanation.** “A changed host key is either expected after a reset or a red flag. I verify the new fingerprint out-of-band on the console before updating the managed known_hosts.”

source.section: 26.25 Scenario 25 — SSH host-key verification fails in CI after a factory reset

lessons.title: Scenario 26 — Redfish sensor collection takes seconds per request
lessons.body:
1. **Symptoms.** GET Chassis/<id>/Sensors?$expand=. takes 8 s; tests time out.

2. **Plausible causes.** Expansion of many members each requiring D-Bus calls; slow sensor daemons; BMC CPU load; TLS renegotiation per request (no keep-alive).

3. **Investigation sequence.** Time with and without $expand; check connection reuse; BMC CPU during request.

4. **Commands/code.**

```code
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{time_total}\n" --cacert lab-ca.pem -H "X-
Auth-Token: $T" https://bmc.example.test/redfish/v1/Chassis/chassis/
Sensors
```

5. **Expected observations.** Expansion dominating; or new TLS handshake each call.

6. **Distinguishing causes.** Expand-only slowness → server-side aggregation; all calls slow → load/connection reuse.

**Corrective actions.** Use Session keep-alive; avoid expand or raise 7. read timeout; report performance against requirements.

8. **Interview-ready explanation.** “I separate client overhead — connection reuse — from server work — expansion and D-Bus fan-out — by timing variants. Then it’s either a test configuration fix or a performance finding against a requirement.”

source.section: 26.26 Scenario 26 — Redfish sensor collection takes seconds per request

lessons.title: Scenario 27 — A test fails only on the first run after BMC boot
lessons.body:
**Symptoms.** First run fails (e.g. sensors missing), reruns pass. 1.

2. **Plausible causes.** Services still initialising (sensor discovery, PLDM discovery); caches cold; readiness gate too weak (only checks Redfish root).

3. **Investigation sequence.** Timestamp failure relative to boot; check service readiness states; measure time until sensors populate.

4. **Commands/code.**

```code
# cat /proc/uptime ; obmcutil state ; systemctl list-jobs
```

5. **Expected observations.** Failures within N minutes of boot; pending systemd jobs.

6. **Distinguishing causes.** Time-correlated with boot → readiness; random → other.

7. **Corrective actions.** Stronger readiness criteria (BMC Ready + no pending jobs + expected sensor count); requirement test for time-to-full-inventory.

8. **Interview-ready explanation.** “If only the first run fails, the system wasn’t fully ready. Redfish answering isn’t enough; I gate on BMC state, pending startup jobs and expected inventory, and measure time-to-ready as a requirement.”

source.section: 26.27 Scenario 27 — A test fails only on the first run after BMC boot

lessons.title: Scenario 28 — An NVMe drive is missing from inventory
lessons.body:
1. **Symptoms.** Drive visible to host OS; missing in BMC Redfish Storage/Drives.

2. **Plausible causes.** NVMe-MI over MCTP (or basic SMBus management) not discovered; drive slot’s SMBus path/mux not configured; drive doesn’t support NVMe-MI over the available binding; BMC daemon not polling that slot.

3. **Investigation sequence.** Check presence signals, bus path, MCTP discovery (message type 0x04 support), relevant daemon logs.

4. **Commands/code.** `# mctp link ; journalctl -b | grep -i nvme # i2cdetect -l                       (bus/mux layout for drive slots)`

5. **Expected observations.** Endpoint absent or lacking NVMe-MI type; mux/bus config missing for that slot.

6. **Distinguishing causes.** No bus response → physical/config; endpoint without NVMe-MI → drive capability; endpoint present, daemon silent → software.

7. **Corrective actions.** Fix platform configuration; document unsupported drives; inventory test comparing host-visible drives with BMC inventory.

8. **Interview-ready explanation.** “The host sees drives over PCIe data paths; the BMC sees them over management paths like SMBus with NVMe-MI over MCTP. A gap means the management path or its configuration is missing, so I trace that path layer by layer.”

source.section: 26.28 Scenario 28 — An NVMe drive is missing from inventory

lessons.title: Scenario 29 — Logs from BMC and test runner appear out of order
lessons.body:
1. **Symptoms.** BMC error appears “after” the test failure it caused.

2. **Plausible causes.** BMC clock drift/offset; time zone differences; buffered logging.

3. **Investigation sequence.** Measure offset (BMC date -u +%s.%N vs runner); check NTP on BMC; normalise all logs to UTC.

4. **Commands/code.**

```code
# date -u +%s.%N ; timedatectl
$ date -u +%s.%N
```

5. **Expected observations.** Offset of seconds; NTP unsynchronised.

6. **Distinguishing causes.** Constant offset → clock; varying → drift or buffering.

7. **Corrective actions.** Enable NTP; record offset at test start; correlation tooling that applies it (Chapter 20).

8. **Interview-ready explanation.** “Causality inverted in logs is a clock problem until proven otherwise. I measure the BMC-to-runner offset and normalise everything to UTC before drawing conclusions.”

source.section: 26.29 Scenario 29 — Logs from BMC and test runner appear out of order

lessons.title: Scenario 30 — The automation account is locked out
lessons.body:
1. **Symptoms.** All jobs fail with 401; admin sees account locked.

2. **Plausible causes.** A negative test used the real account with wrong passwords; a job with a stale password retried; lockout threshold low.

3. **Investigation sequence.** Check AccountService lockout settings and audit logs; identify job/time of failed attempts.

4. **Commands/code.**

```code
$ curl -s --cacert lab-ca.pem -u "$ADMIN" https://bmc.example.test/
redfish/v1/AccountService | python -m json.tool | grep -i lockout
```

5. **Expected observations.** Failed attempts from one job, matching threshold.

6. **Distinguishing causes.** Negative test → test design; stale credential → secret rotation process.

7. **Corrective actions.** Negative-auth tests use throwaway accounts; no retries on 401; credential rotation propagated to CI; alert on lockouts.

8. **Interview-ready explanation.** “Lockouts are usually self-inflicted: a negative test or a retry loop hammering with bad credentials. Authentication-failure tests must use disposable accounts, and clients must never retry 401s blindly.”

lessons.title: Practical exercises with complete solutions
lessons.body:
Write these functions; the reference solutions follow and were tested **[Run]**.

1. decode_mctp_header(raw) → dict of fields; reject wrong header version.

2. parse_sel_elist(text) → list of entries; fail loudly on unparsed lines.

3. get_with_retry(session, url, ...) → retries 502/503/504 and connection errors with exponential backoff, honouring Retry-After (seconds or HTTP date).

4. wait_for(predicate, timeout_s, poll_s, what) → monotonic-deadline polling; testable with an injected clock.

5. supported_commands(bitfield) → decode the 32-byte GetPLDMCommands bitfield.

```code
examples/ch27_solutions.py
 """Chapter 27: reference solutions for the capstone practical exercises."""
 from __future__ import annotations
 import re
 import time
 from collections.abc import Callable
 from dataclasses import dataclass
 from email.utils import parsedate_to_datetime
import requests
# Exercise 1 ---------------------------------------------------------------
def decode_mctp_header(raw: bytes) -> dict[str, int | bool]:
    """Decode the 4-byte MCTP transport header (DSP0236 layout)."""
    if len(raw) < 4:
        raise ValueError(f"need 4 bytes, got {len(raw)}")
    if raw[0] & 0x0F != 1:
        raise ValueError(f"unsupported header version {raw[0] & 0x0F}")
    f = raw[3]
    return {"dest": raw[1], "src": raw[2], "som": bool(f & 0x80), "eom": bool(
f & 0x40),
            "seq": (f >> 4) & 3, "to": bool(f & 0x08), "tag": f & 7}
# Exercise 2 ---------------------------------------------------------------
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class SelEntry:
    record_id: int
    date: str
    time: str
    sensor: str
    event: str
    direction: str
_SEL = re.compile(r"^\s*([0-9a-fA-F]+)\s*\|\s*([^|]+?)\s*\|\s*([^|]+?)\s*\|
\s*([^|]+?)\s*\|"
                  r"\s*([^|]+?)\s*\|\s*(Asserted|Deasserted)\s*$")
def parse_sel_elist(text: str) -> list[SelEntry]:
    """Parse 'ipmitool sel elist'-style lines (id | date | time | sensor |
event | dir).
    Lines that do not match are reported, not silently dropped."""
    entries, bad = [], []
    for line in text.splitlines():
        if not line.strip():
            continue
        m = _SEL.match(line)
        if not m:
            bad.append(line)
            continue
        entries.append(SelEntry(int(m.group(1), 16), *m.group(2, 3, 4, 5, 6)))
    if bad:
        raise ValueError(f"{len(bad)} unparsed SEL line(s), first: {bad[0]!
r}")
    return entries
# Exercise 3 ---------------------------------------------------------------
def retry_after_seconds(value: str | None, default: float) -> float:
    """Retry-After may be delta-seconds or an HTTP date (RFC 9110)."""
    if not value:
        return default
    if value.strip().isdigit():
        return float(value)
    try:
        when = parsedate_to_datetime(value)
        return max(0.0, when.timestamp() - time.time())
    except (TypeError, ValueError):
        return default
def get_with_retry(session: requests.Session, url: str, attempts: int = 4,
                   base_delay: float = 0.5, max_delay: float = 8.0,
                   timeout: tuple[float, float] = (5, 30),
                   sleep: Callable[[float], None] = time.sleep) ->
requests.Response:
    """GET with retries on 502/503/504 and connection errors; honours Retry-
After."""
    last_exc: Exception | None = None
    for attempt in range(attempts):
        try:
            resp = session.get(url, timeout=timeout)
        except (requests.ConnectionError, requests.Timeout) as exc:
            last_exc, resp = exc, None
        if resp is not None and resp.status_code not in (502, 503, 504):
            return resp
        if attempt == attempts - 1:
            break
        delay = min(max_delay, base_delay * 2 ** attempt)
        if resp is not None:
            delay = min(max_delay, retry_after_seconds(resp.headers.get("Retry
-After"), delay))
        sleep(delay)
    if resp is not None:
        return resp            # caller sees the final 5xx and decides
    raise RuntimeError(f"GET {url} failed after {attempts} attempts") from
last_exc
# Exercise 4 ---------------------------------------------------------------
def wait_for(predicate: Callable[[], bool], timeout_s: float, poll_s: float =
0.5,
             what: str = "condition", clock: Callable[[], float] =
time.monotonic,
             sleep: Callable[[float], None] = time.sleep) -> float:
    """Poll until predicate() is true; return elapsed seconds; raise on
timeout."""
    start = clock()
    while True:
        if predicate():
            return clock() - start
        if clock() - start >= timeout_s:
            raise TimeoutError(f"timed out after {timeout_s}s waiting for {wha
 t}")
         sleep(poll_s)
 # Exercise 5 ---------------------------------------------------------------
 def supported_commands(bitfield: bytes) -> list[int]:
     """Decode the 32-byte GetPLDMCommands bitfield into command codes."""
     if len(bitfield) != 32:
         raise ValueError(f"expected 32 bytes, got {len(bitfield)}")
     return [i * 8 + b for i, byte in enumerate(bitfield) for b in range(8) if
 byte >> b & 1]
examples/test_ch27_solutions.py

def test_get_with_retry_against_mock():

sleep=lambda d: None)
```

lessons.title: Suggested next steps for advanced learning
lessons.body:
1. **Run DMTF tools** (Redfish-Service-Validator, Redfish-Interop-Validator) against a test BMC and study every failure.

2. **Read the specs** you use most — DSP0266 (Redfish), DSP0236/ DSP0240 (MCTP/PLDM), DSP0267 (firmware update) — one chapter a week, writing tests for what you read.

3. **Build OpenBMC in QEMU** (the OpenBMC project documents running images in QEMU for supported machines) to have a real Redfish/ IPMI/SSH stack on your laptop.

4. **Contribute** to open-source test tools (OpenBMC test automation, DMTF tools) — the best interview evidence there is.

5. **Learn SPDM** and device attestation; it is becoming standard in platform security.

6. **Add async**: rewrite a collector with asyncio/AsyncSSH to manage fleets.

7. **Observability**: ship structured logs to a search tool and build dashboards of pass rates and flake rates.

8. **Interview practice**: answer five questions from Chapter 25 and one scenario from Chapter 26 aloud every day for a month, recording yourself.

lessons.title: What is an operating system?
lessons.body:
**Definition.** An operating system (OS) is the software layer that manages hardware (CPU, memory, storage, network, devices) and gives programs a safe, uniform way to use it. **Why it exists.** Without an OS, every program would have to drive the disk controller, schedule itself on the CPU, and avoid overwriting other programs’ memory. The OS does this once, correctly, for everyone.

**What it provides:**

| Responsibility | What it means in practice |
| Process management | Runs many programs at once; switches between them (scheduling) |
| Memory management | Gives each process its own virtual memory; prevents one from corrupting another |
| Filesystems | Turns raw blocks on flash/disk into files and directories |
| Device drivers | Talks to hardware: Ethernet, I²C controllers, UARTs, NVMe drives |
| Networking | TCP/IP stack, sockets, routing |
| Security | Users, permissions, capabilities, isolation |
| System calls | The doorway programs use to request all of the above |

lessons.title: Linux: kernel, user space, shell and utilities
lessons.body:
Strictly speaking, **Linux is the kernel** — the core program that owns the hardware. What people call “a Linux system” is the kernel plus user-space software: an init system (usually systemd), a C library (glibc or musl), a shell (Bash, or BusyBox ash on small devices) and utilities ( ls, grep, ip…).

```code
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
|                       USER SPACE                            |
|  Applications:  bmcweb  ipmid  your_test.py  sshd           |
|  Shell:         bash / ash          Utilities: ls grep ip   |
|  Libraries:     glibc / musl, libsystemd, OpenSSL           |
|  Init:          systemd (PID 1)                             |
+---------------------- system calls --------------------------+
|                      KERNEL SPACE                           |
|  Scheduler | Memory mgr | VFS + filesystems | Net stack     |
|  Device drivers: eth, i2c, uart, mtd/mmc, watchdog, gpio    |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
|                        HARDWARE                             |
|  CPU (ARM/x86)  RAM  SPI flash / eMMC  NIC  I2C buses  UART |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
```

**Key terminology**

- **Kernel space** — privileged mode where the kernel runs; a bug here can crash the whole machine (a kernel panic).

- **User space** — where normal programs run; a crash usually kills only that process.

- **System call (syscall)** — a request from user space to the kernel, e.g. open(), `read(), write(), fork().`

- **Shell** — a program that reads commands and runs them (Bash, sh, ash, zsh). The terminal is just the window or serial line that carries text to and from the shell.

- **Utilities** — small programs ( cat, grep, systemctl). On full distributions these come from GNU coreutils and friends; on small embedded images they often come from **BusyBox**, a single binary providing simplified versions of many tools.

| systems | Buildroot | often no package manager on target |

**Important for BMC work:** OpenBMC is built with **Yocto/OpenEmbedded**. The resulting firmware image usually has **no package manager** and a **read-only root filesystem**. You cannot apt install a debugging tool on a BMC; you work with what the image contains, or you build a new image.

| CPU | x86-64, powerful | Often ARM SoC (e.g. ASPEED AST2500/AST2600 in many BMCs) |
| RAM | GBs | Often hundreds of MB up to around 1–2 GB |
| Storage | SSD/HDD, hundreds of GB | SPI NOR flash (tens of MB) or eMMC |
| Root filesystem | Writable ext4/xfs/btrfs | Often read-only squashfs + small writable overlay |
| Tools | Full GNU tools, package | BusyBox or a trimmed tool set; |
| manager | no package manager |
| Updates | Package updates | Whole-image firmware updates |
| Console | Monitor/keyboard, SSH | Serial UART console, SSH, web/ API |
| Uptime expectations | Planned reboots | Must recover by itself (watchdogs) |

lessons.title: Linux in BMCs and server-management platforms
lessons.body:
A **Baseboard Management Controller (BMC)** is a small, separate computer on a server motherboard. It stays powered whenever the server has standby power, even if the main host is off. It lets administrators:

- Power the host on/off and reset it.

- Read sensors (temperature, voltage, fan speed) over I²C/SMBus/PMBus and other buses.

- Inventory hardware (CPUs, DIMMs, drives, PSUs).

- Provide a remote console (serial-over-LAN, KVM).

- Log hardware events.

- Update firmware for itself and sometimes other components.

- Expose management APIs: **Redfish** (REST/JSON over HTTPS), **IPMI** (older binary protocol), and talk to devices internally with **PLDM** over **MCTP**.

**OpenBMC** is an open-source Linux distribution for BMCs, hosted by the Linux Foundation. Under the hood it is “just Linux”: a kernel, systemd, D-Bus, and many daemons. That is excellent news for you — everything in Parts I–III applies directly.

lessons.title: Walkthrough: a hypothetical server BMC (fictional platform “Falcon”)
lessons.body:
```code
              Management network (1 GbE)
                        |
+-----------------------+-------------------------------------+
|  BMC SoC (ARM)        eth0 192.0.2.50                       |
  |  +------------------------------------------------------+   |
  |  | Linux kernel + drivers (i2c, gpio, uart, watchdog)   |   |
  |  | systemd -> services:                                 |   |
  |  |   bmcweb (Redfish/HTTPS :443)   ipmid (IPMI :623/udp)|   |
  |  |   sensor daemons   inventory   logging   fw-update   |   |
  |  |        \______________ D-Bus ______________/         |   |
  |  +------------------------------------------------------+   |
  |   SPI flash (firmware)   RAM   UART (debug console)         |
  +--------+------------+---------------+-------------+---------+
           | I2C        | GPIO          | eSPI/LPC    | MCTP/PLDM
       temp sensors   power button   host CPU      NVMe, NICs
       PSUs, FRU      reset lines    (BIOS/UEFI)   add-in cards
```

Follow a single request: an engineer runs curl https://192.0.2.50/redfish/v1/Chassis/ `chassis/Thermal.`

1. The packet reaches eth0; the kernel’s TCP stack hands it to the process listening on port 443 — **bmcweb**.

2. bmcweb authenticates the user, then asks the sensor daemons for readings **over D- Bus**.

3. A sensor daemon has been reading a temperature chip over **I²C**, via a kernel driver exposed in /sys/class/hwmon/.

4. bmcweb formats the result as Redfish JSON and returns it.

If the API returns an error, the fault could be at any layer: network, bmcweb, D-Bus, a sensor daemon, the kernel driver, the I²C bus, or the sensor chip. **This layered picture**

**is the foundation of every BMC debug session in this book.**

lessons.title: The boot process at a high level
lessons.body:
```code
Power on
  -> ROM code in SoC (fixed, inside the chip)
  -> Bootloader (U-Boot on most BMCs; GRUB/systemd-boot/UEFI on servers)
  -> Linux kernel (+ device tree on ARM)
  -> initramfs (optional small early root filesystem)
  -> Real root filesystem mounted
  -> PID 1: systemd
  -> Targets/services start (network, sshd, bmcweb, ...)
  -> Login prompt / APIs available
```

Chapter 10 examines each stage and how it fails.

lessons.title: Linux filesystem layout
lessons.body:
Linux has a single directory tree starting at / (root). The layout follows the **Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (FHS)**; embedded images follow it loosely.

| Directory | Purpose | BMC note |
| /bin , /sbin , /usr/bin , /usr/ | Programs | Often symlinks to BusyBox |

```code
sbin
```

| /etc | System configuration | May be writable via overlay; changes persist across reboot on many platforms |
| /var | Variable data: logs, caches, | /var/log may be tmpfs (lost at |
| state | reboot) |
| /var/lib | Persistent application state | Often on a writable partition |
| /tmp | Temporary files | Usually tmpfs in RAM |
| /home , /root | User home directories | Usually just /home/root or / |

```code
root
```

| /proc | Virtual: process and kernel | Read for diagnostics information |
| /sys | Virtual: devices, drivers, kernel | hwmon, gpio, i2c, watchdog objects |
| /dev | Device nodes | /dev/i2c-* , /dev/ |

```code
ttyS* , /dev/mtd* , /dev/
   watchdog
```

| /run | Runtime state since boot | PID files, sockets, D-Bus socket (tmpfs) |
| /boot | Kernel and bootloader files | Usually absent on BMC; kernel is in flash |

lessons.title: Hands-on: first look at a system (all [RO])
lessons.body:
```code
uname -a                 # kernel name, version, architecture
cat /etc/os-release      # distribution identity
cat /proc/cpuinfo | head -20
free -h                  # memory summary (BusyBox: free without -h on old builds)
df -h                    # filesystem usage

```

**Sample output (Ubuntu VM, typical):**

```output
$ uname -a
Linux lab-vm 6.8.0-45-generic #45-Ubuntu SMP x86_64 GNU/Linux
$ cat /etc/os-release | head -3
PRETTY_NAME="Ubuntu 24.04.1 LTS"
NAME="Ubuntu"
VERSION_ID="24.04"
```

**Sample output (OpenBMC lab image, fictional but representative):**

```output
root@falcon-bmc:~# uname -m
armv7l
root@falcon-bmc:~# cat /etc/os-release | head -4
ID=openbmc-phosphor
NAME="Phosphor OpenBMC (Phosphor OpenBMC Project Reference Distro)"
VERSION="2.16.0-dev"
VERSION_ID=2.16.0-dev-123-g0abc1234
```

Explanation: armv7l means 32-bit ARM (e.g. AST2500/AST2600 class SoCs); a desktop shows x86_64. /etc/os-release on OpenBMC contains the firmware version string you will later verify after updates (Chapter 19). Exact NAME/ VERSION contents vary by build and vendor.

lessons.title: Exercises
lessons.body:
1. On your lab VM, identify the kernel version, distribution and CPU architecture.

2. List five directories under / and say whether each is a real disk directory or a virtual filesystem.

3. Draw the layers a Redfish GET passes through on a BMC, from network to sensor chip.

4. Which two features of embedded Linux most affect how you install debugging tools on a BMC?

**Solutions**

1. uname -r (kernel), cat /etc/os-release (distribution), uname -m (architecture).

2. Use findmnt /proc /sys /dev /run /tmp — /proc (proc), /sys (sysfs), /dev (devtmpfs), / run (tmpfs) are virtual or RAM-backed; /etc, /usr are on the root filesystem.

3. NIC → kernel TCP stack → bmcweb (port 443) → D-Bus → sensor daemon → kernel hwmon driver → I²C controller driver → I²C bus → sensor chip.

4. No package manager and a read-only root filesystem. Tools must be included at image build time (Yocto), or copied temporarily to a writable location such as /tmp in an authorised lab.

lessons.title: Best practices
lessons.body:
- Start every investigation by identifying **what system you are on**: uname -a, /etc/os-release, uptime, and who you are ( id).

- Never assume a GNU option exists on an embedded target; check --help first.

- Keep a personal “platform card” per lab device: architecture, image version, IPs, console settings, which tools exist.

lessons.title: Paths: absolute versus relative
lessons.body:
- An **absolute path** starts at /: /var/log/syslog. It means the same thing from anywhere.

- A **relative path** starts from the **current working directory**: logs/run1.txt.

- Special names: . (this directory), .. (parent), ~ (your home directory — expanded by the shell).

**Best practice in scripts:** use absolute paths, or compute paths from a known base, because a script’s current directory depends on how it was started (cron, Jenkins and systemd all start in different directories).

lessons.title: Navigation and inspection commands (all [RO])
lessons.body:
| Command | Purpose | Key options |
| pwd | Print working directory | -P resolve symlinks |
| ls | List directory contents | -l long, -a include hidden, -h human sizes, -t sort by time, - r reverse, -d list the directory itself, -i inode |
| cd | Change directory (shell built-in) | cd - previous dir, cd alone goes home |
| tree | Show a directory tree | -L N depth, -a hidden (often not installed) |
| find | Search by name, type, size, | see below time |
| Search a prebuilt filename | fast but database may be stale; | locate |
| database | often not installed |
| file | Detect actual file type from | often missing on BMC images content |
| stat | Detailed metadata | size, inode, permissions, timestamps |

lessons.title: Reading ls -l argument by argument
lessons.body:
```code
$ ls -lh /var/log/syslog
-rw-r----- 1 syslog adm 1.2M Oct 15 09:12 /var/log/syslog
 |          |  |      |   |    |            |
 |          |  owner  grp size  mtime       name
 |          hard link count
 type + permissions (- regular file, d dir, l symlink, c char dev, b block dev)
```

lessons.title: find — the most useful search tool
lessons.body:
```code
Syntax: find <start-dir> <tests> <actions>
  # [RO] All .service files under /lib/systemd/system
  find /lib/systemd/system -name '*.service'
  # [RO] Regular files over 10 MB on the root filesystem only (-xdev: don't cross mounts)
  find / -xdev -type f -size +10M 2>/dev/null
  # [RO] Files changed in the last 30 minutes in /var/log
  find /var/log -type f -mmin -30
  # [RO] Depth-limited listing when tree is missing
  find /etc -maxdepth 1 -type d
```

- -name matches the file name (quote the pattern so the shell does not expand * first).

- -type f regular files, -type d directories, -type l symlinks.

- -size +10M larger than 10 MiB. -mmin -30 modified less than 30 minutes ago; -mtime -1 less than 24 hours.

- 2>/dev/null discards “Permission denied” noise (standard error).

- **Caution:** find ... -delete and find ... -exec rm are **[DISRUPT]**. Always run the same find without the action first and review the list.

source.section: 2.2.2 find — the most useful search tool

lessons.title: Viewing file contents (all [RO])
lessons.body:
| Command | Use |
| cat file | Print whole file (small files only) |
| less file | Page through; /text search, n next, G end, F follow, q quit |
| head -n 20 file | First 20 lines |
| tail -n 50 file | Last 50 lines |
| tail -f file | Follow a growing file (Ctrl+C to stop); -F also survives log rotation (GNU) |
| wc -l file | Count lines ( -w words, -c bytes) |

```code
tail -n 100 /var/log/syslog | less   # [RO] last 100 lines, paged
wc -l /var/log/syslog                # [RO] how big is it in lines?
```

lessons.title: Creating, copying, moving and deleting
lessons.body:
| Command | Label | Notes |
| mkdir -p a/b/c | [MOD] | -p creates parents, no error if it exists |
| touch file | [MOD] | Creates empty file or updates timestamp |
| cp src dst | [MOD] | -r recursive, -p preserve mode/time, -i ask before overwrite, -a archive (GNU) |
| mv src dst | [MOD] | Rename or move; silently overwrites unless -i |
| rm file | [MOD]/[DISRUPT] | No recycle bin. -r recursive, -f force, -i interactive |
| rmdir dir | [MOD] | Removes only empty directories (safe) |

**Safe habits**

```code
mkdir -p ~/lab/ch02 && cd ~/lab/ch02        # work in a sandbox directory
cp -i config.json config.json.bak           # back up before editing
mv -i results.txt archive/                  # -i asks before overwriting
rm -i old_*.log                             # confirm each deletion
ls old_*.log                                # ALWAYS list before rm with a wildcard
```

**Dangerous patterns to recognise**

- rm -rf "$DIR/"* when $DIR is empty becomes rm -rf /*. Chapter 15 shows how to guard against this with ${DIR:?}.

- cp -r src dst behaves differently depending on whether dst already exists (copies into it versus as it).

- mv across filesystems is a copy + delete; interrupted, it can leave partial data.

lessons.title: File extensions versus actual file types
lessons.body:
Linux does **not** use extensions to decide a file’s type. firmware.bin might be a tar archive; report.txt might be gzip-compressed. Use file:

```code
$ file falcon-fw.tar image.bin notes.txt /dev/null
falcon-fw.tar: POSIX tar archive
image.bin:     data
notes.txt:     ASCII text
/dev/null:     character special (1/3)
```

If file is not installed (common on BMCs), inspect the first bytes (“magic numbers”):

```code
head -c 16 image.bin | od -A x -t x1z    # [RO] hex dump of first 16 bytes
```

Gzip starts with 1f 8b; ELF executables with 7f 45 4c 46 (“7fELF”); tar has ustar at byte offset 257.

source.section: 2.5 File extensions versus actual file types

lessons.title: Symbolic links and hard links
lessons.body:
- **Inode** — the on-disk record holding a file’s metadata and data location. A directory entry is just a name → inode mapping.

- **Hard link** — another name pointing to the **same inode**. Deleting one name leaves the data intact until the link count reaches zero. Cannot cross filesystems; cannot (normally) link directories.

- **Symbolic (soft) link** — a small file containing a **path**. It can cross filesystems and point to directories; it breaks (“dangles”) if the target is removed.

```code
cd ~/lab/ch02
echo "hello" > original.txt          # [MOD]
ln original.txt hard.txt             # [MOD] hard link
ln -s original.txt soft.txt          # [MOD] symbolic link
ls -li original.txt hard.txt soft.txt
1311021 -rw-r--r-- 2 user user  6 Oct 15 10:01 hard.txt
1311021 -rw-r--r-- 2 user user  6 Oct 15 10:01 original.txt
1311045 lrwxrwxrwx 1 user user 12 Oct 15 10:01 soft.txt -> original.txt
```

Explanation: hard.txt and original.txt share inode 1311021 and the link count is 2. soft.txt has its own inode and type l. Inode numbers will differ on your system.

```code
rm original.txt
cat hard.txt     # still prints "hello"
cat soft.txt     # cat: soft.txt: No such file or directory  (dangling link)
readlink -f /usr/bin/python3   # [RO] resolve a symlink chain
```

**Embedded relevance:** On BusyBox systems, ls -l /bin/ls usually shows /bin/ls -> / bin/busybox. Many systemd configurations are symlinks under /etc/systemd/system/ `*.wants/.`

lessons.title: Disk usage: du and df (both [RO])
lessons.body:
- df reports **per filesystem**: total, used, available, mount point.

- du reports **per file/directory**: how much space the files you point at consume.

```code
df -h                 # human-readable sizes per mounted filesystem
df -i                 # inode usage (out of inodes = "No space left" with free bytes!)
du -sh /var/log       # total size of a directory
du -h --max-depth=1 /var 2>/dev/null | sort -h   # GNU: biggest subdirectories
du -d 1 /var | sort -n                            # BusyBox-friendly variant
```

**Why du and df can disagree:** a deleted file that is still held open by a process keeps consuming space. df counts it; du cannot see it (no name). Find such files with lsof +L1 (if installed) or ls -l /proc/*/fd 2>/dev/null | grep deleted. Chapter 6 covers this in depth.

lessons.title: Permissions and safe file handling (preview)
lessons.body: ls -l shows permissions such as -rw-r-----. Chapter 3 explains them fully. For now: never make files world-writable to “fix” an error, and never store passwords in world-readable files.

lessons.title: Lab: navigating an unfamiliar embedded filesystem
lessons.body:
You are given SSH access to an unfamiliar lab BMC (or use your VM). Using only [RO] commands, produce a one-page “platform card”.

```code
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# platform_card.sh - read-only survey of an unfamiliar Linux system
echo "== Identity =="
uname -a
cat /etc/os-release 2>/dev/null || cat /etc/issue 2>/dev/null
echo "== Uptime =="
uptime
echo "== Mounts (root, var, tmp) =="
df -h / /var /tmp 2>/dev/null
echo "== Is BusyBox present? =="
ls -l "$(command -v ls)"
echo "== Largest items in /var/log =="
du -a /var/log 2>/dev/null | sort -n | tail -5
echo "== Systemd unit files (first 10) =="
ls /lib/systemd/system/*.service 2>/dev/null | head -10
echo "== Device nodes of interest =="
ls /dev/i2c-* /dev/ttyS* /dev/watchdog* /dev/mtd* 2>/dev/null
```

Run it with bash platform_card.sh > card.txt 2>&1 and read the result. Every command is read-only.

source.section: 2.9 Lab: navigating an unfamiliar embedded filesystem

lessons.title: Exercises
lessons.body:
1. From /var/log, what is the relative path to /etc/hostname?

2. Find all files under /etc modified in the last day.

3. Show the 5 largest directories under /usr.

4. Create a symlink latest.log that points to run_003.log, then explain what happens when run_003.log is renamed.

5. A file named report.pdf will not open. How do you find out what it really is?

6. df -h shows /var 100% used, but du -sh /var shows only 40% of the size. Give two explanations.

**Solutions**

1. ../../etc/hostname.

2. find /etc -type f -mtime -1 2>/dev/null.

3. du -h --max-depth=1 /usr 2>/dev/null | sort -h | tail -5 (BusyBox: du -d 1 /usr | sort `-n | tail -5).`

4. ln -s run_003.log latest.log. After renaming the target, latest.log dangles because a symlink stores a path, not an inode.

5. file report.pdf, or head -c 8 report.pdf | od -c. A real PDF starts with %PDF-.

6. 1. Deleted-but-open files held by a running process; (b) files hidden under a mount point (data written to /var/x before another filesystem was mounted on /var/x); also reserved blocks for root on ext4.

lessons.title: Best practices
lessons.body:
- Use ls/ find before any rm, mv or cp with wildcards.

- Back up configuration files before editing ( cp -p file file.bak.$(date +%Y%m%d%H%M%S)).

- Use find -xdev to stay on one filesystem when hunting large files.

- Check df -i as well as df -h when you see “No space left on device”.

lessons.title: Users, groups and ownership
lessons.body:
- A **user** has a name and a numeric **UID**. root is UID 0 and bypasses most permission checks.

- A **group** has a name and a **GID**. A user has one primary group and may have supplementary groups.

- Every file has an **owner** (user) and a **group**.

- Account data lives in /etc/passwd (names, UIDs, home, shell), /etc/group, and password hashes in /etc/shadow (readable only by root).

- **System/service accounts** (UIDs typically below 1000) run daemons, e.g. www-data,

```code
 systemd-journal, sshd.
id                  # [RO] uid, gid and groups of current user
id nobody           # [RO] another user
groups              # [RO] group names you belong to
getent passwd root  # [RO] account entry (works with LDAP etc. too)
whoami              # [RO]
$ id
uid=1000(asha) gid=1000(asha) groups=1000(asha),4(adm),27(sudo),20(dialout)
```

Explanation: membership in adm allows reading many logs in /var/log on Debian/ Ubuntu; dialout allows access to serial ports /dev/ttyS* and /dev/ttyUSB* — needed for UART work in Chapter 21.

lessons.title: Read, write and execute
lessons.body:
| Bit | On a file | On a directory |
| r (4) | Read contents | List names in it |
| w (2) | Modify contents | Create, delete, rename entries in it |
| x (1) | Execute as a program | Enter it ( cd ) and access entries by name |

Permissions are given for three classes: **u**ser (owner), **g**roup, **o**thers.

```code
-rwxr-x---   owner rwx (7), group r-x (5), others --- (0)  => 750
```

**Important subtlety:** deleting a file requires **write permission on the directory**, not on the file. A read-only file in a writable directory can still be deleted.

lessons.title: Special bits (awareness level)
lessons.body:
- **setuid (4000)** — program runs with the file owner’s UID (e.g. /usr/bin/passwd). Security-sensitive.

- **setgid (2000)** — on a directory, new files inherit the directory’s group (useful for shared test-result folders).

- **sticky (1000)** — on a directory (like /tmp, shown as drwxrwxrwt), users can delete only their own files.

lessons.title: chmod, chown, chgrp, umask
lessons.body:
| Command | Label | Example | Meaning |
| chmod 750 run.sh | [MOD] | numeric | rwx r-x — |
| [MOD] | symbolic | add execute for owner | chmod u+x run.sh |
| chmod go-w file | [MOD] | symbolic | remove write from group and others |
| chmod -R g+rX dir | [MOD] | recursive | X adds execute only to directories (and already-executable files) |
| chown asha:qa file | [MOD], usually needs | change owner and |
| root | group |
| [MOD] | change group (you | chgrp qa file must be a member) |
| umask | [RO] to view | umask 027 sets it for | default permission |
| this shell | mask |

**umask** removes bits from the default creation mode (666 for files, 777 for directories). With umask 022, new files are 644 and directories 755. With umask 077, new files are 600 — useful in scripts that write sensitive data.

```code
umask             # e.g. 0022
( umask 077; echo "token-placeholder" > secret.txt ); ls -l secret.txt
# -rw------- 1 asha asha 18 Oct 15 10:20 secret.txt
```

The parentheses run a **subshell**, so the stricter umask applies only to that command.

lessons.title: sudo and privilege escalation
lessons.body:
sudo <command> runs a single command as root (or another user with -u), if /etc/sudoers allows it. It logs usage (often to the journal or /var/log/auth.log).

```code
sudo -l                    # [RO] what am I allowed to run?
sudo journalctl -p err -b  # [RO] read logs that need privilege
sudo -u postgres psql      # run as another user
```

- **Do:** use sudo for the single command that needs it.

- **Don’t:** run whole scripts or editors as root “to be safe”, or use sudo su - habitually.

- Edit sudoers only with visudo (validates syntax — a broken sudoers file can lock you out).

lessons.title: Diagnosing “Permission denied”
lessons.body:
Work through the **whole path**, not just the final file:

```code
namei -l /opt/tests/run.sh     # [RO] shows permissions of every path component (util-linux)
ls -ld /opt /opt/tests         # [RO] alternative where namei is missing
ls -l /opt/tests/run.sh
id
```

Checklist:

1. Do you have x on **every directory** in the path?

2. For reading/writing: r/ w on the file for your class (owner/group/other)?

3. For running a script: x on the file **and** a valid shebang ( #!/usr/bin/env bash). Alternatively run bash run.sh, which needs only r.

4. Is the filesystem mounted read-only ( findmnt -no OPTIONS /opt)? Then you get “Read-only file system”, a different error.

5. Is the filesystem mounted noexec (common for /tmp)? Executing fails even with x set.

6. Mandatory access control (SELinux/AppArmor) may deny even when permissions allow. Check getenforce or aa-status, and the audit log.

7. Group membership changed? New groups apply only to **new login sessions** ( newgrp or log in again).

lessons.title: Why chmod 777 is bad practice
lessons.body:
777 means anyone on the system can modify or replace this file or directory’s contents. Consequences:

- **Security:** any user or compromised service can modify a script that root later runs → privilege escalation.

- **Integrity:** test results and logs can be silently altered; evidence becomes untrustworthy.

- **It hides the real problem:** the actual fault (wrong owner, missing group, wrong service user) remains and appears again elsewhere.

- Some tools refuse to work with over-permissive files. **SSH refuses private keys readable by others** (“UNPROTECTED PRIVATE KEY FILE”), and may refuse ~/.ssh directories that are group/world-writable (depending on StrictModes).

**Instead:** fix ownership ( chown), add the user to the right group, or set precise modes.

lessons.title: Service accounts and least privilege
lessons.body:
**Least privilege**: every user, script and service gets only the access it needs.

- Run test agents (e.g. a Jenkins agent) as a dedicated non-root user.

- Give that user group access to exactly the devices it needs ( dialout for serial ports), not root.

- systemd services can use User=, Group=, ProtectSystem=, ReadWritePaths= to limit what they touch (Chapter 8).

lessons.title: Safe permissions for scripts, logs and credentials
lessons.body:
| Item | Recommended mode | Why |
| Your scripts | 750 or 755 | Executable; writable only by owner |
| Shared result directory | 2770 with a shared group | setgid keeps group consistent |
| Log files | 640 | Readable by owner and group only |
| Credential/config with secrets | 600 | Owner only |
| ~/.ssh | 700 | Required by SSH |
| SSH private key | 600 | SSH refuses otherwise |
| ~/.netrc | 600 | curl reads credentials from here |

lessons.body:
```code
mkdir -p ~/lab/ch03 && cd ~/lab/ch03
printf '#!/usr/bin/env bash\necho "diag ok"\n' > diag.sh   # [MOD]
./diag.sh                     # bash: ./diag.sh: Permission denied
ls -l diag.sh                 # -rw-r--r--  (no x)
chmod u+x diag.sh && ./diag.sh  # diag ok
chmod 000 diag.sh; bash diag.sh # bash: diag.sh: Permission denied (no r)
chmod 750 diag.sh               # restore sensible mode
```

lessons.title: Exercises
lessons.body:
1. Convert rw-r----- and rwxr-xr-x to numeric.

2. What permissions does a new file get with umask 027?

3. A user can cat /data/results/run1.log but cannot delete it. Why?

4. Write the command to make every directory in results/ enterable by the group without making files executable.

5. A colleague runs chmod -R 777 /opt/testsuite to fix a Jenkins failure. What do you suggest instead?

**Solutions**

1. 640 and 755.

2. 666 & ~027 = 640 → rw-r-----. Directories: 750.

3. Deletion needs write (and execute) permission on /data/results, the directory, not on the file.

4. chmod -R g+rX results/.

5. Find which user Jenkins runs as ( ps -o user= -p <pid> or the agent configuration), then chown -R jenkins:qa /opt/testsuite or add the agent user to the owning group and set chmod -R g+rX (plus g+w only on directories it must write to). Revert the 777.

lessons.title: Best practices
lessons.body:
- Fix ownership, not modes, when the wrong user owns something.

- Use groups to share access; never 777.

- Create secrets with umask 077 and check them with ls -l before use.

- Log what you run with sudo; prefer specific sudo rules for automation users.

lessons.title: Core concepts
lessons.body:
- **Program** — an executable file on disk.

- **Process** — a running instance of a program, with its own memory, open files and a **PID** (process ID).

- **Thread** — an execution path inside a process; threads share the process’s memory. In Linux each thread has its own **TID**.

- **Parent process (PPID)** — the process that created it (via fork()/ clone()). PID 1 (systemd) is the ancestor of everything in user space and adopts orphans.

- **Process states** (column STAT in ps):

| Code | State | Meaning |
| R | Running/runnable | On CPU or waiting for a CPU |
| S | Interruptible sleep | Waiting for an event (most processes, most of the time) |
| D | Uninterruptible sleep | Waiting on I/O inside the kernel; cannot be killed until it returns. Many D processes often mean storage or driver trouble |
| T | Stopped | Paused by a signal (Ctrl+Z, SIGSTOP) or a debugger |
| Z | Zombie | Finished, but parent has not collected its exit status |
| I | Idle kernel thread | Normal |

lessons.title: Foreground and background execution
lessons.body:
```code
sleep 300            # foreground: shell waits; Ctrl+C sends SIGINT
sleep 300 &          # background: shell prints [1] 12345 and returns
jobs                 # [RO] list this shell's jobs
fg %1                # bring job 1 to foreground
# Ctrl+Z             # suspend the foreground job (SIGTSTP)
  bg %1                # resume it in the background
  nohup ./long_test.sh > test.log 2>&1 &   # keep running after logout
```

nohup ignores the hangup signal sent when the terminal closes. For truly long tasks on remote machines, tmux or screen (if installed) are better: you can reattach later.

lessons.title: Inspecting processes (all [RO])
lessons.body:
| Command | Use All processes, BSD-style columns (GNU procps) ps aux |
| ps -ef | All processes, System V style (works on BusyBox too) |
| ps -eo pid,ppid,user,stat,%cpu, | Custom columns, sorted (GNU) |

```code
%mem,rss,etime,cmd --sort=-%mem
```

| ps -p 1234 -o pid,stat,etime,cmd | One process |
| top | Live view; press P sort by CPU, M by memory, 1 per-CPU, q quit |
| htop | Friendlier top (often not installed) |
| pgrep -a sshd | PIDs (and command lines with -a ) matching a name |
| pstree -p | Tree with PIDs (package psmisc; often missing on BMC) |
| cat /proc/<pid>/status | State, memory (VmRSS), threads, UIDs |
| ls -l /proc/<pid>/fd | Open file descriptors |

```code
$ ps -eo pid,ppid,user,stat,%cpu,%mem,etime,cmd --sort=-%cpu | head -5
    PID    PPID USER     STAT %CPU %MEM     ELAPSED CMD
   2381       1 root     Ssl   35.2  4.1    02:13:44 /usr/bin/fake-sensord
    911       1 root     Ss     1.0  0.6  3-01:22:10 /lib/systemd/systemd-journald
      1       0 root     Ss     0.1  0.3  3-01:22:12 /sbin/init
```

Explanation (sample): fake-sensord uses 35% of a CPU and has run for 2 h 13 m, while the system has been up 3 days — it was **restarted** at some point. That mismatch between process age and uptime is a classic clue for a crash/restart loop (Chapter 8). STAT letters: s session leader, l multi-threaded, + foreground group, < high priority, N low priority. **BusyBox note:** BusyBox ps supports few options; often only ps or ps -o `pid,ppid,user,stat,vsz,rss,args. Fall back to reading /proc/<pid>/status and /proc/<pid>/ cmdline.`

lessons.title: Signals, kill and graceful termination
lessons.body:
A **signal** is a notification sent to a process.

| Signal | Number | Default action | Typical use |
| SIGTERM | 15 | Terminate | Polite request to exit; process can clean up. Default of |

```code
kill
```

| SIGINT | 2 | Terminate | Ctrl+C |
| SIGHUP | 1 | Terminate | Terminal closed; many daemons reload config on it |
| SIGKILL | 9 | Kill, cannot be caught | Last resort; no cleanup, may leave lock/temp files |
| SIGSTOP / SIGCONT | 19/18 (x86) | Pause/resume | Freeze a process for inspection |
| SIGQUIT | 3 | Core dump | Ask for a core dump |
| SIGSEGV | 11 | Core dump | Sent by kernel on invalid memory access |

Signal numbers can differ between architectures for some signals — use names.

```code
kill 2381              # [SVC] SIGTERM
kill -TERM 2381        # same, explicit
kill -0 2381 && echo alive   # [RO] checks existence/permission, sends nothing
pkill -f 'python3 my_test.py'   # [SVC] by full command line; check with pgrep -af first!
kill -KILL 2381        # [SVC] only after SIGTERM has had time to work
```

**Graceful stop pattern:** send SIGTERM, wait a few seconds, check, and only then SIGKILL. **On a system managed by systemd, use systemctl stop <unit> instead of kill** — otherwise systemd may restart the process, or be left with a confusing state.

lessons.title: Load average
lessons.body:
```code
$ uptime
 10:42:01 up 3 days,  1:22,  2 users,  load average: 2.15, 1.10, 0.52
```

The three numbers are averages over **1, 5 and 15 minutes** of the number of tasks that are **runnable or in uninterruptible sleep ( D)**. Interpret relative to CPU count ( nproc): a load of 2.15 on a 2-core BMC means it is saturated; on a 32-core server it is light. Rising 1-minute versus 15-minute shows a trend. Because D tasks are included, a high load with low CPU usage often points to **I/O or driver waits**.

lessons.title: Memory
lessons.body:
```code
$ free -h
               total        used        free      shared  buff/cache   available
  Mem:           1.0Gi       610Mi        52Mi        48Mi       340Mi       330Mi
  Swap:             0B          0B          0B
```

- **free** — completely unused. Small is normal; Linux uses spare RAM for cache.

- **buff/cache** — reclaimable file cache (mostly).

- **available** — the kernel’s estimate of memory available for new work without swapping. **Watch this number.**

- BMCs usually have **no swap**; when memory runs out, the OOM killer acts.

Per-process: **RSS** (resident set size) is physical memory in use; **VSZ** is virtual size (often large and less meaningful). /proc/<pid>/status shows VmRSS, VmHWM (peak RSS) and `Threads.`

lessons.title: Tracking memory growth over time (leak hunting)
lessons.body:
```code
pid=$(pgrep -o fake-sensord)          # -o oldest matching
for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do
  printf '%s ' "$(date +%T)"; grep VmRSS "/proc/$pid/status"
  sleep 60
done
```

Steadily increasing VmRSS under constant load suggests a leak; repeat across several restarts to confirm.

source.section: 4.5.3 Tracking memory growth over time (leak hunting)

lessons.title: Open file descriptors
lessons.body:
A **file descriptor (fd)** is a small integer a process uses to refer to an open file, socket, pipe or device. 0 = stdin, 1 = stdout, 2 = stderr.

```code
ls -l /proc/$$/fd               # [RO] your shell's fds
ls /proc/2381/fd | wc -l        # [RO] count fds of a process
cat /proc/2381/limits | grep -i 'open files'   # [RO] per-process limit
ulimit -n                       # [RO] limit for this shell
lsof -p 2381 | head             # [RO] details (if lsof installed)
```

A count that keeps growing indicates an **fd leak**; when it hits the limit, the process gets **“Too many open files” (EMFILE)** — it then cannot open logs, sockets or devices, and failures look random.

lessons.title: Zombie processes
lessons.body:
A **zombie** ( Z, shown as <defunct>) has exited, but its parent has not called wait() to collect the exit status. Zombies use no CPU or memory beyond a process-table entry, so a few are harmless. Many indicate a **bug in the parent**. You **cannot kill a zombie** — it is already dead. Fix or restart the parent; when the parent exits, PID 1 adopts and reaps the zombies.

```code
ps -eo pid,ppid,stat,cmd | awk '$3 ~ /^Z/'     # [RO] list zombies and their parents
```

lessons.title: Out-of-memory (OOM) situations
lessons.body:
When memory is exhausted and cannot be reclaimed, the kernel’s **OOM killer** chooses a process (based on oom_score, roughly memory use adjusted by oom_score_adj) and kills it with SIGKILL.

```code
dmesg -T | grep -iE 'out of memory|oom-kill|killed process'   # [RO] may need root
journalctl -k -b | grep -i oom                                  # [RO] same via journal
cat /proc/2381/oom_score                                        # [RO]
```

**Sample kernel log (fictional):**

```code
[86401.512] fake-sensord invoked oom-killer: gfp_mask=0x140cca(GFP_HIGHUSER_MOVABLE),
order=0, oom_score_adj=0
[86401.530] Out of memory: Killed process 2381 (fake-sensord) total-vm:412344kB, anon-rss:
301220kB, file-rss:0kB, shmem-rss:0kB, UID:0
```

Interpretation: fake-sensord held ~300 MB of anonymous memory when killed; if systemd restarts it and the cycle repeats, you have a memory leak, not a random crash. Exact log wording varies by kernel version.

lessons.title: Resource exhaustion in automated test environments
lessons.body:
Common in CI and long regression runs:

- **Leftover processes** from previous test runs (e.g. orphaned ssh, python or serial-capture processes) holding ports, serial devices or locks.

- **fd leaks** in test harnesses that open SSH sessions or HTTP connections without closing them.

- **Disk filling** with logs and core dumps (Chapter 6).

- **Too many parallel jobs** on one agent → load spikes → timeouts that look like product bugs.

- **PID or thread limits** (cgroup pids.max) in containers.

Defensive habits: track every child process you start and stop it in cleanup (Chapter 15 trap), use timeouts everywhere, and record resource usage at test start and end.

source.section: 4.9 Resource exhaustion in automated test environments

lessons.title: Lab: process investigation
lessons.body:
Simulate a misbehaving process and investigate it with read-only tools.

```code
mkdir -p ~/lab/ch04 && cd ~/lab/ch04
cat > hog.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Simulated misbehaving daemon: burns CPU and leaks file descriptors.
exec 3>/dev/null
i=0
while true; do
  i=$((i+1))
  if (( i % 200000 == 0 )); then
    exec {fd}</dev/null      # open a new fd and never close it (fd leak)
  fi
done
EOF
chmod +x hog.sh
./hog.sh &            # [SVC] starts a background process in your lab
HOG=$!
echo "hog PID=$HOG"
```

Now investigate:

```code
ps -o pid,ppid,stat,%cpu,etime,cmd -p "$HOG"     # 1. Is it running? CPU?
top -b -n 1 | head -15                          # 2. System view (batch mode)
for t in 1 2 3; do ls /proc/$HOG/fd | wc -l; sleep 5; done   # 3. fd growth?
grep -E 'State|VmRSS|Threads' /proc/$HOG/status  # 4. state and memory
cat /proc/loadavg                                # 5. load
kill -TERM "$HOG"; sleep 1; kill -0 "$HOG" 2>/dev/null || echo "stopped"  # 6. cleanup [SVC]
```

**Expected findings:** %CPU near 100 (one core busy), STAT R, the fd count increasing every few seconds, load average rising toward 1. Write a three-line incident note: symptom, evidence, conclusion (“CPU-bound loop with fd leak; growth ~N fds/5s”).

lessons.title: Exercises
lessons.body:
1. Find the five processes using the most memory.

2. How do you tell whether a service process restarted recently without reading logs?

3. A test hangs; ps shows the test’s child ssh in state S. What would D have suggested instead?

4. You see 40 zombie processes with the same PPID. What do you do?

5. Explain load average 4.0 on a 2-core BMC with 10% CPU usage.

**Solutions**

1. ps -eo pid,user,rss,cmd --sort=-rss | head -6 (BusyBox: ps -o pid,rss,args | sort -k2 -n -r | head -6 if rss is supported, else read /proc/*/status).

2. Compare its elapsed time ( ps -o etime= -p PID) with system uptime; or systemctl show `-p NRestarts,ActiveEnterTimestamp <unit>.`

3. S is a normal wait (e.g. for the network). D would mean it is blocked inside the kernel on I/O — e.g. storage or a driver — and could not even be killed.

4. Identify the parent ( ps -p <PPID> -o cmd), collect evidence, then restart the parent service in a controlled way (on a lab system). Report the reaping bug.

5. Load counts tasks in D state, so processes are likely blocked on I/O (flash, NFS, a stuck driver). Check ps for D states, dmesg for I/O errors, and storage health.

lessons.title: Best practices
lessons.body:
- Use systemctl to control services, not kill.

- Measure first (CPU, RSS, fds over time), then conclude.

- Clean up processes you start; record PIDs.

- In CI, record uptime, free, df at the start and end of each job — it explains many “random” failures.

lessons.title: Essentials
lessons.body:
- **Interface** — a network device: eth0, enp3s0, lo (loopback), usb0. BMCs often have eth0/ eth1, and some expose a host-facing interface (e.g. a USB virtual NIC) — names are platform-specific.

- **IP address + prefix** — 192.0.2.50/24 means address 192.0.2.50 in network 192.0.2.0 with a 24-bit mask (255.255.255.0).

- **Gateway / default route** — where packets go when the destination isn’t on a local network.

- **DNS** — translates names to IP addresses. Configured via /etc/resolv.conf (often managed by systemd-resolved or NetworkManager); /etc/hosts provides static entries.

- **Port** — a 16-bit number selecting a service on a host: SSH 22, HTTPS 443 (Redfish), IPMI over LAN 623/UDP.

- **TCP** — connection-oriented (handshake: SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK). **UDP** — connectionless (IPMI LAN uses UDP 623).

lessons.title: The layered method
lessons.body:
Always test from the bottom up and stop at the first layer that fails:

```code
1. Link     : is the cable/interface up?            ip link
2. Address  : do I have the right IP/subnet?         ip addr
3. Route    : do I know how to reach the target?     ip route get <ip>
4. Name     : does the name resolve?                 getent hosts <name>
5. Reach    : does the host answer at all?           ping (if ICMP allowed)
6. Port     : is the TCP port open?                  nc -zv / bash /dev/tcp
7. Service  : does the application respond?          curl -v / ssh -v
8. Auth/App : credentials, TLS, API behaviour        curl -u / response codes
```

| ip -br link | Interfaces and state, brief |

| ss -tunap | All TCP/UDP sockets |
| ping -c 4 -W 2 <ip> | ICMP echo, 4 packets, 2 s wait (Linux iputils) |
| getent hosts <name> | Resolve as the system does (respects /etc/ |

```code
nsswitch.conf , /etc/hosts )
```

| nslookup / dig | Query DNS servers directly (bypass /etc/hosts ) |
| curl -vk --max-time 10 https://<ip>/ | HTTP(S) test, verbose, insecure TLS (lab only) |

```code
redfish/v1/
```

| ssh -v user@host | Verbose SSH handshake debugging |
| traceroute / tracepath | Path hops (often not installed) |
