
system they can cut off your own session.

lessons.title: Reading ip -br addr and ip route
lessons.body:
```code
$ ip -br addr
lo               UNKNOWN        127.0.0.1/8 ::1/128
eth0             UP             192.0.2.10/24 fe80::5054:ff:fe12:3456/64
$ ip route
default via 192.0.2.1 dev eth0 proto dhcp metric 100
192.0.2.0/24 dev eth0 proto kernel scope link src 192.0.2.10
$ ip route get 198.51.100.7
198.51.100.7 via 192.0.2.1 dev eth0 src 192.0.2.10 uid 1000
```

Explanation: traffic to 198.51.100.7 leaves via eth0, through gateway 192.0.2.1, using source 192.0.2.10. If ip route get returns Network is unreachable, there is no matching route.

source.section: 5.3.1 Reading ip -br addr and ip route

lessons.title: Reading ss -tlnp
lessons.body:
```code
State   Recv-Q  Send-Q  Local Address:Port  Peer Address:Port Process
LISTEN  0       128           0.0.0.0:22         0.0.0.0:*     users:(("sshd",pid=702,fd=3))
LISTEN  0       512                 *:443              *:*     users:
(("bmcweb",pid=1190,fd=3))
LISTEN  0       128         127.0.0.1:8080       0.0.0.0:*     users:
(("testsrv",pid=3001,fd=5))
```

0.0.0.0 or * = listening on all addresses. 127.0.0.1:8080 = **only local** connections accepted — a remote client gets “connection refused”. This is a very common misconfiguration.

lessons.title: Testing TCP ports when nc is missing
lessons.body:
Bash has a built-in pseudo-device /dev/tcp/<host>/<port> (a Bash feature, not a real file; it does **not** exist in BusyBox ash or dash):

```code
if timeout 3 bash -c '</dev/tcp/192.0.2.50/443' 2>/dev/null; then
  echo "port 443 open"
else
  echo "port 443 closed/filtered/unreachable"
fi
```

source.section: 5.4 Testing TCP ports when nc is missing

lessons.title: Connection refused versus timeout
lessons.body:
**What happened at network**

| Observation | Meaning level |
| Connection refused | Host replied with TCP RST | The host is reachable, but |
| (immediate) | nothing listens on that port/ address, or a firewall actively rejects |
| Timeout (waits, then fails) | No reply at all | Packets dropped: host down, wrong route, firewall DROP, wrong VLAN, cable |
| No route to host | ICMP host unreachable, or no | Host absent on local network, or |
| ARP reply on local subnet | routing problem |
| Name or service not known | DNS lookup failed | Name resolution problem — the network may be fine |
| TLS error ( SSL certificate | TCP fine; TLS validation failed | Certificate untrusted/expired/ |
| problem ) | hostname mismatch |
| HTTP 401/403 | Service up; auth rejected | Credentials or privileges |
| HTTP 503 / 500 | Service up but backend failing | Investigate the application (e.g. bmcweb ↔ D-Bus) |

lessons.title: Why ping success does not prove a service is available
lessons.body:
ping uses **ICMP** and is answered by the **kernel’s network stack**. It tells you that the host’s kernel is running and routing works. It says **nothing** about:

- whether sshd or bmcweb processes are running,

- whether they listen on the right address and port,

- whether a firewall allows TCP 22/443,

- whether the service is healthy enough to answer (e.g. bmcweb up but its D-Bus backends hung),

- authentication or TLS.

Conversely, **ping failure doesn’t prove the host is down** — many networks block ICMP. A BMC during early boot may answer ping before services start; during a reboot the kernel may answer briefly before shutting down. **Always test the actual service**

**port and protocol.**

source.section: 5.6 Why ping success does not prove a service is available

lessons.title: SSH connectivity
lessons.body:
```code
ssh -v -o ConnectTimeout=10 -o BatchMode=yes root@192.0.2.50 true
```

- -v (up to -vvv) shows each phase: connecting, key exchange, host key verification, authentication.

- -o ConnectTimeout=10 bounds the TCP connect time.

- -o BatchMode=yes disables password prompts — essential in automation, so a missing key fails fast instead of hanging.

- true is a harmless remote command.

**Common SSH failures**

| Message | Cause |
| Connection refused | sshd not running / wrong port |
| Connection timed out | Network path or firewall |
| Host key verification failed / REMOTE HOST | Host key changed — expected after reflashing |
| IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED | a BMC (new keys generated). Verify it really is your device, then remove the old key with ssh- |

```code
keygen -R <host> [MOD]
```

| Permission denied (publickey,password) | Wrong user/key/password, or key permissions too open |
| no matching host key type found | Algorithm mismatch between old/new SSH versions |

**Do not** permanently set StrictHostKeyChecking=no in automation for real environments; it disables protection against man-in-the-middle attacks. In a **lab** where devices are reflashed constantly, a reasoned compromise is a per-lab known_hosts file managed by the test framework, with host-key changes logged.

lessons.title: Firewall and access-control considerations
lessons.body:
- Host firewalls: nftables ( nft list ruleset), iptables ( iptables -L -n -v), firewalld ( firewall-cmd --list-all), ufw status. Reading needs root; all **[RO]** when listing.

- Network ACLs on lab switches, VLAN separation of management networks, and jump hosts are common in data centres. A timeout from your desk but success from the lab jump host points to network policy, not the BMC.

- BMC-side: some BMCs let admins disable protocols (e.g. IPMI over LAN) or restrict accounts — a configuration, not a fault.

- **Do not disable a firewall as a troubleshooting shortcut.** Read the rules and add a specific, documented exception if needed.

lessons.title: Network diagnostics for BMC management interfaces
lessons.body:
```code
BMC=192.0.2.50
ip route get "$BMC"                                   # 1. path
ping -c 3 -W 2 "$BMC"                                 # 2. ICMP (may be blocked)
timeout 3 bash -c "</dev/tcp/$BMC/22"  && echo ssh-port-open
timeout 3 bash -c "</dev/tcp/$BMC/443" && echo https-port-open
curl -sk --max-time 10 -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' "https://$BMC/redfish/v1/"   # 3.
service root
```

The Redfish **service root** /redfish/v1/ is defined by the DMTF Redfish specification to be accessible without authentication on conformant implementations — a good liveness probe. Expect 200. Most other resources need authentication ( 401 without credentials is healthy).

**Interpreting combinations:**

| ping | 22 | 443 | Redfish root | Likely state |
| ✗ | ✗ | ✗ | ✗ | BMC down/ rebooting, network path, or ICMP blocked and services down |
| ✓ | ✗ | ✗ | ✗ | Kernel up; userspace services not (still booting, or failed) |
| ✓ | ✓ | ✗ | ✗ | SSH fine; bmcweb down → inspect via SSH: |

```code
systemctl status
bmcweb
```

| ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | 5xx | bmcweb up; backend (D-Bus services) problem |
| ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | 200 | Basic availability OK |

Also check the BMC’s own view (via SSH or serial console): ip -br addr (did it get the expected IP? DHCP vs static), ip route, ss -tlnp.

source.section: 5.9 Network diagnostics for BMC management interfaces

lessons.title: Exercises
lessons.body:
1. Which command shows which interface would be used to reach 203.0.113.9?

2. curl to a lab service says “Connection refused”. ss -tlnp on the server shows 127.0.0.1:5000. Explain and fix.

3. ping bmc01.example.com says “Name or service not known”, but ping 192.0.2.50 works. Where is the problem?

4. Write a one-line check of TCP port 443 without nc or curl.

5. After reflashing a BMC, SSH fails with “REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED”. What do you do?

**Solutions**

1. ip route get 203.0.113.9.

2. The service listens only on loopback. Configure it to bind 0.0.0.0 (or the specific interface address), restart it [SVC], and confirm with ss -tlnp.

3. Name resolution: check getent hosts bmc01.example.com, /etc/hosts, /etc/resolv.conf, and the DNS record.

4. timeout 3 bash -c '</dev/tcp/192.0.2.50/443' && echo open || echo closed.

5. Confirm (out of band, e.g. via serial console or lab records) that the device was reflashed and the IP is correct; then ssh-keygen -R 192.0.2.50 and reconnect, verifying the new fingerprint if possible.

lessons.title: Best practices
lessons.body:
- Diagnose bottom-up and record each layer’s result.

- Always use timeouts ( --max-time, ConnectTimeout, timeout).

- Test the real protocol and port, not just ping.

- Never disable host-key checking or firewalls globally to “make it work”.

lessons.title: Concepts
lessons.body:
- **Block device** — storage accessed in blocks: /dev/sda, /dev/nvme0n1, /dev/mmcblk0 (eMMC/SD).

- **MTD device** — raw flash (SPI NOR/NAND) accessed through the Memory Technology Device subsystem: /dev/mtd0, /dev/mtdblock0. Common on BMCs. Raw flash has erase blocks and wear; it is **not** a normal disk.

- **Partition** — a section of a device: /dev/sda1, /dev/nvme0n1p2, /dev/mmcblk0p1. Raw flash is divided into MTD partitions defined in the device tree or kernel command line.

- **Filesystem** — the on-disk structure: ext4, xfs, btrfs, vfat; flash-oriented: UBIFS, JFFS2; read-only compressed: squashfs; RAM-based: tmpfs; layered: overlayfs.

- **Mount** — attaching a filesystem to a directory (the **mount point**) in the single tree.

lessons.title: Commands
lessons.body:
| Command | Label | Purpose |
| lsblk -f | [RO] | Block devices, partitions, filesystem types, mount points |
| [RO] | Mount tree; findmnt /var | findmnt shows what filesystem backs a path |
| findmnt -no | [RO] | Script-friendly: root’s device, |
| SOURCE,FSTYPE,OPTIONS / | type, options |
| mount | [RO] with no arguments | List mounts (older style) |
| cat /proc/mounts | [RO] | Kernel’s view; always available, even on BusyBox |
| cat /proc/mtd | [RO] | MTD partitions and names (on flash-based devices) |
| df -hT | [RO] | Usage with filesystem type |
| df -i | [RO] | Inode usage |
| [DISRUPT] | Changes mount state; can risk | mount -o remount,rw /x data on a failing device |
| Command | Label | Purpose |
| umount /x | [DISRUPT] | Detaches; fails if busy |
| mkfs.* , fdisk , flash_erase | [DISRUPT] | Destroy data — never for learning on a real device |

```code
$ lsblk -f
NAME   FSTYPE FSVER LABEL UUID                                 FSAVAIL FSUSE% MOUNTPOINTS
sda
├─sda1 vfat   FAT32       1A2B-3C4D                             505M     1% /boot/efi
└─sda2 ext4   1.0         0f1e2d3c-aaaa-bbbb-cccc-1234567890ab   18G    55% /
```

**Sample (fictional) OpenBMC-style mounts:**

```code
root@falcon-bmc:~# findmnt -no TARGET,SOURCE,FSTYPE,OPTIONS / /var /tmp
/          /dev/mtdblock4   squashfs  ro,relatime
/var       overlay ...      overlay   rw,relatime,lowerdir=...,upperdir=...
/tmp       tmpfs            tmpfs     rw,nosuid,nodev
```

Explanation: the root filesystem is a **read-only squashfs image** in flash; a writable layer (from a read-write flash partition) is laid over parts of it with **overlayfs**; /tmp lives in RAM. Exact layouts differ by OpenBMC platform and flash layout (e.g. static versus UBI layouts, or eMMC-based systems) — always check on your target.

lessons.title: Read-only filesystems
lessons.body:
A filesystem can be read-only because:

1. **By design** — squashfs root on BMCs; writing to /usr fails with “Read-only file system” ( EROFS). Not a fault.

2. **Remounted read-only by the kernel after errors** — ext4 with errors=remount-ro protects data when it detects corruption or I/O errors. **This is a symptom of a**

**storage problem.**

3. **Mounted read-only by configuration** ( /etc/fstab, systemd mount unit, or the image).

Diagnose:

```code
findmnt -no OPTIONS /var | tr ',' '\n' | grep -x ro && echo "read-only"
dmesg -T | grep -iE 'remount|read-only|I/O error|EXT4-fs error|ubifs' | tail
```

**Sample (fictional) kernel log of case 2:**

```code
[52011.3] EXT4-fs error (device mmcblk0p3): ext4_find_entry:1455: inode #131073: comm logger:
reading directory lblock 0
[52011.3] Aborting journal on device mmcblk0p3-8.
[52011.4] EXT4-fs (mmcblk0p3): Remounting filesystem read-only
```

Do **not** simply remount,rw — capture evidence (logs, dmesg), then follow the platform’s recovery procedure (filesystem check offline, reflash, or hardware replacement).

lessons.title: Disk full and inode exhaustion
lessons.body:
**“No space left on device” (ENOSPC)** has three common causes:

| Cause | Check | Typical culprit |
| Blocks exhausted | df -h shows 100% | Large logs, core dumps, test artifacts |
| Inodes exhausted | df -i shows IUse% 100% | Millions of tiny files (session files, per-test temp files) |
| Space held by deleted-but-open | df full, du small | A process still writing to a |
| files | deleted log |

```code
df -h; df -i                                          # [RO]
du -xh / 2>/dev/null | sort -h | tail -15             # [RO] biggest dirs on root fs (GNU)
find /var -xdev -type f -size +5M -exec ls -lh {} + 2>/dev/null   # [RO]
# directories with most files (inode hunt):
find /var -xdev -type f 2>/dev/null | awk -F/ '{NF--; print}' OFS=/ | sort | uniq -c | sort -
n | tail
# deleted-but-open files:
ls -l /proc/[0-9]*/fd 2>/dev/null | grep '(deleted)'
```

**Safe recovery:** compress or move old logs off the device (after copying them as evidence), use the logging tool’s own cleanup ( journalctl --vacuum-size=... is [MOD]), restart a process holding a deleted file only on a lab system with approval [SVC]. Truncating an open log ( : > file.log) frees space immediately but **destroys its content** — copy it first.

lessons.title: Log storage and temporary filesystems
lessons.body:
- **tmpfs** stores files in RAM (and swap). Fast, cleared at reboot, and **consumes memory**. Filling /tmp or a tmpfs /var/log reduces RAM available to processes on a BMC — a disk-full can become an out-of-memory.

- **journald** stores logs in /run/log/journal (volatile, tmpfs) or /var/log/journal (persistent). Many BMC images use volatile or size-limited journals (Chapter 7).

- **Core dumps** can be large; on systemd systems systemd-coredump stores them under / var/lib/systemd/coredump (configurable).

lessons.title: Filesystem permissions and mount options
lessons.body:
Mount options affect behaviour regardless of file modes:

- ro — read-only. noexec — cannot execute programs from this filesystem (common for /tmp, /dev/shm). nosuid — ignore setuid bits. nodev — ignore device nodes.

- A script in /tmp failing with “Permission denied” while ls -l shows x → check for noexec. Run it with bash /tmp/script.sh or place it elsewhere.

lessons.title: Embedded storage constraints
lessons.body:
- **Small capacity** — tens of MB of flash; a debug log at verbose level can fill it in hours.

- **Wear** — flash cells endure a limited number of erase cycles; constant small writes (e.g. logging every second) shorten device life. Flash filesystems (UBIFS, JFFS2) and wear levelling mitigate this.

- **Power-loss safety** — writes interrupted by power cuts can corrupt data; firmware uses atomic update schemes (A/B images). **Partition roles** — typical BMC flash layouts have: bootloader, environment, kernel, • read-only rootfs, read-write partition. Some systems have two flash chips or A/B images for redundancy.

- **Never erase or write MTD partitions to “test”**. Commands like flash_erase, flashcp, dd of=/dev/mtd* are **[DISRUPT]** and can brick a device.

lessons.title: How storage problems break firmware tests and services
lessons.body:
- A service writes its state/config to a full /var → write fails → service exits → systemd restart loop (Chapter 8).

- journald can’t store logs → **missing evidence** exactly when you need it.

- Firmware update needs space to stage the image (often in /tmp, which is RAM) → update fails or the BMC runs out of memory.

- Test harness writes results to a full CI workspace → test framework crashes → reported as “test failure” though the product is fine.

- Read-only remount after flash errors → configuration changes silently fail to persist → “settings lost after reboot” bugs.

source.section: 6.8 How storage problems break firmware tests and services

lessons.title: Lab: simulate disk-full safely with a small tmpfs-like loop file (no root needed)
lessons.body:
Without root you cannot mount, so simulate with a quota-like directory size check, or use a container. Here is a **root-only lab VM** version ([MOD], uses a loop image, doesn’t touch real disks):

```code
# On a disposable lab VM only
truncate -s 5M /tmp/small.img                 # sparse 5 MB file
mkfs.ext4 -q -N 64 /tmp/small.img
# tiny fs with only 64 inodes (it's a file, not a disk)
sudo mkdir -p /mnt/small && sudo mount -o loop /tmp/small.img /mnt/small
sudo chown "$USER" /mnt/small
for i in $(seq 1 100); do touch "/mnt/small/f$i" || { echo "failed at $i"; break; }; done
df -h /mnt/small; df -i /mnt/small            # space free, inodes 100% used
sudo umount /mnt/small && rm /tmp/small.img   # cleanup
```

**Expected:** creation fails around the 50–60th file with “No space left on device” while df -h still shows free space and df -i shows 100% — the inode-exhaustion signature. Exact numbers depend on mkfs defaults.

lessons.title: Exercises
lessons.body:
1. How do you find which filesystem backs /var/lib/myapp?

2. Writes fail with “Read-only file system” in /etc on a BMC. Is it a fault?

3. df -h / shows 62% used but touch /var/x gives “No space left on device”. What do you check?

4. Why is a full /tmp on a BMC also a memory problem?

5. Name two commands you must never run on a production BMC flash for learning.

**Solutions**

1. findmnt -T /var/lib/myapp (the -T option finds the mount containing a path; on BusyBox use df /var/lib/myapp).

2. It depends: on many OpenBMC images /etc is writable via overlay; if it’s read-only, check findmnt -T /etc options and dmesg for remount-after-error messages before concluding.

3. df -i (inodes), df -h /var (it may be a different filesystem), and deleted-open files.

4. /tmp is usually tmpfs, which stores files in RAM.

5. For example flash_erase and dd of=/dev/mtdX (also mkfs.*, fdisk).

lessons.title: Best practices
lessons.body:
- Check df -h, df -i and findmnt early in any investigation involving writes.

- Copy logs off a device before freeing space.

- Treat read-only remounts as hardware/storage evidence.

- Keep debug logging bounded in long tests on flash-based devices.

lessons.title: Why logs matter
lessons.body: Logs are the **flight recorder** of a system. In validation work they let you answer: what happened first, what happened next, and what was the state at failure time? A failure you cannot explain from evidence is a failure you will see again.

lessons.title: Sources of logs
lessons.body:
| Source | Produced by | Where to read it |
| Kernel log | Kernel and drivers ( printk ) | dmesg , journalctl -k |
| System/service logs | Daemons writing to stdout/ | journalctl , /var/log/syslog |
| stderr or syslog under systemd | or /var/log/messages (if a syslog daemon is installed) |
| Application log files | Applications writing their own | e.g. /var/log/nginx/ , test |
| files | harness logs |
| Audit/auth logs | sshd, sudo, PAM, auditd | journalctl -t sshd , /var/ log/auth.log (Debian) or /var/ log/secure (RHEL) |
| BMC event logs | BMC logging services | Via Redfish LogServices and the journal (implementation-specific) |
| Serial console | Everything printed to the | Captured externally (Chapter |
| console, including bootloader | 21) |

**journald** (part of systemd) collects kernel messages, service stdout/stderr, syslog messages and structured metadata (unit name, PID, priority, boot ID) into a binary, indexed journal.

lessons.title: journalctl essentials
lessons.body:
All commands below are **[RO]**. Reading system logs may require root or membership of the systemd-journal or adm group.

| Command | Meaning |
| journalctl | Entire journal, oldest first, in a pager |
| Command | Meaning |
| journalctl -e | Jump to the end |
| journalctl -f | Follow new entries Last 100 lines, no pager (good for scripts) journalctl -n 100 --no-pager |
| journalctl -u bmcweb | One unit ( -u repeatable) |
| journalctl -b | Current boot; -b -1 previous boot Boots recorded in the journal journalctl --list-boots |
| journalctl -k | Kernel messages only (like dmesg ) |
| journalctl -p err | Priority err and more severe ( emerg .. err ); ranges like -p warning..err Time window; also --since "-15min" , "today" , journalctl --since "2026-10-15 09:00" -- |

```code
until "09:30"                                 "yesterday"
```

| journalctl -t sshd | By syslog identifier |
| journalctl _PID=1190 | By field Microsecond timestamps journalctl -o short-precise |
| journalctl -o short-monotonic | Seconds since boot (lines up with dmesg ) |
| journalctl -o json / -o json-pretty | Machine-readable output Journal size journalctl --disk-usage |
| journalctl -g 'timeout' | Grep inside journalctl (needs a build with PCRE2; else pipe to grep ) |
| journalctl --utc | Show times in UTC |

**Priorities (syslog levels):** 0 emerg, 1 alert, 2 crit, 3 err, 4 warning, 5 notice, 6 info, 7 debug. **Older systemd/BusyBox note:** OpenBMC uses systemd, so journalctl is present; some options ( -g, --grep, newer output modes) depend on the systemd version and build options. Check journalctl --version.

lessons.title: dmesg
lessons.body:
dmesg prints the kernel ring buffer — an in-memory, fixed-size buffer. Old messages are overwritten when it fills.

```code
dmesg | tail -50          # [RO] may require root if kernel.dmesg_restrict=1
dmesg -T                  # human-readable time (util-linux; can be inaccurate after suspend)
dmesg -l err,warn         # by level (util-linux)
dmesg -w                  # follow (util-linux)
```

dmesg -C / -c **clear** the buffer — **[MOD] and destroys evidence**. Never use them during an investigation. Timestamps like [ 12.345678] are **seconds since boot** (monotonic), not wall-clock time.

lessons.title: Timestamps and log correlation
lessons.body:
Correlating events requires a **common time base**:

- Wall-clock time (journald default, syslog, application logs) depends on the system clock. On a BMC, the clock may be wrong at early boot until NTP or the host sets it — timestamps can **jump**.

- Monotonic time ( dmesg, journalctl -o short-monotonic) counts from boot and never jumps, but resets each boot.

- Different machines (test host, BMC, Jenkins agent) have **different clocks and time zones**. Convert to **UTC** and record each clock’s offset at test start.

**Practical rule:** in your harness, log date -u +%FT%T.%3NZ on the test host and date -u on the device at start and end of each test. You can then compute the offset and align logs.

lessons.title: Boot-specific logs
lessons.body:
```code
journalctl --list-boots           # [RO]
journalctl -b -1 -p warning --no-pager | tail -50   # previous boot's last warnings
journalctl -b -1 -n 30            # last 30 lines before the previous shutdown/crash
```

Previous-boot logs exist only if the journal is **persistent** (stored on flash/disk), not volatile. If --list-boots shows only boot 0, logs from before the last reboot are gone — capture them over serial or remote logging instead.

lessons.title: Persistent versus volatile logs
lessons.body:
| Mode | Location | Survives reboot? | Typical on |
| Volatile | /run/log/journal | No | Many embedded |
| (tmpfs) | systems (protects flash) |
| Persistent | /var/log/journal | Yes | Servers; some BMC configurations |

```code
Controlled by Storage= in /etc/systemd/journald.conf ( volatile, persistent, auto, none).
```

With auto, the journal is persistent only if /var/log/journal exists. Size limits: SystemMaxUse=, RuntimeMaxUse=. Check effective state:

```code
journalctl --disk-usage
ls -d /var/log/journal /run/log/journal 2>/dev/null
```

lessons.title: Missing logs and logging failures
lessons.body:
When a log you expect is absent, ask:

1. **Was it rotated or vacuumed?** Size limits drop old entries.

2. **Was it volatile and lost at reboot?**

3. **Was the service logging somewhere else?** (its own file, or stdout redirected)

4. **Was the message rate-limited?** journald rate-limits noisy services ( RateLimitIntervalSec=, RateLimitBurst=) and logs “Suppressed N messages from unit”. The kernel also rate-limits (“callbacks suppressed”).

5. **Was the disk full?** journald cannot write.

6. **Did the system die before flushing?** A hard reset/watchdog may lose the last seconds. The serial console often holds them.

7. **Is your clock filter wrong?** --since in local time versus UTC, or the clock jumped.

lessons.title: Log rotation and storage limitations
lessons.body:
Classic text logs are rotated by **logrotate** ( /etc/logrotate.conf, /etc/logrotate.d/): renamed app.log → app.log.1 → app.log.2.gz, with copytruncate or a post-rotate signal so the program writes to a new file. Tools that keep a file open ( tail -f) must handle rotation ( tail -F). When collecting evidence, include rotated files: zgrep searches compressed logs.

```code
zgrep -h 'ERROR' /var/log/app.log* | sort | tail     # [RO]
```

lessons.title: Kernel messages that matter to hardware validation
lessons.body:
Examples (wording varies with drivers and kernel versions; **sample, fictional values**):

```code
i2c i2c-3: ... timeout / transfer error / NACK          -> I2C bus or device not responding
aspeed-i2c-bus 1e78a100.i2c-bus: ... timed out          -> controller-level timeout (ASPEED-
specific driver)
lm75 3-0048: probe failed / error -121                   -> -121 is -EREMOTEIO: no ACK from
device
nvme nvme0: I/O 12 QID 3 timeout, reset controller      -> NVMe command timeout
mmcblk0: error -110 transferring data                   -> -110 is -ETIMEDOUT
ftgmac100 1e660000.ethernet eth0: Link is Down          -> link lost
watchdog: watchdog0: ... / "Watchdog ... reset"         -> watchdog activity
EXT4-fs error ... Remounting filesystem read-only       -> storage error
Out of memory: Killed process ...                       -> OOM
```

Negative numbers are **errno** values: -5 EIO, -6 ENXIO, -16 EBUSY, -19 ENODEV, -22 EINVAL, -110 ETIMEDOUT, -121 EREMOTEIO. Look them up in errno.h or with errno `from the moreutils package, or python3 -c 'import errno,os; print(errno.errorcode[121], os.strerror(121))'.`

source.section: 7.10 Kernel messages that matter to hardware validation

lessons.title: Sample logs (fictional) and a systematic investigation
lessons.body:
**Scenario:** A regression test “sensor_read_all” failed at 09:14:32 UTC on BMC falcon-bmc. You have collected journalctl -b -o short-precise --utc output. Extract:

```code
  Oct 15 09:13:58.104 falcon-bmc systemd[1]: Started Fake Sensor Daemon.
  Oct 15 09:14:02.511 falcon-bmc kernel: i2c i2c-3: bus recovery failed
  Oct 15 09:14:02.512 falcon-bmc kernel: lm75 3-0048: read failed: -110
  Oct 15 09:14:02.530 falcon-bmc fake-sensord[2381]: ERROR sensor TEMP_INLET read error
  errno=110
  Oct 15 09:14:05.530 falcon-bmc fake-sensord[2381]: ERROR sensor TEMP_INLET read error
  errno=110
  Oct 15 09:14:08.530 falcon-bmc fake-sensord[2381]: WARNING sensor TEMP_INLET marked
unavailable
Oct 15 09:14:31.900 falcon-bmc bmcweb[1190]: GET /redfish/v1/Chassis/chassis/Thermal 200
Oct 15 09:14:32.010 falcon-bmc test-agent[4410]: FAIL sensor_read_all: TEMP_INLET Reading
null
```

**Step-by-step investigation**

1. **Define the symptom precisely:** “Redfish Thermal returned HTTP 200 but TEMP_INLET reading was null at 09:14:32.”

2. **Bound the time window:** from the last known good state (daemon started 09:13:58) to the failure (09:14:32).

3. **Find the first meaningful error:** not the test FAIL (that’s the last symptom), but 09:14:02.511 i2c i2c-3: bus recovery failed, immediately followed by the driver read failure with -110 (timeout).

4. **Follow the chain:** kernel I²C timeout → daemon read errors (errno 110) → sensor marked unavailable → Redfish reports null → test fails. Each later line is explained by the earlier one.

5. **Hypotheses:** (a) device at bus 3 address 0x48 not responding (hardware, power, cable/riser), (b) bus held low by another device, (c) I²C controller/driver issue, (d) test environment (e.g. a board variant without that sensor).

6. **Next evidence:** does this happen on other boards? Does i2c-3 show errors for other addresses? Did the sensor ever read successfully this boot? What changed since the last pass (firmware version, hardware)?

7. **Report:** “Symptom: null reading. First error: I²C bus 3 timeout at 09:14:02.511. Root cause **not yet confirmed**; leading hypothesis: device 3-0048 not responding.”

Notice how the HTTP 200 shows the API layer was healthy — the problem lives lower.

source.section: 7.11 Sample logs (fictional) and a systematic investigation

lessons.title: Exercises
lessons.body:
1. Show only error-level-or-worse messages from the current boot for unit ssh.service.

2. Show the last 50 kernel messages from the previous boot.

3. Show all messages between 09:00 and 09:30 today in UTC with microsecond timestamps.

4. A colleague runs dmesg -c “to clean up before the test”. Why is this harmful?

5. journalctl --list-boots shows one entry, but the device rebooted twice today. Explain.

**Solutions**

1. journalctl -b -u ssh.service -p err --no-pager (the unit is named sshd.service on some distributions; OpenBMC commonly uses dropbear, often socket-activated per connection).

2. journalctl -k -b -1 -n 50 --no-pager.

3. journalctl --utc --since "$(date -u +%F) 09:00" --until "$(date -u +%F) 09:30" -o `short-precise.`

4. It clears the ring buffer, destroying kernel evidence that may explain the failure. If you need markers, write one instead: logger "TEST START sensor_read_all" or (root) `echo "TEST START" > /dev/kmsg.`

5. The journal is volatile ( /run/log/journal), so previous boots weren’t kept.

lessons.title: Best practices
lessons.body:
- Insert markers ( logger "TEST START <id>") at test boundaries.

- Collect logs as text **and** keep time in UTC.

- Never clear logs before collecting them.

- Collect previous-boot logs immediately after an unexpected reboot.

lessons.title: What systemd does
lessons.body:
**systemd** is the init system (PID 1) and service manager on most modern distributions and on OpenBMC. It:

- starts services in parallel, respecting dependencies,

- supervises them and restarts them per policy,

- captures their output into the journal,

- manages mounts, sockets, timers, devices and targets as **units**,

- tracks every process of a service in a **cgroup**, so it can stop them all.

lessons.title: Units and service files
lessons.body:
| Unit type | Suffix | Purpose |
| Service | .service | A daemon or one-shot task |
| Socket | .socket | Socket activation (start service on first connection) |
| Target | A group/synchronisation point | .target |

```code
( multi-user.target )
```

| Timer | .timer | Scheduled activation (cron replacement) |
| Mount | .mount | A mount point |
| Path | .path | Activation on file changes |
| Device | .device | Kernel devices (from udev) |

**Locations** (highest precedence first):

1. /etc/systemd/system/ — administrator overrides and drop-ins ( <unit>.d/*.conf)

2. /run/systemd/system/ — runtime-generated

3. /lib/systemd/system/ or /usr/lib/systemd/system/ — shipped by packages/image

**Template units** have @ in their name: serial-getty@.service becomes serial-getty@ttyS0.service; %i inside the file is replaced by the instance ( ttyS0). OpenBMC uses templates heavily (e.g. per-chassis/per-host instances).

lessons.title: Anatomy of a service file
lessons.body:
```code
# /etc/systemd/system/fake-sensord.service  (lab example)
[Unit]
Description=Fake Sensor Daemon (lab)
After=network.target
Wants=network.target
StartLimitIntervalSec=60
StartLimitBurst=5
[Service]
Type=simple
User=sensord
EnvironmentFile=-/etc/default/fake-sensord
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/fake-sensord --config /etc/fake-sensord.conf
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=2
TimeoutStartSec=30
[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
```

| Directive | Meaning |
| After= / Before= | Ordering only — start after X, if both are starting. Does not pull X in |
| Wants= | Weak dependency: also start X; continue if X fails |
| Requires= | Strong dependency: if X fails to start or is stopped, this unit is stopped too |
| BindsTo= | Stronger: stop when X disappears |
| Type=simple | Ready as soon as the process starts |
| Type=exec | Ready once the binary has been successfully executed |
| Type=forking | Classic daemon that forks; ready when parent exits |
| Type=notify | Ready when the process calls |

```code
sd_notify("READY=1")
```

| Type=oneshot | Runs to completion (often with |

```code
RemainAfterExit=yes )
```

| Type=dbus | Ready when it acquires BusName= on D-Bus (common in OpenBMC) |

```code
no , on-failure , always , on-abnormal … Restart=
```

| RestartSec= | Delay before restart |
| StartLimitIntervalSec= / StartLimitBurst= | Rate limit: more than Burst starts in Interval → unit enters failed state with start-limit-hit (in [Unit] section on current systemd) |
| TimeoutStartSec= | Max time to become ready; exceeded → failed with timeout |
| EnvironmentFile=-path | Load variables; leading - means “ignore if missing” |

**Common confusion:** After= without Wants=/ Requires= only orders; Requires= without After= starts both in parallel.

lessons.title: Service-changing commands
lessons.body:
| Command | Label | Effect |
| systemctl start <unit> | [SVC] | Start now |
| systemctl stop <unit> | [SVC] | Stop now — on a BMC, stopping bmcweb ends Redfish access; stopping networking can cut you off [DISRUPT] |
| systemctl restart <unit> | [SVC] | Stop + start |
| [SVC] | Ask service to reload config (if | systemctl reload <unit> supported) |
| systemctl enable/disable | [MOD] | Boot-time behaviour (creates/ |
| <unit> | removes symlinks) |
| systemctl daemon-reload | [MOD]/[SVC] | Re-read unit files after editing them |
| systemctl reset-failed | [MOD] | Clears failed state and start- |
| <unit> | limit counter — do this only after you’ve captured evidence |
| [MOD] | Create a drop-in override safely | systemctl edit <unit> |
| systemctl mask <unit> | [DISRUPT] | Prevent a unit from starting at all |
| systemctl reboot | [DISRUPT] | Reboot |

**Rule:** capture status, show, and journalctl -u output **before** restarting anything. A restart resets state and can destroy evidence.

lessons.title: Reading systemctl status
lessons.body:
```code
● fake-sensord.service - Fake Sensor Daemon (lab)
     Loaded: loaded (/etc/systemd/system/fake-sensord.service; enabled; preset: enabled)
     Active: activating (auto-restart) (Result: exit-code) since Wed 2026-10-15 09:20:11 UTC;
1s ago
    Process: 5120 ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/fake-sensord --config /etc/fake-sensord.conf
(code=exited, status=78)
   Main PID: 5120 (code=exited, status=78)
        CPU: 12ms
Oct 15 09:20:11 lab fake-sensord[5120]: config: cannot open /etc/fake-sensord.conf: No such
file or directory
Oct 15 09:20:11 lab systemd[1]: fake-sensord.service: Main process exited, code=exited,
  status=78/CONFIG
  Oct 15 09:20:11 lab systemd[1]: fake-sensord.service: Failed with result 'exit-code'.
```

Line by line:

- **Loaded** — the file path (did it pick up the file you think?), enabled at boot.

- **Active: activating (auto-restart)** — it failed and systemd is waiting RestartSec to restart: a **restart loop** in progress.

- **status=78** — exit code. 78 is EX_CONFIG in BSD sysexits.h; systemd shows its name ( 78/CONFIG). Exit code meanings are defined by the program itself, so always check the program’s own message.

- The log line gives the real reason: a missing config file.

Other Result values: signal (killed by a signal, e.g. SIGSEGV → crash, SIGKILL → OOM or watchdog), timeout, core-dump, start-limit-hit, watchdog (systemd’s service watchdog WatchdogSec= expired).

lessons.title: Failed services and restart loops
lessons.body:
Symptoms: NRestarts increasing, process age much lower than uptime, repeating log patterns, eventually start-limit-hit.

```code
systemctl show fake-sensord -p NRestarts,Result,ExecMainStatus,ActiveEnterTimestamp
journalctl -u fake-sensord -b --no-pager | grep -E 'Started|Main process exited|Failed' | tai
l -20
```

Typical causes: missing/invalid config, missing dependency (file, device node, D-Bus service), port already in use, permission problems (service User= cannot read files), crash (SIGSEGV), OOM, storage full/read-only.

lessons.title: Startup timeouts
lessons.body:
Type=notify or Type=dbus services must signal readiness. If they hang during initialisation (e.g. waiting for a device or another D-Bus service that never appears), `systemd kills them after TimeoutStartSec and logs start operation timed out. Terminating.`

Look for what the service was waiting on in its log and in systemctl list-jobs.

lessons.title: Environment variables and configuration errors
lessons.body:
Services **do not** inherit your shell environment. Under systemd, a service gets a minimal environment plus Environment=/ EnvironmentFile= values. A program that works from your shell but fails as a service often depends on PATH, HOME or a variable you set

```code
in .bashrc.
  systemctl show fake-sensord -p Environment,EnvironmentFiles,User,WorkingDirectory
  cat /proc/<pid>/environ | tr '\0' '\n'    # [RO] actual environment of a running process
  (root)
```

lessons.title: Dependency failures
lessons.body:
```code
systemd[1]: Dependency failed for Fake Sensor Daemon (lab).
systemd[1]: fake-sensord.service: Job fake-sensord.service/start failed with result
'dependency'.
```

The unit itself never ran; **look at the dependency** that failed ( systemctl list-dependencies fake-sensord, then the status of each Requires= unit).

lessons.title: Lab: diagnose a service that repeatedly fails to start (lab VM with systemd and sudo)
lessons.body:
This lab creates a deliberately broken service. **Run only on a disposable lab VM.** All files are named lab-* for easy cleanup.

```code
# 1. Create the program [MOD]
sudo tee /usr/local/bin/lab-sensord >/dev/null <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Lab daemon: requires a config file with interval=<seconds>
CONF="${LAB_CONF:-/etc/lab-sensord.conf}"
if [[ ! -r "$CONF" ]]; then
  echo "ERROR cannot read config $CONF" >&2
  exit 78
fi
interval=$(sed -n 's/^interval=//p' "$CONF")
if ! [[ "$interval" =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]]; then
  echo "ERROR invalid interval '$interval' in $CONF" >&2
  exit 78
fi
while true; do echo "reading sensors"; sleep "$interval"; done
EOF
sudo chmod 755 /usr/local/bin/lab-sensord
# 2. Create the unit [MOD]
sudo tee /etc/systemd/system/lab-sensord.service >/dev/null <<'EOF'
[Unit]
Description=Lab sensor daemon
StartLimitIntervalSec=30
StartLimitBurst=4
[Service]
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/lab-sensord
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=2
EOF
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl start lab-sensord      # [SVC]
```

**Investigate (read-only):**

```code
sleep 12
systemctl status lab-sensord --no-pager
systemctl show lab-sensord -p Result,NRestarts,ExecMainStatus
journalctl -u lab-sensord -b --no-pager | tail -15
```

**Expected observations:** after ~4 failed starts in 30 s, Active: failed (Result: start- `limit-hit); journal shows ERROR cannot read config /etc/lab-sensord.conf repeated and Start request repeated too quickly. Exit status 78.`

**Fix part 1:** create the config with a bad value.

```code
echo "interval=abc" | sudo tee /etc/lab-sensord.conf
sudo systemctl reset-failed lab-sensord && sudo systemctl start lab-sensord
journalctl -u lab-sensord -n 5 --no-pager    # -> ERROR invalid interval 'abc'
```

**Fix part 2:**

```code
echo "interval=5" | sudo tee /etc/lab-sensord.conf
sudo systemctl reset-failed lab-sensord && sudo systemctl start lab-sensord
systemctl is-active lab-sensord               # active
journalctl -u lab-sensord -n 3 --no-pager     # reading sensors
```

**Cleanup:**

```code
sudo systemctl stop lab-sensord
sudo rm /etc/systemd/system/lab-sensord.service /usr/local/bin/lab-sensord /etc/lab-
sensord.conf
sudo systemctl daemon-reload; sudo systemctl reset-failed
```

**What this lab teaches:** the first error was in the journal on the very first start; start-limit-hit is a consequence, not a cause; reset-failed is needed before systemd will try again; and fixing one error can expose the next.

lessons.title: Exercises
lessons.body:
1. What’s the difference between After=network.target and Requires=network.target?

2. Write a shell condition that prints “DOWN” if bmcweb is not active.

3. A service shows Result: signal and status=9/KILL. Name two possible senders.

4. Why does a program run fine from your shell but fail as a service with “command not found”?

5. Where would you look to see the effective unit file including overrides?

**Solutions**

1. After= only orders startup; Requires= makes the unit depend on network.target being started successfully (and stop if it stops).

2. systemctl is-active --quiet bmcweb || echo DOWN.

3. The OOM killer (check dmesg), systemd itself after a stop timeout ( TimeoutStopSec → SIGKILL), or a person/script running kill -9.

4. Different PATH and environment; use absolute paths in ExecStart or set `Environment=PATH=....`

5. systemctl cat <unit>.

lessons.title: Best practices
lessons.body:
- Inspect first, change second; save the evidence.

- Use systemctl edit drop-ins instead of editing shipped unit files.

- Prefer systemctl is-active --quiet in scripts.

- Record NRestarts at test start and end — a growing count is a hidden failure even when tests pass.

lessons.title: Kernel responsibilities (recap)
lessons.body: Scheduling, memory management, filesystems, networking, **device drivers**, interrupt handling, timers, security enforcement. For validation engineers, the most important point: **the kernel is the boundary between hardware behaviour and software behaviour**, and its log is often the first place hardware problems appear.

lessons.title: Device discovery, drivers and device nodes
lessons.body:
1. **Discovery** — the kernel learns what hardware exists. On PCs: enumeration of buses (PCIe, USB) and ACPI. On ARM BMCs: the **device tree (DT)**, a data structure passed by the bootloader describing SoC peripherals and board devices (e.g. “an LM75 sensor at I²C bus 3 address 0x48”).

2. **Binding** — the kernel matches each device to a **driver** ( compatible strings in DT, IDs for PCI/USB) and calls the driver’s **probe** function. Probe success = device ready; probe failure is logged.

3. **Exposure** — drivers expose devices through **device nodes** in /dev (character or block devices, created by devtmpfs/udev) and through **sysfs attributes** in /sys.

A device that is present in the device tree but whose probe fails will be **missing** from / sys/class/... and /dev, and the services depending on it will fail later — the classic “device appears in one interface but not another” case.

source.section: 9.2 Device discovery, drivers and device nodes

**Sample (fictional) output:**

```output
== /sys/class/hwmon/hwmon2 (lm75)
temp1_input=31500
== /sys/class/hwmon/hwmon3 (aspeed_pwm_tacho)
fan1_input=8400
fan2_input=0
```

Explanation: 31500 = 31.5 °C. fan2_input=0 could mean a stopped fan, a missing fan, or an unpopulated connector — not automatically a fault; compare with the board’s expected population.

```code
# [RO] Is a driver bound to I2C device 3-0048?
ls -l /sys/bus/i2c/devices/3-0048/driver 2>/dev/null || echo "no driver bound (or device not
instantiated)"
```

**Caution about i2cdetect/ i2cget/ i2cset (i2c-tools):** i2cdetect probes addresses by sending transactions and **can disturb some devices**; it skips addresses in use by drivers by default and asks for confirmation. i2cset **writes registers — [DISRUPT]** (it can change voltage regulators, fan controllers, or EEPROM contents). Use them only on authorised lab hardware, with the hardware team’s register documentation, and prefer sysfs reads first.

lessons.title: Interrupts
lessons.body:
An **interrupt** is a hardware signal telling the CPU “something happened” (packet arrived, transfer done). /proc/interrupts shows counters:

```code
grep -E 'i2c|eth|ttyS' /proc/interrupts      # [RO]
```

Take two samples a few seconds apart: a counter that **does not change** while you expect activity suggests the device isn’t signalling (or the driver uses polling); a counter **increasing extremely fast** can indicate an interrupt storm (a stuck line), which can starve the CPU.

lessons.title: Device-driver errors
lessons.body:
Typical patterns (wording driver-specific):

- probe of 3-0048 failed with error -121 — device didn’t acknowledge (absent, unpowered, wrong address, bus fault).

- ... timed out / -110 — transaction timed out.

- ... -EPROBE_DEFER (-517) messages during boot — driver waits for a dependency; usually resolved later in boot. Persistent deferral means a missing dependency (clock, regulator, GPIO).

- firmware: failed to load xyz.bin (-2) — firmware file missing from the filesystem.

lessons.title: Kernel oops and panic
lessons.body:
- **Oops** — the kernel detected a serious bug (e.g. bad pointer dereference) in kernel code. It prints a register dump and **call trace**, kills the offending task, and may continue in a possibly unstable state. The system is marked “tainted”.

- **Panic** — a fatal error; the kernel stops. With panic=N on the command line (or kernel.panic sysctl), it reboots after N seconds. panic_on_oops turns oopses into panics.

**Sample (fictional, abbreviated) oops:**

```code
[  845.120] Unable to handle kernel NULL pointer dereference at virtual address 00000008
[  845.120] pgd = (ptrval)
[  845.121] Internal error: Oops: 5 [#1] SMP ARM
[  845.121] Modules linked in:
[  845.122] CPU: 0 PID: 2381 Comm: fake-sensord Tainted: G        W         6.6.0 #1
[  845.123] PC is at lab_sensor_read+0x2c/0x90
[  845.124] Backtrace:
[  845.124] [<c05a1b2c>] (lab_sensor_read) from [<c05a0f10>] (hwmon_attr_show+0x48/0x10c)
```

What to record: the first line (type of fault), Comm/ PID (the process context, not necessarily the culprit), PC is at (function where it crashed), the backtrace, kernel version, and what was happening (test step). Panics often happen **too fast to reach persistent storage** — the serial console capture is the most reliable evidence. Some systems store crash logs with **pstore/ramoops** in reserved RAM, readable after reboot under /sys/fs/pstore/ (if configured).

lessons.title: Watchdogs and unexpected reboots
lessons.body:
A **watchdog** is a timer that resets the system if software stops “petting” (refreshing) it — protecting against hangs.

- **Hardware watchdog** — in the SoC (BMCs typically have several); opened via /dev/ watchdog*. On many systems **systemd pets it** ( RuntimeWatchdogSec= in /etc/systemd/ system.conf). If PID 1 or the kernel hangs, the hardware resets the BMC.

- **Service watchdog** — systemd’s per-service WatchdogSec=; the service must send WATCHDOG=1 via sd_notify; otherwise systemd kills/restarts it ( Result: watchdog).

- **Host watchdog** — the BMC can implement a watchdog for the host (IPMI watchdog commands) — distinguish from the BMC’s own.

**Warning:** writing to /dev/watchdog **arms** the hardware watchdog on many drivers; if you then stop writing, the board resets. Opening it can also conflict with systemd. **[DISRUPT]** — do not touch it for learning.

**Evidence of a watchdog reset:**

- Boot reason registers exposed by the platform (e.g. bootstatus in /sys/class/watchdog/watchdog0/bootstatus if the driver supports it; ASPEED platforms may expose reset cause differently — implementation-specific).

- The previous boot’s log ends abruptly with no shutdown messages ( journalctl -b -1 `-n 30).`

- Serial console shows the bootloader banner without a preceding “reboot: Restarting system”.

- systemd logs about watchdog timeouts, kernel “soft lockup”/“hard LOCKUP”/“hung task” messages before the reset.

lessons.title: Hardware errors versus software failures
lessons.body:
| Evidence | Points toward hardware | Points toward software |
| Failure follows a specific board/ | ✓ |

slot/cable when swapped

| Failure follows a firmware | ✓ |

version, independent of board

| Kernel bus errors (NACK, | ✓ (or driver) |

timeouts, CRC, ECC) before application errors

| Application exception/crash | ✓ |

without lower-level errors

| Failure depends on temperature, | ✓ |

voltage, physical handling

| Failure is 100% deterministic for | ✓ (usually) |

a given input

| Intermittent with specific timing/ | Either — needs controlled |
| load | experiments |

lessons.title: Gathering evidence without changing hardware state
lessons.body:
1. **Prefer reading** from /sys, /proc, logs and management APIs.

2. **Don’t reload drivers, unbind/bind devices, write registers or reset buses** unless the test plan calls for it and you have approval.

3. **Snapshot first:** save dmesg, journal, /sys/bus/i2c/devices listing, hwmon values, ip - s link, /proc/interrupts (twice), uptime.

4. **Note the time** and keep the system powered if the failure state is valuable to the hardware team — a reboot can erase the fault.

5. **Record what you did**, including read-only commands, in order.

```code
# [RO] Hardware evidence snapshot (run as root on a lab device)
OUT="/tmp/hwsnap_$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ)"
mkdir -p "$OUT"
dmesg > "$OUT/dmesg.txt" 2>&1
cat /proc/interrupts > "$OUT/interrupts_1.txt"; sleep 5; cat /proc/interrupts > "$OUT/
interrupts_2.txt"
ls -l /sys/bus/i2c/devices/ > "$OUT/i2c_devices.txt" 2>&1
for h in /sys/class/hwmon/hwmon*; do echo "$h $(cat "$h/name" 2>/dev/null)"; done > "$OUT/
hwmon.txt"
ip -s link > "$OUT/ip_link_stats.txt" 2>&1
cat /proc/cmdline /proc/version > "$OUT/kernel.txt"
uptime > "$OUT/uptime.txt"
echo "saved to $OUT"
```

Copy $OUT off the device ( scp -r) before any reboot, because /tmp is usually RAM.

lessons.title: Exercises
lessons.body:
1. How do you check whether a driver is bound to I²C device 5-0050?

2. Convert temp1_input=45250 to °C.

3. A board reboots every ~2 hours with no shutdown messages. List three pieces of evidence you’d collect.

4. Why is running i2cset to “check a device” inappropriate?

5. What does a backtrace’s Comm: fake-sensord tell you, and what doesn’t it tell you?

**Solutions**

1. ls -l /sys/bus/i2c/devices/5-0050/driver.

2. 45.25 °C.

3. Previous-boot journal tail ( journalctl -b -1 -n 50), serial console capture across the reboot, watchdog/reset-cause information, kernel lockup/hung-task messages, memory trend (OOM), uptime at each reboot.

4. It writes to device registers and can change hardware behaviour or corrupt data (e.g. EEPROM, regulators); it’s not a read-only check.

5. It shows which process context was running when the kernel faulted; the bug is usually in the kernel function at PC, which the process merely triggered.

lessons.title: Best practices
lessons.body:
- Snapshot evidence before touching anything.

- Keep serial console capture running during hardware and reboot tests.

- Distinguish what the kernel reported from what the application inferred.
