source.section: 10.1 Boot stages and their failure signatures

lessons.title: Service startup ordering
lessons.body:
systemd starts units in parallel, constrained by After=/ Before= and dependencies. Boot delays usually come from one slow unit on the critical chain, often a Type=notify/ dbus unit waiting for something, or systemd-networkd-wait-online waiting for a link.

```code
systemd-analyze                          # [RO] total time: kernel + userspace
systemd-analyze blame | head -15         # [RO] slowest units
systemd-analyze critical-chain bmcweb.service   # [RO]
journalctl -b | grep -iE 'timed out|dependency failed|failed to start'
```

blame shows time-to-ready per unit, not necessarily the cause — a unit may be slow because it waited for another.

lessons.title: Boot loops
lessons.body:
A boot loop is a repeated cycle of start → failure → reset. Causes:

- Kernel panic with panic=N auto-reboot.

- Watchdog reset because boot takes longer than the watchdog timeout or something hangs.

- A service that triggers reboot on failure (e.g. units with FailureAction=reboot or OnFailure= reboot targets).

- Firmware image corruption — bootloader falls back or retries.

- Hardware: power instability, brown-outs.

Evidence: serial capture across several cycles (find the **last line before each reset**), counting cycles and their period, journalctl --list-boots (if persistent) and each boot’s tail.

lessons.title: Failed firmware boot scenarios
lessons.body:
After a firmware update, the new image may fail to boot. Robust platforms use:

- **Dual images (A/B or primary/backup)** — the bootloader boots the alternate image after N failed attempts, or a watchdog-based fallback switches flash side.

- **Boot counters** in bootloader environment variables.

- **Golden/recovery images** — minimal images used for recovery.

How these work is **platform-specific** (U-Boot configuration, flash layout, the BMC’s update daemon). Before reflash tests, learn: How do I know which image booted? How do I trigger and observe fallback in the lab? What is the recovery procedure if both fail (e.g. external flash programmer)?

lessons.title: Reboot validation
lessons.body:
A reboot test is more than “does it come back?”. Define pass criteria explicitly:

1. **Pre-checks:** record firmware version, uptime, boot ID ( cat /proc/sys/kernel/random/ boot_id), service states, sensor count, time.

2. **Trigger** the reboot through the intended interface (Redfish Manager.Reset, systemctl reboot, IPMI mc reset cold) **[DISRUPT]** on a lab system.

3. **Observe going down:** service port closes (confirms it actually rebooted, not just a network blip).

4. **Observe coming up** with a bounded timeout: ping → SSH port → Redfish root 200 → key services active.

5. **Post-checks:** new boot ID differs; uptime small; same firmware version; no failed units; no new critical log entries; sensors and inventory complete; time synchronised; NRestarts normal.

6. **Record timings:** down time, time to ping, to SSH, to API ready. Track them across runs — growing boot time is a regression.

**Boot ID** is the cleanest proof that a reboot happened: it is a random value regenerated each boot.

lessons.title: Boot logs and previous-boot logs
lessons.body:
```code
journalctl --list-boots
journalctl -b -1 -n 50 --no-pager      # end of the previous boot: how did it end?
journalctl -b -1 -p err --no-pager     # errors during the previous boot
journalctl -b 0 -p err --no-pager      # errors in this boot
```

A **clean shutdown** ends with lines such as Reached target ... Shutdown, systemd-shutdown[1]: ..., kernel reboot: Restarting system. An abrupt end with ordinary runtime messages suggests a crash, watchdog reset, power loss or external reset.

lessons.title: Recovery and rollback concepts
lessons.body:
- **Recovery** — returning a device to a working state: reboot, factory reset (**[DISRUPT]**, erases configuration), booting the alternate image, reflashing via an external path.

- **Rollback** — returning to the previous known-good firmware. Some update stacks keep the old image until the new one is confirmed.

- Always know the recovery path before testing something risky.

lessons.title: Evidence collection after unexpected restarts
lessons.body:
Order matters — volatile evidence disappears first:

1. Save the serial console capture (it’s outside the device).

2. Immediately save journalctl -b -1 (if persistent) and journalctl -b 0.

3. Save /sys/fs/pstore/* if present (crash records — may be removed once read and cleared by a service).

4. Record reset cause / watchdog bootstatus if available.

5. Save dmesg of the new boot (early boot messages can show reset reasons and storage errors).

6. Note uptime, boot ID, firmware version, time.

7. Record what the test was doing at the last log line.

lessons.title: Decision tree: BMC unreachable after reboot
lessons.body:
```code
START: BMC not reachable after reboot (Redfish/SSH fail)
|
+-- 1. Did the reboot actually start? (was the port down at some point?
|      boot ID changed? console shows shutdown?)
|      NO  -> reboot command failed/ignored: check API response, task status, logs.
|      YES -> continue
|
+-- 2. Is there serial console output? (Chapter 21)
|      NO OUTPUT AT ALL -> power/hardware/flash/bootloader very early:
|                         verify console wiring & baud; check power; escalate to HW.
|      STUCK IN U-BOOT  -> image/env problem: record messages; follow platform
|                         recovery (alternate image) - do not erase flash.
|      KERNEL PANIC / LOOP -> capture full panic text; note image version; check
|                         whether fallback image boots.
|      REACHES LOGIN    -> continue
|
+-- 3. Log in via console. Is the network configured?
|      `ip -br addr`, `ip route`
|      NO IP / WRONG IP -> DHCP vs static config lost? network service failed?
|                         `systemctl status systemd-networkd`; journal for network.
|      LINK DOWN        -> cable/switch/PHY; `ethtool eth0` if available; dmesg link msgs.
|      IP OK            -> continue
|
+-- 4. Can the test host reach it? (ping, ip route get, ARP)
|      NO  -> network path: switch port, VLAN, ARP cache on host, duplicate IP,
|             firewall. Compare from a second machine on the same subnet.
|      YES -> continue
|
+-- 5. Are services listening? `ss -tlnp` | `systemctl --failed`
|      bmcweb/ssh not running -> `systemctl status`, `journalctl -u`; first error.
|      Running but not listening on expected port/address -> config.
|      Listening -> continue
|
+-- 6. Is it still booting? `systemctl is-system-running`
|      "starting"   -> wait with bounded timeout; check `systemctl list-jobs`.
|      "degraded"   -> some unit failed: `systemctl --failed`.
|      "running"    -> continue
|
+-- 7. Service up but requests fail? (TLS, auth, 5xx)
|      TLS error  -> new certificate after reflash; client trust settings.
|      401        -> credentials reset by update/factory defaults?
|      5xx        -> backend D-Bus services (Chapter 18).
|
END: Document symptom, first error, stage reached, evidence, hypothesis.
```

source.section: 10.9 Decision tree: BMC unreachable after reboot

lessons.title: Exercises
lessons.body:
1. Which command proves that a reboot really happened between two checks?

2. systemctl is-system-running returns degraded. What next?

3. The previous boot’s last journal line is an ordinary sensor log entry at 03:12:44. What does this suggest?

4. List the six measurements you’d record for each cycle of a 100-reboot stress test.

5. Why can’t you rely on the journal to diagnose a bootloader failure?

**Solutions**

1. Compare /proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id before and after (also uptime).

2. systemctl --failed, then status and journal of each failed unit.

3. The system stopped abruptly (crash, watchdog, power loss, or external reset) — no shutdown sequence was logged; look at console capture and reset cause.

4. For example: time to port-down, time to ping, time to SSH, time to API ready, failed-unit count, critical journal entries (plus firmware version and boot ID).

5. The bootloader runs before Linux and journald exist; only the serial console (or bootloader-specific logs) shows those messages.

lessons.title: Best practices
lessons.body:
- Capture serial console for every reboot or firmware test.

- Use boot IDs, not just uptime, to prove reboots.

- Define pass criteria for “back up” — not just ping.

- Never factory-reset or erase flash to “see if it helps” without approval and evidence collection.

lessons.title: Shell versus terminal
lessons.body:
- **Terminal (emulator)** — the window (or serial line) that displays text and sends keystrokes: GNOME Terminal, Windows Terminal, PuTTY, minicom.

- **Shell** — the program interpreting commands: **Bash** (GNU Bourne-Again Shell), **dash** ( /bin/sh on Debian/Ubuntu), **BusyBox ash** ( /bin/sh on many embedded systems, including many OpenBMC images), zsh.

- **POSIX sh** — the standard shell language. Bash supports POSIX plus extensions ( [[ ]], arrays, $(( )) extras, /dev/tcp, {a..z}, local, mapfile…).

**Portability rule:** if a script starts with #!/bin/sh, write POSIX-only syntax. If it uses Bash features, start it with #!/usr/bin/env bash (or #!/bin/bash) and make sure Bash exists on the target. **Many BMC images do not ship Bash** — check with command -v bash. Scripts that will run on the BMC may need to be POSIX sh; scripts running on your test host can use Bash.

lessons.title: How Bash processes a command line
lessons.body:
Understanding this order removes most quoting mysteries:

1. **Tokenise** into words and operators ( |, >, &&, ;…), respecting quotes.

2. **Expansions**, in order: brace ( {a,b}) → tilde ( ~) → parameter/variable ( $var) → arithmetic ( $(( ))) → command substitution ( $( )) → **word splitting** (unquoted results split on IFS) → **pathname expansion** (globbing: *, ?, [...]) → quote removal.

3. **Redirections** are set up.

4. The command runs.

Steps 2’s word splitting and globbing apply **only to unquoted expansions**. That’s why quoting variables matters.

source.section: 11.2 How Bash processes a command line

lessons.title: Commands, arguments and quoting
lessons.body:
```code
echo hello world            # 2 arguments: "hello", "world"
echo "hello   world"        # 1 argument, spaces preserved
echo 'cost: $5 and $(date)' # single quotes: completely literal
echo "today: $(date +%F)"   # double quotes: $ expansions happen, no splitting/globbing
echo "a \"quoted\" word"    # backslash escapes inside double quotes
echo $'tab:\there'          # ANSI-C quoting (Bash): \t becomes a tab
```

| Quote | $var expanded? | $(cmd) ? | Word splitting/globbing? |
| none | yes | yes | yes |
| "..." | yes | yes | no |
| '...' | no | no | no |

**The golden rule: quote every variable expansion — "$var" — unless you**

**specifically want splitting or globbing.**

```code
file="test results.log"
touch "$file"
ls -l $file        # WRONG: ls receives "test" and "results.log"
ls -l "$file"      # right
```

lessons.title: Variables and the environment
lessons.body:
```code
name="falcon-bmc"          # no spaces around =
echo "$name"
echo "${name}_01"          # braces delimit the name
export BMC_HOST=192.0.2.50 # exported: visible to child processes
env | grep BMC_            # [RO] view environment
BMC_PORT=443 ./check.sh    # set only for this one command
unset name
```

- A **shell variable** exists only in the current shell.

- An **environment variable** is exported and inherited by child processes. Children cannot change the parent’s environment.

- Common ones: HOME, USER, PATH, PWD, SHELL, LANG/ LC_ALL (affects sorting and tool output!), TZ.

**Tip for automation:** set LC_ALL=C when parsing command output in scripts — localized output (other languages, different decimal separators, different sort orders) breaks parsers.

lessons.title: PATH and executable lookup
lessons.body:
When you type ping, the shell looks for (in this order): aliases, shell **functions**, **built- ins** (e.g. cd, echo, test), then searches each directory in $PATH left to right.

```code
echo "$PATH"                 # /usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin:...
type ls cd ping              # [RO] how each name resolves
command -v jq || echo "jq not installed"   # portable existence check (use this in scripts)
which python3                # external tool; less reliable than command -v
hash -r                      # forget cached locations after installing something
```

- The current directory is **not** in PATH (for safety), hence ./script.sh.

- Cron, systemd and Jenkins provide **minimal PATHs** — a frequent cause of “command not found” in automation. Use absolute paths or set PATH at the top of scripts.

lessons.title: Standard input, output and error
lessons.body:
| Stream | fd | Default |
| stdin | 0 | keyboard / terminal |
| stdout | 1 | terminal |
| stderr | 2 | terminal |
| Syntax | Meaning |
| cmd > out.txt | stdout to file (truncate) — [MOD] of the file |
| cmd >> out.txt | append |
| cmd 2> err.txt | stderr to file |
| cmd > all.txt 2>&1 | both to file (order matters: redirect stdout first, then point 2 at 1) |
| cmd &> all.txt | Bash shorthand for the above |
| cmd 2>/dev/null | discard errors |
| cmd < in.txt | stdin from file |
| cmd <<'EOF' ... EOF | here-document (quoted 'EOF' → no expansion inside) |
| cmd <<< "text" | here-string (Bash) |
| cmd1 \| cmd2 | stdout of cmd1 → stdin of cmd2 |
| cmd1 \|& cmd2 | stdout and stderr (Bash) |
| cmd \| tee log.txt | show and save |

```code
ls /etc /nonexistent > out.txt 2> err.txt
cat out.txt    # listing of /etc
cat err.txt    # ls: cannot access '/nonexistent': No such file or directory
```

**Common mistake:** cmd 2>&1 > file sends stderr to the terminal (fd 2 was copied before fd 1 was redirected). **Bash set -o noclobber** makes > refuse to overwrite existing files (use >| to force) — a useful safety net in interactive sessions.

lessons.title: Exit codes
lessons.body:
Every command returns an **exit status** 0–255. **0 means success**; non-zero means failure (meaning is command-specific).

```code
grep -q root /etc/passwd; echo $?     # 0 (found)
grep -q nosuchuser /etc/passwd; echo $?  # 1 (not found)
grep -q x /nonexistent; echo $?       # 2 (error)
```

Conventions: 126 found but not executable; 127 command not found; 128+N killed by signal N (e.g. 130 = Ctrl+C/SIGINT, 137 = SIGKILL, 143 = SIGTERM); timeout returns 124 when the time limit is reached. $? holds the status of the **last** command — read it immediately or save it: rc=$?. **Pipelines:** the status of a | b is the status of b by default. With set -o pipefail, it’s the last non-zero status in the pipeline. ${PIPESTATUS[@]} (Bash) lists all.

```code
false | true; echo "$?"                         # 0  (failure hidden!)
set -o pipefail; false | true; echo "$?"        # 1
grep ERROR missing.log | wc -l; echo "${PIPESTATUS[@]}"   # 2 0
```

lessons.title: Command substitution
lessons.body:
```code
now=$(date -u +%FT%TZ)
kernel=$(uname -r)
count=$(grep -c ERROR app.log)   # grep -c prints the count (and returns 1 if count is 0!)
echo "At $now kernel $kernel had $count errors"
```

Use $(...), not backticks — it nests cleanly and is easier to read. Trailing newlines are stripped from the result.

lessons.title: Pipes and redirection together
lessons.body:
```code
# Top 5 most frequent error messages in a log (all [RO])
grep -i 'error' app.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -5
```

Each stage runs as a separate process, concurrently. A pipeline is a flow of text; design each stage to do one job.

lessons.title: Wildcards and globbing
lessons.body:
| Pattern | Matches |
| * | Any string (not leading . by default) |
| ? | One character |
| [abc] , [0-9] | One character from the set |
| [!0-9] | One character not in the set |
| {a,b,c} | Brace expansion — not a glob; generates words even if files don’t exist Recursive (Bash with shopt -s globstar ) |

```code
ls *.log
ls run_??.log
echo file_{1..3}.txt       # file_1.txt file_2.txt file_3.txt
```

**Traps:**

- If nothing matches, Bash leaves the pattern **as is** ( *.log stays literally *.log). shopt -s nullglob makes it expand to nothing; shopt -s failglob makes it an error.

- Globs inside quotes are **not** expanded: ls "*.log" looks for a file literally named `*.log.`

- find -name '*.log' — quote so that find, not the shell, interprets the pattern.

lessons.title: Quoting special characters
lessons.body:
Characters with special meaning: space tab newline | & ; ( ) < > $ \ ” ’ * ? [ ] # ~ = % { } !`

- # starts a comment only at the start of a word.

- ! triggers history expansion in interactive Bash inside double quotes: echo "done!" may fail interactively; use single quotes.

- Filenames beginning with - look like options: use ./-file or -- ( rm -- -file).

lessons.title: Complete runnable example
lessons.body:
```code
  #!/usr/bin/env bash
  # env_report.sh - demonstrate variables, substitution, redirection and exit codes
  # Usage: ./env_report.sh [output_file]
  out="${1:-env_report.txt}"           # default if no argument given
  {
    echo "Report generated: $(date -u +%FT%TZ)"
    echo "User: ${USER:-unknown}  Host: $(hostname)"
    echo "Shell: $BASH_VERSION"
    echo "PATH entries:"
    # shellcheck disable=SC2086  # intentional word splitting of PATH entries
    printf '  %s\n' ${PATH//:/ }
    for tool in jq curl ip ss timeout; do
      if command -v "$tool" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
        echo "  tool $tool: present"
      else
        echo "  tool $tool: MISSING"
      fi
    done
  } > "$out"
  echo "wrote $out ($(wc -l < "$out") lines)"
Run: bash env_report.sh /tmp/r.txt; echo "exit=$?"; cat /tmp/r.txt. Expected: wrote /tmp/
```

r.txt (N lines), exit 0, and a report listing which tools exist. (The ${PATH//:/ } line is a deliberate, commented exception to “always quote”, since PATH entries are known not to contain spaces in this context.)

lessons.title: Exercises
lessons.body:
1. Why does rm $f fail when f="my file.txt"? Fix it.

2. Redirect both stdout and stderr of make to build.log while still seeing output on screen.

3. Make grep pattern file | sort fail when grep errors.

4. What exit code does a command killed by SIGTERM produce in Bash?

5. A cron job says jq: command not found but jq works interactively. Why?

**Solutions**

1. Word splitting produces two arguments. Use rm -- "$f".

2. make 2>&1 | tee build.log.

3. set -o pipefail (and check $?), or check ${PIPESTATUS[0]}.

4. 143 (128 + 15).

5. Cron’s minimal PATH doesn’t include where jq is installed (e.g. /usr/local/bin); set PATH in the crontab or script, or use the absolute path.

lessons.title: Best practices
lessons.body:
- Quote expansions; use -- before user-supplied filenames.

- Use $(...), command -v, printf (more predictable than echo for data).

- Set LC_ALL=C when parsing output; set PATH explicitly in automation.

lessons.title: Variable assignment and parameter expansion
lessons.body:
| Expansion | Result |
| ${var} | Value |
| ${var:-default} | Value, or default if unset/empty |
| ${var:=default} | Same, and assigns default |
| ${var:?message} | Value, or exit with message if unset/empty (great safety guard) |
| ${var:+alt} | alt if var is set and non-empty |
| ${#var} | Length |
| ${var#prefix} / ${var##prefix} | Remove shortest/longest matching prefix |
| ${var%suffix} / ${var%%suffix} | Remove shortest/longest matching suffix |
| ${var/old/new} / ${var//old/new} | Replace first/all (Bash) |
| ${var:offset:length} | Substring (Bash) |
| ${var^^} / ${var,,} | Upper/lower case (Bash 4+) |

```code
path="/var/log/tests/run_042.log"
echo "${path##*/}"     # run_042.log      (basename)
echo "${path%/*}"      # /var/log/tests   (dirname)
echo "${path%.log}.json"   # /var/log/tests/run_042.json
fw="falcon-v2.16.0-rc3"
echo "${fw#falcon-v}"  # 2.16.0-rc3
host="${BMC_HOST:-192.0.2.50}"
```

lessons.title: Arithmetic
lessons.body:
```code
count=5
count=$((count + 1))
(( count > 3 )) && echo "big"
echo $(( 7 / 2 ))      # 3 — integer only
awk 'BEGIN { printf "%.2f\n", 7/2 }'   # 3.50 — use awk (or bc) for decimals
```

Leading zeros mean **octal** in $(( )): $(( 08 + 1 )) is an error. Strip zeros or use $ `((10#08 + 1)).`

lessons.title: Tests: [ ] versus [[ ]]
lessons.body:
- [ ... ] (same as test) is POSIX and works in BusyBox ash. Quote everything inside it.

- [[ ... ]] is Bash: no word splitting inside, supports &&, ||, pattern matching ==, regex =~.

- (( ... )) is for arithmetic.

| String test | Meaning empty [ -z "$s" ] |
| [ -n "$s" ] | non-empty |
| [ "$a" = "$b" ] | equal ( == works in Bash [[ ]] ) not equal [ "$a" != "$b" ] |
| [[ $s == fw-* ]] | glob match (Bash) |
| [[ $s =~ ^v[0-9]+\.[0-9]+$ ]] | regex (Bash; don’t quote the regex) |
| Numeric test | Meaning |
| [ "$a" -eq "$b" ] | equal ( -ne , -lt , -le , -gt , -ge ) |
| (( a < b )) | arithmetic comparison (Bash) |

**Trap:** [ "$a" > "$b" ] is a **redirection** creating a file named $b! Use -gt or (( )).

| File test | True if |
| -e | exists regular file -f |
| -d | directory |
| -r / -w / -x | readable / writable / executable by you exists and size > 0 -s |
| -L | symlink |
| -S | socket |
| -c / -b | character / block device |
| f1 -nt f2 | f1 newer than f2 |

lessons.title: if / elif / else
lessons.body:
```code
if [ -f /etc/os-release ]; then
  . /etc/os-release
  echo "Distribution: ${PRETTY_NAME:-unknown}"
elif [ -f /etc/issue ]; then
  head -1 /etc/issue
else
  echo "unknown distribution"
fi
```

if tests the **exit status** of any command — [ is just a command:

```code
if grep -q 'ERROR' run.log; then echo "errors found"; fi
if ping -c1 -W2 192.0.2.50 >/dev/null 2>&1; then echo up; else echo down; fi
```

lessons.title: case
Loops
lessons.body:
```code
# for over a list
for svc in sshd cron systemd-journald; do
  printf '%-20s %s\n' "$svc" "$(systemctl is-active "$svc" 2>/dev/null)"
done
# for over files (safe with spaces; nullglob avoids literal pattern)
shopt -s nullglob
for f in /var/log/*.log; do
  printf '%8s %s\n' "$(wc -l < "$f")" "$f"
done
# C-style for (Bash)
for (( i = 1; i <= 3; i++ )); do echo "attempt $i"; done
# while reading lines safely
while IFS= read -r line; do
  printf 'line: %s\n' "$line"
done < /etc/hostname
# until: loop until a condition becomes true
tries=0
until [ -e /tmp/ready.flag ] || [ "$tries" -ge 5 ]; do
  tries=$((tries + 1)); sleep 1
done
```

IFS= read -r preserves leading spaces and backslashes — always use this form. **Pipe-into-while trap:** cmd | while read ...; do count=$((count+1)); done runs the loop in a **subshell** (in Bash, by default), so count is lost after the loop. Use process `substitution: while ...; done < <(cmd).` break exits the loop; continue skips to the next iteration; break 2 exits two nested loops.

lessons.title: Reading user input
lessons.body:
```code
read -r -p "BMC address: " bmc
read -r -s -p "Password: " pw; echo    # -s hides typing; don't log it
read -r -t 10 -p "Continue? [y/N] " ans || ans="n"   # 10 s timeout
```

In automation, avoid interactive input — take values from arguments, environment variables or files.

lessons.title: Positional arguments
lessons.body:
| Variable | Meaning |
| $0 | Script name |
| $1 … $9 , ${10} | Arguments |
| $# | Number of arguments |
| "$@" | All arguments as separate words (use this) |
| "$*" | All arguments as one string |
| shift | Drop $1 , renumber |

lessons.title: Script 1: connectivity checker
lessons.body:
```code
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# check_connectivity.sh - check ping and TCP ports for a host (read-only)
# Usage: check_connectivity.sh <host> [port ...]
# Exit: 0 all checks passed, 1 some check failed, 2 usage error
usage() { echo "Usage: $0 <host> [port ...]  (default ports: 22 443)" >&2; }
if [ "$#" -lt 1 ]; then usage; exit 2; fi
host="$1"; shift
if [ "$#" -eq 0 ]; then set -- 22 443; fi
failures=0
if ping -c 2 -W 2 "$host" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "PASS ping $host"
else
  echo "WARN ping $host failed (ICMP may be blocked; not counted as failure)"
fi
for port in "$@"; do
  case "$port" in
    ''|*[!0-9]*) echo "SKIP invalid port '$port'"; failures=$((failures + 1)); continue ;;
  esac
  if timeout 3 bash -c "exec 3<>/dev/tcp/$host/$port" 2>/dev/null; then
    echo "PASS tcp $host:$port"
  else
    echo "FAIL tcp $host:$port"
    failures=$((failures + 1))
  fi
done
if [ "$failures" -eq 0 ]; then exit 0; else exit 1; fi
```

**Run:** bash check_connectivity.sh localhost 22 9 (on a VM with sshd). **Expected:**

```output
PASS ping localhost, PASS tcp localhost:22, FAIL tcp localhost:9, exit status 1. If sshd
```

isn’t running, 22 also fails. Notes: ping -W is iputils syntax (Linux); macOS uses -t for a deadline. /dev/tcp requires Bash. The host is validated only loosely here; Chapter 13 adds input validation.

lessons.title: Script 2: service status checker
lessons.body:
```code
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# check_services.sh - report systemd service states (read-only)
# Usage: check_services.sh service1 [service2 ...]
# Exit: 0 all active, 1 any not active, 2 usage/no systemd
if [ "$#" -eq 0 ]; then
  echo "Usage: $0 <service> [service ...]" >&2; exit 2
fi
if ! command -v systemctl >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "ERROR systemctl not found (no systemd here?)" >&2; exit 2
fi
not_active=0
for svc in "$@"; do
  state=$(systemctl is-active "$svc" 2>/dev/null)
  [ -n "$state" ] || state="unknown"
  case "$state" in
    active) echo "PASS $svc is active" ;;
    *)
      echo "FAIL $svc is $state"
      restarts=$(systemctl show "$svc" -p NRestarts --value 2>/dev/null)
      [ -n "$restarts" ] && echo "     NRestarts=$restarts"
      not_active=$((not_active + 1))
      ;;
  esac
done
exit $(( not_active > 0 ? 1 : 0 ))
```

systemctl show -p X --value prints only the value (systemd 230+; older versions print `X=value).`

lessons.title: Script 3: required files checker
lessons.body:
```code
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# check_files.sh - verify required files exist, are readable and non-empty
# Usage: check_files.sh file1 [file2 ...]
missing=0
for f in "$@"; do
  if [ ! -e "$f" ]; then
    echo "FAIL missing: $f"; missing=$((missing + 1))
  elif [ ! -r "$f" ]; then
    echo "FAIL not readable: $f"; missing=$((missing + 1))
  elif [ -f "$f" ] && [ ! -s "$f" ]; then
    echo "WARN empty: $f"
  else
    echo "PASS $f"
  fi
done
[ "$missing" -eq 0 ]
```

The last line’s exit status becomes the script’s exit status. Example: bash `check_files.sh /etc/hostname /etc/nonexistent → PASS /etc/hostname, FAIL missing: /etc/` nonexistent, exit 1.

lessons.title: Exercises
lessons.body:
1. Print the file extension of name="results.tar.gz" as gz and as tar.gz.

2. Write a loop that waits up to 60 s (polling every 5 s) for TCP 443 on a host.

3. Why does [ $x = abc ] give “unary operator expected” when x is empty?

4. Rewrite cat list.txt | while read h; do n=$((n+1)); done; echo $n so $n is correct.

5. Write a case that maps HTTP codes: 2xx OK, 401/403 AUTH, 5xx SERVER, else OTHER.

**Solutions**

1. ${name##*.} → gz; ${name#*.} → tar.gz. 2.

```code
for i in $(seq 1 12); do
  timeout 3 bash -c "</dev/tcp/$host/443" 2>/dev/null && { echo up; break; }
  sleep 5
done
```

(Track a found flag if you need to know whether it never came up.) 3. Unquoted empty

```code
$x disappears, leaving [ = abc ]. Quote: [ "$x" = abc ]. 4. n=0; while IFS= read -r h; do
n=$((n+1)); done < list.txt; echo "$n". 5.
  case "$code" in
    2??) echo OK ;; 401|403) echo AUTH ;; 5??) echo SERVER ;; *) echo OTHER ;;
  esac
```

lessons.title: Best practices
lessons.body:
- Validate arguments early; print usage to stderr; exit 2 for usage errors.

- Define exit codes clearly (0 pass, 1 check failed, 2 usage/environment error).

- Use case for string dispatch; (( )) for numbers.

lessons.title: Functions
lessons.body:
```code
log() {                         # definition (POSIX-compatible form)
  printf '%s [%s] %s\n' "$(date -u +%FT%TZ)" "$1" "$2" >&2
}
log INFO "starting"             # invocation: like a command
```

- Arguments inside a function are $1, $2, $@, $# (the script’s own arguments are hidden).

- return N sets the function’s exit status (0–255). Without return, the status is that of the last command.

- To **return data**, print it to stdout and capture with $(...); use the status for success/failure.

- local var limits a variable to the function (Bash; also supported by BusyBox ash and dash, though not strictly POSIX).

```code
get_disk_pct() {          # prints percent used for a mount point, returns 1 on error
  local mount="$1" pct
  pct=$(df -P "$mount" 2>/dev/null | awk 'NR==2 { gsub("%","",$5); print $5 }')
  [ -n "$pct" ] || return 1
  printf '%s\n' "$pct"
}
if pct=$(get_disk_pct /); then
  echo "root is ${pct}% full"
else
  echo "could not read disk usage"
fi
```

df -P (POSIX output format) guarantees one line per filesystem, making parsing reliable even with long device names.

lessons.title: Arrays (Bash)
lessons.body:
```code
services=(sshd cron "my service")        # indexed array
echo "${services[0]}"                    # sshd
echo "${#services[@]}"                   # 3
for s in "${services[@]}"; do echo "[$s]"; done   # quotes keep "my service" intact
services+=(rsyslog)                      # append
declare -A thresholds=( [disk]=90 [mem]=85 )   # associative (Bash 4+)
thresholds[load]=4
for key in "${!thresholds[@]}"; do echo "$key=${thresholds[$key]}"; done
mapfile -t lines < /etc/hostname         # read file into array (Bash 4+)
```

BusyBox ash/dash **have no arrays**; use positional parameters ( set -- a b c) or newline-separated strings there.

lessons.title: Input validation
Command-line options with getopts
Configuration files — safely
lessons.body:
Sourcing a config ( . config.sh) **executes** it — anyone who can edit the file can run code as you. For simple key=value configs, parse instead:

```code
load_config() {     # reads KEY=VALUE lines; ignores comments; only allowed keys
  local file="$1" key value
  [ -r "$file" ] || return 1
  while IFS='=' read -r key value; do
    key="${key//[[:space:]]/}"
    case "$key" in
      ''|\#*) continue ;;
      BMC_HOST|SSH_PORT|HTTPS_PORT|DISK_WARN_PCT|SERVICES|LOG_LINES|CMD_TIMEOUT)
        printf -v "CFG_$key" '%s' "$value" ;;
      *) echo "WARN ignoring unknown key '$key'" >&2 ;;
    esac
  done < "$file"
}
```

printf -v name assigns to a variable whose name is computed — safe here because names come from an allow-list, unlike eval.

lessons.title: Script organisation
lessons.body:
A maintainable script layout:

```code
#!/usr/bin/env bash          1. shebang
# header: purpose, usage,    2. documentation
#   exit codes, deps
set -uo pipefail             3. strict-ish settings (Chapter 15)
readonly VERSION=1.0         4. constants
defaults                     5. default configuration
functions                    6. helpers then checks
main() { ... }               7. main logic
main "$@"                    8. single entry point
```

Libraries: put shared helpers in lib/common.sh and source it with a path relative to the script:

```code
SCRIPT_DIR=$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)
# shellcheck source=lib/common.sh
. "$SCRIPT_DIR/lib/common.sh"
```

lessons.title: Project: diagkit.sh — a reusable diagnostic utility
lessons.body:
This utility has separate functions for connectivity, services, storage and logs; supports options and a config file; uses timeouts; is read-only; and produces a summary with a meaningful exit code.

```code
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# diagkit.sh - modular read-only Linux diagnostic utility
# Usage: diagkit.sh [-c config] [-H host] [-s "svc1 svc2"] [-t secs] [-o outdir] [-h]
# Exit codes: 0 all PASS, 1 at least one FAIL, 2 usage/config error
# Requires: bash 4+, coreutils; optional: systemctl, journalctl, timeout
set -uo pipefail
readonly VERSION="1.0"
CFG_BMC_HOST=""
CFG_SSH_PORT=22
CFG_HTTPS_PORT=443
CFG_DISK_WARN_PCT=90
CFG_SERVICES=""
CFG_LOG_LINES=200
CFG_CMD_TIMEOUT=5
OUTDIR=""
declare -A RESULTS=()
declare -a ORDER=()
usage() {
  cat >&2 <<EOF
diagkit $VERSION - read-only diagnostics
Usage: $0 [-c config] [-H host] [-s "svc ..."] [-t secs] [-o outdir] [-h]
  -c FILE   config file with KEY=VALUE lines
  -H HOST   host to test for connectivity (optional)
  -s LIST   space-separated systemd services to check
  -t SECS   per-command timeout (default $CFG_CMD_TIMEOUT)
  -o DIR    directory to save collected logs (default: none)
EOF
}
log() { printf '%s [%s] %s\n' "$(date -u +%FT%TZ)" "$1" "$2" >&2; }
record() {   # record <check-name> <PASS|WARN|FAIL|SKIP> <detail>
  local name="$1" status="$2" detail="$3"
  ORDER+=("$name")
  RESULTS["$name"]="$status|$detail"
  log "$status" "$name: $detail"
}
run_t() {    # run a command with the configured timeout if 'timeout' exists
  if command -v timeout >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    timeout "$CFG_CMD_TIMEOUT" "$@"
  else
    "$@"
  fi
}
load_config() {
  local file="$1" key value
  [ -r "$file" ] || { log ERROR "cannot read config $file"; return 1; }
  while IFS='=' read -r key value; do
    key="${key//[[:space:]]/}"
    case "$key" in
      ''|\#*) continue ;;
      BMC_HOST|SSH_PORT|HTTPS_PORT|DISK_WARN_PCT|SERVICES|LOG_LINES|CMD_TIMEOUT)
        printf -v "CFG_$key" '%s' "$value" ;;
      *) log WARN "ignoring unknown config key '$key'" ;;
    esac
  done < "$file"
}
check_connectivity() {
  local host="$CFG_BMC_HOST" port
  if [ -z "$host" ]; then record connectivity SKIP "no host configured"; return 0; fi
  for port in "$CFG_SSH_PORT" "$CFG_HTTPS_PORT"; do
    if run_t bash -c "exec 3<>/dev/tcp/$host/$port" 2>/dev/null; then
      record "tcp_$port" PASS "$host:$port reachable"
    else
      record "tcp_$port" FAIL "$host:$port not reachable within ${CFG_CMD_TIMEOUT}s"
    fi
  done
}
check_services() {
  local svc state
  if [ -z "$CFG_SERVICES" ]; then record services SKIP "no services configured"; return 0; fi
  if ! command -v systemctl >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    record services SKIP "systemctl not available"; return 0
  fi
  for svc in $CFG_SERVICES; do        # intentional splitting of a space-separated list
    state=$(run_t systemctl is-active "$svc" 2>/dev/null)
    [ -n "$state" ] || state="unknown"
    if [ "$state" = "active" ]; then
      record "svc_$svc" PASS "active"
    else
      record "svc_$svc" FAIL "state=$state"
    fi
  done
}
check_storage() {
  local line mount pct ipct
  while read -r line; do
    mount=$(awk '{print $6}' <<<"$line")
    pct=$(awk '{gsub("%","",$5); print $5}' <<<"$line")
    [[ $pct =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] || continue
    if (( pct >= CFG_DISK_WARN_PCT )); then
      record "disk_$mount" FAIL "${pct}% used (threshold ${CFG_DISK_WARN_PCT}%)"
    else
      record "disk_$mount" PASS "${pct}% used"
    fi
  done < <(df -P -x tmpfs -x devtmpfs 2>/dev/null | tail -n +2)
  ipct=$(df -Pi / 2>/dev/null | awk 'NR==2 {gsub("%","",$5); print $5}')
  if [[ $ipct =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]]; then
    if (( ipct >= CFG_DISK_WARN_PCT )); then record inodes_root FAIL "${ipct}% inodes used"
    else record inodes_root PASS "${ipct}% inodes used"; fi
  else
    record inodes_root SKIP "inode usage unavailable"
  fi
}
check_logs() {
  local errs
  if ! command -v journalctl >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    record logs SKIP "journalctl not available"; return 0
  fi
  errs=$(run_t journalctl -b -p err --no-pager -q 2>/dev/null | wc -l)
  if (( errs == 0 )); then
    record journal_errors PASS "no err-level entries this boot (or no permission to read)"
  else
    record journal_errors WARN "$errs err-level entries this boot"
  fi
  if [ -n "$OUTDIR" ]; then
    mkdir -p "$OUTDIR" || { record log_save FAIL "cannot create $OUTDIR"; return 0; }
    run_t journalctl -b -n "$CFG_LOG_LINES" --no-pager > "$OUTDIR/journal_tail.txt" 2>&1
    run_t dmesg > "$OUTDIR/dmesg.txt" 2>&1 || true
    record log_save PASS "saved logs to $OUTDIR"
  fi
}
summary() {
  local name status detail fails=0 warns=0
  printf '\n%-28s %-5s %s\n' CHECK STATUS DETAIL
  for name in "${ORDER[@]}"; do
    IFS='|' read -r status detail <<<"${RESULTS[$name]}"
    printf '%-28s %-5s %s\n' "$name" "$status" "$detail"
    [ "$status" = FAIL ] && fails=$((fails + 1))
    [ "$status" = WARN ] && warns=$((warns + 1))
  done
  printf '\nTotal: %d checks, %d FAIL, %d WARN\n' "${#ORDER[@]}" "$fails" "$warns"
  (( fails == 0 ))
}
main() {
  local opt config=""
  while getopts ":c:H:s:t:o:h" opt; do
    case "$opt" in
      c) config="$OPTARG" ;;
      H) CFG_BMC_HOST="$OPTARG" ;;
      s) CFG_SERVICES="$OPTARG" ;;
        t) CFG_CMD_TIMEOUT="$OPTARG" ;;
        o) OUTDIR="$OPTARG" ;;
        h) usage; exit 0 ;;
        :) echo "Option -$OPTARG requires a value" >&2; usage; exit 2 ;;
        \?) echo "Unknown option -$OPTARG" >&2; usage; exit 2 ;;
      esac
    done
    shift $((OPTIND - 1))
    if [ -n "$config" ]; then load_config "$config" || exit 2; fi
    [[ $CFG_CMD_TIMEOUT =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] || { echo "Invalid timeout" >&2; exit 2; }
    log INFO "diagkit $VERSION starting on $(hostname)"
    check_connectivity
    check_services
    check_storage
    check_logs
    if summary; then exit 0; else exit 1; fi
  }
  main "$@"
```

**Example config ( diagkit.conf):**

```code
  # diagkit configuration
  BMC_HOST=127.0.0.1
  SSH_PORT=22
  HTTPS_PORT=443
  DISK_WARN_PCT=90
  SERVICES=cron systemd-journald
  LOG_LINES=200
  CMD_TIMEOUT=5
Run: bash diagkit.sh -c diagkit.conf -o /tmp/diag_out
```

**Example output (illustrative — your checks and values will differ):**

```output
2026-10-15T09:41:02Z [INFO] diagkit 1.0 starting on lab-vm
2026-10-15T09:41:02Z [PASS] tcp_22: 127.0.0.1:22 reachable
2026-10-15T09:41:02Z [FAIL] tcp_443: 127.0.0.1:443 not reachable within 5s
...
CHECK                        STATUS DETAIL
tcp_22                       PASS  127.0.0.1:22 reachable
tcp_443                      FAIL  127.0.0.1:443 not reachable within 5s
svc_cron                     PASS  active
svc_systemd-journald         PASS  active
disk_/                       PASS  55% used
inodes_root                  PASS  12% inodes used
journal_errors               WARN  3 err-level entries this boot
log_save                     PASS  saved logs to /tmp/diag_out
Total: 8 checks, 1 FAIL, 1 WARN
```

Exit status: 1 (one FAIL). Note that log lines go to **stderr** and the summary to **stdout**, so diagkit.sh > summary.txt captures a clean report.

**Design points to explain in an interview:**

- Each check is independent; a failing check doesn’t stop others (no set -e).

- Results are collected in data structures, then reported — separation of checking from reporting.

- Read-only: nothing is restarted or modified (except writing to the chosen output directory).

- Missing tools produce SKIP, not crashes.

- Config is parsed with an allow-list, never sourced.

lessons.title: Exercises
lessons.body:
1. Add a check_memory function that FAILs when MemAvailable is below 10% of MemTotal `(read /proc/meminfo).`

2. Why does diagkit.sh not use set -e?

3. Make -s accept services separated by commas as well as spaces.

4. Why is printf -v "CFG_$key" acceptable here but eval "CFG_$key=$value" is not?

**Solutions** 1.

```code
check_memory() {
  local total avail pct
  total=$(awk '/^MemTotal:/ {print $2}' /proc/meminfo)
  avail=$(awk '/^MemAvailable:/ {print $2}' /proc/meminfo)
  if [ -z "$total" ] || [ -z "$avail" ]; then record memory SKIP "meminfo incomplete";
return 0; fi
  pct=$(( avail * 100 / total ))
  if (( pct < 10 )); then record memory FAIL "${pct}% available"
  else record memory PASS "${pct}% available"; fi
}
```

(Add check_memory to main.) MemAvailable exists in kernels 3.14+. 2. Checks are expected to fail sometimes; the script must continue and report all results. set -e would abort at the first non-zero status. 3. In check_services, normalise first: local list="$ {CFG_SERVICES//,/ }" and loop over $list. 4. printf -v assigns the value literally to a variable whose name is restricted by the allow-list. eval would execute any shell syntax in $value (e.g. $(rm ...)).

lessons.title: Best practices
lessons.body:
- One function, one responsibility; report through a single record mechanism.

- Make exit codes part of the interface and document them.

- Run shellcheck on every script (static analysis that catches quoting and logic bugs).

lessons.title: grep — find lines
lessons.body:
| Option | Meaning ignore case -i |
| -v | invert (lines not matching) |
| -c | count matching lines show line numbers -n |
| -E | extended regex ( + ? \| () without backslashes) |
| -F | fixed string (no regex — fast, safe for literal text) print only the matching part -o |
| -w | whole word |
| -A N / -B N / -C N | context lines after/before/around |
| -r / -R | recursive |
| -l | list files with matches |
| -q | quiet: exit status only |
| -m N | stop after N matches |

```code
grep -c ERROR boot.log                       # 4
grep -E 'ERROR|WARNING' boot.log | wc -l     # 6
grep -n -B1 -A2 'probe failed' boot.log      # context around the first hardware error
grep -oE 'code=E[0-9]+' boot.log | sort | uniq -c
```

Expected output of the last command:

```code
1 code=E1104
3 code=E1203
```

lessons.title: Regular expressions
lessons.body:
| Element | BRE ( grep , sed ) | ERE ( grep -E , sed -E , awk ) |
| Any char | . | . |
| Zero or more | * | * |
| One or more | \+ (GNU) | + |
| Optional | \? (GNU) | ? |
| Alternation | \| (GNU) | \| |
| Group | \( \) | ( ) |
| Count | \{2,3\} | {2,3} |
| Start/end | ^ $ | ^ $ |
| Element | BRE ( grep , sed ) | ERE ( grep -E , sed -E , awk ) |
| Class | [0-9] , [[:digit:]] , [[:space:]] | same |

Prefer -E for readability. Escape a literal dot as \.. **PCRE** ( grep -P, with \d, lookarounds) is GNU-only and often missing on embedded systems — avoid it in portable scripts.

```code
grep -E '^[0-9]{4}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2}T09:00:0[5-9]' boot.log   # 09:00:05–09:00:09
grep -E 'status=[0-9]+/[A-Z]+' boot.log
```

lessons.title: cut, tr, sort, uniq
lessons.body:
```code
cut -d' ' -f3 boot.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn   # messages per source
      6 systemd[1]:
      3 kernel:
      2 bmcweb[455]:
      1 phosphor-fan[480]:
      1 fake-sensord[530]:
      1 fake-sensord[502]:
      1 fake-sensord[471]:
      1 fake-sensord[402]:
```

Because each fake-sensord process has a different PID, its lines are counted separately. Strip the PIDs with sed (normalising variable tokens before counting is a key log-analysis habit):

```code
cut -d' ' -f3 boot.log | sed -E 's/\[[0-9]+\]//; s/:$//' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
      6 systemd
      5 fake-sensord
      3 kernel
      2 bmcweb
      1 phosphor-fan
```

- cut -d DELIM -f N — field N with a single-character delimiter; -c 1-19 — characters 1–19.

- tr 'a-z' 'A-Z' — translate characters; tr -d '\r' — delete carriage returns (from Windows or serial logs); tr -s ' ' — squeeze repeated spaces.

- sort — -n numeric, -r reverse, -k2,2 by field 2, -t: delimiter, -u unique, -h human sizes (GNU), -s stable.

- uniq works on **adjacent** duplicates only → always sort first. -c count, -d only duplicates.

lessons.title: sed — stream editing
lessons.body:
```code
sed -n '5,8p' boot.log                       # print lines 5-8
sed -n '/Starting Fake/,/Failed with/p' boot.log   # print a range between patterns
sed 's/falcon-bmc/BMC/' boot.log | head -2   # substitute (output only; file unchanged)
sed -E 's/.*code=(E[0-9]+).*/\1/;t;d' boot.log     # extract codes; delete others (GNU 't;d'
idiom)
```

- s/old/new/ first match per line; s/old/new/g all matches.

- -n with p prints only selected lines.

- -E extended regex; \1 back-reference to group 1.

- **sed -i edits files in place — [MOD]**. GNU uses sed -i, BSD/macOS needs sed -i ''; BusyBox supports -i. Make a backup: sed -i.bak 's/a/b/' file.

lessons.title: awk — fields, conditions and calculations
lessons.body:
awk splits each line into fields $1, $2, … (default separator: whitespace), NF = number of fields, NR = line number, $0 = the whole line.

```code
awk '{print $3}' boot.log | head -3               # third field
awk '$4 == "ERROR"' boot.log                      # lines whose 4th field is ERROR
awk '/ERROR/ {n++} END {print n+0, "errors"}' boot.log     # count (n+0 prints 0 if none)
awk -F'[][]' '{print $2}' kern.log | head -3      # dmesg timestamps (field separator [ or ])
```

**Count by severity:**

```code
awk '{for (i=4;i<=NF;i++) if ($i ~ /^(ERROR|WARNING|INFO)$/) {c[$i]++; break}}
     END {for (k in c) printf "%-8s %d\n", k, c[k]}' boot.log | sort
ERROR    4
INFO     1
WARNING  2
```

**Extract key=value pairs (sensor and code) and tabulate:**

```code
grep ERROR boot.log |
awk '{ s=""; c="";
       for (i=1;i<=NF;i++) {
         if ($i ~ /^sensor=/) s=substr($i,8);
         if ($i ~ /^code=/)   c=substr($i,6);
       }
       print s, c }' | sort | uniq -c
      3 TEMP_INLET E1203
      1 TEMP_OUTLET E1104
```

**Time difference between first and last error (seconds, same day):**

```code
grep ERROR boot.log | awk '{
  split(substr($1,12,12), t, ":");          # HH:MM:SS.mmm
  s = t[1]*3600 + t[2]*60 + t[3];
  if (NR==1) first=s; last=s
} END { printf "errors span %.3f s\n", last-first }'
errors span 9.645 s
```

lessons.title: Filtering timestamps and severity
lessons.body:
ISO-8601 timestamps ( 2026-10-15T09:00:05Z) **sort lexically in time order**, so string comparison works:

```code
awk '$1 >= "2026-10-15T09:00:05" && $1 < "2026-10-15T09:00:10"' boot.log
```

For dmesg-style seconds-since-boot:

```code
awk -F'[][]' '$2+0 >= 40 && $2+0 <= 100' kern.log   # messages between 40 s and 100 s
```

For journals, filter at the source: journalctl --since/--until -p warning.

lessons.title: Counting errors and warnings per minute (rate)
lessons.body:
```code
awk '/ERROR|WARNING/ { print substr($1,1,16) }' boot.log | sort | uniq -c
      6 2026-10-15T09:00
```

substr($1,1,16) truncates to the minute; use 1,13 for hourly buckets — a quick way to spot error bursts in long runs.

lessons.title: Extracting service names and error codes from systemd lines
lessons.body:
```code
grep -E '\.service: (Main process exited|Failed with result)' boot.log |
  sed -E 's/.*systemd\[1\]: ([^:]+): .*status=([0-9]+)\/([A-Z]+).*/\1 exit=\2 (\3)/; t;
s/.*systemd\[1\]: ([^:]+): Failed.*/\1 failed/'
fake-sensord.service exit=1 (FAILURE)
fake-sensord.service failed
fake-sensord.service exit=1 (FAILURE)
```

lessons.title: The first meaningful error
lessons.body:
```code
grep -nE 'error|fail|timed out|ERROR' -i boot.log | head -1
3:2026-10-15T09:00:02.410Z falcon-bmc kernel: lm75 3-0048: probe failed with error -121
```

The first error is the **kernel probe failure** for the sensor at I²C bus 3, address 0x48 — not the daemon errors that follow. The daemon’s “device not found” (E1203) is a downstream consequence. That ordering is the whole game in log analysis.

lessons.title: Processing large log files efficiently
lessons.body:
- **Filter early:** put the most selective grep first; later stages process less data.

- grep -F for literal strings is much faster than regexes.

- LC_ALL=C grep ... avoids slow multibyte locale handling (often a large speed-up on big files).

- Don’t cat file | grep — grep pattern file saves a process (minor, but cleaner).

- Avoid shell while read loops for millions of lines — awk is far faster.

- For compressed logs: zgrep, zcat file.gz | awk ....

- Use grep -m to stop early, tail -c to read only the end of huge files.

- Use sort -S 50% --parallel=4 (GNU) for big sorts; on BusyBox, prefer awk aggregation to avoid sorting.

lessons.title: Handling spaces and unusual filenames safely
lessons.body:
```code
# WRONG: breaks on spaces/newlines in names
for f in $(find logs -name '*.log'); do wc -l $f; done
# RIGHT: null-delimited
find logs -name '*.log' -print0 | while IFS= read -r -d '' f; do
  printf '%s %s\n' "$(wc -l < "$f")" "$f"
done
# RIGHT: let find run the command
find logs -name '*.log' -exec wc -l {} +
# RIGHT: xargs with null delimiters
find logs -name '*.log' -print0 | xargs -0 grep -l 'ERROR'
```

Never parse ls output in scripts; filenames may contain spaces, newlines or leading dashes.

source.section: 14.12 Handling spaces and unusual filenames safely

lessons.title: GNU versus BusyBox portability
lessons.body:
**BusyBox (typical; depends**

| Feature | GNU on build config) |
| grep -P (PCRE) | Yes (if built with PCRE) | Usually no |
| grep -E , -o , -c , -A/-B | Yes | Usually yes |
| Yes | Yes ( -r also) | sed -E |
| sed -i | Yes | Yes |
| awk | gawk/mawk | BusyBox awk: POSIX-ish; no gawk extensions ( strftime absent in some builds, no gensub , no asort ) |
| sort -h , -V , --parallel | Yes | Often missing |
| date -d "string" | Flexible parsing | Limited formats |
| find -printf | Yes | No |
| xargs -0 | Yes | Usually yes |
| ls --time-style , du --max- | Yes | Use du -d |

```code
depth
```

| readlink -f | Yes | Usually yes BusyBox (typical; depends |
| Feature | GNU on build config) |
| timeout | coreutils | Present in many builds; older ones use -t SECS syntax |
| Long options ( --quiet ) | Yes | Often only short options |

**Strategy:** do heavy parsing on the **test host** (full GNU tools, Python), and keep on-device commands simple: collect raw output, copy it back, analyse it there.

lessons.title: Exercises (use the sample files)
lessons.body:
1. Count WARNING lines.

2. List unique PIDs of fake-sensord.

3. Print kernel messages from kern.log mentioning i2c-3, with only the timestamp and message.

4. How many times did fake-sensord exit? How many distinct PIDs ran?

5. Produce a CSV time,source,level,message for ERROR/WARNING lines.

6. Find the gap between consecutive i2c-3: transfer timed out messages in kern.log.

**Solutions**

1. grep -c WARNING boot.log → 2.

2. grep -oE 'fake-sensord\[[0-9]+\]' boot.log | grep -oE '[0-9]+' | sort -un → 402, 471, 502, 530.

3. grep 'i2c-3' kern.log | sed -E 's/^\[ *([0-9.]+)\] /\1 /'.

4. grep -c 'fake-sensord.service: Main process exited' boot.log → 2 exits logged; 4 distinct PIDs (some exits not logged in this extract — note evidence may be incomplete). 5.

```code
grep -E ' (ERROR|WARNING) ' boot.log | awk '{
  src=$3; sub(/\[[0-9]+\]:$/,"",src); sub(/:$/,"",src);
  msg=""; for (i=5;i<=NF;i++) msg = msg (i>5?" ":"") $i;
  gsub(/"/,"\"\"",msg);
  printf "%s,%s,%s,\"%s\"\n", $1, src, $4, msg }'
```

1. grep 'transfer timed out' kern.log | awk -F'[][]' '{t=$2+0; if (NR>1) printf "%.3f\n", t-p; p=t}' → 74.880.

lessons.title: Best practices
lessons.body:
- Normalise variable tokens before counting.

- Report the first meaningful error, then the chain.

- Keep sample logs in your repository as test fixtures for parsers.

lessons.title: Conditional execution
lessons.body:
```code
mkdir -p out && echo "created"          # run second only if first succeeded
ping -c1 -W1 "$host" >/dev/null || echo "host down"    # run second only if first failed
cmd || { echo "cmd failed" >&2; exit 1; }   # group with { ...; } (note spaces and ;)
```

**Trap:** a && b || c is **not** if/else — c also runs when b fails. Use a real if when that matters.

```code
if ! output=$(systemctl is-active sshd 2>&1); then

fi
```

lessons.title: Strict modes and their trade-offs
lessons.body:
| Setting | Effect | Trade-off |
| set -u | Using an unset variable is an | Catches typos; requires $ |
| error | {var:-} for optional variables |
| set -o pipefail | Pipeline fails if any stage fails | grep returning 1 (no match) now fails the pipeline — handle intentionally |
| set -e | Exit when a command fails | Many surprising exceptions (below) |

lessons.title: Why set -e is not a complete error-handling strategy
lessons.body:
set -e (errexit) is **ignored or behaves surprisingly** in many contexts:

1. **Commands in conditions** ( if cmd, while cmd, cmd && ..., cmd || ...) never trigger it — and in a function called from such a context, errexit is disabled for the whole function body:

```code
set -e
check() { false; echo "still running!"; }
if check; then echo "check passed?!"; fi   # prints both lines
```

1. **Command substitution in assignments with local**: local x=$(false) succeeds because local succeeded.

2. **Subshells and $(...)**: errexit is not inherited into command substitutions by default (Bash shopt -s inherit_errexit changes that, Bash 4.4+).

3. **Pipelines** without pipefail: only the last command counts.

4. **Arithmetic**: (( count++ )) returns status 1 when the result is 0 — killing a script under set -e at the first increment from 0.

5. It **exits silently** — no message saying what failed unless you add an ERR trap.

6. Diagnostic scripts must **continue after failures** to collect all evidence; aborting on the first failure loses data.

**Recommended approach:** use set -uo pipefail, check critical commands explicitly with if/ ||, report clearly, and decide deliberately where to stop. Optionally use set -e for small linear scripts (installers, build steps) **with** an ERR trap that reports the line:

```code
set -Eeuo pipefail
trap 'echo "ERROR line $LINENO: $BASH_COMMAND (exit $?)" >&2' ERR
```

( -E makes the ERR trap apply inside functions.)

lessons.title: Traps and cleanup
lessons.body:
trap 'commands' SIGNALS runs commands when the script receives signals or exits.

```code
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# trap_demo.sh - temp dir cleanup and child process termination on exit
set -uo pipefail
workdir=$(mktemp -d "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/diag.XXXXXX") || exit 2
child_pid=""
cleanup() {
  local rc=$?
  if [ -n "$child_pid" ] && kill -0 "$child_pid" 2>/dev/null; then
    kill -TERM "$child_pid" 2>/dev/null
    wait "$child_pid" 2>/dev/null
  fi
  rm -rf -- "${workdir:?}"
  echo "cleanup done (exit $rc)" >&2
  exit "$rc"
}
trap cleanup EXIT
  trap 'echo "interrupted" >&2; exit 130' INT
  trap 'echo "terminated" >&2; exit 143' TERM
  sleep 300 &           # simulated long-running capture
  child_pid=$!
  echo "working in $workdir, child $child_pid"
  sleep 2
  echo "done"
```

Run it and press Ctrl+C after 1 s: you’ll see interrupted, then the EXIT trap runs cleanup (kills sleep 300, removes the directory) and the exit code is 130. Without the trap, sleep 300 would keep running as an orphan.

- EXIT runs on any exit (normal, exit, or after INT/TERM handlers call exit).

- SIGKILL cannot be trapped — cleanup can never be 100% guaranteed; design for leftovers (e.g. stale lock detection, Chapter 16).

lessons.title: Temporary files
lessons.body:
```code
tmpfile=$(mktemp) || exit 2                 # /tmp/tmp.XXXXXXXXXX, mode 600
tmpdir=$(mktemp -d -t diag.XXXXXX) || exit 2
```

Never use predictable names like /tmp/output.txt — concurrent runs collide and other users could pre-create the file (symlink attacks). Always remove temp files in a trap.

lessons.title: Timeouts
lessons.body:
```code
timeout 10 some_command                     # SIGTERM after 10 s; exit status 124 if timed
out
timeout -k 5 10 some_command                # then SIGKILL 5 s later if still alive
timeout --foreground 30 ssh ...             # when running interactively from a terminal
```

Built-in tool timeouts are better when available: curl --connect-timeout 5 --max-time 20, `ssh -o ConnectTimeout=10 -o ServerAliveInterval=5 -o ServerAliveCountMax=3, ping -W.`

lessons.title: Retry loops with bounded attempts
lessons.body:
```code
retry() {   # retry <attempts> <delay_s> <command...>; returns last status
  local attempts="$1" delay="$2" n=1 rc
  shift 2
  while true; do
    "$@"; rc=$?
    if [ "$rc" -eq 0 ]; then return 0; fi
    if [ "$n" -ge "$attempts" ]; then
      echo "retry: giving up after $n attempts (last rc=$rc): $*" >&2
      return "$rc"
    fi
    echo "retry: attempt $n failed (rc=$rc); sleeping ${delay}s" >&2
    sleep "$delay"
    n=$((n + 1)); delay=$((delay * 2))           # exponential backoff
  done
}
retry 5 2 curl -skf --max-time 5 -o /dev/null "https://192.0.2.50/redfish/v1/"
```

Rules: always **bound** retries; **log** each failure; **back off**; and retry only **transient** failures (a 401 won’t fix itself — retrying hides real bugs). In test reports, record that retries happened.

lessons.title: Logging and timestamps
lessons.body:
```code
LOG_FILE="${LOG_FILE:-./run_$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ).log}"
log() {
  local level="$1"; shift
  printf '%s %-5s %s\n' "$(date -u +%FT%T.%3NZ)" "$level" "$*" | tee -a "$LOG_FILE" >&2
}
log INFO "starting test"
```

%3N (milliseconds) is GNU date; BusyBox date doesn’t support %N — use whole seconds there. Use UTC; include enough context (host, test id) in each line; never log secrets. To send all output of a script to a log while still seeing it:

```code
exec > >(tee -a "$LOG_FILE") 2>&1     # Bash process substitution
```

lessons.title: Signal handling summary
lessons.body:
| Signal | Typical source | Script response |
| INT | Ctrl+C | Clean up, exit 130 |
| TERM | kill , systemd stop, Jenkins | Clean up, exit 143 abort, timeout |
| HUP | Terminal closed | Clean up or ignore ( nohup ) |
| KILL | kill -9 , OOM | Cannot handle — no cleanup |

Note: Bash defers trap execution until the current foreground command finishes. To react promptly while waiting on a long child, run it in the background and wait for it ( wait is interruptible).

source.chapter: 15 Error Handling and Reliable Bash Automation

lessons.title: Idempotent operations
lessons.body:
An operation is **idempotent** if running it twice has the same effect as running it once. Automation reruns things constantly, so aim for this:

| Not idempotent | Idempotent |
| mkdir out (fails if exists) | mkdir -p out |
| echo "x=1" >> conf (duplicates) | grep -qx 'x=1' conf \|\| echo 'x=1' >> conf |
| ln -s a b (fails if exists) | ln -sfn a b |

```code
useradd tester                                id tester >/dev/null 2>&1 \|\| useradd
                                             tester
```

lessons.title: Quoting variables safely and avoiding destructive wildcards
lessons.body:
```code
# DANGER: if OUTDIR is empty or unset, this becomes rm -rf /*
rm -rf "$OUTDIR"/*
# SAFER: ${var:?} aborts if empty/unset
rm -rf -- "${OUTDIR:?OUTDIR not set}"/*
# SAFER STILL: validate the path first
case "$OUTDIR" in
  /tmp/diag.*|"$HOME"/lab/*) rm -rf -- "${OUTDIR:?}" ;;
  *) echo "refusing to delete unexpected path: $OUTDIR" >&2; exit 2 ;;
esac
```

Other habits: cd "$dir" || exit 1 (never continue in the wrong directory); use -- before filenames; preview with echo or ls before destructive commands; prefer find ... -print first, then -delete.

lessons.title: Debugging scripts
lessons.body:
```code
bash -n script.sh          # syntax check only (doesn't run)
bash -x script.sh args     # trace each command after expansion
set -x; ...; set +x        # trace only a section
PS4='+ ${BASH_SOURCE##*/}:${LINENO}: ' bash -x script.sh   # trace with file:line
shellcheck script.sh       # static analysis (install the shellcheck package)
```

bash -x shows **expanded** values — the fastest way to discover why [ $x = y ] misbehaves. Be careful: traces print variable values, so **never trace scripts handling secrets into shared logs**.

lessons.body:
- **Test with bad input**: no arguments, empty strings, spaces in names, unreachable hosts.

- **Test failure paths**: missing tools (temporarily shadow with a function or a modified PATH in a test), permission denied, full disk (Chapter 6 lab).

lessons.title: Complete example: a reliable remote log collector
lessons.body:
```code
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# collect_remote_logs.sh - collect read-only diagnostics from a lab device over SSH
# Usage: collect_remote_logs.sh -H host [-u user] [-o outdir] [-t timeout]
# Exit: 0 all collected, 1 partial, 2 usage, 3 cannot connect
set -uo pipefail
host="" user="root" outdir="" tmo=20
usage() { echo "Usage: $0 -H host [-u user] [-o outdir] [-t timeout_s]" >&2; }
while getopts ":H:u:o:t:h" o; do
  case "$o" in
    H) host="$OPTARG" ;; u) user="$OPTARG" ;; o) outdir="$OPTARG" ;;
    t) tmo="$OPTARG" ;; h) usage; exit 0 ;; *) usage; exit 2 ;;
  esac
done
[ -n "$host" ] || { usage; exit 2; }
[[ $tmo =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] || { echo "bad timeout" >&2; exit 2; }
outdir="${outdir:-./logs_${host}_$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ)}"
mkdir -p -- "$outdir" || exit 2
log() { printf '%s %s\n' "$(date -u +%FT%TZ)" "$*" | tee -a "$outdir/collector.log" >&2; }
ssh_opts=(-o BatchMode=yes -o ConnectTimeout=10 -o ServerAliveInterval=5 -o
ServerAliveCountMax=3)
# Fixed list of read-only commands: name|command
cmds=(
  "uname|uname -a"
  "os_release|cat /etc/os-release"
  "uptime|uptime"
  "boot_id|cat /proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id"
  "df|df -h"
  "mem|cat /proc/meminfo"
  "failed_units|systemctl --failed --no-pager"
  "journal_err|journalctl -b -p err --no-pager"
  "journal_tail|journalctl -b -n 500 --no-pager"
  "dmesg|dmesg"
)
if ! timeout "$tmo" ssh "${ssh_opts[@]}" "$user@$host" true 2>>"$outdir/collector.log"; then
  log "ERROR cannot connect to $user@$host"
  exit 3
fi
failed=0
for entry in "${cmds[@]}"; do
  name="${entry%%|*}"; cmd="${entry#*|}"
  if timeout "$tmo" ssh "${ssh_opts[@]}" "$user@$host" "$cmd" \
       > "$outdir/$name.txt" 2> "$outdir/$name.err"; then
    log "OK   $name"
  else
    rc=$?
    log "FAIL $name (rc=$rc)"
    failed=$((failed + 1))
  fi
  [ -s "$outdir/$name.err" ] || rm -f -- "$outdir/$name.err"
done
log "collected into $outdir ($failed failures)"
[ "$failed" -eq 0 ] && exit 0 || exit 1
```

Points to note: the command list is fixed and read-only (no user input reaches the remote shell); each command gets its own timeout, output and error file; a failure in one doesn’t stop others; exit codes distinguish “couldn’t connect” (an infrastructure problem) from “partial collection”. Authentication relies on SSH keys ( BatchMode=yes) — no passwords in the script.

lessons.title: Exercises
lessons.body:
1. Why does (( errors++ )) crash a set -e script when errors=0?

2. Write a guard that refuses to run unless WORKDIR starts with /tmp/.

3. Make a function require_cmd that exits 2 with a message if a tool is missing.

4. Your trap deletes the temp dir, but after kill -9 the dir remains. Is your script wrong?

5. What does exit code 124 mean from timeout?

**Solutions**

1. The arithmetic expression evaluates to 0 (post-increment returns the old value), so (( )) returns status 1 and set -e exits. Use errors=$((errors + 1)).

2. case "${WORKDIR:-}" in /tmp/?*) ;; *) echo "unsafe WORKDIR" >&2; exit 2 ;; esac.

3. require_cmd() { command -v "$1" >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "missing required command:

```code
$1" >&2; exit 2; }; }.
```

4. No — SIGKILL cannot be trapped. Handle leftovers on the next run (e.g. clean old diag.* dirs older than a day) or let the OS clean /tmp.

5. The command was killed because the time limit expired.

lessons.title: Best practices
lessons.body:
- set -uo pipefail, explicit checks, informative errors, and an EXIT trap.

- Every external call has a timeout; every retry is bounded.

- Logs: UTC, levels, no secrets.

lessons.title: Cron fundamentals
lessons.body:
cron runs commands on a schedule. Edit **your** crontab with crontab -e ([MOD]); list it with crontab -l ([RO]).

```code
# ┌ minute (0-59)
# │ ┌ hour (0-23)
# │ │ ┌ day of month (1-31)
# │ │ │ ┌ month (1-12)
# │ │ │ │ ┌ day of week (0-7, 0 and 7 = Sunday)
# │ │ │ │ │
  */5 * * * *  /home/asha/bin/health_check.sh >> /home/asha/logs/health.log 2>&1
  0 2 * * 1-5  /home/asha/bin/nightly_collect.sh
```

*/5 = every 5 minutes; 1-5 = Monday to Friday. **Cron’s environment is minimal** — no .bashrc, short PATH, often SHELL=/bin/sh, working directory = home. Therefore: absolute paths, set PATH at the top of the crontab or script, redirect output (otherwise cron tries to email it), and test with env -i `HOME="$HOME" PATH=/usr/bin:/bin bash script.sh to simulate.`

**systemd timers** are the modern alternative: logs go to the journal, Persistent=true runs missed jobs, dependencies are supported. User timers work without root

```code
( systemctl --user). Example ~/.config/systemd/user/health.timer with OnCalendar=*:0/5
paired with health.service; enable with systemctl --user enable --now health.timer. (User
```

services may need loginctl enable-linger to run when you’re logged out — which requires appropriate rights.)

lessons.title: Lock files: avoiding duplicate execution
lessons.body:
If a 5-minute job sometimes takes 7 minutes, two copies overlap. Use flock (util-linux):

```code
  #!/usr/bin/env bash
  # health_check.sh - periodic, non-overlapping health check (user-level)
  set -uo pipefail
  LOCK="${XDG_RUNTIME_DIR:-/tmp}/health_check.lock"
  exec 9>"$LOCK" || exit 2
  if ! flock -n 9; then
  echo "$(date -u +%FT%TZ) another instance is running; skipping"
  exit 0
fi
# ... checks go here; the lock is released automatically when the script exits
echo "$(date -u +%FT%TZ) load=$(cut -d' ' -f1 /proc/loadavg) mem_avail_kB=$(awk '/
MemAvailable/{print $2}' /proc/meminfo)"
```

flock -n fails immediately if the lock is held; the kernel releases it when fd 9 closes (even after kill -9), so there are no stale locks. Where flock isn’t available (some BusyBox builds), use mkdir as an atomic lock and a PID check:

```code
lockdir="/tmp/health_check.lockdir"
if mkdir "$lockdir" 2>/dev/null; then
  echo $$ > "$lockdir/pid"
  trap 'rm -rf -- "$lockdir"' EXIT
else
  oldpid=$(cat "$lockdir/pid" 2>/dev/null)
  if [ -n "$oldpid" ] && kill -0 "$oldpid" 2>/dev/null; then
    echo "already running (pid $oldpid)"; exit 0
  fi
  echo "removing stale lock from pid ${oldpid:-unknown}"
  rm -rf -- "$lockdir" && mkdir "$lockdir" && echo $$ > "$lockdir/pid" || exit 2
  trap 'rm -rf -- "$lockdir"' EXIT
fi
```

(The stale-lock branch has a small race between check and removal; acceptable for single-user lab tools, which is why flock is preferred.)

lessons.title: Periodic health checks
lessons.body:
Design principles:

- Each run is **short, bounded** (timeouts) and **read-only**.

- Output is **one structured line per run** (or JSON lines), easy to graph and grep.

- Thresholds are configurable; alert on **state changes** (OK→FAIL), not every failing sample.

```code
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# periodic_probe.sh - append one JSON line per run (user-level)
set -uo pipefail
host="${1:?usage: $0 <host>}"
out="${2:-$HOME/probe_${host}.jsonl}"
ts=$(date -u +%FT%TZ)
start=$(date +%s)
if timeout 5 bash -c "exec 3<>/dev/tcp/$host/443" 2>/dev/null; then https=true; else https=fa
lse; fi
if timeout 5 bash -c "exec 3<>/dev/tcp/$host/22" 2>/dev/null; then ssh=true; else ssh=false;
fi
dur=$(( $(date +%s) - start ))
printf '{"ts":"%s","host":"%s","https":%s,"ssh":%s,"probe_s":%d}\n' \
  "$ts" "$host" "$https" "$ssh" "$dur" >> "$out"
```

Analyse later: grep -c '"https":false' ~/probe_192.0.2.50.jsonl, or load into Python/ pandas.

lessons.title: Log rotation concepts for your own logs
lessons.body:
Without root you may not configure system logrotate, but you can rotate your own logs:

```code
rotate_log() {   # rotate_log <file> <max_bytes> <keep>
  local f="$1" max="$2" keep="$3" i size
  [ -f "$f" ] || return 0
  size=$(wc -c < "$f")
  [ "$size" -lt "$max" ] && return 0
  for (( i = keep - 1; i >= 1; i-- )); do
    [ -f "$f.$i" ] && mv -f -- "$f.$i" "$f.$((i + 1))"
  done
  mv -f -- "$f" "$f.1"
  : > "$f"
}
rotate_log "$HOME/logs/health.log" 1048576 5    # keep 5 x 1 MiB
```

User-level logrotate also works with your own config and state file: logrotate -s `~/.logrotate.state ~/logrotate.conf.`

source.section: 16.4 Log rotation concepts for your own logs

lessons.title: Background processes, timeouts and cancellation
lessons.body:
```code
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# parallel_ping.sh - probe several hosts in parallel with a global deadline
set -uo pipefail
hosts=("$@")
[ "${#hosts[@]}" -gt 0 ] || { echo "usage: $0 host..." >&2; exit 2; }
declare -A pids=()
tmpd=$(mktemp -d) || exit 2
trap 'kill "${pids[@]}" 2>/dev/null; rm -rf -- "$tmpd"' EXIT
for h in "${hosts[@]}"; do
  ( timeout 10 ping -c 3 -W 2 "$h" >/dev/null 2>&1; echo $? > "$tmpd/$h" ) &
  pids[$h]=$!
done
for h in "${hosts[@]}"; do
  wait "${pids[$h]}"
  rc=$(cat "$tmpd/$h" 2>/dev/null || echo 99)
  if [ "$rc" -eq 0 ]; then echo "UP   $h"; else echo "DOWN $h (rc=$rc)"; fi
done
```

- & starts each probe in the background; $! is its PID.

- wait PID collects each result; total time ≈ the slowest probe, bounded by timeout 10.

- The EXIT trap kills any remaining children if the script is cancelled (e.g. Jenkins abort sends SIGTERM).

lessons.body:
```code
  # Sample system resources every 10 s into a CSV while a test runs (user-level)
  monitor_resources() {   # monitor_resources <outfile> <interval_s>
    local out="$1" iv="$2"
    echo "ts,load1,mem_avail_kB,root_used_pct" > "$out"
    while true; do
      printf '%s,%s,%s,%s\n' "$(date -u +%FT%TZ)" \
        "$(cut -d' ' -f1 /proc/loadavg)" \
        "$(awk '/MemAvailable/{print $2}' /proc/meminfo)" \
        "$(df -P / | awk 'NR==2{gsub("%","",$5);print $5}')" >> "$out"
      sleep "$iv"
    done
  }
  monitor_resources /tmp/res.csv 10 &
  MON_PID=$!
  trap 'kill "$MON_PID" 2>/dev/null' EXIT
  # ... run the long test here ...
For one process: ps -o pid,rss,%cpu,etime -p <pid> in a loop, or /usr/bin/time -v cmd
```

(GNU time) for peak RSS of a command.

lessons.title: Safe execution in CI environments
lessons.body:
- **Never prompt.** Use BatchMode=yes, -y flags, and fail fast when input is missing.

- **Bound everything:** per-command timeouts and a job-level timeout.

- **Workspace-relative paths:** write into $WORKSPACE (Jenkins) or a mktemp -d dir; never into shared global paths.

- **Unique names:** include build number/job ID in output paths so parallel jobs don’t collide.

- **Clean up** processes and temp files in traps; CI agents are long-lived.

- **Exit codes carry meaning:** 0 pass, 1 test failure, 2 usage/config, 3 infrastructure (device unreachable). Chapter 25 maps these into Jenkins results.

- **No secrets in logs:** don’t set -x around credential handling; use the CI system’s credential masking.

- **Locks for shared devices:** two jobs testing the same BMC at once produce nonsense; use Jenkins lock (Lockable Resources plugin) or a lock on a shared file system.

lessons.title: Exercises
lessons.body:
1. Write a crontab line running ~/bin/probe.sh every 10 minutes on weekdays from 08:00 to 18:59.

2. Why should a cron script not rely on ~/.bashrc?

3. Demonstrate that flock -n prevents overlap: start a script that holds the lock for 30 s and run a second copy.

4. How would you stop all background children if your script receives SIGTERM?

5. Why alert on state changes rather than on each failing sample?

**Solutions**

1. */10 8-18 * * 1-5 /home/<user>/bin/probe.sh >> /home/<user>/logs/probe.log 2>&1.

2. Cron doesn’t run an interactive shell, so .bashrc isn’t read; environment variables, aliases and PATH changes from it don’t apply.

3. Script: exec 9>/tmp/t.lock; flock -n 9 || { echo busy; exit 0; }; sleep 30. Run bash t.sh & bash t.sh → the second prints busy.

4. Track child PIDs and trap 'kill "${pids[@]}" 2>/dev/null' EXIT plus trap 'exit 143' TERM; or kill the process group ( kill -- -$$ when the script is a group leader — use with care).

5. To avoid alert storms and to highlight transitions, which carry the diagnostic information (when did it start failing?).

lessons.title: Best practices
lessons.body:
- Lock, bound, log, rotate.

- One structured line per periodic sample.

- Treat CI agents as shared, long-lived machines — clean up everything you start.

lessons.title: What OpenBMC is
lessons.body:
**OpenBMC** is an open-source Linux distribution for Baseboard Management Controllers, developed under the Linux Foundation. It is built with the **Yocto Project / OpenEmbedded** build system: machine-specific “meta layers” describe each platform (SoC, board, devices), and the build produces a firmware image (kernel + root filesystem + bootloader pieces) for that machine. Design principles you’ll notice everywhere:

- **systemd** manages all services.

- **D-Bus** is the internal “data bus”: services publish objects (sensors, inventory, states, software images, logs) and others read or change them through D-Bus.

- Interfaces are defined centrally in the **phosphor-dbus-interfaces** repository (YAML definitions under the xyz.openbmc_project.* namespace), so services agree on property names and types.

- External APIs (**bmcweb** for Redfish/web, **ipmid** for IPMI) are translators: they map protocol requests to D-Bus calls.

lessons.title: High-level architecture
lessons.body:
```code
          External clients: Redfish (HTTPS), Web UI, IPMI (RMCP+/UDP 623), SSH
                     |                     |                  |
+--------------------v---------------------v------------------v-------------+
|  bmcweb (Redfish + web UI backend)   ipmid (IPMI)    sshd/dropbear        |
|                     \                    |                                |
|                      \________ D-Bus (system bus) _______________________ |
```

lessons.title: Linux userspace services and systemd
lessons.body:
Each daemon is a systemd service. Many OpenBMC unit names are the D-Bus service name, e.g. xyz.openbmc_project.State.BMC.service — making it easy to map a missing D- Bus service to its unit. Many units are **templates** ( ...@.service) instantiated per host/ chassis, and many use Type=dbus so systemd considers them started when they claim their bus name.

**Read-only inspection on a lab BMC:**

```code
systemctl list-units --type=service --no-pager | grep -E 'xyz|phosphor|bmcweb|ipmi'
systemctl --failed --no-pager
systemctl status bmcweb --no-pager            # may be socket-activated: also check
bmcweb.socket
systemctl list-dependencies multi-user.target --no-pager | head -40
journalctl -u bmcweb -b --no-pager | tail -50
```

**Socket activation note:** on many builds bmcweb.socket listens on port 443 and starts bmcweb.service on demand. If bmcweb.service shows inactive but the socket is active, Redfish may still work — check both units and ss -tlnp.

lessons.title: systemd dependencies and BMC state targets
lessons.body:
OpenBMC uses **systemd targets** to represent state transitions (for example host power-on/off sequences), with services hooked into those targets. Platform-specific power sequencing is often implemented as services wanted by such targets. The exact target names vary; explore with:

```code
systemctl list-units --type=target --no-pager | grep -i obmc
systemctl list-dependencies obmc-host-start@0.target --no-pager   # example name; verify on
your platform
```

When a host power-on fails, the failure is often a service inside the power-on target — the same systemd debugging technique as Chapter 8 applies.

lessons.title: D-Bus and IPC concepts (introduction)
lessons.body: **IPC** (inter-process communication) is how separate processes exchange data: pipes, sockets, shared memory, message buses. **D-Bus** is a message bus: processes connect to a **bus daemon** (on OpenBMC usually dbus-daemon or dbus-broker), and send method calls, receive replies, and broadcast signals. Chapter 18 covers it in depth.

lessons.body:
Clients don’t hard-code which daemon owns a sensor. They ask the **ObjectMapper**

```code
( xyz.openbmc_project.ObjectMapper at /xyz/openbmc_project/object_mapper) questions like
“which services implement xyz.openbmc_project.Sensor.Value under /xyz/openbmc_project/
```

sensors?” bmcweb uses this heavily. If the ObjectMapper is unhealthy, many APIs fail at once — a useful clue.

lessons.title: Firmware images and update concepts (overview)
lessons.body: An OpenBMC firmware image typically bundles kernel, root filesystem and other pieces, often with a **MANIFEST** describing the image (purpose, version) and **signatures** if image verification is enabled. The update service (phosphor-bmc-code-mgmt) validates the image, creates a software object on D-Bus with a **Version** and **Activation** state, writes the image to flash when activation is requested, and the BMC reboots into it. Redfish exposes this through **UpdateService** and **FirmwareInventory**. Chapter 19 covers the workflow and its failures.

lessons.title: How management APIs relate to internal services
lessons.body: Example 1 — **Redfish thermal reading:** GET /redfish/v1/Chassis/<id>/Sensors/... (or the older .../Thermal) → bmcweb → ObjectMapper lookup for sensor objects associated with that chassis → Get of xyz.openbmc_project.Sensor.Value property Value from the sensor daemon → JSON response. Example 2 — **IPMI mc info:** ipmitool sends a Get Device ID request → network IPMI daemon → ipmid command handler → reads version information (from D-Bus/software objects or configured data) → response bytes. Example 3 — **Redfish BMC reset:** POST .../Managers/bmc/Actions/Manager.Reset → bmcweb → sets a transition property on the BMC state object (phosphor-state-manager) → systemd reboot. **Debugging consequence:** when an API call fails, ask “which D-Bus service and object does it depend on?” and inspect that service directly (Chapter 18). A Redfish 500/503 often means bmcweb is fine but a backend service is missing, slow or returned an error.

lessons.title: Common sources of BMC failures
lessons.body:
| Category | Examples |
| Hardware | Sensor not responding on I²C, missing FRU EEPROM, fan failure, flash wear |
| Kernel/driver | Probe failures, device-tree mismatch with board revision, driver timeouts |
| Category | Examples |
| Configuration | entity-manager config doesn’t match board, wrong thresholds, network config lost |
| Service | Daemon crash/restart loop, D-Bus name not acquired, startup timeout, dependency failed |
| Resources | Memory leak → OOM; flash or tmpfs full; too many sessions |
| Firmware update | Image incompatible, signature failure, interrupted flash, version mismatch after reboot |
| Time | Wrong clock → TLS failures, confusing logs |
| Network | Wrong VLAN, DHCP failure, duplicate IP, shared- NIC (NC-SI) issues |

lessons.title: Practical exercise: build a map of your lab BMC
lessons.body:
On an authorised lab BMC or a QEMU OpenBMC image, collect (all [RO]):

```code
cat /etc/os-release
systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running --no-pager | wc -l
systemctl --failed --no-pager
ss -tlnp 2>/dev/null || netstat -tlnp
busctl list --no-pager | grep -c xyz.openbmc_project
busctl tree xyz.openbmc_project.ObjectMapper --no-pager | head -30
journalctl --list-boots --no-pager
df -h; free
```

Write a one-page map: image version, number of running services, failed units, listening ports and owning daemons, number of xyz.openbmc_project services, persistent or volatile journal, free storage and memory. This map is your **baseline** — the reference you compare against when something breaks (Chapter 26).
