lessons.title: What version control is and why it matters

source.section: 1.1 What version control is and why it matters

lessons.title: Git versus GitHub and other hosting services
lessons.body:
| Git | GitHub / GitLab / Gerrit / Bitbucket |
| What it is | A program on your computer | A server that hosts Git repositories |
| Works offline | Yes | No |
| Stores history | Yes, fully, in .git/ | Yes, a copy |
| Adds | — | Web UI, pull/merge requests, code review, permissions, CI integration, issue tracking |

Git is **distributed**: every clone contains the full history. GitHub is one company’s hosting service. OpenBMC, for example, uses **Gerrit** for code review and mirrors repositories on GitHub. Many companies run GitLab or Bitbucket internally. The Git commands in this part work identically everywhere; only the review workflow (pull request vs merge request vs Gerrit change) differs.

source.section: 1.2 Git versus GitHub and other hosting services

lessons.title: Local and remote repositories
lessons.body:
- A **local repository** is the .git/ folder on your machine plus your files.

- A **remote** is another copy of the repository, usually on a server, that you fetch from and push to. By convention the main remote is called origin.

```code
Your laptop                                   Server (GitHub / GitLab / Gerrit)
┌───────────────────────────────┐             ┌──────────────────────┐
│ working directory (files)     │             │ origin               │
│ staging area (index)          │  git push   │  main, feature/x,    │
│ local repo (.git: commits)    │ ──────────► │  tags ...            │
│ remote-tracking: origin/main  │ ◄────────── │                      │
└───────────────────────────────┘  git fetch  └──────────────────────┘
```

origin/main on your laptop is a **remote-tracking branch**: your last known picture of the server’s main. It only updates when you run git fetch or git pull.

lessons.title: The three areas: working directory, staging area, history
lessons.body:
This is the most important idea in Git.

```code
working directory  ── git add ──►  staging area  ── git commit ──►  history
      ▲                                │                                │
      └──────── git restore ───────────┘◄──── git restore --staged ─────┘
```

1. **Working directory**: the files you edit.

2. **Staging area** (also called the index): the exact snapshot you are preparing for the next commit. You choose what goes in with git add.

3. **History**: commits. Each commit is a full snapshot of the staged files plus author, date, message and a pointer to its parent commit(s).

**How it works internally.** Git stores content as objects in .git/objects, named by a hash of their content: blobs (file contents), trees (directories) and commits (snapshot + metadata + parent). A **branch** is just a small file containing one commit hash. HEAD says which branch you are on. Because objects are named by their content hash, Git can detect any corruption or tampering, and identical files are stored once.

**Why a staging area?** It lets you commit part of your work. For example, you fixed a test and also changed a local debug setting; you stage and commit only the test fix.

source.section: 1.4 The three areas: working directory, staging area, history

lessons.title: Important terminology
lessons.body:
| Term | Meaning |
| Repository (repo) | The project folder plus its .git history |
| Commit | A saved snapshot with a message and a unique ID (hash) |
| Hash / SHA | The commit ID, e.g. 7341583 (short) or 40/64 hex characters (full) |
| Branch | A movable name pointing to a commit |
| HEAD | Pointer to what you currently have checked out |
| Remote | Another copy of the repository, e.g. origin |
| Clone | Copy a remote repository to your machine, including history |
| Tracked / untracked | Whether Git already knows about a file |
| Index / staging area | The snapshot being prepared for the next commit |

lessons.title: Hands-on: the core commands
lessons.body:
The following session was **[EXECUTED]** in an empty folder (hashes will differ for you).

First, tell Git who you are (once per machine):

```code
$ git config --global user.name "Asha Rao"
$ git config --global user.email "asha@example.com"
$ git config --global init.defaultBranch main
```

lessons.title: git init and git status
lessons.body:
```code
$ mkdir bmc-tests && cd bmc-tests
$ git init
Initialized empty Git repository in .../bmc-tests/.git/
$ printf 'def test_ping():\n    assert True\n' > test_ping.py
$ mkdir reports && touch reports/junit.xml
$ git status
On branch main
No commits yet
Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
    reports/
    test_ping.py
nothing added to commit but untracked files present (use "git add" to track)
```

**Interpretation:** Git sees two untracked items. reports/ is generated output and must never be committed. That is the job of .gitignore.

lessons.title: .gitignore
lessons.body:
```code
$ printf 'reports/\n__pycache__/\n.venv/\n' > .gitignore
$ git status --short
?? .gitignore
?? test_ping.py
```

reports/ disappeared from the list. ?? means “untracked”.

lessons.title: git add and git commit
lessons.body:
```code
$ git add .gitignore test_ping.py
$ git status --short
A  .gitignore
A  test_ping.py
$ git commit -m "Add first smoke test and .gitignore"
[main (root-commit) 7341583] Add first smoke test and .gitignore
 2 files changed, 5 insertions(+)
 create mode 100644 .gitignore
 create mode 100644 test_ping.py
$ git log --oneline
7341583 Add first smoke test and .gitignore
```

A means “added to the staging area”. After the commit the working tree is clean.

lessons.title: git diff, git show, git log
lessons.body:
| Command | Shows |
| git diff | working directory vs staging area (unstaged changes) |
| git diff --staged | staging area vs last commit (what you are about to commit) |
| git diff main..feature/x | differences between two branches |
| git show <commit> | one commit: message, author and its diff |
| git log --oneline --graph --all | compact history of all branches as a graph |
| git log -p -- tests/test_power.py | history of one file with diffs |
| git log --author=asha --since=2.weeks | filtered history |

**Habit worth building:** always run git diff --staged before git commit. It is the cheapest code review you will ever do, and it catches debug prints, hardcoded IP addresses and passwords before they enter history.

source.section: 1.6.4 git diff, git show, git log

lessons.title: git restore
lessons.body:
| You want to… | Command |
| Throw away unstaged edits to a file | git restore tests/test_power.py |
| Unstage a file but keep the edits | git restore --staged tests/test_power.py |
| Get a file back as it was in a commit | git restore --source=HEAD~2 config.py |

git restore <file> **permanently discards** uncommitted edits to that file. There is no undo, because those edits were never stored in Git.

lessons.title: git clone
lessons.body:
```code
$ git clone https://github.com/<your-user>/bmc-tests.git        # HTTPS
$ git clone git@github.com:<your-user>/bmc-tests.git            # SSH
$ git clone --depth 1 --branch v1.0.0 <url>                     # shallow, one tag
```

A clone sets up origin, downloads all history (unless --depth is used) and checks out the default branch.

lessons.title: A good .gitignore for a Python test-automation repository
lessons.body:
```code
# Python
__pycache__/
*.py[cod]
.venv/
venv/
*.egg-info/
.pytest_cache/
# Generated by every test run - never commit
reports/
artifacts/
*.log
# Local secrets and machine-specific config
.env
*.local.yaml
# Firmware images and large binaries belong in an artifact store, not Git
*.mtd
*.tar
images/
```

Two warnings:

1. .gitignore only affects **untracked** files. If reports/junit.xml was already committed, adding reports/ to .gitignore does nothing. Remove it from the index first: git rm -r --cached reports/ then commit.

2. .gitignore is not a security control. It helps prevent accidents, but a file added with git add -f is still committed. Chapter 5 covers secret scanning.

source.section: 1.7 A good .gitignore for a Python test-automation repository

lessons.title: Common mistakes and troubleshooting
lessons.body:
| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
| fatal: not a git repository | You are outside the repo folder | cd into it; git rev-parse --show-toplevel shows the root |
| Author identity unknown | user.name/user.email not set | set them with git config |
| Commit contains reports/ | committed before .gitignore | git rm -r --cached reports/ |
| existed | and commit |
| nothing to commit but you | you edited a file in another | check pwd and git status |
| edited | clone |
| Huge repository | binaries/firmware images | Chapter 5: remove and use an |
| committed | artifact store or Git LFS |

lessons.title: Practical exercise 1.1 — version a Python automation project
lessons.body:
**Task.** Create a repository sensor-checks containing checks/limits.py with a function `in_range(value, low, high), a test file tests/test_limits.py with three tests, a .gitignore,` and three commits: (1) project skeleton, (2) function and tests, (3) a fix to the boundary condition. Then show the history and the diff of the fix.

**Solution.**

```code
  mkdir sensor-checks && cd sensor-checks && git init
  mkdir checks tests
  printf '__pycache__/\n.venv/\nreports/\n.pytest_cache/\n' > .gitignore
  touch checks/__init__.py
  git add . && git commit -m "Create project skeleton"
  cat > checks/limits.py <<'EOF'
  def in_range(value, low, high):
      return low < value < high
  EOF
  cat > tests/test_limits.py <<'EOF'
  from checks.limits import in_range
  def test_inside():  assert in_range(12.0, 11.4, 12.6)
  def test_below():   assert not in_range(11.0, 11.4, 12.6)
  def test_on_limit(): assert in_range(11.4, 11.4, 12.6)   # limit itself is allowed
  EOF
  git add . && git commit -m "Add in_range check and tests"
  python -m pytest -q          # test_on_limit fails: the boundary is wrong
  sed -i 's/low < value < high/low <= value <= high/' checks/limits.py
  git diff                       # review before staging
  git commit -am "Fix in_range: include the limit values"
git log --oneline
git show HEAD                  # the fix and its message
```

The deliberately failing third test shows the value of committing tests with the code: the history now explains why the comparison changed.

source.section: 1.9 Practical exercise 1.1 — version a Python automation project

lessons.title: Best practices
lessons.body:
- Commit small, logical changes with messages that explain why.

- Review git diff --staged before every commit.

- Create .gitignore in the very first commit.

- Never commit generated reports, virtual environments, firmware images or secrets.

- Record the test-code commit hash in every test report (Chapter 14 shows how).

lessons.title: Why branches exist
lessons.body:
A branch lets you work on a change **in isolation**. Your half-finished test_firmware_update.py should not break the nightly regression that runs from main. You develop on feature/fw-update-test, get it reviewed, and merge it when it works.

Internally a branch is only a 41-byte file under .git/refs/heads/ containing a commit hash. Creating a branch is instant and costs nothing.

lessons.title: Creating, switching and deleting branches
lessons.body:
```code
git branch                          # list local branches (* = current)
git branch -a                       # include remote-tracking branches
git switch -c feature/fan-tests     # create and switch (Git 2.23+)
git switch main                     # switch back
git branch -d feature/fan-tests     # delete (refuses if not merged)
git branch -D feature/fan-tests     # force delete (unmerged work becomes hard to find)
git push origin --delete feature/fan-tests   # delete on the remote
```

Older tutorials use git checkout -b; it still works. git switch and git restore were added to split checkout’s two jobs into clearer commands.

lessons.title: Branch types used by teams
lessons.body:
| Branch | Purpose | Lifetime |
| main (or master) | Always-working integration | permanent branch; nightly regression runs here |
| feature/<topic> | One change: a new test, a fix | days |
| release/<version> | Stabilise test code that | months matches a firmware release |
| Urgent fix to a release branch | hours/days | hotfix/<topic> |

For embedded validation, release/ branches matter: when firmware 2.16 is in the field, you may need the test suite as it was for 2.16 while main already targets 2.17.

lessons.title: Merging
lessons.body:
**Fast-forward merge.** If main has not moved since you branched, Git just moves the main pointer forward. No merge commit is created. **[EXECUTED]**

```code
$ git switch -c feature/add-retries
$ echo 'MAX_RETRIES = 1' >> config.py
$ git commit -qam "Add MAX_RETRIES"
$ git switch main
$ git merge feature/add-retries
Updating 03507a7..60c8c40
Fast-forward
 config.py | 1 +
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
```

**Three-way merge.** If both branches have new commits, Git combines them using three snapshots: the common ancestor, your branch and the other branch. The result is a **merge commit** with two parents.

```code
        o---o  feature/longer-timeout
       /     \
o---o---o-----M   main   (M = merge commit, two parents)
```

lessons.title: Merge conflicts
lessons.body: A conflict happens when both branches changed the **same lines** differently. Git cannot know which is correct, so it stops and asks you.

lessons.title: Lab 2.1 — create and resolve a conflict [EXECUTED]
lessons.body:
Setup: config.py contains REDFISH_TIMEOUT_S = 10. One engineer raises it to 30 on a feature branch because the BMC reboots slowly; another changes it to 15 on main.

```code
$ git switch -c feature/longer-timeout
$ sed -i 's/REDFISH_TIMEOUT_S = 10/REDFISH_TIMEOUT_S = 30/' config.py
$ git commit -qam "Increase Redfish timeout for slow reboot"
$ git switch main
$ sed -i 's/REDFISH_TIMEOUT_S = 10/REDFISH_TIMEOUT_S = 15/' config.py
$ git commit -qam "Tune Redfish timeout to 15 s"
$ git merge feature/longer-timeout
Auto-merging config.py
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in config.py
Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.
```

Inspect:

```code
$ git status
On branch main
You have unmerged paths.
  (fix conflicts and run "git commit")
  (use "git merge --abort" to abort the merge)
Unmerged paths:
  (use "git add <file>..." to mark resolution)
    both modified:   config.py
$ cat config.py
BMC_HOST = "127.0.0.1"
<<<<<<< HEAD
REDFISH_TIMEOUT_S = 15
=======
REDFISH_TIMEOUT_S = 30
>>>>>>> feature/longer-timeout
MAX_RETRIES = 1
```

- Between <<<<<<< HEAD and =======: your current branch (main).

- Between ======= and >>>>>>>: the branch being merged.

**Resolve safely.** This is an engineering decision, not a text-editing chore. Ask: why did each person change it? Here the 30 s value is based on measured reboot time, so it wins. Edit the file to the final content, remove all markers, then:

```code
$ grep -n '<<<<<<<\|>>>>>>>' config.py     # must print nothing
$ python -m pytest -q                       # run tests before concluding
$ git add config.py
$ git commit --no-edit
$ git log --oneline --graph
*   335fbb7 Merge branch 'feature/longer-timeout'
|\
| * 8087f19 Increase Redfish timeout for slow reboot
* | f9293ac Tune Redfish timeout to 15 s
|/
* 60c8c40 Add MAX_RETRIES
* 03507a7 Add test configuration
```

**Safety rules for conflicts**

1. If unsure, git merge --abort returns you to the state before the merge.

2. Never resolve by blindly picking “ours” or “theirs” for the whole file.

3. Run the tests after resolving; a syntactically clean merge can still be wrong.

4. Talk to the other author when the intent is unclear.

5. Use git diff before git add to check the final result.

source.section: 2.5.1 Lab 2.1 — create and resolve a conflict [EXECUTED]

lessons.title: Rebasing
lessons.body:
git rebase main (run on your feature branch) takes your commits and **replays** them on top of the latest main, giving a straight-line history. **[EXECUTED]**

```code
$ git switch feature/sensor-test
$ git rebase main
Successfully rebased and updated refs/heads/feature/sensor-test.
$ git log --oneline --graph -3
* 18e07e9 Add sensor test helper      <- new hash: the commit was rewritten
* 0104f1e Add other module
* abed0e8 Revert "Enable debug logging"
```

**Rebase rewrites history**: your commits get new hashes. That is fine for commits only you have. It is dangerous for commits other people already based work on.

**The golden rule:** do not rebase commits that have been pushed to a branch other people use. Rebasing your own feature branch before opening (or updating) a pull request is normal; after a rebase you push with git push --force-with-lease, which refuses to overwrite the remote if someone else pushed in the meantime.

| Merge | Rebase |
| History | true history, with merge | linear, rewritten commits |
| Safe on shared branches | yes | no |
| Conflict resolution | once | possibly once per replayed commit |
| Typical use | integrating into main | updating your private feature branch |

Interactive rebase (git rebase -i HEAD~4) lets you squash “fix typo” commits into meaningful ones before review.

lessons.title: Merge requests and pull requests
lessons.body: A **pull request** (GitHub, Bitbucket) or **merge request** (GitLab) asks for your branch to be merged into another, with review and automated checks. Gerrit uses **changes** with patch sets instead of branches, but the idea is the same: no code reaches main without review and passing CI.

lessons.title: Keeping a branch synchronised
lessons.body:
```code
git fetch origin                   # update origin/* without touching your files
git switch feature/fan-tests
git rebase origin/main             # private branch: replay on latest main
# or
git merge origin/main              # shared branch: merge main in
```

Sync often (daily). Small, frequent syncs mean small conflicts.

lessons.title: Protecting shared branches
Exercise 2.1
lessons.body:
Create two branches from main, each adding a different test to the **end of the same file** tests/test_power.py. Merge both into main. Why do you get a conflict even though the tests are different? Resolve it so both tests survive.

**Solution.** Both branches inserted lines at the same position (after the last line), so Git sees two different edits to the same region. Resolve by keeping both blocks, one after the other, removing the markers, running pytest, then git add and git commit. Teams reduce this by keeping one test topic per file.

lessons.title: Exercise 2.2
lessons.body:
Your feature branch has five commits: “add test”, “fix typo”, “wip”, “fix test”, “address review”. Make it two meaningful commits before review.

**Solution.** git rebase -i origin/main, mark the commits to fold as squash (or fixup), keep two pick lines, edit messages, then git push --force-with-lease. Only do this on your own branch.

lessons.title: The feature development workflow
lessons.body:
```code
1. git switch main && git pull           # start from the latest main
2. git switch -c feature/psu-redundancy-test
3. edit -> run tests locally -> git add -p -> git diff --staged -> git commit
4. git fetch && git rebase origin/main   # stay current (private branch)
5. git push -u origin feature/psu-redundancy-test
6. open a pull request; CI runs automatically
7. address review comments with new commits
8. merge when approved and CI is green; delete the branch
```

git add -p stages hunks interactively, so unrelated edits stay out of the commit.

lessons.title: Code review workflow
lessons.body:
Reviewers of test code should check:

- Does the test check the requirement, not just “no exception”?

- Are assertions specific, with useful failure messages?

- Are timeouts bounded? Are waits polling with a deadline instead of fixed sleep?

- Does the test clean up (power state, configuration) even when it fails?

- Does it need exclusive hardware? Is that declared (marker, lock)?

- No hardcoded IP addresses, passwords or tokens.

- Will it be stable in CI, or does it depend on timing or order?

lessons.title: Commit message conventions
lessons.body:
A widely used format (from the Git project itself):

```code
Short summary in imperative mood, about 50 characters
Explain WHY the change is needed and what it does, wrapped at ~72
characters. Mention the firmware behaviour, bug ID or requirement.
  Fixes: BMC-1234
```

Many teams also use **Conventional Commits** (fix:, feat:, test:, ci: prefixes), which tools can use to generate release notes. Pick one convention and enforce it in review. Examples for test code:

```code
  test: add redundancy check for PSU hot-removal
  fix(ci): publish JUnit report even when pytest crashes
  ci: run smoke suite on every pull request
Bad: update, fix, changes, asdf.
```

lessons.title: Pull request quality checks
lessons.body:
A good pull request:

1. Has one purpose. “Add PSU test **and** refactor the client **and** bump pytest” is three PRs.

2. Describes what, why and how it was tested (e.g. “ran smoke + PSU suite on simulator; lab run #812”).

3. Is small enough to review in under 30 minutes.

4. Passes automated checks: tests, lint, report publishing.

5. Mentions any new hardware, credential or Jenkins requirement.

lessons.title: Tagging and releases
lessons.body:
A **tag** is a permanent name for a commit, typically a version. Use annotated tags (they store author, date and message). **[EXECUTED]**

```code
$ git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "First regression baseline"
$ git tag -n
v1.0.0          First regression baseline
$ git push origin v1.0.0          # tags are not pushed by default
$ git describe
v1.0.0
```

In embedded validation, tag the test suite version that qualified a firmware release, e.g. tests-fw-2.16.0, so the exact qualification can be rerun later.

lessons.title: Cherry-picking
lessons.body:
git cherry-pick <commit> copies one commit onto your current branch as a new commit. Typical use: a test fix landed on main and must also go to release/2.16.

```code
  git switch release/2.16
  git cherry-pick -x a1b2c3d     # -x records "cherry picked from commit a1b2c3d"
python -m pytest -m smoke      # always re-test on the target branch
git push
```

Use it for small, self-contained fixes. Cherry-picking large features creates duplicate commits and confusing history.

lessons.title: Reverting commits
lessons.body:
git revert <commit> creates a **new** commit that undoes an earlier one. History is preserved, so it is safe on shared branches. **[EXECUTED]**

```code
$ git revert --no-edit HEAD
[main abed0e8] Revert "Enable debug logging"
 1 file changed, 1 deletion(-)
$ git log --oneline -3
abed0e8 Revert "Enable debug logging"
d72bc44 Enable debug logging
335fbb7 Merge branch 'feature/longer-timeout'
```

Reverting a merge commit needs -m 1 to say which parent is the mainline.

lessons.title: Reset versus revert
lessons.body:
git reset moves the current branch pointer to another commit.

| Mode | Branch pointer | Staging area | Working files | Typical use |
| --soft | moved | keeps changes | unchanged | redo the last |
| staged | commit message/ content |
| --mixed (default) | moved | reset | unchanged | unstage everything, keep edits |
| --hard | moved | reset | overwritten | throw away local work completely |

**[EXECUTED]**

```code
$ git commit -qam "WIP wrong commit"
$ git reset --soft HEAD~1
$ git status --short
M  config.py          # the change is back in staging, the commit is gone
                                   git revert             git reset
```

| Rewrites history | no | yes (for the branch it moves) |
| Safe after push to shared branch | yes | no |

```code
git revert             git reset
```

| Effect | new “undo” commit | commits disappear from the branch |

**Operations that rewrite history** (avoid on shared branches): reset (of pushed commits), rebase, commit --amend, cherry-pick-then-force-push replacements, filter-repo/ filter-branch, and any push --force. They change commit hashes, so everyone who already has the old commits gets diverged histories and confusing conflicts. Use them only on private branches, or with team agreement (for example, when removing a leaked secret).

lessons.title: Recovering from common mistakes
lessons.body:
| Mistake | Recovery |
| Wrong last commit message (not pushed) | git commit --amend |
| Forgot a file in last commit (not pushed) | git add file && git commit --amend --no-edit |
| Committed to main instead of a branch (not | git branch feature/x then git reset --hard |
| pushed) | origin/main on main |
| Bad commit already pushed | git revert <hash> |
| Deleted a branch with unmerged work | find it in git reflog, then git branch <name> |

```code
<hash>
```

| reset --hard too far | git reflog, then git reset --hard HEAD@{n} |
| Uncommitted edits needed elsewhere | git stash push -m "msg", later git stash pop |

**Lab 3.1 — recover a deleted branch with the reflog [EXECUTED].** The reflog records every position HEAD has had, locally, for about 90 days by default.

```code
$ git switch -qc temp
$ echo 'Y=2' >> config.py && git commit -qam "Important experiment"
$ git switch -q main
$ git branch -D temp
Deleted branch temp (was bf1ab86).
$ git reflog -5
abed0e8 HEAD@{0}: checkout: moving from temp to main
bf1ab86 HEAD@{1}: commit: Important experiment
abed0e8 HEAD@{2}: checkout: moving from main to temp
abed0e8 HEAD@{3}: reset: moving to HEAD~1
a94d406 HEAD@{4}: commit: WIP wrong commit
$ git branch recovered bf1ab86
$ git log --oneline -1 recovered
bf1ab86 Important experiment
```

Uncommitted work is **not** in the reflog. Commit (or stash) often.

lessons.title: Reviewing diffs before committing
lessons.body:
```code
git status
git diff                         # what is not staged yet
git add -p                       # stage only what belongs in this commit
git diff --staged                # final check
git diff --staged --stat         # quick list of files
git diff --staged | grep -iE 'password|token|secret|BEGIN .*PRIVATE KEY'
```

lessons.title: Managing test scripts and configuration safely
lessons.body:
- Keep **non-secret** configuration in Git (config/sim.yaml, timeouts, expected sensors). Keep **secrets** out of Git; inject them at runtime (Chapter 19).

- Provide templates (config/lab.example.yaml) with placeholders; real lab files live in a private repository or are generated by the pipeline.

- Separate test logic (Python) from environment data (YAML), so the same tests run on simulator and lab (Projects 2 and 3).

- Review configuration changes as carefully as code: a wrong expected_firmware makes every run fail or, worse, pass against the wrong firmware.

source.section: 3.11 Managing test scripts and configuration safely

lessons.title: Exercises
lessons.body:
**3.1** You pushed a commit that changed a test threshold incorrectly; three colleagues already pulled. Undo it. **Solution:** git revert <hash>, push. Do not reset: it would rewrite shared history.

**3.2** A fix on main (c0ffee1) must go to release/2.16. **Solution:** git switch release/2.16 && git cherry-pick -x c0ffee1, run the release smoke suite, push via a PR targeting the release branch.

**3.3** Your last local commit contains a debug print(password). Not pushed. **Solution:** remove the line, git add, git commit --amend --no-edit, verify with git show. If it **was** pushed, treat it as a leaked secret (Chapter 5): rotate the credential first.

lessons.title: Creating and organising repositories
lessons.body: Choose a clear name (bmc-regression-tests, not scripts2), a default branch (main), a licence for public projects, and an owner (personal account or organisation). Teams usually keep one repository per independent component: test framework, test suites, pipeline library. Do not mix unrelated projects.

lessons.title: A repository structure for test automation
lessons.body:
```code
bmc-regression-tests/
├── README.md               # what, how to run, requirements, limitations
├── Jenkinsfile             # pipeline definition, reviewed like code
├── requirements.txt        # pinned dependencies
├── pytest.ini              # markers, test paths, defaults
├── .gitignore
├── CODEOWNERS              # who must review which paths (GitHub/GitLab)
├── config/
│   ├── sim.yaml
│   └── lab.example.yaml    # template only
├── src/<package>/          # framework / client code
├── tests/
│   ├── smoke/
│   └── regression/
├── scripts/                # setup, diagnostics, log collection
└── docs/                   # architecture, how to add a test
```

This is exactly the shape of Projects 2 and 3.

source.section: 4.2 A repository structure for test automation

lessons.title: README files
lessons.body: A README answers, in this order: what is this; how do I run it (copy-paste commands); what does it need (Python version, hardware, credentials, plugins); how is it organised; how do I add a test; known limitations; who owns it. The three project READMEs in Part VII are worked examples.

lessons.title: Issues, pull requests and reviews
lessons.body:
- **Issues** track bugs, test gaps and tasks. Link PRs to issues (“Fixes #42”).

- **Pull requests** carry the change, the discussion and the CI results.

- **Reviews**: reviewers can comment, approve or request changes.

- **CODEOWNERS** automatically requests reviews from the right people:

```code
# CODEOWNERS
/Jenkinsfile           @org/test-infra
/src/                  @org/test-infra
/tests/firmware/       @org/fw-validation
```

lessons.title: Branch protection and required checks
lessons.body:
GitHub offers **branch protection rules** and the newer **rulesets** (Settings → Rules). Typical settings for main:

| Setting | Why |
| Require a pull request before merging | no unreviewed changes |
| Require approvals (1–2) | four-eyes principle |
| Require status checks to pass (e.g. ci/jenkins/ | broken tests cannot merge |

```code
smoke)
```

| Require branches to be up to date | CI tested the actual merge result |
| Block force pushes and deletion | protects history |
| Require signed commits (optional) | authorship assurance |

A status check is a pass/fail result that CI reports to the commit. Jenkins reports it through the GitHub Branch Source / Checks integration (Chapter 18). GitLab: “protected branches” + “pipelines must succeed”. Gerrit: the Verified label set by CI.

lessons.title: Release tags
lessons.body: Create releases from annotated tags (v1.2.0). On GitHub, a Release adds notes and downloadable assets to a tag. For test suites, record which firmware versions the release qualified.

lessons.title: Repository secrets
lessons.body: GitHub Actions has encrypted **repository/organisation/environment secrets** (Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions). They are injected into workflow runs and masked in logs. They are **not** visible to Jenkins; Jenkins has its own Credentials store (Chapter 19). Secrets are not passed to workflows triggered from forks by default, which protects against malicious pull requests.

lessons.title: GitHub Actions fundamentals — a comparison with Jenkins
lessons.body:
A minimal workflow that runs Project 1’s tests on every push and pull request **[REVIEWED]**:

```code
# .github/workflows/tests.yml
name: tests
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
jobs:
  pytest:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 15
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v7
        with:
          python-version: "3.13"
      - run: pip install -r requirements.txt
      - run: python -m pytest --junitxml=reports/junit.xml
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        if: always()
        with:
          name: reports
          path: reports/
```

| Concept | Jenkins | GitHub Actions |
| Pipeline definition | Jenkinsfile (Groovy DSL) | .github/workflows/*.yml |
| Runs on | agents you operate | GitHub-hosted or self-hosted runners |
| Hardware labs | natural fit (agents in the lab) | needs self-hosted runners in the lab |
| Secrets | Credentials plugin | Actions secrets |
| Extensions | plugins | marketplace actions |
| Test reports | JUnit plugin, trends | artifacts; reports need extra actions |

```code
Version note: actions/checkout@v7, actions/setup-python@v7 and actions/upload-artifact@v7
```

were the major versions shown in the official READMEs in October 2026; check them again before use.

Embedded teams commonly use Jenkins for hardware-in-the-loop work because agents can live inside the lab network next to the devices.

source.section: 4.8 GitHub Actions fundamentals — a comparison with Jenkins

lessons.title: CI status checks
lessons.body: When Jenkins finishes a build for a commit, it can post success/failure/pending to the hosting service. The PR page shows the result and, with branch protection, blocks merging until it is green. If the check never appears, see Chapter 18 (webhook or credentials problems).

lessons.title: Public versus private repositories
lessons.body:
| Public | Private |
| Who can read | anyone | invited people/teams |
| Use for | portfolio, open source | employer code, lab configuration |
| Risk | any secret is exposed to the | still leaks via forks, copies, |
| world instantly | laptops |

**Rule:** employer code, internal hostnames, lab IP plans, logs from real products and firmware images never go into a public repository, even “temporarily”.

lessons.title: Preventing credential and proprietary-code exposure
lessons.body:
1. Use synthetic data and simulators for public projects (as this book does).

2. Keep .env, *.local.yaml, keys and dumps in .gitignore.

3. Enable secret scanning and push protection where available (GitHub offers both).

4. Add a pre-commit secret scanner (e.g. gitleaks or detect-secrets) locally and in CI.

5. Review git diff --staged for hostnames, IPs, serial numbers, customer names.

6. Read your employer’s policy before publishing anything derived from work.

lessons.title: Exercises
lessons.body:
**4.1** Create a public GitHub repository for Project 1, protect main (PR required, one approval, required check), and add the Actions workflow above. Open a PR that breaks a test and confirm merge is blocked. **Solution outline:** Settings → Rules → New branch ruleset (or Branches → Add rule), target main, enable “Require a pull request”, “Require status checks” (select pytest after it has run once), “Block force pushes”. The failing PR shows a red ✗ and the merge button is disabled.

**4.2** Write a CODEOWNERS file that requires the infra team for Jenkinsfile and scripts/, and the firmware team for tests/firmware/. **Solution:** see the CODEOWNERS example above, adding /scripts/ @org/test-infra.

lessons.title: HTTPS
lessons.body:
Hosting services no longer accept your account password for Git over HTTPS; GitHub stopped in August 2021. Use a **personal access token** (fine-grained where possible) or a credential manager.

| Error | Likely cause using account password remote: Support for password authentication |

```code
was removed
```

wrong/expired token, missing scope fatal: Authentication failed for

```code
'https://...'
```

| remote: Repository not found (but it exists) | token lacks access to that repo/org, or SSO not authorised |
| 403 | authenticated but no permission |

lessons.title: SSH
lessons.body:
```code
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "asha@example.com"     # creates ~/.ssh/id_ed25519(.pub)
cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub                       # add this PUBLIC key to your account
ssh -T git@github.com                           # test: prints a greeting with your
username
ssh -vT git@github.com                          # verbose: which key was offered?
```

| Error | Cause | Fix |
| Permission denied (publickey) | key not added, wrong key | add key; ssh-add; ~/.ssh/ |
| offered | config IdentityFile |
| Host key verification failed | host not in known_hosts | verify fingerprint from the provider’s docs, then add |
| WARNING: REMOTE HOST | host key changed (or MITM) | stop, verify with the provider |
| IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED! | before updating |

Never “fix” host-key errors with StrictHostKeyChecking=no in CI: it disables the protection against connecting to an impostor.

lessons.title: Remote URL problems
lessons.body:
```code
git remote -v                                  # show remotes
git remote set-url origin git@github.com:org/bmc-tests.git
git ls-remote origin                           # does the remote answer? which branches?
```

Typical problems: typo in the URL, HTTPS URL used with an SSH-only setup, renamed repository, corporate proxy blocking SSH (port 22).

lessons.title: Merge conflicts — quick reference
lessons.body: git status lists conflicted files; git diff shows markers; git merge --abort or git rebase --abort undoes; git mergetool opens a visual tool; resolve, test, git add, then git commit (merge) or git rebase --continue (rebase).

lessons.title: Detached HEAD
lessons.body:
HEAD normally points to a branch. If you check out a tag or a commit, it points directly to the commit: **detached HEAD**. **[EXECUTED]**

```code
$ git switch --detach HEAD~2
HEAD is now at 335fbb7 Merge branch 'feature/longer-timeout'
$ git status | head -1
HEAD detached at 335fbb7
```

Looking around is safe. If you make commits here and then switch away, they belong to no branch and are easy to lose. Fix: git switch -c rescue-branch before leaving. Jenkins checks out commits in detached HEAD on purpose: it builds an exact commit, not a moving branch.

lessons.title: Accidental commits
lessons.body:
| Situation | Fix |
| Committed to wrong branch, not pushed | git branch correct-branch; git reset --hard HEAD~1 on the wrong one |
| Committed a generated file | git rm --cached file, add to .gitignore, commit |
| Committed a secret, not pushed | amend/reset it away and still consider it exposed if it left your machine |
| Committed a secret, pushed | rotate immediately, then clean history (below) |

lessons.title: Large files and unwanted artifacts
lessons.body:
Git keeps every version of every file forever. A 64 MB firmware image committed ten times is 640 MB in every clone, and every Jenkins checkout.

- Prevent: .gitignore for *.mtd, *.tar, images/, reports/.

- Store binaries in an artifact repository (Artifactory, Nexus, S3, Jenkins archives) and reference them by version and checksum.

- If a team truly needs versioned binaries in Git, use **Git LFS**, which stores pointers in Git and contents on a separate server.

- Find what is big: git rev-list --objects --all | git cat-file --batch-check='%

```code
(objecttype) %(objectname) %(objectsize) %(rest)' | sort -k3 -n | tail
```

Removing from the latest commit does **not** shrink the repository; the file is still in history. Removing it from history requires a rewrite (below).

lessons.title: Secret detection and credential rotation
lessons.body:
If a password, token or private key reaches a remote repository:

1. **Rotate first.** Revoke/change the credential immediately. Assume it is compromised: clones, forks, CI caches and bots may already have it. Cleaning history does not “un-leak” a secret.

2. Check access logs for misuse, and tell your security team.

3. Remove it from history with **git-filter-repo** (recommended by the Git project over git filter-branch), coordinate a force push, ask everyone to re-clone, and ask the host to purge cached views if needed.

4. Add a scanner so it does not recur.

```code
# [CONCEPT] remove a file from all history (rewrites every hash - coordinate first!)
pip install git-filter-repo
git filter-repo --invert-paths --path config/lab-secrets.yaml
```

GitHub’s documentation page “Removing sensitive data from a repository” walks through the provider-specific steps.

lessons.title: Safe use of .gitignore
lessons.body:
- Ignore patterns are relative to the .gitignore location; /reports/ matches only at the root; reports/ anywhere.

- !keep.me re-includes a file.

- Debug a rule: git check-ignore -v path/to/file prints which rule matched.

- Commit .gitignore; personal patterns go in .git/info/exclude.

lessons.title: Recovering lost work
lessons.body:
| Lost what | Where to look |
| Commits after reset/rebase/branch delete | git reflog |
| Stashed changes | git stash list; dropped stash: git fsck --lost-found (dangling commits) |
| Uncommitted, never staged edits | not in Git: editor history/backups only |
| Staged but never committed | git fsck --lost-found can find dangling blobs |

lessons.title: Debugging failed checkout operations in Jenkins
lessons.body:
Jenkins’ Git plugin runs ordinary Git commands on the **agent**, using credentials from the Jenkins Credentials store. So debug it like Git, but on the agent, as the agent’s user.

| Console message | Likely cause | Investigation |
| Cannot run program "git" | Git not installed on the agent | which git on the agent; Global |
| or not on PATH | Tool Configuration |
| wrong credential ID, key not | check job’s credential; test | Permission denied (publickey) |
| added as deploy key | with ssh -T as the agent user |
| Host key verification failed | agent’s known_hosts lacks the | Git Host Key Verification |
| server | Configuration in Manage Jenkins → Security; add the verified key |
| Couldn't find any revision to | branch specifier wrong (*/main | check branch name and |
| build | vs */master) | refspec |
| commit not fetched (shallow | increase depth or disable | fatal: reference is not a |
| tree | clone, force-pushed) | shallow; check force pushes |
| timeouts on clone | huge repo / slow network | shallow clone, reference repo, clean large files, increase checkout timeout |
| an earlier Git process crashed | clean workspace (cleanWs() / | index.lock: File exists |
| in the workspace | wipe workspace) |

Reproduce manually:

```code
# on the agent, as the jenkins user
cd /tmp && GIT_TRACE=1 GIT_SSH_COMMAND="ssh -v" git ls-remote git@github.com:org/bmc-
tests.git
```

source.section: 5.10 Debugging failed checkout operations in Jenkins

lessons.title: Troubleshooting scenarios
lessons.body:
**Scenario 5.1 — “It works on my laptop but Jenkins can’t clone.”** Laptop uses your personal SSH key; Jenkins uses a deploy key credential. Check the job’s credential ID, confirm the deploy key is on the repository (read-only is enough), confirm host key verification on the agent. Prevention: one documented service credential per repository, least privilege.

**Scenario 5.2 — “My PR shows 400 changed files.”** You committed .venv/. Remove with git rm -r --cached .venv, add to .gitignore, amend or add a commit, force-push your feature branch with --force-with-lease.

**Scenario 5.3 — “A lab password is in a public repo commit from yesterday.”** Rotate the password now; review BMC access logs; report; then filter-repo and force-push; enable push protection and a pre-commit scanner.

lessons.title: Exercises
lessons.body:
**5.1** In a scratch repository, commit a file lab.env containing BMC_PASSWORD=example, then make it disappear from the latest commit and from history. **Solution:** for practice only (no real secret): git rm --cached lab.env, add lab.env to .gitignore, commit; then pip `install git-filter-repo and git filter-repo --invert-paths --path lab.env (on a fresh` clone, as the tool requires); verify with git log --all -- lab.env (no output). With a real secret, rotation would come first.

**5.2** A Jenkins checkout fails with Couldn't find any revision to build. Write your investigation steps. **Solution:** read the branch specifier in the job (*/master vs */main); run git ls-remote <url> as the agent user with the job’s credential to list real branch names; fix the specifier; for multibranch jobs, rescan the repository.

**5.3** You see HEAD detached at v1.0.0 and you have made two commits. Save them. **Solution:** git switch -c fix-from-v1 before switching away; if you already left, find the commits in git reflog and create the branch at the right hash.

lessons.title: Continuous Integration (CI)
lessons.body:
**Continuous Integration** means every change is merged into a shared branch frequently (at least daily) and every change is **automatically built and tested**. The goal is to find integration problems minutes after they are introduced, while the author still remembers the change, instead of weeks later during a release crunch.

CI is a practice supported by a tool. Installing Jenkins does not give you CI if people keep long-lived branches and nobody looks at red builds.

lessons.title: Continuous Delivery versus Continuous Deployment
lessons.body:
| Continuous Delivery | Continuous Deployment |
| Every change is built, tested | yes | yes |

and packaged

| Every passing change is | yes | yes |

releasable

| Release to production | a human decides | automatic |
| Common in firmware | yes (a release manager | rare: shipping firmware to |
| approves) | devices has physical risk |

For BMC firmware, “deployment” usually means publishing a validated image to a release repository or flashing it on lab fleets, not pushing to customers automatically.

lessons.title: Build, test, package and deployment stages
lessons.body:
```code
code change
    │
    ▼
┌────────┐   ┌──────────┐   ┌────────────┐   ┌───────────┐   ┌───────────┐
│ Source │──►│  Build   │──►│ Unit/fast  │──►│ Integration│──►│ Package & │
│ (Git)  │   │ (deps,   │   │ tests      │   │ / HW tests │   │ publish   │
└────────┘   │ compile) │   └────────────┘   └───────────┘   └───────────┘
             └──────────┘         │                │               │
                                  ▼                ▼               ▼
                            reports, logs,  results, logs,   artifact with
                            quality gate    quality gate      version + hash
```

- **Build**: create the thing to test (firmware image, Python venv, container).

- **Test**: fast tests first, slow/hardware tests later.

- **Package**: produce a versioned, checksummed artifact.

- **Deploy/release**: put the artifact somewhere it will be used.

source.section: 6.3 Build, test, package and deployment stages

lessons.title: Feedback loops
lessons.body:
The value of CI is fast, trustworthy feedback. Design for it:

| Loop | Target time | Example |
| Developer laptop | seconds–minutes | unit tests, simulator smoke |
| Pull request CI | < 15 minutes | lint, unit, simulator suite |
| Post-merge on hardware | < 1 hour | smoke on one lab BMC |
| Nightly | hours | full regression across platforms |
| Release qualification | days | stress, update/rollback, long-run |

Slow feedback is ignored. Unreliable feedback (flaky tests) is worse: people learn to click “rebuild” instead of reading failures.

lessons.title: Automated regression
lessons.body: A **regression** is something that used to work and now does not. Automated regression testing reruns the existing suite on every new build, so a firmware change that breaks fan control is caught the same day. The suite only protects what it checks: missing assertions are silent gaps.

lessons.title: Quality gates
Pipeline triggers
lessons.body:
| Trigger | Use |
| Push / webhook | run on every change |
| Pull request | validate before merge |
| Schedule (cron) | nightly/weekly full regression |
| Upstream job | firmware build finished → run tests on the new image |
| Manual with parameters | rerun a suite against a chosen firmware |
| SCM polling | fallback when webhooks are impossible (Chapter 18) |

lessons.title: Artifacts and reports
lessons.body:
- **Artifacts**: files kept after the build: JUnit XML, HTML report, logs, BMC snapshots, pip freeze, firmware metadata.

- **Reports**: human/machine views of results: test counts, failures, trends.

Rule: **the workspace is temporary; artifacts are evidence.** Anything needed to investigate a failure next week must be archived, because agents are cleaned and devices are reflashed.

lessons.title: Benefits and limitations
lessons.body:
| Benefits | Limitations |
| Defects found early and cheaply | Only as good as the tests and assertions |
| Repeatable, documented process | Pipelines are software: they have bugs and need maintenance |
| Exact link between code, firmware and results | Hardware is scarce: queues and contention |
| Less manual effort per run | Flaky tests destroy trust |
| Evidence for audits and releases | Security: CI has credentials and network access |

lessons.title: CI/CD in embedded firmware and hardware validation
lessons.body:
Embedded pipelines add physical steps: flash an image, power-cycle, wait for boot, talk over Redfish/IPMI/SSH/UART, collect console logs, restore the device. These steps are slow, can fail for physical reasons (cable, PDU, network switch), and can leave a device unusable. Chapter 7 explains the architecture that copes with this.

```code
firmware commit ─► firmware build ─► image + version + checksum
                                            │ triggers
                                            ▼
test-code commit ─► test pipeline: reserve device ─► flash (lab) ─► health check
                                            │
                       smoke ─► regression ─► collect logs ─► publish results
                                            │
                                   release device (always)
```

source.section: 6.10 CI/CD in embedded firmware and hardware validation

lessons.title: Exercises
lessons.body:
**6.1** Classify each as CI, continuous delivery, or continuous deployment: (a) every merged firmware change produces a signed image ready for release approval; (b) every PR runs unit tests; (c) every passing build is automatically installed on all production servers. **Solution:** (a) continuous delivery, (b) CI, (c) continuous deployment.

**6.2** Propose three quality gates for a BMC regression pipeline. **Solution (examples):** health check must pass before tests; firmware version must match the requested build; JUnit report must exist with ≥ N tests; zero smoke failures before regression starts.

lessons.title: The big picture
lessons.body:
```code
┌─────────────┐  webhook   ┌──────────────────────┐
│ Git hosting │──────────► │ Jenkins controller   │  schedules, stores results,
│ (code, PRs) │ ◄──status──│ (no builds on it)    │  credentials, UI
└─────────────┘            └─────────┬────────────┘
                                     │ dispatches by label
         ┌───────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────┐
         ▼                           ▼                             ▼
┌─────────────────┐        ┌───────────────────┐        ┌────────────────────┐
│ build agents    │        │ test agents       │        │ lab agents         │
│ label: build    │        │ label: linux &&   │        │ label: bmc-lab     │
│ firmware builds │        │ python3 (sim,     │        │ in lab network     │
│ (Yocto/bitbake) │        │ unit, containers) │        │ serial adapters    │
└───────┬─────────┘        └───────────────────┘        └─────────┬──────────┘
        │ publishes image                                         │ Redfish/SSH/UART
        ▼                                                         ▼
┌─────────────────┐                                     ┌────────────────────┐
│ artifact store  │ ── image + checksum ───────────────►│ DUTs: BMC boards,  │
│ (images, logs)  │                                     │ PDUs, serial, JTAG │
└─────────────────┘                                     └────────────────────┘
```

lessons.title: Source control
lessons.body: Separate repositories (or directories) for firmware, test framework, test suites and pipeline libraries, each versioned. A test result should record **all** of: firmware version/ commit, test-suite commit, framework version, configuration version, device identity.

lessons.title: Jenkins controller and agents
lessons.body: The **controller** schedules jobs, stores configuration, credentials and build history, and serves the UI. **Agents** run the actual work. Best practice is to run **zero executors on the controller**, so that untrusted or heavy build steps never execute where all credentials live (Chapter 9).

lessons.title: Build environments
lessons.body: Firmware builds (OpenBMC uses the Yocto Project/BitBake) need large disks, many CPUs and caches (downloads, sstate cache). Test-code “builds” are light: create a Python virtual environment and install pinned dependencies, ideally in a container.

lessons.title: Test environments
lessons.body:
| Environment | Contents | Use |
| Simulation | Python simulator, mock Redfish | PR checks, framework tests service |
| Emulation | QEMU running a BMC image | boot/service tests without |
| (OpenBMC supports some | boards QEMU machines) |
| Hardware lab | real boards, PDUs, serial | regression, update, power, sensors |

Each layer catches different defects. Simulation catches test-code bugs cheaply; only hardware catches real sensor, timing and flash problems.

lessons.title: Test devices and lab infrastructure
lessons.body: A typical bench: DUT (server/BMC board), managed PDU for remote power cycling, serial console server or USB-serial adapter, management network switch, sometimes a JTAG/flash programmer for recovery, and the lab agent machine. An **inventory** (YAML file, database or Lockable Resources labels) records each device’s address, platform, capabilities and owner.

lessons.title: Hardware reservation and resource contention
lessons.body:
Two jobs using the same BMC at once produce garbage: one reboots it while the other reads sensors; both open the same serial port; one flashes firmware the other is testing. Solutions, from simplest to most capable:

| Mechanism | Scope | Notes |
| One agent per device, 1 | per agent | simple; wastes agent capacity |

executor

| per job | does not stop other jobs | disableConcurrentBuilds() |
| Lockable Resources plugin | whole Jenkins | named devices or labelled |
| lock() | pools; recommended |
| File lock on the agent (Project 3 | one machine | protects against local scripts |
| DeviceLock) | too |
| Mechanism | Scope | Notes |
| Lab reservation service | whole lab | needed when humans and multiple CI systems share devices |

Always combine reservation with **timeouts** (do not hold a device forever) and **release in a finally/post block**.

lessons.title: Firmware image management
lessons.body:
- Store images in an artifact repository with immutable versions.

- Record a checksum (SHA-256) and verify it on the agent before flashing.

- Record build metadata: firmware commit, build number, build options, signing key ID.

- Never test “latest.bin”: resolve “latest” to an exact version at the start of the pipeline and log it.

lessons.title: Test orchestration
lessons.body: The pipeline orchestrates; Python executes. Jenkins decides where and in which order (reserve, prepare, run suite, collect, release). pytest and the framework decide how a test talks to the device. Keeping this split (Chapter 12) lets you run the same tests from a laptop.

lessons.title: Result collection, log retention, reporting, notifications
lessons.body:
- **Collect**: JUnit XML, HTML report, framework logs, device snapshots (Redfish JSON), console/UART logs, journalctl from the BMC, environment metadata.

- **Retain**: Jenkins buildDiscarder keeps N builds; important results (release qualification) go to long-term storage.

- **Report**: JUnit trends in Jenkins; a short classified failure summary.

- **Notify**: the right owner, with the failure category and a link (Chapter 22).

source.section: 7.10 Result collection, log retention, reporting, notifications

lessons.title: Why embedded CI/CD differs from web pipelines
lessons.body:
| Aspect | Typical web app | Embedded / BMC validation |
| Test target | containers, created on demand | scarce physical boards |
| Parallelism | scale out freely | limited by devices; locking required |
| Duration | minutes | flash + boot alone can take 10– 30 minutes |
| Aspect | Typical web app | Embedded / BMC validation |
| Failure sources | mostly code | code, firmware, hardware, cabling, power, network |
| Cleanup | delete container | restore power state, config, maybe reflash/recover |
| Risk | rollback a deploy | a bad flash can brick a board |
| Evidence | app logs | console/UART, BMC journal, sensor data, timing |
| Security | cloud credentials | lab credentials, physical access, isolated networks |

source.section: 7.11 Why embedded CI/CD differs from web pipelines

lessons.title: Exercises
lessons.body:
**7.1** Draw the architecture for a team with 2 platforms × 3 boards each, one firmware build per hour, and PR checks on test code. **Solution outline:** build agents for firmware; artifact store; container-based agents for PR simulation; two lab agents (one per platform, label bmc-lab && platform-a), Lockable Resources with labels platform-a (3 resources) and platform-b; nightly full regression; post-build smoke triggered by firmware builds.

**7.2** List the evidence you would archive for a failed firmware-update test. **Solution:** image name, version, SHA-256; before/after version; update task status history with timestamps; console log across reboot; BMC journal; Redfish snapshots; test log; Jenkins console; agent diagnostics.

lessons.title: Build tools and dependency installation
lessons.body: For Python test code, “build” means: choose an interpreter, create an isolated environment, install exact dependencies. Tools: venv + pip (standard library, used in this book), or newer tools such as uv or Poetry. The principles are identical.

lessons.title: Virtual environments
lessons.body:
A virtual environment is a folder with its own Python and site-packages, so projects do not share or break each other’s dependencies.

```code
python3 -m venv .venv             # create
. .venv/bin/activate              # activate (Linux/macOS);
Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
which python                      # .../.venv/bin/python
deactivate
```

Always run tools as python -m pip and python -m pytest: that guarantees they use the interpreter you think they use.

lessons.title: Requirements files and dependency pinning
lessons.body:
```code
# requirements.txt (Project 2)
pytest==9.1.1
pytest-html==4.2.0
pytest-timeout==2.4.0
requests==2.34.2
PyYAML==6.0.3
```

== pins exact versions. Without pins, a new release of a dependency can change behaviour overnight, and last night’s “regression” is really a pytest upgrade. Pinning direct dependencies is the minimum; for full reproducibility also pin transitive dependencies (pip freeze > constraints.txt, or a lock file from a tool like pip-tools or uv). Every pipeline in this book archives pip freeze output so you can see exactly what ran.

Update pins deliberately: a pull request “bump pytest to X”, with CI green.

lessons.title: Reproducible environments
lessons.body: Reproducible means: same inputs → same environment → same results. Inputs include the Python version, OS packages, dependency versions, environment variables, configuration files and the test-code commit. Pinning, containers (Chapter 21) and recording metadata get you most of the way.

lessons.title: Python project structure
lessons.body:
```code
p1-sensor-ci/
├── src/sensortools/      # importable package ("src layout": tests can't
│   ├── __init__.py       #  accidentally import from the working directory)
│   ├── parser.py
│   ├── thresholds.py
│   └── cli.py
├── tests/
│   ├── conftest.py       # shared fixtures
│   ├── test_parser.py
│   ├── test_thresholds.py
│   └── test_cli.py
├── pytest.ini            # configuration
├── requirements.txt
└── scripts/run_tests.sh
```

pytest.ini for Project 1:

```code
[pytest]
testpaths = tests
pythonpath = src
addopts = -ra --strict-markers
markers =
    smoke: fast checks run on every commit
junit_family = xunit2
```

- pythonpath = src adds src to sys.path for tests.

- -ra prints a short summary of all non-passing outcomes.

- --strict-markers makes a typo like @pytest.mark.smok an error instead of a silently unselected test.

lessons.title: Running pytest from the command line
lessons.body:
| Command | Effect |
| python -m pytest | run everything under testpaths |
| python -m pytest -q | quieter output one test python -m pytest tests/ |

```code
test_parser.py::test_parse_valid_line
```

| python -m pytest -k "threshold and not cli" | select by name expression |
| python -m pytest -m smoke | select by marker stop at first failure python -m pytest -x |
| python -m pytest --lf | rerun last failures (local debugging) more detail python -m pytest -vv --tb=long |
| python -m pytest --junitxml=reports/junit.xml | machine-readable report list tests without running python -m pytest --collect-only -q |

source.section: 8.6 Running pytest from the command line

lessons.title: Test selection and markers
lessons.body:
```code
@pytest.mark.smoke
def test_parse_valid_line(): ...
```

**[EXECUTED]** Project 1 has 15 tests, 3 marked smoke:

```code
$ python -m pytest -m smoke -q
...                                                                      [100%]
3 passed, 12 deselected in 0.02s
```

lessons.title: Exit codes
lessons.body:
pytest’s exit code tells the pipeline what kind of outcome happened:

| Code | Meaning |
| 0 | all collected tests passed |
| 1 | tests ran and some failed |
| 2 | interrupted, including errors during collection |
| 3 | internal error |
| 4 | command-line usage error |
| 5 | no tests collected |
| 6 | warnings exceeded --max-warnings |

**[EXECUTED]** each case, in Project 1:

```code
$ python -m pytest -q                              # one test deliberately broken
FAILED tests/test_thresholds.py::test_evaluate_p12v[11.4-critical] - Assertio...
1 failed, 14 passed in 0.05s
rc=1
$ python -m pytest -q -m nosuchmarker              # nothing selected
rc=5
$ python -m pytest -q --bogus                      # bad option
rc=4
$ python -m pytest -q                              # file with a syntax error added
ERROR tests/test_broken.py
!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!! Interrupted: 1 error during collection !!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!
1 error in 0.33s
rc=2
```

This distinction is the foundation of good pipelines: **exit 1 means the product (or test expectations) failed; exit 2–5 mean the test run itself is broken.** A pipeline that treats every non-zero code the same loses that information; a pipeline that ignores non-zero codes reports broken runs as green.

lessons.title: Environment variables
lessons.body:
Use environment variables for things that change per run or are secret:

```code
import os
timeout = float(os.environ.get("REDFISH_TIMEOUT_S", "10"))   # default + override
password = os.environ["BMC_PASSWORD"]                          # required: KeyError if
missing
```

Prefer failing fast with a clear message over silently using a default for anything that matters (Project 2’s config.py raises ConfigError if lab credentials are missing).

lessons.title: Configuration management
lessons.body:
Order of precedence used throughout this book (highest first):

1. Pipeline parameters / environment variables (e.g. EXPECTED_FW)

2. Target configuration file (config/sim.yaml, config/bmc-lab-01.yaml)

3. Defaults in code

Validate configuration at startup: required keys, allowed values, **no secrets in files** (Project 3’s loader rejects password: keys).

lessons.title: Test reports and artifacts
lessons.body:
```code
python -m pytest \
  --junitxml=reports/junit.xml \
  --html=reports/report.html --self-contained-html
```

JUnit XML is for machines (Jenkins). HTML (pytest-html plugin) is for people. Keep both, plus the console log.

lessons.title: Lab 8.1 — a local pipeline before Jenkins [EXECUTED]
lessons.body:
Project 1’s scripts/run_tests.sh runs the same stages Jenkins will run:

```code
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Local "pipeline": the same steps Jenkins runs, so CI failures can be reproduced
locally.
# Usage: scripts/run_tests.sh [pytest marker expression, e.g. "smoke"]
set -euo pipefail
MARKER="${1:-}"
PYTHON="${PYTHON:-python3}"
REPORT_DIR="reports"
echo "== 1. Create virtual environment"
"$PYTHON" -m venv .venv
# shellcheck disable=SC1091
. .venv/bin/activate
echo "== 2. Install pinned dependencies"
python -m pip install --quiet --upgrade pip
python -m pip install --quiet -r requirements.txt
echo "== 3. Run tests"
mkdir -p "$REPORT_DIR"
ARGS=(--junitxml="$REPORT_DIR/junit.xml" --html="$REPORT_DIR/report.html" --self-
contained-html)
if [[ -n "$MARKER" ]]; then ARGS+=(-m "$MARKER"); fi
set +e
python -m pytest "${ARGS[@]}" 2>&1 | tee "$REPORT_DIR/pytest-console.log"
RC=${PIPESTATUS[0]}
set -e
echo "== pytest exit code: $RC"
exit "$RC"
```

Key techniques:

- set -euo pipefail: stop on errors, unset variables and failures inside pipes.

- set +e around pytest: we want to capture its exit code, not abort.

- ${PIPESTATUS[0]}: the exit code of pytest, not of tee. Without it, the pipeline would always see tee’s success (0). This is a classic cause of “failed tests reported as passed”.

- The script exits with pytest’s code, so callers (and Jenkins) see the truth.

Output:

```output
$ scripts/run_tests.sh
== 1. Create virtual environment
== 2. Install pinned dependencies
== 3. Run tests
platform linux -- Python 3.13.16, pytest-9.1.1, pluggy-1.6.0
rootdir: .../p1-sensor-ci
configfile: pytest.ini
testpaths: tests
plugins: html-4.2.0, metadata-3.1.1
collected 15 items
tests/test_cli.py ..                                                     [ 13%]
tests/test_parser.py .......                                             [ 60%]
tests/test_thresholds.py ......                                          [100%]
----- generated xml file: .../reports/junit.xml -----
- Generated html report: file:///.../reports/report.html -
============================== 15 passed in 0.06s ==============================
== pytest exit code: 0
```

lessons.title: Exercises
lessons.body:
**8.1** Add a regression marker to Project 1 and mark the CLI tests with it. What happens if you forget to register it in pytest.ini? **Solution:** with --strict-markers, collection fails with “‘regression’ not found in markers configuration option”, exit code 2 (an error during collection). Register it under markers =.

**8.2** Change run_tests.sh so that exit code 5 (no tests) is treated as a failure with a clear message. **Solution:** after computing RC: if [[ $RC -eq 5 ]]; then echo "ERROR: marker '$MARKER' selected no tests"; fi and keep exit "$RC" (5 is already non-zero, so the run fails).

lessons.title: What Jenkins does
lessons.body: Jenkins is an open-source automation server. It watches for events (a commit, a schedule, a button click), runs the steps you defined on a suitable machine, records the console output and results, keeps artifacts, and reports status back. Almost all of its useful features (Git, Pipeline, JUnit, credentials binding, locking) come from **plugins** on top of a small core.

lessons.title: Controller and agent architecture
lessons.body:
```code
┌──────────────────── Jenkins controller ────────────────────┐
│  web UI / REST API     job configs     build history        │
│  scheduler + queue     credentials     plugin code          │
│  JENKINS_HOME on disk  (executors: 0 recommended)           │
└──────────────┬───────────────────────────┬──────────────────┘
               │ remoting channel (TCP/WebSocket/SSH)
      ┌────────▼────────┐          ┌───────▼─────────┐
      │ agent: linux-01 │          │ agent: lab-01   │
      │ labels: linux   │          │ labels: bmc-lab │
      │  python3 docker │          │  platform-a     │
      │ executors: 4    │          │ executors: 1    │
      │ workspaces/...  │          │ /dev/ttyUSB0    │
      └─────────────────┘          └─────────────────┘
```

| Term | Meaning |
| Controller | The Jenkins server process: UI, scheduling, configuration, results |
| Agent | A machine (or container) connected to the controller that runs build steps |
| Node | Generic word for the controller or any agent |
| Executor | A slot for one concurrent build (or pipeline node block) on a node |
| Term | Meaning |
| Label | A tag on an agent (linux, python3, bmc-lab) used to select where to run |
| Job / Project | A configured task, e.g. “bmc-regression” |
| Build / Run | One execution of a job, numbered #1, #2… |
| Workspace | A directory on the agent where a build checks out and works |
| Queue | Builds waiting for a free executor with a matching label |

**How a build flows:** trigger → build enters the queue → scheduler finds an online node whose labels match and which has a free executor → the agent creates or reuses the workspace → steps run on the agent and stream their output to the controller → results and archived files are stored in JENKINS_HOME on the controller.

lessons.title: JENKINS_HOME and build history
lessons.body: JENKINS_HOME (e.g. /var/lib/jenkins for Linux packages, /var/jenkins_home in the official container) contains global configuration, jobs/<name>/config.xml, jobs/<name>/builds/<n>/ (logs, test results, archived artifacts), plugins and encrypted credentials. **Back it up**, and keep it on fast, reliable storage. Use buildDiscarder so build history does not fill the disk.

lessons.title: Freestyle jobs versus Pipeline jobs
lessons.body:
| Freestyle | Pipeline |
| Definition | web forms | Jenkinsfile code (Groovy-based DSL) |
| Version control | config lives in Jenkins | Jenkinsfile lives in Git, reviewed with the code |
| Multi-stage flow, parallelism | limited | native (stages, parallel, |

```code
matrix)
```

| Survives controller restart | no (build is lost) | yes for most steps (durable) |
| Conditional logic, locking, | plugin-dependent, awkward | first-class |

retries

| Learning curve | lowest | moderate |
| Recommended for new work | quick experiments | yes |

Freestyle is still useful to learn the moving parts (Chapter 10). Everything serious in this book is a Pipeline.

lessons.title: Installing Jenkins in a local lab
lessons.body: **Requirements (October 2026):** Jenkins LTS needs **Java 21 or Java 25**. Java 17 is no longer supported by current releases; an unsupported Java version prevents the controller from starting. Check jenkins.io → Documentation → Java support policy before installing. Give it at least 4 GB RAM and 50 GB disk for a lab.

source.section: 9.5 Installing Jenkins in a local lab

lessons.title: Option A — container (any OS with Docker) [REVIEWED]
lessons.body:
```code
docker volume create jenkins-data
docker run --name jenkins --restart=on-failure --detach \
  --publish 8080:8080 --publish 50000:50000 \
  --volume jenkins-data:/var/jenkins_home \
  jenkins/jenkins:lts-jdk21
docker exec jenkins cat /var/jenkins_home/secrets/initialAdminPassword
```

- Port 8080: web UI. Port 50000: inbound (TCP) agents; not needed for WebSocket or SSH agents.

- The named volume keeps JENKINS_HOME when the container is replaced.

- The official image has no Docker CLI. The Jenkins documentation shows how to build a custom image (with docker-ce-cli and the docker-workflow plugin) plus a Docker-in-Docker sidecar if pipelines must build containers. You do not need that for this book’s projects.

source.section: 9.5.1 Option A — container (any OS with Docker) [REVIEWED]

lessons.title: Option B — Linux package
lessons.body:
Debian/Ubuntu and Red Hat-family packages are published by the Jenkins project. The repository signing key rotates periodically, so copy the current commands from jenkins.io/doc/book/installing/linux/ rather than from old blog posts. After installation, Jenkins runs as a systemd service:

```code
sudo systemctl status jenkins
sudo journalctl -u jenkins -f              # controller log
sudo cat /var/lib/jenkins/secrets/initialAdminPassword
```

lessons.title: Option C — other platforms
lessons.body: Windows has an MSI installer (runs as a Windows service); macOS can use Homebrew (brew install jenkins-lts); any OS can run the generic WAR with java -jar jenkins.war --httpPort=8080. Paths, service managers and default users differ: Linux package → user jenkins, home /var/lib/jenkins; container → /var/jenkins_home; WAR → ~/.jenkins of the user who started it.

lessons.title: First-run setup
lessons.body:
1. Open http://localhost:8080, paste the initial admin password.

2. “Install suggested plugins” (includes Pipeline, Git, Credentials, Timestamper, Workspace Cleanup and others). Then add **JUnit** if missing, **HTML Publisher** (optional), **Lockable Resources** (for hardware), **Pipeline Graph View** (optional visualisation).

3. Create an admin user. Set the Jenkins URL (Manage Jenkins → System).

4. Set the controller’s executors to **0** (Manage Jenkins → Nodes → Built-In Node → Configure).

lessons.title: Adding a Linux agent
lessons.body:
Prepare the agent machine:

```code
sudo apt-get install -y openjdk-21-jre-headless git python3 python3-venv
sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash jenkins
```

Then in Jenkins: Manage Jenkins → Nodes → New Node, type Permanent Agent:

| Field | Example |
| Name | linux-01 |
| Number of executors | 2 (1 for hardware-attached agents) |
| Remote root directory | /home/jenkins/agent |
| Labels | linux python3 |
| Usage | “Only build jobs with label expressions matching this node” |
| Launch method | “Launch agents via SSH” (SSH Build Agents plugin) or inbound agent |

For an **inbound** agent, the node page shows the exact command to run on the agent, of `the form java -jar agent.jar -url <controller-url> -secret <secret> -name linux-01 -` webSocket -workDir /home/jenkins/agent. Copy it from the page (the secret is node-specific; treat it as a credential) and run it as a service on the agent.

lessons.title: Basic administration and troubleshooting
lessons.body:
| Problem | Where to look |
| UI down | systemctl status jenkins, journalctl -u |

```code
jenkins, container docker logs jenkins
```

| Builds stuck in queue | hover the queued item: “Waiting for next available executor on ‘bmc-lab’” means no online agent with that label is free |
| Agent offline | Nodes → agent → Log; Java version, network, secret, disk space |
| Problem | Where to look |
| Disk full | old builds (add buildDiscarder), huge artifacts, workspaces |
| Slow controller | builds running on the controller, too many plugins, large logs |
| Something odd after upgrade | Manage Jenkins → System Log, plugin compatibility warnings |

Useful pages: Manage Jenkins → System Information (properties, environment), Script Console (administrators only: it runs arbitrary code with full rights).

lessons.title: Plugin management and compatibility
lessons.body:
- Install only plugins you need; each one is code running with controller privileges and a possible security advisory.

- Update regularly, but test upgrades on a staging controller first.

- Read the plugin’s page for required Jenkins version and dependencies.

- Manage Jenkins → Plugins shows available updates and security warnings.

- Pin plugin versions for reproducible controllers (e.g. a plugins.txt used with jenkins-plugin-cli when building a controller image).

**Core vs plugin** (this book flags it everywhere):

| Feature | Provided by |
| Jobs, builds, agents, labels, executors, queue | core |
| Pipeline / Jenkinsfile | Pipeline plugin suite |
| Git checkout | Git plugin (+ Git client) |
| junit step, test trends | JUnit plugin |
| archiveArtifacts, fingerprint | core (exposed to Pipeline as steps) |
| withCredentials | Credentials Binding plugin (storage: Credentials plugin) |
| lock | Lockable Resources plugin Timestamper plugin timestamps() |
| cleanWs() | Workspace Cleanup plugin HTML Publisher plugin publishHTML |
| readJSON, readYaml | Pipeline Utility Steps plugin |
| Multibranch + GitHub PRs | Branch API + GitHub Branch Source plugins |

lessons.title: Exercises
lessons.body:
**9.1** Install Jenkins in a container, set controller executors to 0, add one agent labelled

```code
linux python3, and run a Pipeline job with pipeline { agent { label 'python3' } stages
{ stage('hi') { steps { sh 'python3 --version' } } } }. Expected: the console shows
Running on linux-01 in /home/jenkins/agent/workspace/... and the Python version.
```

**9.2** Stop the agent and start the job again. **Expected:** the build waits in the queue with “There are no nodes with the label ‘python3’” (or “…is offline”). This is how a missing lab agent looks.

lessons.title: Lab 10.1 — a Freestyle job that runs Project 1’s pytest suite [REVIEWED]
lessons.body:
New Item → Freestyle project → name p1-freestyle.

**1. General.** Tick Restrict where this project can be run, label expression linux && python3. Tick Discard old builds (max 30).

**2. Source Code Management → Git.** Repository URL of your Project 1 repository; credentials (if private); branch specifier */main.

**3. Build Triggers.** For now, none (build manually). Options: Build periodically (cron syntax, e.g. H 2 * * *), Poll SCM, GitHub hook trigger (needs the GitHub plugin), Build after other projects are built.

H spreads load: H 2 * * * means “some fixed minute between 02:00 and 02:59, chosen per job”, so 50 nightly jobs do not all start at 02:00.

**4. Build Environment.** Tick Delete workspace before build starts (Workspace Cleanup plugin) and Add timestamps to the Console Output (Timestamper plugin).

**5. Build Steps → Execute shell.**

```code
#!/bin/bash
# Freestyle runs this with '/bin/sh -xe' unless a shebang is given: we use bash
# for PIPESTATUS. -e is still wanted for the setup commands.
set -euo pipefail
python3 -m venv .venv
. .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -q -r requirements.txt
mkdir -p reports
set +e
python -m pytest --junitxml=reports/junit.xml 2>&1 | tee reports/pytest-console.log
rc=${PIPESTATUS[0]}
set -e
echo "pytest exit code: $rc"
# exit 1 = test failures: let the JUnit publisher mark the build UNSTABLE.
# anything else non-zero = the run is broken: fail the build.
if [ "$rc" -eq 1 ]; then exit 0; fi
exit "$rc"
```

Why not simply python -m pytest ...? In Freestyle, a non-zero exit marks the build **FAILURE**. Test failures would then look the same as a broken environment. Why not || true? That hides every error, including “no tests collected” (5) and collection errors (2). The pattern above keeps those distinctions.

**6. Post-build Actions.**

- Publish JUnit test result report → reports/junit.xml (JUnit plugin). It marks the build UNSTABLE if any test failed, and FAILURE if the file is missing (unless “allow empty results” is ticked; do not tick it).

- Archive the artifacts → reports/** (core).

**7. Save → Build Now.**
