lessons.title: Scenario 2 — Git checkout fails with authentication error
lessons.body:
- Symptoms: Permission denied (publickey) or Authentication failed in the checkout stage.

- **Likely causes:** wrong credential ID; deploy key removed; token expired; SSO not authorised.

- **Investigation:** job’s credential; repository deploy keys; test as the agent user.

- Commands: GIT_SSH_COMMAND="ssh -v" git ls-remote git@host:org/repo.git (as jenkins on the agent).

- **Expected:** “Offering public key … Authentication refused” or no key offered.

- **Corrective:** fix/rotate the credential, re-add the deploy key. **Prevention:** documented service credentials with expiry monitoring; read-only • deploy keys.

- **Answer:** “Checkout runs Git on the agent with the job’s credential, so I reproduced it as the agent user with verbose SSH and found the deploy key had been removed during a repo migration.”

source.section: 33.2 Scenario 2 — Git checkout fails with authentication error

lessons.title: Scenario 3 — Tests pass locally but fail in CI
lessons.body:
- **Symptoms:** green on laptop, red in Jenkins.

- **Likely causes:** unpinned dependency, different Python, local files not in Git, environment variables set locally, time zone/locale, test order, network access.

- **Investigation:** reproduce with CI’s commit, pip-freeze.txt, parameters and command.

- Commands: git checkout <GIT_COMMIT>; python -m venv /tmp/v; /tmp/v/bin/pip install

```code
-r pip-freeze.txt; <copied pytest command>
```

- **Expected:** failure reproduces once environment matches.

- **Corrective:** pin/add missing dependency; commit missing file; make tests independent of local env.

- **Prevention:** run_local.sh mirroring CI; fresh venvs.

- **Answer:** “I rebuilt the exact CI environment from the archived freeze file; the failure reproduced: a transitive dependency had a new release. I pinned it and added a constraints file.”

source.section: 33.3 Scenario 3 — Tests pass locally but fail in CI

lessons.title: Scenario 4 — JUnit reports are missing
lessons.body:
- **Symptoms:** No test report files were found; build FAILURE.

- **Likely causes:** pytest never ran (earlier failure), wrong path, different working directory (dir()), report deleted by cleanup before publishing, pytest killed.

- **Investigation:** console order of steps; ls -R reports before junit.

- Commands: sh 'ls -la reports || true' in post { always } before junit.

- **Expected:** directory absent or file in a different path.

- **Corrective:** fix path; publish before cleanWs(); ensure pytest runs with --junitxml.

- **Prevention:** allowEmptyResults: false; standard REPORT_DIR variable.

- **Answer:** “The report path was relative to a dir() block, so junit looked in the wrong folder. I standardised REPORT_DIR and kept missing reports as a hard failure.”

lessons.title: Scenario 5 — A firmware test hangs until the pipeline timeout
lessons.body:
- **Symptoms:** build ABORTED after 90 minutes; last line is in a firmware test.

- **Likely causes:** request without timeout; infinite wait loop; device hung; serial read blocking. **Investigation:** last log lines, which operation, device console at that time. •

- Commands: add pytest-timeout (timeout = 120), requests.get(..., timeout=10), `timeout(time: 15, unit: 'MINUTES', activity: true).`

- **Expected:** a per-test timeout now fails just that test with a stack trace showing the blocking call.

- **Corrective:** bounded polling with deadline; timeouts on every call.

- **Prevention:** code review rule “every wait has a deadline”; per-test timeouts.

- **Answer:** “The pipeline timeout gave no useful evidence. I added per-test and per-call timeouts, so the next hang failed the single test with the stack trace pointing at an unbounded poll loop.”

source.section: 33.5 Scenario 5 — A firmware test hangs until the pipeline timeout

lessons.title: Scenario 6 — Two jobs try to use the same BMC
lessons.body:
- **Symptoms:** random reboots during sensor tests; both jobs fail inconsistently.

- **Likely causes:** no locking; two jobs pointing at the same config.

- **Investigation:** overlapping build timelines; BMC event log shows unexpected resets.

- Commands: lock(resource: 'bmc-lab-01') { ... }

- **Expected:** second job waits “Waiting for lock on bmc-lab-01”.

- **Corrective:** add locks to every job that touches the device.

- **Prevention:** framework refuses to run lab tests without a lock (e.g. checks `LOCKED_RESOURCE env or holds DeviceLock).`

- **Answer:** “Timelines overlapped and the BMC log showed a reset from the other job. I added Lockable Resources locks and made the framework take a local lock too.”

source.section: 33.6 Scenario 6 — Two jobs try to use the same BMC

lessons.title: Scenario 7 — BMC unreachable after reboot
lessons.body:
- **Symptoms:** tests after a reboot error with connection refused/timeouts.

- **Likely causes:** boot slower than fixed sleep; network config lost after reboot; boot failure; IP changed (DHCP).

- **Investigation:** console log of the boot; time-to-ready history; ping vs Redfish vs SSH.

- Commands: device.wait_until_ready(timeout_s=600, poll_s=5); UART capture during reboot.

- **Expected:** either ready later than expected or boot stops with an error on console.

- **Corrective:** replace sleep with polling; if boot fails, file defect / recover device.

- **Prevention:** record boot time each run; alert on growth.

- **Answer:** “A fixed sleep was shorter than boot after the new firmware. Polling with a deadline fixed the test, and the recorded boot time showed a 60-second increase that we reported as a firmware regression.”

lessons.title: Scenario 8 — Jenkins agent disconnects during regression
lessons.body:
- **Symptoms:** ChannelClosedException, build FAILURE/ABORTED mid-suite.

- **Likely causes:** agent host reboot, network blip, OOM, disk full.

- **Investigation:** agent log, system journal on agent, memory/disk graphs.

- Commands: journalctl --since "2 hours ago" on agent; df -h; dmesg | grep -i oom.

- **Expected:** OOM kill of the agent JVM or network events.

- **Corrective:** fix resource issue; health-check device before reuse; rerun.

- **Prevention:** monitoring, retry(conditions: [agent()]) around node allocation for idempotent stages, classify as infra.

- **Answer:** “The agent JVM was OOM-killed. I fixed memory, treated the device as suspect until a health check passed, and classified the run as infrastructure so nobody chased a firmware bug.”

source.section: 33.8 Scenario 8 — Jenkins agent disconnects during regression

lessons.title: Scenario 9 — Test fails because dependencies differ between environments
lessons.body:
- **Symptoms:** TypeError from a library API change.

- **Likely causes:** unpinned dependency.

- **Investigation:** compare pip freeze of good vs bad builds.

- Commands: diff <(curl -s .../good/artifact/pip-freeze.txt) <(curl -s .../bad/ `artifact/pip-freeze.txt)`

- **Expected:** one package version changed.

- **Corrective:** pin; adapt code deliberately later.

- **Prevention:** lock files, scheduled dependency-update PRs.

- **Answer:** “Diffing archived freeze files between builds showed a new library release; I pinned it and scheduled the upgrade as a reviewed change.”

source.section: 33.9 Scenario 9 — Test fails because dependencies differ between environments

lessons.title: Scenario 10 — A failed test is reported as successful
lessons.body:
- **Symptoms:** console shows FAILED, build is green.

- **Likely causes:** exit code lost (| tee without pipefail, || true, wrapper ignoring code), skipMarkingBuildUnstable, wrong report published (old file).

- **Investigation:** read the sh step; check exit-code handling and published file timestamps.

- Commands: def rc = sh(returnStatus: true, script: '''#!/bin/bash ... exit $ `{PIPESTATUS[0]}''')`

- **Expected:** rc 1 now visible; build UNSTABLE.

- **Corrective:** propagate exit codes; clean reports/ at start.

- **Prevention:** a “canary” failing test in a pipeline self-test job to prove failures turn red.

- **Answer:** “pytest’s output was piped through tee under /bin/sh, so the step saw tee’s exit code. I switched to bash with PIPESTATUS and added a self-test that proves a failing test turns the build unstable.”

source.section: 33.10 Scenario 10 — A failed test is reported as successful

lessons.title: Scenario 11 — A retry hides an intermittent firmware defect
lessons.body:
- **Symptoms:** nightly green, but console shows reruns (R); field reports of the same symptom.

- **Likely causes:** --reruns enabled globally.

- **Investigation:** rerun counts per test across builds; first-attempt failure messages.

- **Commands:** grep consoles for rerun; remove --reruns; run the test 50× on hardware.

- **Expected:** reproducible intermittent failure (e.g. 1 in 10).

- **Corrective:** file the defect with evidence; remove blanket reruns.

- **Prevention:** reruns only for listed tests with tickets; report rerun count as a separate signal.

- **Answer:** “Reruns turned an intermittent firmware race into a green build: the JUnit file showed zero failures. I removed blanket reruns, reproduced 1 in 10 failures, and the firmware team fixed a race in the fan service.”

source.section: 33.11 Scenario 11 — A retry hides an intermittent firmware defect

lessons.title: Scenario 12 — Secrets appear in build logs
lessons.body:
- **Symptoms:** a password visible in console or archived log.

- **Likely causes:** Groovy interpolation, set -x, debug print, transformed secret not masked.

- **Investigation:** find the step; check how the secret reached the output.

- **Commands:** use sh 'cmd "$BMC_PASSWORD"' (single quotes), set +x, Python logging mask.

- **Expected:** or no mention at all.

- **Corrective:** rotate the secret; delete affected logs; fix code.

- **Prevention:** review checklist, masking in framework logs, least privilege.

- **Answer:** “First I rotated the password and deleted the builds’ logs, then fixed a debug print in a helper; now logs are masked and the review checklist forbids printing request objects.”

source.section: 33.12 Scenario 12 — Secrets appear in build logs

lessons.title: Scenario 13 — Health check fails with HTTP 401 after a weekend
lessons.body:
- **Symptoms:** health exit 11; all lab jobs failing.

- **Likely causes:** password rotated on BMC but not in Jenkins; account locked after failed logins; BMC reflashed to defaults.

- **Investigation:** try the credential manually (securely); check BMC account status/ logs.

- Commands: curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' -u "$BMC_USER:$BMC_PASSWORD" `https://$DUT/redfish/v1/Managers inside withCredentials.`

- **Expected:** 401.

- **Corrective:** update the Jenkins credential (same ID); unlock account.

- **Prevention:** rotation procedure updating Jenkins in the same change; lockout-aware retries (do not retry auth).

- **Answer:** “The health gate correctly reported AUTH; the BMC had been reflashed to defaults. We updated provisioning so reflashing re-creates the CI account.”

source.section: 33.13 Scenario 13 — Health check fails with HTTP 401 after a weekend

lessons.title: Scenario 14 — pytest exits 5 in nightly
lessons.body:
- **Symptoms:** “no tests ran”, FAILURE.

- **Likely causes:** marker renamed; SUITE parameter value changed; tests moved out `of testpaths.`

- Investigation: --collect-only -m <marker>.

- Commands: python -m pytest --collect-only -q -m regression

- **Expected:** 0 selected.

- **Corrective:** fix marker mapping.

- **Prevention:** --strict-markers; self-test that each suite selects ≥ N tests.

- **Answer:** “A refactor renamed the marker; exit 5 failed the build as designed. I added a self-test that asserts each suite selects a minimum number of tests.”

lessons.title: Scenario 15 — Collection error after a merge
lessons.body:
- **Symptoms:** exit 2, ERROR collecting tests/....

- **Likely causes:** syntax/import error; plugin declared in non-root conftest; missing dependency.

- **Investigation:** first error in output.

- Commands: python -m pytest --collect-only -q

- **Expected:** traceback pointing at the file.

- **Corrective:** fix code; move pytest_plugins to root conftest.

- **Prevention:** PR checks run collection; pre-commit compileall.

- **Answer:** “Collection errors stop everything, so we treat exit 2 as a pipeline failure and run a fast collect-only check on every PR.”

source.section: 33.15 Scenario 15 — Collection error after a merge

lessons.title: Scenario 16 — Lock never released / jobs queue forever
lessons.body:
- **Symptoms:** “Waiting for lock on bmc-lab-01” for hours.

- **Likely causes:** a job holding the lock is stuck (no timeout); manual reservation forgotten.

- **Investigation:** Lockable Resources page shows the holder. **Commands:** stage timeout around locked work; lock(..., timeoutForAllocateResource: • `60, timeoutUnit: 'MINUTES').`

- **Expected:** stuck job identified.

- **Corrective:** abort the holder; release.

- **Prevention:** timeouts inside locks; minimal lock scope; alerts on long waits.

- **Answer:** “A hung job held the lock without a timeout. I added stage timeouts inside lock blocks and a bounded wait for acquiring the lock.”

source.section: 33.16 Scenario 16 — Lock never released / jobs queue forever

lessons.title: Scenario 17 — Serial port busy
lessons.body:
- Symptoms: SerialException: could not open port /dev/ttyUSB0: [Errno 16] Device or `resource busy.`

- **Likely causes:** a human’s picocom session; previous job’s process still running; two jobs.

- **Investigation:** find which process holds the port on the agent; check for a human console session or an orphaned process from an aborted build.

- Commands: fuser -v /dev/ttyUSB0 or lsof /dev/ttyUSB0; ps -fp <pid>.

- **Expected:** a PID holding the port (picocom, or a python capture process).

- **Corrective:** stop it; ensure close in finally.

- **Prevention:** lock serial ports as resources; background capture processes owned by the pipeline and killed in post.

- **Answer:** “An orphaned capture process from an aborted build held the port; now captures are started and stopped by the pipeline and the port is part of the device lock.”

lessons.title: Scenario 18 — Firmware update task stuck at a percentage
lessons.body:
- **Symptoms:** update test fails after update_timeout_s with “still Running”.

- **Likely causes:** flash write hang; image incompatible; BMC service crash.

- **Investigation:** recorded status history; console; journal of the software manager.

- Commands: Project 3 UpdateReport steps; journalctl -u <software manager service> over SSH if reachable.

- **Expected:** stalled progress, maybe errors in journal.

- **Corrective:** classify FIRMWARE_REGRESSION; recover device per lab procedure.

- **Prevention:** bounded waits; evidence capture in finally.

- **Answer:** “Because the orchestrator records every poll and the console tail even on failure, the report showed progress stalled at 75 % with a flash driver error, which went straight into the defect.”

source.section: 33.18 Scenario 18 — Firmware update task stuck at a percentage

lessons.title: Scenario 19 — Wrong firmware tested
lessons.body:
- **Symptoms:** results don’t match the release; version check fails or nobody checked.

- **Likely causes:** flash step skipped; “latest” resolved differently; wrong device.

- **Investigation:** device-reported version vs parameter; build metadata.

- Commands: smoke test_firmware_version_matches_expected.

- **Expected:** mismatch.

- **Corrective:** reflash; rerun.

- **Prevention:** exact versions only; version assertion in smoke.

- **Answer:** “The smoke suite asserts the device-reported version equals the requested one, so testing the wrong image fails in seconds.”

lessons.title: Scenario 20 — Intermittent HTTP 503 from the BMC
lessons.body:
- **Symptoms:** random tests fail with 503.

- **Likely causes:** BMC web server overloaded/restarting; too many sessions; real defect.

- **Investigation:** timing correlation; BMC journal for web service restarts; session count.

- **Commands:** log each request’s status/latency; count 5xx per run.

- **Expected:** bursts after specific operations.

- **Corrective:** if service crashes → product defect; if test overload → reduce concurrency.

- **Prevention:** classify 5xx separately; trend it.

- **Answer:** “5xx is the BMC telling us it’s unhealthy, so we treat it as a product signal, not something to retry away; the journal showed the web service restarting after a large log request.”

source.section: 33.20 Scenario 20 — Intermittent HTTP 503 from the BMC

lessons.title: Scenario 21 — Tests depend on order
lessons.body:
- **Symptoms:** pass in full run, fail alone (or vice versa).

- **Likely causes:** earlier test sets state later ones rely on.

- **Investigation:** run the failing test alone; random order on unit tests.

- Commands: python -m pytest tests/x.py::test_y; -p randomly (pytest-randomly).

- **Expected:** failure depends on a missing precondition.

- **Corrective:** fixtures establish preconditions.

- **Prevention:** isolation reviews; random order in CI for unit tests.

- **Answer:** “The test assumed the host was powered on by a previous test; a fixture now ensures the precondition and restores it.”

lessons.title: Scenario 22 — Build queue very long
lessons.body:
- **Symptoms:** builds wait an hour before starting.

- **Likely causes:** too few lab agents/devices; long lock scopes; jobs on the wrong labels.

- **Investigation:** queue reasons; lock holders; stage durations.

- **Commands:** move setup/analysis outside lock; beforeAgent true.

- **Expected:** locks held only during device stages.

- **Corrective:** restructure; add capacity where justified.

- **Prevention:** monitor queue time per label.

- **Answer:** “Jobs held the device lock during venv creation and report generation; narrowing the lock cut device occupancy by 30 %.”

lessons.title: Scenario 23 — Disk full on agent
lessons.body:
- **Symptoms:** No space left on device at random steps (pip install, git checkout, report writing).

- **Likely causes:** workspaces never cleaned; large logs or firmware images in workspaces; growing pip/docker caches.

- **Investigation:** which directories grow; which jobs leave large workspaces.

- Commands: df -h /home/jenkins; du -sh /home/jenkins/agent/workspace/* | sort -h | `tail.`

- **Expected:** a few job workspaces holding GBs (images, old reports, venvs).

- **Corrective:** clean the workspaces; add post { cleanup { cleanWs() } }; move images to an artifact store.

- **Prevention:** buildDiscarder; disk monitoring; the environment-check stage fails early below a free-space threshold (Project 2’s env_check.sh requires 500 MB).

- **Answer:** “Old workspaces with firmware images filled the disk; we now clean workspaces after archiving, and the environment check fails fast with a clear message when space is low.”

lessons.title: Scenario 24 — Pipeline green but HTML report empty or unstyled
lessons.body:
- **Symptoms:** JUnit results fine, but the HTML report page is blank or has no styling in Jenkins.

- **Likely causes:** Jenkins’ Content Security Policy blocking the report’s scripts/styles; report not self-contained.

- **Investigation:** open the browser developer console on the report page; download the file and open it locally.

- **Commands:** regenerate with --self-contained-html; browser console → look for CSP violation messages.

- **Expected:** CSP violation messages in the console; the downloaded file renders correctly.

- **Corrective:** view downloaded copies, or configure a resource root URL (Manage Jenkins → Security) so user content is served from a separate origin.

- **Prevention:** treat JUnit as the verdict source; HTML is a convenience view; avoid relaxing CSP globally.

- **Answer:** “Jenkins’ CSP blocked the report’s inline content; the results themselves were fine. We configured a resource root URL so reports render safely instead of weakening CSP.”

source.section: 33.24 Scenario 24 — Pipeline green but HTML report empty or unstyled

lessons.title: Scenario 25 — PR from a fork tries to print credentials
lessons.body:
- **Symptoms:** a reviewer notices a PR adding env dumps or network calls to a helper script.

- **Likely causes:** malicious or careless contribution.

- **Investigation:** did any build with credentials run this PR? Which agents and which credentials were bound?

- **Commands:** check the PR’s build console and the job’s branch-source trust settings; search the console for the injected output.

- **Expected:** the PR build ran in the simulation pool with no credentials bound, so nothing sensitive was printed.

- **Corrective:** if a credential was exposed, rotate it immediately; close the PR; delete affected logs.

- **Prevention:** untrusted PRs run without credentials and without lab access; Jenkinsfile taken from the target branch for untrusted authors; maintainer approval before hardware runs.

- **Answer:** “Fork PRs only run simulation on isolated agents with no secrets, so the attempt exposed nothing; we still reviewed trust settings and added the case to our security checklist.”

source.section: 33.25 Scenario 25 — PR from a fork tries to print credentials

lessons.title: Scenario 26 — Duplicate builds for each push
lessons.body:
- **Symptoms:** two identical builds start for every commit.

- **Likely causes:** both webhook and pollSCM configured; branch and PR both discovered for the same commit; two jobs watching the same repository.

- **Investigation:** read “Started by …” at the top of each build’s console; check the job’s triggers and branch-source behaviours.

- **Commands:** compare consoles: Started by GitHub push by … vs Started by an SCM change (polling).

- **Expected:** two different trigger causes for the same commit.

- **Corrective:** keep one trigger path (webhook), exclude branches that are also filed as PRs, remove the duplicate job.

- **Prevention:** a documented trigger policy; disableConcurrentBuilds(abortPrevious: true) for rapid pushes; periodic indexing only as a safety net.

- **Answer:** “The consoles showed two causes: webhook and polling. I kept the webhook with daily indexing as a fallback, and builds halved.”

source.section: 33.26 Scenario 26 — Duplicate builds for each push

lessons.title: Scenario 27 — Agent can’t access /dev/ttyUSB0
lessons.body:
- Symptoms: PermissionError: [Errno 13] Permission denied: '/dev/ttyUSB0' on one lab agent only.

- **Likely causes:** agent user not in the dialout group; container started without --device; device enumerated under a different name.

- **Investigation:** compare user groups and device ownership with a working agent.

- Commands: groups jenkins; ls -l /dev/ttyUSB0 /dev/serial/by-id/; fix with sudo usermod -aG dialout jenkins and restart the agent service.

- **Expected:** device owned by group dialout, agent user not a member.

- **Corrective:** add the group, restart the agent (group changes need a new login session).

- **Prevention:** agent provisioning adds the group; env check verifies the port is readable; use stable /dev/serial/by-id names in config.

- **Answer:** “The new agent’s user lacked the dialout group; provisioning now adds it and the environment check verifies the port before tests start.”

lessons.title: Scenario 28 — Test passes against the simulator, fails on hardware
lessons.body:
- **Symptoms:** simulator run green; lab run red on the same test commit.

- **Likely causes:** simulator model differs from the platform (resource IDs, units, schema details, timing); or a real product defect.

- **Investigation:** compare the real response (collected snapshot) with the simulator’s response for the failing resource.

- Commands: python scripts/collect_logs.py in lab mode; diff <(jq -S . artifacts/ `bmc_snapshot/manager.json) <(jq -S . sim_manager.json).`

- **Expected:** a structural difference (e.g. chassis ID, threshold format) or a genuinely wrong value.

- **Corrective:** fix configuration/adapter mapping and improve the simulator; or file a product defect if the value is wrong.

- **Prevention:** keep sanitised real response samples to update the simulator; contract tests that run the adapter against recorded responses.

- **Answer:** “The real platform used a different chassis ID and threshold format; the adapter now reads IDs from config, and the simulator was updated from sanitised real responses.”

source.section: 33.28 Scenario 28 — Test passes against the simulator, fails on hardware

lessons.title: Scenario 29 — Upstream firmware build triggers the test job with empty parameters
lessons.body:
- **Symptoms:** downstream regression runs with empty EXPECTED_FW and tests whatever is on the board.

- **Likely causes:** upstream build job: call omits parameters; new job’s first run has no registered parameters.

- **Investigation:** downstream build’s Parameters page and “Started by upstream project” cause; upstream Jenkinsfile.

- Commands: upstream: build job: 'bmc-regression', parameters: [string(name:

```code
'EXPECTED_FW', value: env.FW_VERSION)]; downstream: if (!params.EXPECTED_FW)
{ error('EXPECTED_FW is required') }.
```

- **Expected:** parameters page shows an empty value.

- **Corrective:** pass parameters explicitly; validate them at the start of the downstream pipeline.

- **Prevention:** fail fast on missing required parameters; never fall back to “whatever is installed”.

- **Answer:** “The downstream job now validates its parameters and fails with ‘EXPECTED_FW is required’ instead of silently testing the wrong firmware.”

source.section: 33.29 Scenario 29 — Upstream firmware build triggers the test job with empty parameters

lessons.title: Scenario 30 — Evidence for an old failure is gone
lessons.body:
- **Symptoms:** a defect needs logs from a run two weeks ago; workspace cleaned, device reflashed, build discarded.

- **Likely causes:** evidence kept only in workspaces; short buildDiscarder retention; no long-term export.

- **Investigation:** what was archived for that build, and what the retention policy is.

- **Commands:** check the build’s Build Artifacts list;

```code
buildDiscarder(logRotator(numToKeepStr: '…', artifactNumToKeepStr: '…')) in the
```

Jenkinsfile.

- **Expected:** only the console log survived, or the build itself was rotated away.

- **Corrective:** reproduce if possible; for the future, archive evidence in `post { always }.`

- **Prevention:** archive reports and device evidence for every run; longer retention (or “keep forever”) for release qualification; export summaries to long-term storage.

- **Answer:** “Evidence lives in archived artifacts, not workspaces or devices; release-qualification builds are kept permanently and summaries exported.”

source.section: 33.30 Scenario 30 — Evidence for an old failure is gone

lessons.title: Scenario 31 — Time-dependent failures right after BMC reboot
lessons.body:
- **Symptoms:** TLS certificate or session-token checks fail only in the first minutes after a reboot.

- **Likely causes:** BMC clock not yet synchronised (NTP/RTC), so certificates look “not yet valid”; framework timers based on wall-clock time jump.

- **Investigation:** compare BMC time with agent time in the evidence; check NTP status on the BMC.

- **Commands:** Redfish GET /redfish/v1/Managers/{id} → DateTime; over SSH date -u and timedatectl (if available).

- **Expected:** BMC time far off agent time until sync completes.

- **Corrective:** include “time synchronised” in readiness; use time.monotonic() for all framework timers (Project 3 does).

- **Prevention:** readiness checks that cover clock state; record BMC time in evidence.

- **Answer:** “After reboot the BMC clock was hours off until NTP synced; readiness now waits for time sync and our timers use monotonic time.”

source.section: 33.31 Scenario 31 — Time-dependent failures right after BMC reboot

lessons.title: Scenario 32 — Regression duration creeps up over months
lessons.body:
- **Symptoms:** nightly regression grew from 4 h to 5.6 h without many new tests.

- **Likely causes:** fixed sleeps added; slower BMC responses or boot (firmware); more retries.

- **Investigation:** compare per-test durations and stage times between old and new builds; boot-time trend.

- **Commands:** python -m pytest --durations=30; compare JUnit time attributes across builds; read waited_s from readiness logs.

- **Expected:** a few tests or operations (e.g. Redfish latency, boot) account for most of the growth.

- **Corrective:** remove sleeps; report firmware latency/boot regressions with data.

- **Prevention:** track duration metrics per test and per operation; alert on budget overruns.

- **Answer:** “Trend data showed Redfish latency doubling across firmware builds, a product regression we reported with timing evidence, and we removed two fixed sleeps that hid it.”

source.section: 33.32 Scenario 32 — Regression duration creeps up over months

lessons.title: Pipeline troubleshooting checklist
lessons.body:
1. Which stage failed first? (graph/console)

2. Pipeline problem or product problem? (exit code, category)

3. What exactly ran? (commit, params, freeze, config, agent, device, firmware)

4. Was the environment healthy before? (env check, health/preflight)

5. Does it reproduce? (same inputs locally or on the same agent)

6. What changed since the last good run? (Changes page, freeze diff, firmware diff)

7. Is the evidence sufficient? If not, improve collection before rerunning.

8. Fix, then add a guard so the same failure is reported earlier/clearer next time.

lessons.title: Practical exercises with solutions
lessons.body:
**P1.** Add a pipeline self-test stage to Project 1 that fails if the smoke marker selects fewer `than 3 tests. Solution: sh '. .venv/bin/activate && test "$(python -m pytest --collect-only -q -m smoke | grep -c "::")" -ge 3'.`

**P2.** In Project 2, add a simulator fault manager_unhealthy that makes the manager report Health: Critical; verify the health check exits 12. Solution: in backend.py store manager_health in state ("OK", or "Critical" if the fault is set); in server.py return `{"State": "Enabled", "Health": s["manager_health"]}; run BMC_SIM_FAULTS=manager_unhealthy python scripts/health_check.py; echo $? → 12.`

**P3.** In Project 3, add an ipmi_sel_entries() optional capability returning a list, implemented in the simulator, with a regression test asserting no entries of severity “Critical”. Solution: add a method to DeviceAdapter raising UnsupportedOperation; implement in SimulatedDevice returning sample entries (add a fault sel_critical); test in `tests/device/test_sel.py; skip on adapters raising UnsupportedOperation with pytest.skip.`

**P4.** Write a Jenkins stage that runs smoke on every branch but regression only on main, without occupying a lab agent on other branches. Solution: stage('Regression') { when `{ beforeAgent true; branch 'main' } agent { label 'bmc-lab' } steps { ... } }.`

**P5.** Make Project 2’s pipeline send one email when the health check fails and none for product failures. Solution: see Exercise 22.1.

lessons.title: Capstone acceptance criteria
lessons.body:
Your capstone (extend Project 2 or 3 in your own public repo) is complete when:

1. Fresh clone → one documented command runs the suite on the simulator.

2. Jenkins pipeline (executed on your own Jenkins) with: checkout, env validation, venv, self-tests, health gate, selectable suites, diagnostics in finally, classification, JUnit + HTML publishing, archive, cleanup.

3. Exit codes mapped deliberately; a failing test → UNSTABLE; a broken run → FAILURE; proven by screenshots or console excerpts.

4. At least four simulator faults demonstrating PRODUCT, INFRA/LAB, AUTH and TEST_CODE categories.

5. No secrets in the repository; credentials via bindings; log masking.

6. Locking demonstrated (two concurrent builds, the second waits).

7. README with architecture, verification status table, limitations.

8. Unit tests for helper code (classifier, config) in CI.

9. GitHub branch protection with the CI check required.

10. A 2-minute spoken explanation recorded or rehearsed.

lessons.title: Executive Summary of My Profile
lessons.body:
**Bottom line:** your profile is a credible **4.5-year firmware validation engineer**: about 3 years 10 months on SSD firmware (March 2022 to December 2025, Chennai) and about 9 months on OpenBMC (January 2026 to now, Bengaluru), all at HCLTech, with Python automation, Linux, Jenkins and Git. That combination is genuinely in demand in Bengaluru. SSD/NVMe and BMC/OpenBMC validation roles appear at storage and semiconductor MNCs, server OEMs and engineering-services firms, and the JDs repeat the same requirements: Python, Linux, CI, and protocol knowledge such as NVMe/PCIe or Redfish/IPMI/PLDM/MCTP (Micron JD; Infobell OpenBMC JD).

**The weakness is the resume, not necessarily your experience.** It names no protocols, no tools beyond Python, Jenkins and Git, no test counts, no release counts and no measured improvements. That means an interviewer will build the whole conversation by probing. You win by turning every generic bullet into a specific, numbered, first-person story. You lose by guessing at protocols you have not used. **Where interviewers will spend their time.** SSD is your deepest experience, so expect deep NVMe questions. OpenBMC is your current role and is what most BMC interviewers care about, but at 9 months they will test whether you understand the architecture or only ran test suites. Protocol questions (Redfish, IPMI, MCTP, PLDM, I2C, UART) will come because they are standard in BMC roles, but your resume does not claim them. Answer at the level you really know them.

Wherever an answer describes project details that only you know, it is marked **[adapt to your real work]**. Replace those parts with what actually happened, or drop them. **Never say a sentence in this handbook that is not true for you.** Facts the source notes could not verify are marked **(verify)**.

lessons.title: Header and contact block
lessons.body: **What's there:** name, title, Bengaluru, phone, email, LinkedIn. **Risk:** the email on the resume is different from the address on the account this handbook was prepared from. That may be deliberate, but **check that the resume email and phone are the ones you actively monitor**, and that they match your LinkedIn and Naukri profiles. Recruiters drop candidates who don't respond. **LinkedIn:** interviewers will open it. Make sure the titles and dates match the resume exactly (Software Engineer, Mar 2022 – Dec 2025; Senior Software Engineer, Jan 2026 – present). A mismatch looks like inflation.

lessons.title: Professional summary
lessons.body:
"Dynamic Senior Software Engineer with 4+ years of experience in Embedded Software Testing, Firmware Validation, and Python-based automation. Specialized in SSD and OpenBMC firmware validation with strong expertise in Linux debugging, test automation, and log analysis. Proven track record of enhancing test coverage, improving defect detection…"

1. **May ask:** "Walk me through your 4 years." "What does 'specialized' mean, given you've done OpenBMC for under a year?" "What does 'strong expertise in Linux debugging' look like? Give an example."

2. **Why:** to check that the summary matches the details, and to find the weakest claim.

3. **Knowledge needed:** Linux debugging tools (dmesg, journalctl, grep/awk, lspci, systemctl), the SSD and BMC validation life cycle.

4. **Practical:** one concrete Linux debugging story per project.

5. **Follow-ups:** "How much did coverage increase? From what to what?" "How did you measure defect detection?"

**6**. **Cross-question:** "'Proven track record' — proven how?"

7. **Suspicion risk: HIGH.** "Dynamic", "strong expertise" and "proven track record" with no numbers read as template language. Rewrite it (Section 17).

**2.3 Current designation: Senior Software Engineer (Jan 2026** – **present, Bengaluru)**

1. **May ask:** "What changed when you became Senior? Do you mentor anyone? Do you own a test area?"

2. **Why:** the title and the timing (it starts with a new project and a new city) suggest a promotion. The interviewer wants to know whether it reflects responsibility or tenure.

3. **Knowledge:** how your team is structured, and who assigns, reviews and signs off tests.

4. **Practical:** anything you own end to end: a feature area, a nightly job, onboarding a junior, reviewing test cases.

5. **Follow-ups:** "How big is your team? Who do you report to?"

**6**. **Cross-question:** "You've been Senior for 9 months on a domain you've known for 9 months. Why should we treat you as senior in BMC?"

7. **Suspicion risk: MEDIUM.** An honest answer covers it. See Section 15.

**2.4 Previous role: Software Engineer (Mar 2022** – **Dec 2025, Chennai)**

1. **May ask:** "Was this the same company? Why did you move from SSD to OpenBMC?"

2. **Why:** the resume lists the two roles like separate jobs. Clarify that it was an internal move within HCLTech.

3. **Practical:** the reason for the move (project ramp-down, a new account, your request, promotion). Give a true, neutral reason.

4. **Suspicion risk: LOW**, as long as it is explained.

lessons.title: Total experience: "4+ years"
lessons.body: You started in March 2022, so as of October 2026 you have about **4 years 7 months**. Say "about four and a half years". The **PUC in 2020** → **job in March 2022** timeline will be noticed: what were you doing between 2020 and 2022, and how did you get a software role with only PUC at the time? Have a one-line factual answer ready. If you joined through a company early-career or work-integrated-learning programme that combined a job with a sponsored degree, say so plainly; it is a positive story. (Verify the name and details of your own programme before you mention it.)

lessons.title: Companies and projects
lessons.body: Both projects are at HCLTech, an engineering-services company. **Interviewers know that services engineers work on a client's product**, so they will ask "Which client? Which product?" You are probably under NDA. The safe answer is: "It's a client engagement, so I can't name the customer, but I can describe the product class: enterprise NVMe SSD firmware [adapt], and an OpenBMC-based server management controller on [AST2600-class hardware — adapt]. I can walk through the technical work in detail." This is normal and accepted. Never invent a client name.

lessons.title: Programming languages
lessons.body: Python is your only language. Expect **one live coding exercise**: parse a log, count errors, dedupe a list, validate a JSON response, compare version strings (common tester exercises). You will also face **"read this snippet** — **what's wrong?"** on mutable default arguments, is vs == , and exceptions. If shell scripting is part of your daily work, add "Bash" to the resume. If not, don't.

lessons.title: Testing tools
lessons.body: **No testing tools are named**: no pytest, Robot, nvme-cli, fio, ipmitool, Redfish validator or Jira. That is the single easiest fix. List only the tools you actually used. Interviewers will assume you used some of them and will ask "Which tools?" in round one.

lessons.title: Automation
lessons.body:
The claims are "Developed Python-based scripts to automate firmware execution, validation workflows" (SSD) and "Developed and automated Python-based test cases… CI integration" (OpenBMC). Expect: "How many scripts or test cases? What framework? How were results reported? What happens when a test fails mid-run? How did Jenkins trigger it?" Have the **architecture of your automation** ready: config → device access layer (SSH, serial, HTTP, CLI wrappers) → test cases → logging → report → CI.

**2.11 Protocols, hardware interfaces, APIs, firmware/BMC technologies** None are named. In an OpenBMC validation role you almost certainly touched **Redfish** and possibly **IPMI**. In SSD validation you almost certainly touched **NVMe admin commands, SMART, firmware download/commit and PCIe enumeration**. Confirm for yourself which ones you really used and be ready to say so. For MCTP/PLDM/I2C/KCS, answer at concept level and label it honestly: "I know this from study, not from hands-on work."

lessons.title: Projects
lessons.body: There are two projects, both with "Execution & Validation" in the name. **"Execution" signals a test-execution role.** The interviewer will test whether you also **designed** tests, **wrote** automation and **debugged** failures, or only ran suites someone else wrote. Your bullets claim design and automation, so you need concrete examples of each.

lessons.title: Responsibilities
lessons.body: These all appear on the resume: executing validation workflows, developing Python tests, root-cause analysis, defect reproduction with cross-functional teams, release support. Expect "Walk me through a typical day/sprint", "Who are the cross-functional teams?" (firmware developers, hardware, platform, program management) and "What did you hand over to developers when you filed a bug?"

lessons.title: Key achievements
lessons.body:
"Automated repetitive validation tasks, reducing manual testing effort significantly. Improved defect detection efficiency… Contributed to stable firmware releases by identifying critical issues early."

**Suspicion risk: HIGH.** These three bullets have no numbers, no tasks named and no critical issue described. Every one of them will be met with "By how much?" or "Which one?" Before any interview, fill in templates like these with your real figures: "Automated [N] manual [firmware update / power-cycle / smoke] test cases in Python, cutting a regression pass from [X hours] to [Y hours]." [adapt to your real work] "Filed [N] firmware defects across [M] releases, [K] of them rated critical/high." [adapt to your real work] "Found a [data-integrity / boot hang / update failure] issue in [pre-release build] that was fixed before customer release." [adapt to your real work]

If you don't know exact numbers, use honest approximations and say "approximately". **Never invent numbers you can't explain.**

**2.15 Certifications** There are none. That is not disqualifying for validation roles. An ISTQB Foundation certificate is cheap insurance for testing-fundamentals rounds (ISTQB CTFL), but skills matter far more.

lessons.title: Education
lessons.body: **BCA, SASTRA University, 2025; PUC Science, 2020.** You completed the BCA while working full time from March 2022. Expect: "Was it regular, distance or online?" "How did you manage both?" "Why BCA and not engineering?" State the mode **exactly as it appears on your certificate**, because background verification will check it (Dheya on distance degrees and BGV). Some MNC JDs specify "Bachelor's/Master's in CS or Engineering" (Micron JD), so ATS filters may reject a BCA. Section 17 covers how to handle that.

lessons.title: Other information
lessons.body: The "Declaration" line is outdated in modern resumes. It's harmless, but it uses space you could give to a "Tools" line. There is no notice-period or location-preference line; recruiters will ask, so know the answer.

lessons.title: "4+ years of experience in Embedded Software Testing, Firmware Validation, and Python-based automation"
lessons.body:
**[ON RESUME** — **must defend]**

**B:** What is embedded software testing? How is it different from web or app testing? **I:** What's the difference between firmware validation and firmware verification? **A:** How do you test firmware behaviour that depends on timing or power state? **P:** What was your test setup? (host machine, DUT, connections) **S:** A firmware build passes all your functional tests but fails at the customer site. What went wrong in your test strategy? **T:** The DUT hangs only on every 50th boot. How do you catch it?

**F:** How much of your 4 years was manual and how much automation?

**Expected answer:**

"Embedded testing means the software under test runs on dedicated hardware, so the hardware state is part of every test: power, resets, thermal conditions, link state. Logs come from the device itself, over a serial console, dmesg or the BMC journal, not from a browser. For the first [three years and ten months] I validated SSD firmware on Linux hosts. We flashed each release candidate, ran functional, firmware-update, power-cycle and regression suites, and analysed failures from host logs and drive logs. Since January I've done the same for OpenBMC firmware: build sanity, Redfish and [IPMI — adapt] interface checks, reboot and update flows. Roughly [X%] of my time is automation development and maintenance, and the rest is execution and triage [adapt to your real work]. On validation versus verification: verification asks 'did we build it to spec?' and validation asks 'does it work in the real system for the real use case?' In practice our team used 'validation' for both [adapt]."

**3.2 "Specialized in SSD and OpenBMC firmware validation" [ON RESUME** — **must defend] B:** What is an SSD controller's firmware responsible for? What is a BMC? **I:** How is BMC firmware validation different from SSD firmware validation? **A:** What is common between NVMe firmware update and OpenBMC code update? **P:** Which SSD form factor and interface did you test? Which BMC SoC? **S:** You're asked to validate a BMC that manages NVMe drives. What would you test? **T:** The drive's temperature shows in nvme smart-log but not in Redfish. Where do you look? **F:** You've done OpenBMC for 9 months. Is "specialized" fair?

**Expected answer:** "SSD firmware runs inside the drive controller. It handles the NVMe command set, the flash translation layer, wear levelling, error correction and power-loss handling, and the host only sees it through the NVMe interface. A BMC is a separate controller on the server board that monitors health, logs events and allows remote management even when the host is off (Linux Foundation). The validation discipline is the same: download the image, activate it, reboot, verify the version, then run regression, power-cycle and negative tests. The NVMe flow is Firmware Image Download plus Firmware Commit (nvme-cli fw-commit). The OpenBMC flow is upload, Ready, Activate, reboot, functional (OpenBMC code-update). On 'specialized': I'd call SSD my deep area and OpenBMC my current, growing area. I'm comfortable being tested on both, and I'll tell you where my BMC knowledge stops." That last sentence defuses the cross-question. Say it.

**3.3 "Strong expertise in Linux debugging, test automation, and log analysis" [ON RESUME** — **must defend]**

**B:** How do you see kernel messages? Service logs? **I:** How would you find every error in the last boot of a systemd service? **A:** How would you trace why a process hangs? **P:** Give me the exact commands you'd run when an SSD disappears from the host. **S:** A log is 4 GB. How do you find the first failure? **T:** journalctl shows nothing for the failing service. What next? **F:** What's the most useful Linux command you used daily?

**Expected answer:**

"My daily set is dmesg -T for kernel messages, such as NVMe timeouts and PCIe AER errors, journalctl -u <service> -b -p err on the BMC, and grep/awk/sed/sort/uniq for slicing logs. For a drive that drops I run lspci to see whether it's still enumerated, lspci -vvv to compare the negotiated link speed and width with capability, then dmesg for 'timeout, aborting' or 'controller is down; will reset' (Linux nvme pci.c), then nvme list and nvme smart-log . For a 4 GB log I don't open it. I grep -n -m1 for the first error signature, then sed -n a window around that line number. In Python I'd stream it with a generator so it never loads into memory. If the journal is empty for a service, I check whether the service even started ( systemctl status ), whether it crashed before logging, or whether the journal is volatile and was lost on reboot."

**3.4 "Proven track record of enhancing test coverage, improving defect detection" [ON RESUME** — **must defend] B:** What is test coverage in firmware testing? **I:** How do you find coverage gaps? **A:** How do you measure defect detection effectiveness? **P:** Name one gap you found and closed. **S:** A customer finds a bug your suite missed. What do you do? **F:** By how much did coverage improve?

**Expected answer:**

"For us, coverage meant requirement or feature coverage, not code coverage. We mapped features to test cases, for example every NVMe log page or every Redfish resource we support, and looked for features with no test or only happy-path tests [adapt]. One gap I closed was [negative firmware-update cases: corrupted image, wrong slot, power loss during commit — adapt]. I added [N] cases and they caught [describe]. Defect detection effectiveness is bugs found by us versus bugs found after release. When something escapes, I write a test that reproduces it, add it to regression, and ask why our suite missed it: missing configuration, too few iterations, or the wrong environment."

**3.5 OpenBMC: "Executed comprehensive validation workflows for OpenBMC firmware, ensuring system stability,**

**compliance, and high-quality releases." [ON RESUME** — **must defend] B:** What is OpenBMC? What's in a BMC firmware image? **I:** What does your validation workflow for a new BMC build look like? **A:** "Compliance" — compliance with what? Redfish schema? DMTF validators? A customer spec? **P:** Which interfaces do you test: Redfish, IPMI, WebUI, SSH? **S:** The new build boots, but Redfish returns 503 for the first 2 minutes. Pass or fail? **T:** After update, the BMC shows the old version. Why? **F:** How many builds per week? How long does a full cycle take?

**Expected answer:** "When a build lands, I first verify the image: version string, target machine. Then I update the BMC and confirm the new version is the functional one, for example FirmwareVersion under /redfish/v1/Managers/bmc and /etc/os-release on the BMC. Then smoke checks: BMC reaches Ready ( obmcutil state ), systemctl --failed is empty, network/SSH/HTTPS work, the Redfish service root responds, and basic power on/off works. Then the regression suites: [list your real areas — sensors, event logs, users, network, firmware update, power control — adapt]. By 'compliance' I mean [our product requirements / Redfish schema checks with the DMTF Service Validator — adapt only if true]. On 503 at startup: a BMC is legitimately not ready right after boot, so I'd check the spec or requirement for readiness time. If it settles to 200 within the agreed window, it's a pass. My automation should wait for BMC Ready, not use fixed sleeps. If the old version shows after update, the usual causes are that the BMC wasn't rebooted after activation (the running image only changes after reboot), the activation failed, or the MANIFEST machine name didn't match (code-update.md)."

source.section: 3.1 "4+ years of experience in Embedded Software Testing, Firmware Validation, and Python-based automation"

lessons.title: OpenBMC: "Developed and automated Python-based test cases, improving regression coverage and enabling
lessons.body:
**efficient debugging through detailed log and root-cause analysis." [ON RESUME** — **must defend]**

**B:** Which Python libraries did you use? **I:** How does a test collect logs automatically on failure? **A:** How do you keep tests independent when they share one BMC? **P:** Show me the structure of one test case. **S:** A test passes locally but fails in Jenkins. Why? **T:** A Redfish test intermittently times out. Test bug or firmware bug? **F:** How many test cases did you automate?

**Expected answer:** "We used [pytest — adapt] with requests for Redfish, [paramiko for SSH — adapt] and subprocess for ipmitool. A session-scoped fixture logs in once and deletes the Redfish session at the end. Each test does its precondition check, the action, then assertions on status code and payload. On failure a hook collects first-failure data: journalctl from the BMC, the Redfish event log and the console capture, attached to the report [adapt]. The tests share one BMC, so each test restores what it changes. For example, a PATCH test reads the original value first and restores it in teardown. For intermittent timeouts I re-run that one test in a loop with timestamps and capture the journal at the moment of failure. If bmcweb or the backend daemon logs an error or restarts, it's firmware. If the BMC is healthy and only my client timed out, I check my timeout values and the network. I automated [N] cases covering [areas — adapt]."

**significantly enhance regression testing efficiency through automation and CI integration." [ON RESUME** — **must**

### defend]

**B:** Who were the cross-functional teams? **I:** What do you include in a bug report so a developer can reproduce it? **A:** How did CI integration change the regression process? **P:** What exactly is "significantly"? **S:** A developer says "not reproducible, closing". What do you do? **F:** What process did you optimize?

**Expected answer:** "I worked mainly with the BMC firmware developers, the platform and hardware team, and our test leads [adapt]. A good report has the build version, platform, exact steps, expected versus actual, frequency (for example 3 of 20 runs), logs captured at the failure (journal, Redfish event log, console), and whether it reproduces on the previous build. If a developer can't reproduce it, I offer to reproduce it on my bench with them watching, or give them my script so they can run it. Usually the difference is configuration or timing. Before CI, regression was triggered manually and the results were collected by hand. After we put it in Jenkins, the suite ran [nightly / on each build — adapt] and published JUnit results and logs automatically. That took [X hours of manual effort per cycle down to Y — fill in real numbers]."

**3.8 SSD: "Performed end-to-end validation of SSD firmware across Linux environments by executing both manual**

**and automated test suites for multiple firmware releases." [ON RESUME** — **must defend]**

**B:** Was it NVMe or SATA? Which form factor (M.2, U.2, AIC)? **I:** What does "end-to-end" cover? **A:** How do you validate a firmware upgrade without losing user data? **P:** Which Linux distros and kernels? Which tools? **S:** A firmware release improves performance but SMART media errors increase. Ship or not? **T:** After firmware update, the drive enumerates at Gen3 instead of Gen4. Debug it. **F:** How many releases did you validate?

**Expected answer (assuming NVMe** — **adapt if SATA):**

"End-to-end for us meant from receiving the firmware binary to sign-off. That covered flashing via nvme fw-download and nvme fw-commit , verifying the new revision in nvme id-ctrl and nvme fw-log , then functional suites (admin commands, log pages, features), I/O and data-integrity runs with fio verify, power-cycle and reboot loops, and upgrade/downgrade between N-1 and N [adapt]. For data preservation, we write a known pattern before the update, update under I/O or idle, then read back and verify. On Gen3 vs Gen4: I compare LnkCap and LnkSta in lspci -vvv . If the link trained down, I check whether it happens with the old firmware too. If yes, it's likely slot or signal integrity. If no, it's a firmware link-training regression, and I file it with both lspci outputs and dmesg. We validated about [N] releases over [period — adapt]."

**3.9 SSD: "Developed Python-based scripts to automate firmware execution, validation workflows, and test**

**processes, improving efficiency and reducing manual effort." [ON RESUME** — **must defend]**

**B:** How does Python run nvme-cli commands? **I:** How do you parse nvme smart-log output in Python? **A:** How do you automate a power-cycle loop with checks each iteration? **P:** Describe one script line by line. **S:** Your script runs for 12 hours and dies at hour 11. How do you avoid losing results? **F:** How much manual effort did you save?

**Expected answer:**

```code
"I wrapped the CLI tools with subprocess.run([...], capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=..., check=True) . For
```

parsing I preferred JSON output where nvme-cli supported it ( -o json ), and regex otherwise. One script I wrote was a [power-cycle loop — adapt]. Each iteration it powered the DUT off through [a controllable PDU / relay / IPMI — adapt], waited, powered on, waited for the device to enumerate with a timeout, then captured nvme list , the SMART log and dmesg. It compared the SMART counters with the previous iteration (power cycles +1, unsafe shutdowns as expected) and stopped on the first anomaly with all logs saved. To survive crashes, every iteration's results are written to disk immediately, as JSON lines, so a crash at hour 11 loses one iteration, not eleven hours. It replaced [a manual procedure of X minutes per cycle — adapt]."

**3.10 SSD: "Conducted detailed log-based failure analysis to identify firmware defects and collaborated with**

**cross-functional teams to support release cycles." [ON RESUME** — **must defend]**

**B:** Which logs exist for an SSD? **I:** How do you tell a host issue from a drive firmware issue? **A:** What is telemetry and when do you pull it? **P:** Walk me through your hardest SSD failure. **T:** dmesg shows "I/O … QID … timeout, aborting" then "reset controller". Interpret it.

**Expected answer:**

"On the host side there's dmesg (NVMe driver timeouts, resets, PCIe AER) plus our test logs. On the drive side there's the SMART/Health log, the Error Information log, the Firmware Slot log, and telemetry (Host-Initiated and Controller-Initiated logs that the vendor decodes) (kernel nvme.h log IDs). That timeout sequence means the driver didn't get a completion in time. It first sends an Abort, and on a second timeout it resets the controller (pci.c). Repeated aborts followed by a reset point to firmware hung on a command. 'CSTS=0xffffffff' instead points to the device dropping off the bus, which is link or power. Before any power cycle I capture telemetry, the error log and SMART, because a power cycle can destroy the evidence. My hardest failure was [describe — adapt]."

**3.11 Key achievements (all three bullets) [ON RESUME** — **must defend]**

**Q:** Which repetitive task did you automate first? How long did it take manually?

**Q:** What does "defect detection efficiency" mean? How was it measured?

**Q:** Name one critical issue you found early.

**Expected answer (structure):** "The first thing I automated was [X], which took about [Y] minutes per run, [Z] times per release. After automation it ran unattended in [Jenkins/overnight], and I only reviewed failures. On defect detection: we started capturing logs automatically at failure, so I could file defects with root-cause evidence the same day instead of re-running to reproduce. A critical issue I caught early was [describe in one line — adapt]."

If you cannot fill these in truthfully, **remove the bullets** rather than defend empty claims.

**3.12 "CI/CD (Jenkins, Git/GitHub)" [ON RESUME** — **must defend]**

**B:** What is CI/CD? Freestyle vs Pipeline? **I:** What's in your Jenkinsfile? **A:** How do you stop two jobs from using one DUT at once? **P:** How are results shown in Jenkins? **T:** The pipeline fails at checkout. What do you check? **F:** Did you write pipelines or only trigger them?

**Expected answer:** "Our regression ran as a [declarative pipeline / freestyle job — adapt] on a lab agent connected to the DUT. Stages were checkout, flash or update the firmware, run pytest with --junitxml , then in post { always { junit …; archiveArtifacts … } } publish the results and logs. To keep jobs off the same bench, you use agent labels with one executor, or the Lockable Resources plugin's lock() step (plugin docs). I [wrote / modified / mainly triggered and maintained — be precise] the pipeline. Git was for the test repo: feature branches, pull requests, review."

**3.13 Education [ON RESUME** — **must defend]**

**Q:** Regular or distance? Full-time job and degree at once — how?

**Q:** What did you study in BCA that helps your job?

**Answer (adapt to the truth):** "I completed my BCA from SASTRA University in 2025, [in online/distance/work-integrated mode — state exactly as on the certificate], while working full time at HCLTech. Weekdays were project work, and evenings and weekends were coursework and exams. It was hard, but it gave me the CS fundamentals (data structures, OS, networks, DBMS) that I use when debugging Linux and writing Python."

lessons.title: Most Likely Interview Questions
lessons.body:
The questions are ranked by probability for your resume. Each one has the reason it's asked, a strong answer, key points, a likely follow-up and an answer to that follow-up. 🔴 **VERY HIGH PROBABILITY** 🔴**1. Tell me about yourself.** Why: opener; checks whether your story matches the resume. Answer: use the 90-second intro (Section 14). Key points: about 4.5 years; SSD → OpenBMC; Python automation, Linux debugging, CI; one achievement with a number. Follow-up: "Why did you move from SSD to BMC?" → "The project moved me to a new OpenBMC programme in Bengaluru [adapt]. It made sense for me because BMC validation builds directly on what I did in SSD: firmware update flows, logs, power and reset testing, now at platform level." 🔴**2. Explain your current OpenBMC project. What exactly do you do?** Why: it's your current role; they're checking depth and ownership. Answer: use the 2-minute project answer (Section 13). Key points: platform class; interfaces tested; your automation; one bug; the process improvement. Follow-up: "What's the architecture of OpenBMC?" → give the Section 7 diagram verbally: U-Boot, Linux kernel, systemd, phosphor daemons on D-Bus, bmcweb for Redfish, ipmid for IPMI. 🔴**3. Explain your SSD validation project.** Why: your longest experience. Key points: NVMe (confirm), form factor, tools (nvme-cli, fio), test categories, one bug, automation. Follow-up: "How do you update SSD firmware?" → nvme fw-download with --xfer , then nvme fw-commit with slot and action. Action 1 activates at next reset, action 3 activates immediately without reset if FRMW bit 4 is supported. Then verify with fw-log and id-ctrl (nvme-cli; libnvme). 🔴**4. What did you automate with Python? Show me how.** Why: your resume's main technical claim. Answer: framework layers (config, device access, tests, logging, reporting, CI). Pick one script and explain it end to end. Follow-up: "Write a function that counts ERRORs in a log by module." → see Section 10.4. 🔴**5. How do you validate a new firmware build?** Why: the core job. Answer: entry check (version, checksum, release notes) → flash/update → verify version → smoke → targeted tests for changed areas → full regression → compare against the previous build's results → report. Follow-up: "What if smoke fails?" → stop, don't run full regression, report the build as rejected with logs, and confirm the failure isn't environmental by checking the previous build on the same bench. 🔴**6. Tell me about the most difficult bug you found.** Why: proves real experience and debugging skill. Answer: STAR: symptom, frequency, logs, isolation steps (A/B firmware, different DUT, different host), root cause as the developer confirmed it, your role, the fix verified, the regression test added. Follow-up: "What did you do versus the developer?" → be exact: "I narrowed it to X and gave them Y. They found the code fix." 🔴**7. What is Redfish? How have you used it?** Why: the standard BMC API. Answer: "DMTF's RESTful API for server management: HTTPS and JSON, schema-defined resources under /redfish/v1 (DSP0266). I used it to [read FirmwareVersion, power-control the host, query sensors and event logs — adapt only what's true]." Follow-up: "How do you authenticate?" → Basic auth, or POST to /redfish/v1/SessionService/Sessions and use the returned X-Auth-Token , then DELETE the session at the end (OpenBMC Redfish cheatsheet). 🔴**8. How do you decide whether a failure is hardware, firmware, software or a test issue?** Answer: reproduce → compare with the last known-good firmware on the same hardware (fails on both = environment or hardware; fails only on new = firmware) → swap DUT, cable or slot (failure follows the DUT = hardware) → check whether the script's assumptions changed (it fails without any firmware change = test or infra) → look at what the logs say. Follow-up: "Give an example." Use one real case. 🔴**9. Smoke vs sanity, regression vs retesting, severity vs priority.** Answer: Section 6 definitions with firmware examples (ISTQB glossary). 🔴**10. Which Linux commands do you use for debugging?** `Answer: dmesg -T , journalctl -u … -b -p err , systemctl status/--failed , lspci -vvv , lsblk , nvme list , grep -` n/-C , awk , tail -f , df -h , ps , top , ip a , ss -tulpn , scp . Give one example of a time each one helped. 🔴**11. How did you integrate tests with Jenkins?** Answer: Section 11 Jenkinsfile; --junitxml , junit step, archived logs, triggers, labelled agents. Follow-up: "What if the DUT is offline when the job starts?" → a pre-check stage pings or SSHes the DUT and aborts as an infrastructure failure (not a test failure), and notifies the lab owner. 🔴**12. Why are you looking for a change?** Answer: Section 15. It should be forward-looking, about depth in BMC/platform validation and a product-company environment, and never negative about HCLTech. 🟠 **HIGH PROBABILITY** 🟠**1. What is a BMC, and what happens when it boots?** U-Boot loads the kernel, initramfs and device tree; the kernel mounts a read-only squashfs root plus a read-write overlay; systemd starts; the phosphor services start; BMC state goes from NotReady to Ready (flash-layout; state manager). Follow-up: "Where are logs kept, and do they survive reboot?" /tmp and /run are tmpfs and are lost; /var persists. So capture logs before rebooting. 🟠**2. What is D-Bus in OpenBMC?** It's the IPC bus that every daemon publishes its objects on, under /xyz/openbmc_project/… . The ObjectMapper finds which service owns a path, and busctl inspects it (object-mapper). Follow-up: "How would you read host `state?" busctl get-property xyz.openbmc_project.State.Host /xyz/openbmc_project/state/host0` xyz.openbmc_project.State.Host CurrentHostState (standard form, (verify) on your build). 🟠**3. What is IPMI? Give some ipmitool commands.** ipmitool -I lanplus -H -U -P

chassis power status , sdr list , sel list , mc info , sol activate . Lanplus is IPMI 2.0 RMCP+ and is required for SOL (ipmitool man). Follow-up: "Why is the industry moving to Redfish?" IPMI has security issues in the spec itself (cipher 0, RAKP hash disclosure) (Rapid7), a binary format and a limited data model. Redfish is HTTPS/JSON and schema-driven. 🟠**4. Explain NVMe queues.** The host writes 64-byte commands into a submission queue in host memory and rings the tail doorbell. The controller fetches and executes them, posts a 16-byte completion with a phase bit and raises MSI-X. The host processes completions and writes the CQ head doorbell (OSDev NVMe). Follow-up: "Why is NVMe faster than AHCI?" Up to 64K queues × 64K commands versus 1 queue of 32, no locking, and fewer register accesses (NVMe overview). 🟠**5. What is SMART? Which fields do you check?** Critical warning, composite temperature (Kelvin), available spare vs threshold, percentage used, unsafe shutdowns, media errors, error log entries (libnvme types.h). Follow-up: "How do you verify a graceful vs surprise power-off?" Unsafe shutdowns should increment only when the controller didn't get CC.SHN before power loss. 🟠**6. How do you design a power-cycle test?** Precondition (known data written), loop N times: power off (graceful or surprise), wait, power on, wait for enumeration within a timeout, check link speed/width, SMART deltas, error log, dmesg, data verify; stop on the first anomaly with logs saved. 🟠**7. Explain the defect lifecycle and what goes in a bug report.** New → Assigned → Open → Fixed → Retest → Verified/Closed, plus Reopened, Rejected, Duplicate and Deferred (ISTQB). Report fields: build, platform, steps, expected/actual, frequency, logs, severity, regression info. 🟠**8. Write a Python script to call a Redfish API and validate the response.** See Section 10.3. 🟠**9. What is pytest's fixture? Scope?** Function (default), class, module, package, session. A yield fixture splits setup and teardown, and fixtures in conftest.py are shared (pytest fixtures). 🟠**10. How do you handle flaky tests?** Don't hide them with reruns. Rerun once to classify, track the flake rate, find the cause (timing, missing readiness wait, shared state, environment), and treat a real intermittent firmware failure as a defect with frequency data. 🟡 **MEDIUM PROBABILITY** 🟡**1. How does a BMC firmware update work in OpenBMC?** Upload the .mtd.tar (with its MANIFEST) via Redfish UpdateService. The image appears as a software object in Ready. Activation moves it to Active. Reboot makes it functional (code-update.md). Follow-up: "What blocks an update?" The MANIFEST MachineName not matching OPENBMC_TARGET_MACHINE , or a signature or key problem. 🟡**2. What are Redfish status codes 200/201/202/204/400/401/403/404/405/412/500/503?** See Section 8.1. Follow-up: "When does Redfish return 202?" For async operations, with a Location header pointing to a task monitor (DSP0266). 🟡**3. What is Yocto/BitBake?** Yocto is the build system that produces the OpenBMC image. BitBake runs the recipes: . setup then bitbake obmc-phosphor-image (openbmc README). [NOT ON RESUME — answer honestly about whether you built images.] 🟡**4. What is fio? How do you test data integrity?** Use --verify=crc32c --verify_fatal=1 --verify_dump=1 , and verify_state_save/load across power loss (fio HOWTO). 🟡**5. Git merge vs rebase; revert vs reset; bisect.** See Section 5.4. 🟡**6. What is UART and how do you capture boot logs?** TX/RX/GND, typically 115200 8N1; kernel console=ttyS,115200n8 (kernel serial console); capture with pyserial or picocom. 🟡**7. BVA and equivalence partitioning with a firmware example.** Fan PWM 0–100: test −1, 0, 1, 99, 100, 101. 🟡**8. Where do you see yourself in five years?** See Section 15. 🟢 **LOW PROBABILITY (but possible in BMC-heavy panels)** 🟢**1. What is MCTP?** DMTF's transport for management messages between the BMC and devices, independent of the physical bus (SMBus/I2C, PCIe VDM, etc.). Endpoints are addressed by 8-bit EIDs (DSP0236). [NOT ON RESUME — answer honestly] 🟢**2. What is PLDM?** DMTF data models over MCTP for monitoring, FRU, BIOS and firmware update (OpenBMC PLDM design). [NOT ON RESUME] 🟢**3. Explain I2C START/STOP and ACK.** START is SDA falling while SCL is high; STOP is SDA rising while SCL is high; the receiver ACKs by pulling SDA low on the 9th clock (NXP UM10204). [NOT ON RESUME] 🟢**4. What is KCS?** The host-side system interface to the BMC for in-band IPMI, driven by Linux ipmi_si (kernel IPMI docs). [NOT ON RESUME] 🟢**5. What is NVMe-MI?** NVMe management of drives out-of-band by the BMC, over SMBus or PCIe VDM, carried as MCTP message type 0x04 (NVMe-MI Q&A). This is a good bridge between your two projects. 🟢**6. Python GIL; threads vs processes vs asyncio.** Threads suit I/O-bound work like polling BMCs, processes suit CPU-bound work like parsing huge logs, and asyncio gives cooperative concurrency (Python glossary: GIL).

lessons.body:

| NVMe, SSD firmware, PCIe basics | [IMPLIED BY ROLE — likely asked, revise] | Deep | 9 |
| Redfish, REST API testing | [IMPLIED BY ROLE — likely asked, revise] | Medium-deep | 5.2, 8.1 [IMPLIED BY ROLE — likely asked, revise] IPMI (ipmitool, SEL/SDR) Medium 8.2 |
| UART / serial console | [IMPLIED BY ROLE — likely asked, revise] | Medium | 8.6 |

Stress, performance, power-cycle
