questions.answer: parallel { stage ... } or matrix; pitfalls: shared workspace files, limited executors, shared hardware needing locks, failFast choices.

questions.question: How do you prevent two builds using the same BMC?
questions.answer: Lockable Resources: lock(resource: 'bmc-x') or label pools with quantity; keep lock scope tight; release automatically at block end.

questions.question: How do test results appear in Jenkins?
questions.answer: pytest writes JUnit XML; the junit step (JUnit plugin) parses it, shows results and trends, and marks the build UNSTABLE on failures.

questions.question: What do you archive for embedded test runs?
questions.answer: JUnit/HTML reports, console logs, device snapshots, console/UART and journal logs, environment metadata, pip freeze, classification summary.

questions.question: A JUnit report is missing. How should the pipeline behave?
questions.answer: Fail with a clear message (allowEmptyResults: false where tests must run), because missing results mean the run is broken, not passed.

questions.question: How do you distinguish test failures from pipeline failures?
questions.answer: Map exit codes (pytest 1 → UNSTABLE; 2–5 → FAILURE), health gates before tests, typed exceptions and classification per test.

questions.question: When is retry appropriate?
questions.answer: Idempotent, transient operations (checkout, pip install, readiness polling), and agent-loss conditions; not for test suites or non-idempotent device actions.

questions.question: How do you design timeouts?
questions.answer: Operation timeouts < per-test < stage < pipeline; inactivity timeouts for hangs; every wait is a poll with a deadline.

questions.question: Risks of building pull requests?
questions.answer: PR code runs on your agents with whatever credentials and network access the build has. Use trusted Jenkinsfiles for untrusted PRs, isolated agents, no secrets, manual approval for hardware.

questions.question: How do you harden a Jenkins controller?
questions.answer: Authentication + authorisation, no controller executors, updated core/plugins, few plugins, HTTPS, restricted Script Console, backups, sandboxed pipelines.

questions.question: CI vs CD vs continuous deployment?
questions.answer: CI: integrate and test every change; continuous delivery: every change releasable with a manual release decision; continuous deployment: automatic release.

questions.question: How would you migrate Freestyle jobs to Pipeline?
questions.answer: Inventory jobs, write equivalent Jenkinsfiles (one stage per build step, post for publishers), run both in parallel for a while, compare results, switch triggers, archive the old jobs.

questions.question: How does a webhook-triggered PR build report back to GitHub?
questions.answer: Branch source plugin builds the PR, then posts a commit status/check; branch protection requires it before merging.

questions.question: Write test cases for a BMC firmware update via Redfish.
questions.answer: "Positive cases: update to N+1 with ApplyTime Immediate; with OnReset (then reset); verify FirmwareVersion and FirmwareInventory; verify settings like network and users persist; downgrade to N-1 if supported; update with the same version. Negative cases: corrupted tar, wrong machine image (MANIFEST MachineName mismatch should be rejected) (code-update.md), unsigned image, a second upload while one is in progress (expect a 4xx/503), a ReadOnly user attempting the update (403), and power loss during activation, which should recover via the alternate image if the platform has dual flash. Non-functional: update time, host stays up during BMC update, logs show the update events."

source.section: 6.3 Embedded testing questions with model answers

questions.question: How do you test a reboot scenario?
questions.answer: "Define the reboot type: BMC reboot ( Manager.Reset ), host warm reboot, host cold power cycle, AC cycle. For each iteration: trigger, wait for readiness with a timeout (BMC Ready, Redfish 200, host OS ping), verify state (versions, sensors present, no new error logs, no failed services), save logs, continue. Stop on the first failure, preserve evidence, and report the iteration number and timing."

source.section: 6.3 Embedded testing questions with model answers

questions.question: What's your entry and exit criteria for a firmware release?
questions.answer: "Entry: the build is delivered with release notes, it boots, and smoke passes. Exit: the planned suites are executed, the pass rate meets the target, there are no open critical or high defects without an approved waiver, known issues are documented, and the report is signed off (ISTQB)."

source.section: 6.3 Embedded testing questions with model answers

questions.question: How do you prioritise when there's no time for a full regression?
questions.answer: "Risk-based: first the areas the release notes say changed, then features that depend on them, then historically flaky or high-defect areas, then customer-critical paths such as firmware update, power control and data integrity. I state explicitly what was not run." **Common mistakes in embedded testing answers:** forgetting power and reset as test variables; no stopping strategy for loops; not preserving logs; treating intermittent failures as "cannot reproduce" without frequency data.

source.section: 6.3 Embedded testing questions with model answers

questions.question: How do you test BMC functionality?
questions.answer: "Interface by interface: Redfish, IPMI, WebUI, SSH. Feature by feature: power control, sensors, event logs, inventory/FRU, firmware update, users and roles, network, time/NTP, LEDs, factory reset, BMC reboot persistence. Each gets positive, negative and persistence-across-reboot cases. [Name the subset you actually own — adapt.]"

questions.question: How do you debug BMC issues?
questions.answer: "Layered: console/UART if it isn't booting; network if it's unreachable; obmcutil state and systemctl --failed for service health; journalctl -u <unit> -b for the failing daemon; busctl to check whether the D-Bus object exists and has the right value; then the Redfish/IPMI front end. I capture logs before rebooting, because /tmp and /run are lost."

questions.question: How do you collect BMC logs?
questions.answer: " journalctl (whole boot, or per unit, -o json-pretty when I need fields like REDFISH_MESSAGE_ID (redfish logging)), the `Redfish EventLog at /redfish/v1/Systems/system/LogServices/EventLog/Entries , obmcutil listlogs , a BMC dump via` phosphor-debug-collector/dreport, and the UART console capture. In automation, a failure hook pulls these automatically. [adapt]"

questions.question: How do you verify a firmware build before testing it?
questions.answer:
"Check the tarball's MANIFEST ( version , MachineName ), the checksum against the release notes, and that the version string matches what's expected. After the update, confirm /etc/os-release ( VERSION_ID , BUILD_ID ) and Redfish

```code
FirmwareVersion match."
```

questions.question: How do you validate a new firmware build?
questions.answer: Use the checklist in 7.8.

questions.question: How do you perform regression testing on BMC?
questions.answer: "Smoke on every build; full regression [nightly / per drop — adapt] in Jenkins; compare results with the previous build so new failures stand out; re-run new failures once to separate flaky from deterministic; file real regressions with build-to-build evidence. The upstream project's openbmc-test-automation suite organises tests the same way, in buckets like HW_CI and CT_basic_run run against OPENBMC_HOST (openbmc-test-automation)."

questions.question: How do you test reboot scenarios?
questions.answer: "BMC reboot via Manager.Reset with GracefulRestart (REDFISH-cheatsheet), reboot over SSH, ipmitool mc reset cold , AC cycle. Host reboot via ComputerSystem.Reset . Each iteration: wait for Ready, verify version, network, sensors and settings, and that there are no new error logs or failed units. Also check that the host keeps running during a BMC reboot, since a BMC reboot shouldn't power off the host, and that the power restore policy is applied after an AC cycle."

questions.question: How do you identify whether an issue is hardware, firmware or software?
questions.answer: "Reproduce on a second board with the same firmware. If it follows the board, it's likely hardware. Reproduce on the same board with the previous firmware. If the old firmware is fine, it's a firmware regression. If both pass but my test fails, I check the test and environment. For a BMC sensor, I check the hardware path directly: i2cdetect on the bus, /sys/class/hwmon , versus what the daemon publishes on D-Bus."

questions.question: How do you report a firmware defect?
questions.answer: "Title with symptom and area; build and platform; steps; expected vs actual; frequency; logs (journal, event log, dump, console); last known good build; severity proposal; my analysis so far, clearly labelled as hypothesis."

questions.question: How do you validate fixes?
questions.answer: "Re-run the exact reproduction on the fix build, at least as many iterations as the original failure rate demands. If it failed 1 in 50, I run a few hundred. Then run regression on the surrounding area. Add the reproduction to the automated suite."

questions.question: What is the difference between in-band and out-of-band management?
questions.answer: "In-band goes through the host OS, for example ipmitool -I open via /dev/ipmi0 using KCS. Out-of-band goes to the BMC's own network interface (Redfish over HTTPS, IPMI over LAN) and works even when the host is off or hung (kernel IPMI)."

questions.question: What is SOL?
questions.answer: "Serial-over-LAN: the host's serial console redirected over the network. Use ipmitool -I lanplus … sol activate , and exit with ~. (ipmitool man). OpenBMC also exposes it over SSH."

questions.question: What is a factory reset on OpenBMC?
questions.answer: " Manager.ResetToDefaults with ResetAll . It clears /var , /home and /etc after reboot, so I verify that the network, users and settings return to defaults (code-update.md; REDFISH-cheatsheet)."

questions.question: What is the host power systemd chain?
questions.answer: `" obmc-host-start@0.target requires obmc-host-startmin@0.target , which pulls in obmc-chassis-poweron@0.target and` start_host@0.service . Failures route via OnFailure to a quiesce target (openbmc-systemd). If the host won't power on, systemctl list-jobs shows what's stuck."

questions.question: What is the Redfish Service Validator?
questions.answer: "A DMTF tool that walks the Redfish tree with GETs and checks every payload against the schema: missing, unknown or wrongly-typed properties, enum values, URIs. You install it with pip install redfish_service_validator and run it against -r https://<bmc> . A good regression gate is to compare its error count with the previous build (Service Validator)." [Say whether you ran it — only if true.]

questions.question: What are sensors and thresholds in OpenBMC?
questions.answer: See 7.5. Thresholds are Warning and Critical, High and Low. Crossing one should create a log entry and change Redfish health.

questions.question: Default OpenBMC credentials?
questions.answer: root / 0penBmc (zero, not O) on upstream (REDFISH-cheatsheet). Products should change them, so testing that defaults are disabled or forced to change is a security case.

questions.question: What's the difference between phosphor-hwmon and dbus-sensors?
questions.answer: "Both publish sensors to D-Bus. phosphor-hwmon is configured per machine at build time. dbus-sensors is configured at runtime from entity-manager JSON based on detected hardware (sensor-architecture; the entity-manager detail is (verify))."

questions.question: How does a Redfish sensor get its data?
questions.answer: "The daemon reads hardware (hwmon/I2C) and publishes on D-Bus. Mapper associations link sensors to a chassis ( all_sensors ). bmcweb looks those up and builds /redfish/v1/Chassis/<id>/Sensors (sensor-architecture)."

questions.question: What would you check if the event log has no entries after an event?
questions.answer: "Is phosphor-logging running? Was an entry created on D-Bus ( obmcutil listlogs )? Is bmcweb reading the right log service? Was the log cleared or rotated? Is time wrong, so the entry is there but sorted oddly?"

questions.question: What is a namespace? Why have more than one?
questions.answer: It's a separately addressable LBA range with its own format, used for multi-tenant isolation, different LBA formats, or attaching to different controllers. It's created with Namespace Management (0x0D) and attached with Namespace Attachment (0x15). Then run nvme ns-rescan (spec practice).

questions.question: What's the difference between a controller reset and an NVM subsystem reset?
questions.answer: A controller reset (CC.EN 1 → 0 → 1, nvme reset ) resets one controller. An NVM subsystem reset ( nvme subsystem-reset ) resets the whole subsystem, including the link (nvme-cli docs). Some firmware activations need one or the other (status 0x111 vs 0x110).

questions.question: What is APST and why does it matter in validation?
questions.answer: Autonomous Power State Transition (feature 0x0C) moves the drive into low-power states on its own. Buggy entry/exit is a classic cause of timeouts and drive drops, which is why the kernel suggests disabling it when a controller goes down (pci.c).

questions.question: How do you verify data integrity across power loss?
questions.answer: Use fio with verify and state save, cut power mid-write, then verify only. On drives with PLP, every acknowledged write must survive. On client drives without PLP, only flushed data is guaranteed (fio HOWTO; PLP behaviour is (verify) against the product spec).

questions.question: Why does SMART temperature show ~310?
questions.answer: It's in Kelvin, so 310 K ≈ 37 °C (libnvme).

questions.question: What's MTFA?
questions.answer: Maximum Time for Firmware Activation, in 100 ms units in Identify Controller. It's the longest I/O pause allowed during immediate activation (libnvme).

questions.question: Explain PRP vs SGL.
questions.answer: Both describe the data buffers for a command. PRPs are page-pointer lists. SGLs are scatter-gather descriptors. The Linux driver uses SGLs above sgl_threshold (32K default) when the device supports them (pci.c).

questions.question: What would you include in an SSD firmware bug report?
questions.answer: Firmware revision (old and new), drive model and serial (masked if needed), host and kernel, nvme-cli version, exact commands, iteration count, dmesg, SMART and error log before and after, telemetry, fio job file and verify_dump output, and whether it reproduces on N-1.

questions.question: Why precondition before measuring performance?
questions.answer: See 5.6. FOB results overstate steady-state performance.

questions.question: What's write amplification?
questions.answer:
NAND writes divided by host writes. GC and wear-levelling make it greater than 1, especially at high fill and with random writes. It shows up as steady-state drops and endurance consumption (conceptual).

**Common mistakes:**

Saying NVMe "replaces PCIe". NVMe is a protocol that runs over PCIe. Not knowing SMART temperature is in Kelvin. Treating 0x10B/0x111 as failures. Running fio write tests on a mounted filesystem. Comparing performance without preconditioning. Power-cycling before collecting telemetry.

questions.question: "How did you integrate regression with CI?"
questions.answer:
"[Describe the real trigger: nightly cron / upstream FW build / manual with parameters]. Tests ran on a labelled bench agent, results came back as JUnit, and logs were archived. Before CI we [manual process, time]. After, [time, effort] [adapt with numbers]." **"A regression pipeline fails. Is it Jenkins, automation, firmware or hardware?"** See Section 12, scenario 7. **"How do you avoid two jobs flashing the same board?"** Lockable resources or a dedicated agent per bench with one executor. **"How would you run the same suite on 5 platforms?"** A matrix or parallel stage over platform labels, each acquiring its own lock. **"Where do secrets live?"** In the Jenkins credentials store, never in the repo, and masked in logs.

**Common mistakes:** saying "Jenkins runs tests" without explaining agents and how they reach hardware; no artifact or log retention strategy; treating every red build as a firmware bug.

questions.question: Tell me about yourself.
questions.answer: use the 90-second intro (Section 14).
followUps: "Why did you move from SSD to BMC?" → "The project moved me to a new OpenBMC programme in Bengaluru [adapt]. It made sense for me because BMC validation builds directly on what I did in SSD: firmware update flows, logs, power and reset testing, now at platform level."
questions.why: opener; checks whether your story matches the resume.
questions.keyPoints: about 4.5 years; SSD → OpenBMC; Python automation, Linux debugging, CI; one achievement with a number.

questions.question: Explain your current OpenBMC project. What exactly do you do?
questions.answer: use the 2-minute project answer (Section 13).
followUps: "What's the architecture of OpenBMC?" → give the Section 7 diagram verbally: U-Boot, Linux kernel, systemd, phosphor daemons on D-Bus, bmcweb for Redfish, ipmid for IPMI.
questions.why: it's your current role; they're checking depth and ownership.
questions.keyPoints: platform class; interfaces tested; your automation; one bug; the process improvement.

questions.question: Explain your SSD validation project.
questions.answer: Key points: NVMe (confirm), form factor, tools (nvme-cli, fio), test categories, one bug, automation.
followUps: "How do you update SSD firmware?" → nvme fw-download with --xfer , then nvme fw-commit with slot and action. Action 1 activates at next reset, action 3 activates immediately without reset if FRMW bit 4 is supported. Then verify with fw-log and id-ctrl (nvme-cli; libnvme).
questions.keyPoints: NVMe (confirm), form factor, tools (nvme-cli, fio), test categories, one bug, automation.

questions.question: What did you automate with Python? Show me how.
questions.answer: framework layers (config, device access, tests, logging, reporting, CI). Pick one script and explain it end to end.
followUps: "Write a function that counts ERRORs in a log by module." → see Section 10.4.

questions.question: Tell me about the most difficult bug you found.
questions.answer: STAR: symptom, frequency, logs, isolation steps (A/B firmware, different DUT, different host), root cause as the developer confirmed it, your role, the fix verified, the regression test added.
followUps: "What did you do versus the developer?" → be exact: "I narrowed it to X and gave them Y. They found the code fix."
questions.why: proves real experience and debugging skill.

questions.question: What is Redfish? How have you used it?
questions.answer: "DMTF's RESTful API for server management: HTTPS and JSON, schema-defined resources under /redfish/v1 (DSP0266). I used it to [read FirmwareVersion, power-control the host, query sensors and event logs — adapt only what's true]."
followUps: "How do you authenticate?" → Basic auth, or POST to /redfish/v1/SessionService/Sessions and use the returned X-Auth-Token , then DELETE the session at the end (OpenBMC Redfish cheatsheet).

questions.question: How do you decide whether a failure is hardware, firmware, software or a test issue?
questions.answer: reproduce → compare with the last known-good firmware on the same hardware (fails on both = environment or hardware; fails only on new = firmware) → swap DUT, cable or slot (failure follows the DUT = hardware) → check whether the script's assumptions changed (it fails without any firmware change = test or infra) → look at what the logs say.
followUps: "Give an example." Use one real case.

questions.question: Smoke vs sanity, regression vs retesting, severity vs priority.
questions.answer: Section 6 definitions with firmware examples (ISTQB glossary).

questions.question: Which Linux commands do you use for debugging?
questions.answer: `Answer: dmesg -T , journalctl -u … -b -p err , systemctl status/--failed , lspci -vvv , lsblk , nvme list , grep -` n/-C , awk , tail -f , df -h , ps , top , ip a , ss -tulpn , scp . Give one example of a time each one helped.

questions.question: How did you integrate tests with Jenkins?
questions.answer: Section 11 Jenkinsfile; --junitxml , junit step, archived logs, triggers, labelled agents.
followUps: "What if the DUT is offline when the job starts?" → a pre-check stage pings or SSHes the DUT and aborts as an infrastructure failure (not a test failure), and notifies the lab owner.

questions.question: Why are you looking for a change?
questions.answer:
Section 15. It should be forward-looking, about depth in BMC/platform validation and a product-company environment, and never negative about HCLTech.

🟠 **HIGH PROBABILITY** 🟠**1. What is a BMC, and what happens when it boots?** U-Boot loads the kernel, initramfs and device tree; the kernel mounts a read-only squashfs root plus a read-write overlay; systemd starts; the phosphor services start; BMC state goes from NotReady to Ready (flash-layout; state manager).
followUps: "Where are logs kept, and do they survive reboot?" /tmp and /run are tmpfs and are lost; /var persists. So capture logs before rebooting. 🟠**2. What is D-Bus in OpenBMC?** It's the IPC bus that every daemon publishes its objects on, under /xyz/openbmc_project/… . The ObjectMapper finds which service owns a path, and busctl inspects it (object-mapper). "How would you read host `state?" busctl get-property xyz.openbmc_project.State.Host /xyz/openbmc_project/state/host0` xyz.openbmc_project.State.Host CurrentHostState (standard form, (verify) on your build). 🟠**3. What is IPMI?

Give some ipmitool commands.** ipmitool -I lanplus -H -U -P

chassis power status , sdr list , sel list , mc info , sol activate . Lanplus is IPMI 2.0 RMCP+ and is required for SOL (ipmitool man). "Why is the industry moving to Redfish?" IPMI has security issues in the spec itself (cipher 0, RAKP hash disclosure) (Rapid7), a binary format and a limited data model. Redfish is HTTPS/JSON and schema-driven. 🟠**4. Explain NVMe queues.** The host writes 64-byte commands into a submission queue in host memory and rings the tail doorbell. The controller fetches and executes them, posts a 16-byte completion with a phase bit and raises MSI-X. The host processes completions and writes the CQ head doorbell (OSDev NVMe). "Why is NVMe faster than AHCI?" Up to 64K queues × 64K commands versus 1 queue of 32, no locking, and fewer register accesses (NVMe overview). 🟠**5. What is SMART?

Which fields do you check?** Critical warning, composite temperature (Kelvin), available spare vs threshold, percentage used, unsafe shutdowns, media errors, error log entries (libnvme types.h). "How do you verify a graceful vs surprise power-off?" Unsafe shutdowns should increment only when the controller didn't get CC.SHN before power loss. 🟠**6. How do you design a power-cycle test?** Precondition (known data written), loop N times: power off (graceful or surprise), wait, power on, wait for enumeration within a timeout, check link speed/width, SMART deltas, error log, dmesg, data verify; stop on the first anomaly with logs saved. 🟠**7. Explain the defect lifecycle and what goes in a bug report.** New → Assigned → Open → Fixed → Retest → Verified/Closed, plus Reopened, Rejected, Duplicate and Deferred (ISTQB). Report fields: build, platform, steps, expected/actual, frequency, logs, severity, regression info. 🟠**8. Write a Python script to call a Redfish API and validate the response.** See Section 10.3.

🟠**9. What is pytest's fixture?

Scope?** Function (default), class, module, package, session. A yield fixture splits setup and teardown, and fixtures in conftest.py are shared (pytest fixtures).

🟠**10. How do you handle flaky tests?** Don't hide them with reruns. Rerun once to classify, track the flake rate, find the cause (timing, missing readiness wait, shared state, environment), and treat a real intermittent firmware failure as a defect with frequency data.

questions.question: What is PLDM?
questions.answer: DMTF data models over MCTP for monitoring, FRU, BIOS and firmware update (OpenBMC PLDM design).

questions.question: Explain I2C START/STOP and ACK.
questions.answer: START is SDA falling while SCL is high; STOP is SDA rising while SCL is high; the receiver ACKs by pulling SDA low on the 9th clock (NXP UM10204).

questions.question: What is KCS?
questions.answer: The host-side system interface to the BMC for in-band IPMI, driven by Linux ipmi_si (kernel IPMI docs).

questions.question: Python GIL; threads vs processes vs asyncio.
questions.answer: Threads suit I/O-bound work like polling BMCs, processes suit CPU-bound work like parsing huge logs, and asyncio gives cooperative concurrency (Python glossary: GIL).

This report is the bridge into Part VIII’s final phase. This plan turns the handbook into 180 study sessions, one per day, in eight phases that follow the chapter dependency map: Python fundamentals, data and functions, intermediate Python, the standard library and packaging, pytest and quality, APIs and tooling, embedded automation and frameworks, and finally the capstone and interview preparation. Every session names the chapters, exercises or project steps to do, and a concrete “done when” check, so you always know whether a day is finished. options: Sets are sorted, so they use binary search
Hashing gives average O(1) lookup versus O(n) scanning

scenarios.title: A Redfish endpoint works manually but fails in automation
scenarios.prompt: A Redfish endpoint works manually but fails in automation. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: curl returns 200 for GET /redfish/v1/Systems/system; the pytest suite gets 401 (or 400, or SSLError) on the same URL.

steps.label: Plausible causes
steps.text: Missing/incorrect auth header in the client; token from a different session; data= instead of json= on POST; curl using -k while Python verifies TLS; proxy variables (HTTPS_PROXY) affecting Python only; URL joining errors (double slash, missing /redfish/v1); different user/role.

steps.label: Investigation sequence
steps.text: (a) Log the exact prepared request from Python (method, URL, headers redacted). (b) Run curl with -v and compare. (c) Check environment variables in the test process. (d) Repeat the Python call in a REPL with the same config.

steps.label: Commands/code
steps.text:
```code
$ curl -v --cacert lab-ca.pem -H "X-Auth-Token: $TOKEN" https://
bmc.example.test/redfish/v1/Systems/system
$ env | grep -i -E "proxy|requests_ca_bundle|ssl_cert"
import logging, http.client
http.client.HTTPConnection.debuglevel = 1      # prints request lines and
headers
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG)       # urllib3 debug logs
```

steps.label: Expected observations
steps.text: A difference: missing X-Auth-Token, Content- `Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded, a proxy CONNECT, //redfish,` or a TLS verify failure that curl skipped with -k.

steps.label: Distinguishing causes
steps.text: 401 → auth header/session; 400 MalformedJSON → body encoding; SSLError → trust store; ProxyError/odd 403 from a proxy page → proxy variables; 404 → URL construction.

steps.label: Corrective actions
steps.text: Use json=; centralise URL joining and auth in the client; configure verify with the lab CA; set NO_PROXY for lab hosts; add a unit test that asserts the exact URL and headers.

steps.label: Interview-ready explanation
steps.text: “When manual works and automation doesn’t, I diff the two requests byte by byte. The difference is almost always in headers, body encoding, TLS trust or environment — like curl using -k while Python verifies certificates, or a proxy variable on the CI agent. Once found, I fix it in the client’s single request path and add a unit test so it can’t regress.”

scenarios.title: A BMC stops responding after a firmware update
scenarios.prompt: A BMC stops responding after a firmware update. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: Update task reached 100%; BMC rebooted; Redfish, SSH and IPMI time out for more than 15 minutes.

steps.label: Plausible causes
steps.text: Still booting (first boot after update can be slow: migrations, key generation); boot failure/loop (bad image, failed activation); network config lost (DHCP vs static reset, VLAN, MAC change); services failing to start; watchdog reset loop; rollback to the alternate image.

steps.label: Investigation sequence
steps.text: (a) Console: is it booting, looping, or stuck? (b) Is the IP still assigned (ARP/ping on the management network, DHCP server leases)? (c) Port checks 22/443/623. (d) If the console has a login: check network config and failed services. (e) Check which image is running (A/B).

steps.label: Commands/code
steps.text:
```code
  $ nc -vz -w 3 bmc.example.test 443 ; nc -vz -w 3 bmc.example.test 22
  $ ip neigh | grep 192.0.2.10                    # did the MAC change?
# (console)  ip -br addr ; systemctl --failed ; journalctl -b -p err ;
obmcutil state
```

steps.label: Expected observations
steps.text: One of: repeating U-Boot banners (boot loop); kernel panic text; a login prompt with no IP address; services failed (bmcweb, network); a different firmware version than expected (rollback).

steps.label: Distinguishing causes
steps.text: Boot loop/panic → image/activation; login + no IP → network configuration; IP present but ports closed → services; old version → rollback; slow but progressing → readiness timeout too short.

steps.label: Corrective actions
steps.text: Recover via alternate image or recovery procedure; file a bug with console log; set a realistic readiness deadline based on measured first-boot time; add console capture to all update tests; verify network config persistence as a test.

steps.label: Interview-ready explanation
steps.text: “My first tool is the console, because it’s the only interface that works when the network stack doesn’t. It tells me in seconds whether the BMC is boot-looping, panicking, booted without network, or just slow. That decides whether it’s an image problem, a config-persistence problem or a test timing problem.”

source.section: 26.2 Scenario 2 — A BMC stops responding after a firmware update

scenarios.title: UART logs stop unexpectedly during boot
scenarios.prompt: UART logs stop unexpectedly during boot. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: Console capture shows U-Boot and early kernel messages, then nothing, though the BMC becomes reachable over the network.

steps.label: Plausible causes
steps.text: Kernel switched console to another UART (console= in bootargs); baud change after the boot loader; console log level lowered; getty not running on that tty; the capture program lost the USB adapter (re-enumeration on power cycle); another program stole the port.

steps.label: Investigation sequence
steps.text:
(a) Check capture logs for adapter errors/ `gaps. (b) Over SSH: cat /proc/cmdline, cat /proc/consoles, systemctl status serial-getty@*.`
Compare with previous firmware’s bootargs. (d) Check lsof on the capture host.

steps.label: Commands/code
steps.text:
```code
# cat /proc/cmdline         (e.g. console=ttyS4,115200n8)
# cat /proc/consoles
$ lsof /dev/serial/by-id/usb-*        # capture host: who has the port
open?
```

steps.label: Expected observations
steps.text: Console now ttyS5, or baud differs, or a second process holding the port, or capture log shows a SerialException at the time of power cycle.

steps.label: Distinguishing causes
steps.text: Garbage instead of silence → baud; complete silence with correct port → console moved or getty missing; capture exception → adapter/USB.

steps.label: Corrective actions
steps.text: Fix bootargs/getty configuration (bug if unintended); open the port with exclusive=True; power the adapter independently; reconnect logic that records gaps.

steps.label: Interview-ready explanation
steps.text: “Silence after a certain point usually means the console moved, not that the system stopped. I check /proc/ cmdline and /proc/consoles over SSH and compare with the previous build. If the capture tool lost the adapter, the capture log shows it — that’s why my capture records gaps.”

scenarios.title: An IPMI command returns an error only on one platform
scenarios.prompt: An IPMI command returns an error only on one platform. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: ipmitool raw 0x06 0x04 (Get Self Test Results) returns rsp=0xc1 on platform B; works on A.

steps.label: Plausible causes
steps.text: Command optional and not implemented on B; different IPMI stack/OEM providers; privilege differences (would be 0xD4); command disabled by a filter/allow-list on B; firmware bug.

steps.label: Investigation sequence
steps.text: (a) Decode the code: 0xC1 = invalid command. (b) Check B’s documentation/feature list. (c) Check B’s IPMI provider configuration or command allow-list. (d) Compare firmware lineage of A and B.

steps.label: Commands/code
steps.text:
```code
$ ipmitool -I lanplus -H bmcB.example.test -U automation -E -
C 17 raw 0x06 0x04
$ ipmitool ... mc info          # IPMI version, additional device support
# journalctl -u phosphor-ipmi-net* -n 50     (BMC side; unit names vary)
```

steps.label: Expected observations
steps.text: Consistent 0xC1 on B; documentation lists the command as unsupported, or a provider library absent from B’s image.

steps.label: Distinguishing causes
steps.text: 0xC1 → not implemented/filtered; 0xD4 → privilege; 0xD5 → state; transport error → session/cipher. Requirements decide if 0xC1 is a bug.

steps.label: Corrective actions
steps.text: If required, file a bug for B; otherwise make the test platform-aware (capability in config) and mark expected behaviour per platform.

steps.label: Interview-ready explanation
steps.text: “I decode the completion code first. 0xC1 means the BMC answered but doesn’t implement that command, which is legal for optional commands. Then requirements decide: either it’s a product gap on that platform, or my test assumed a capability it shouldn’t.”

scenarios.title: An MCTP endpoint cannot be discovered
scenarios.prompt: An MCTP endpoint cannot be discovered. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: A NIC’s PLDM sensors are missing; mctpd shows no endpoint for it.

steps.label: Plausible causes
steps.text: Device unpowered/absent; wrong bus or address in configuration; MCTP interface for that bus not created; device firmware has MCTP disabled; bus stuck or mux channel wrong; static EID conflict; device answered but message type list lacks PLDM.

steps.label: Investigation sequence
steps.text: Presence → bus health → interface → configuration → device capability → analyser.

steps.label: Commands/code
steps.text:
(BMC, authorised)
```code
# mctp link ; mctp addr ; mctp route
# dmesg | grep -i -E "i2c|mctp"
# i2cdetect -y 7            # only if probing bus 7 is approved
# journalctl -u mctpd -b
```

steps.label: Expected observations
steps.text: Missing interface (config), I²C errors (bus), NACK at the address (device/power/mux), or endpoint present without PLDM message type.

steps.label: Distinguishing causes
steps.text: No ACK at address → physical/power/mux; ACK but no MCTP response → device firmware/MCTP disabled; endpoint present, PLDM missing → capability; EID duplicates → configuration conflict.

steps.label: Corrective actions
steps.text: Fix platform configuration, enable MCTP in device firmware, repair bus issues, resolve EID allocation; add a discovery test comparing expected endpoints by UUID.

steps.label: Interview-ready explanation
steps.text: “I walk up the stack: is the device powered and ACKing on the bus, is the MCTP interface for that bus configured, does the device answer MCTP control messages, and does it list PLDM in its message types. Each step rules out a layer, and a bus analyser settles disagreements.”

scenarios.title: A PLDM request times out intermittently
scenarios.prompt: A PLDM request times out intermittently. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: About 1 in 300 GetSensorReading requests to EID 12 time out.

steps.label: Plausible causes
steps.text: Bus contention/arbitration loss; device busy (should send NOT_READY but drops instead); timeout too tight relative to latency tail; lost packets/reassembly errors; late responses mismatched; BMC CPU load delaying the requester.

steps.label: Investigation sequence
steps.text: (a) Collect per-request latency histograms. (b) Correlate timeouts with other bus traffic and BMC load. (c) Check kernel logs for I²C errors at those times. (d) Look for late responses with old instance IDs. (e) Analyser capture around a failure.

steps.label: Commands/code
steps.text:
```code
import statistics, time
lat, fails = [], 0
for _ in range(1000):
    t0 = time.monotonic()
    try:
        pldm.get_tid(12)
        lat.append(time.monotonic() - t0)
    except Exception:                      # counting failures in a
diagnostic loop
        fails += 1
print(f"fails={fails} p50={statistics.median(lat):.3f}s p99={sorted(lat)[i
nt(0.99*len(lat))]:.3f}s")
```

steps.label: Expected observations
steps.text: Either p99 close to the timeout (tight timeout), failures clustered with other traffic (contention), I²C errors (bus), or responses arriving after timeout (late).

steps.label: Distinguishing causes
steps.text: Latency tail → timeout/performance; clustered with traffic → contention; kernel bus errors → physical layer; late matched responses → requester logic.

steps.label: Corrective actions
steps.text: Adjust timeout within spec timing; coordinate pollers; fix device firmware (NOT_READY instead of silence); fix stale-response handling; add a soak test with failure-rate threshold.

steps.label: Interview-ready explanation
steps.text: “Intermittent timeouts need statistics, not anecdotes. I measure the latency distribution and failure correlation. If successful responses crowd near the timeout, the timeout or device performance is the issue; if failures cluster with other bus traffic, it’s contention; kernel I²C errors point to the physical layer.”

scenarios.title: An SSH command succeeds manually but fails in Jenkins
scenarios.prompt: An SSH command succeeds manually but fails in Jenkins. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: ssh bmc 'obmcutil state' works on your laptop; Jenkins `step fails with Host key verification failed or command not found or` hangs.

steps.label: Plausible causes
steps.text: Unknown host key on the agent; different user/ key; no agent forwarding; PATH differences in non-interactive shells; DNS/route differences; the command prompting for input (no TTY) and hanging.

steps.label: Investigation sequence
steps.text: Reproduce on the agent as the Jenkins user with BatchMode=yes, -vvv, and print environment remotely.

steps.label: Commands/code
steps.text:
```code
$ sudo -u jenkins ssh -vvv -o BatchMode=yes automation@bmc.example.test 'e
cho $PATH; which obmcutil'
```

steps.label: Expected observations
steps.text: Host key prompt (fails under BatchMode), “Permission denied (publickey)”, or a PATH without the tool’s directory.

steps.label: Distinguishing causes
steps.text: Host key message → known_hosts provisioning; publickey → credential binding; not found → PATH/full path; hang → interactive prompt.

steps.label: Corrective actions
steps.text: Provision known_hosts for the agent; bind the 7. key via Jenkins credentials; use absolute paths; always use BatchMode=yes and timeouts.

steps.label: Interview-ready explanation
steps.text: “Jenkins runs as a different user, non-interactively, from a different machine. I reproduce exactly that context with BatchMode and verbose logging; the cause is usually host keys, credentials or PATH, and the fix belongs in agent provisioning, not in disabling checks.”

source.section: 26.7 Scenario 7 — An SSH command succeeds manually but fails in Jenkins

scenarios.title: An I²C device does not acknowledge requests
scenarios.prompt: An I²C device does not acknowledge requests. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: Reads from 0x4C on bus 9 raise ENXIO; device worked last week.

steps.label: Plausible causes
steps.text: Device unpowered (host off — many devices are on host power rails); mux channel not selected; address changed (strap/board revision); bus stuck; 7-bit/8-bit address confusion in a new script; kernel driver now owns it.

steps.label: Investigation sequence
steps.text: Check host power state → mux topology → i2cdetect (if approved) → kernel logs → board revision → analyser.

steps.label: Commands/code
steps.text:
```code
# obmcutil state                 (is the host on?)
# i2cdetect -l                   (bus numbering, muxes)
# dmesg | grep -i i2c
```

steps.label: Expected observations
steps.text: Host off; a mux bus number changed after a kernel update; UU for the address; or SDA held low.

steps.label: Distinguishing causes
steps.text: All addresses NACK → bus/mux/power; only this one → device, address, strap; UU → driver ownership.

steps.label: Corrective actions
steps.text: Power the host before testing; use stable bus naming from configuration; read via driver interfaces; recover/repair the bus.

steps.label: Interview-ready explanation
steps.text: “A NACK on the address means no one answered there. I check whether the device is powered — often it’s on a host rail — whether the mux channel or bus numbering changed, and whether a kernel driver owns it. Only after that do I suspect the device.”

source.section: 26.8 Scenario 8 — An I²C device does not acknowledge requests

scenarios.title: Tests pass individually but fail during parallel execution
scenarios.prompt: Tests pass individually but fail during parallel execution. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: pytest test_x.py::test_y passes; pytest -n 4 fails randomly in power and session tests.

steps.label: Plausible causes
steps.text: Shared BMC state (power, settings); session limit exhaustion; session-scoped fixtures running per worker; name collisions in created resources; rate limiting.

steps.label: Investigation sequence
steps.text: Run with -n 4 -v and record worker IDs; inspect which tests overlap in time; check BMC session count during run.

steps.label: Commands/code
steps.text:
```code
$ pytest -n 4 --dist loadgroup -v
@pytest.mark.xdist_group("bmc01-power")       # serialise power tests on
one worker
def test_power_cycle(redfish, ipmi): ...
```

steps.label: Expected observations
steps.text: Failures coincide with a power test on another worker, or 401/503 as sessions max out.

steps.label: Distinguishing causes
steps.text: Correlated with state-changing tests → shared state; 401/503 → resource limits; duplicate-name errors → naming.

steps.label: Corrective actions
steps.text: Group/serialise state-changing tests per BMC; unique names; bound workers; parallelise across BMCs instead.

steps.label: Interview-ready explanation
steps.text: “Parallel failures that vanish in isolation mean shared state or shared limits. A physical BMC is a single resource; I serialise tests that change its state with xdist groups or locks, and parallelise across BMCs.”

source.section: 26.9 Scenario 9 — Tests pass individually but fail during parallel execution

scenarios.title: A regression suite produces inconsistent results
scenarios.prompt: A regression suite produces inconsistent results. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: Same firmware, same suite: 3–12 failures per night, different tests each time.

steps.label: Plausible causes
steps.text: Timing assumptions (sleeps); order dependence; other jobs on the BMC; environmental noise; real product intermittency; resource leaks over the run.

steps.label: Investigation sequence
steps.text: Collect a failure history per test; compute flake rates; correlate with time, order, worker, concurrent jobs; inspect failure messages for patterns (timeouts vs assertions).

steps.label: Commands/code
steps.text:
```code
$ pytest -p randomly -v              # (pytest-randomly) expose order
dependence
$ pytest --count 50 -x tests/test_suspect.py   # (pytest-repeat) quantify
one test
```

steps.label: Expected observations
steps.text: Failures cluster: e.g. tests right after a reboot test; or all timeouts at one point in the night when another job runs.

steps.label: Distinguishing causes
steps.text: Order-dependent → isolation; time-dependent → environment; uniformly random with product errors → product intermittency.

steps.label: Corrective actions
steps.text: Replace sleeps with condition polling; restore state; lock BMCs; file product bugs with rates; quarantine visibly while fixing.

steps.label: Interview-ready explanation
steps.text: “Inconsistent results are data. I build per-test history and look for correlation with order, time and concurrency. That separates test design problems from environment and from genuine product intermittency, which then gets a bug with a measured rate.”

source.section: 26.10 Scenario 10 — A regression suite produces inconsistent results

scenarios.title: 401 errors appear halfway through a long Redfish run
scenarios.prompt: 401 errors appear halfway through a long Redfish run. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: First 200 tests pass; then most fail with 401; next night same pattern.

steps.label: Plausible causes
steps.text: Session leak hitting the BMC’s session limit; session timeout during a long idle test; password rotation mid-run; account lockout.

steps.label: Investigation sequence
steps.text: Query SessionService/Sessions at failure; check account status; review fixtures for missing logout.

steps.label: Commands/code
steps.text:
```code
$ curl -s --cacert lab-ca.pem -u "$ADMIN" https://bmc.example.test/
redfish/v1/SessionService/Sessions | python -m json.tool
```

steps.label: Expected observations
steps.text: Session count at maximum, all from the automation account.

steps.label: Distinguishing causes
steps.text: Max sessions → leak; few sessions and token idle long → timeout; account locked → lockout.

steps.label: Corrective actions
steps.text: Context-manager clients in yield fixtures; session-count check at suite end; re-login logic only where justified.

steps.label: Interview-ready explanation
steps.text: “Failures that start at a consistent test count, not a consistent time, smell like resource exhaustion. Listing active sessions confirmed a leak from a fixture whose teardown didn’t run; I fixed the lifecycle and added a test that session count returns to baseline.”

source.section: 26.11 Scenario 11 — 401 errors appear halfway through a long Redfish run

scenarios.title: Redfish returns 503 for minutes after every BMC reboot
scenarios.prompt: Redfish returns 503 for minutes after every BMC reboot. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: After reboot, service root returns 503 for ~90 s, then 200.

steps.label: Plausible causes
steps.text: Normal start-up (services initialising); bmcweb waiting on dependent daemons; slow storage/key generation on first boot.

steps.label: Investigation sequence
steps.text: Measure time-to-ready over several reboots; check journal ordering of service starts; compare with requirements.

steps.label: Commands/code
Expected observations
steps.text: Consistent readiness time; journal shows services coming up.

steps.label: Distinguishing causes
steps.text: Consistent and within requirement → expected; growing or exceeding requirement → defect; random 503s later → different problem.

steps.label: Corrective actions
steps.text: Readiness gate before tests; a dedicated test asserting time-to-ready meets the requirement.

steps.label: Interview-ready explanation
steps.text: “A BMC isn’t ready the moment it answers TCP. I gate suites on a readiness check with a deadline and measure time-to-ready as its own requirement-backed test, so start-up behaviour is validated rather than tripping unrelated tests.”

source.section: 26.12 Scenario 12 — Redfish returns 503 for minutes after every BMC reboot

scenarios.title: A firmware update task stays “Running” forever
scenarios.prompt: A firmware update task stays “Running” forever. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: TaskState = Running at 60% for 30 minutes.

steps.label: Plausible causes
steps.text: Update process hung; task resource not updated after a BMC reboot (stale task); device-side PLDM update stalled; storage write slow/failing.

steps.label: Investigation sequence
steps.text: Check BMC uptime (did it reboot mid-task?), journal of the software manager and pldmd, device state via PLDM GetStatus if applicable, storage errors.

steps.label: Commands/code
steps.text:
```code
# journalctl -u xyz.openbmc_project.Software.BMC.Updater -b    (unit names
vary)
# journalctl -u pldmd -b | tail -50
# cat /proc/uptime
```

steps.label: Expected observations
steps.text: Error messages from the updater, a reboot that orphaned the task, or a stalled transfer.

steps.label: Distinguishing causes
steps.text: Uptime reset → orphaned task; updater error → failure not propagated to task state (bug); PLDM stall → device side.

steps.label: Corrective actions
steps.text: File bug for task-state propagation; test with hard deadline and evidence collection; verify final version independently of task state.

steps.label: Interview-ready explanation
steps.text: “A task that never finishes is either a hung update or a task that lost track of a finished or failed update — often across a reboot. I check uptime and updater logs, and my tests always verify the final version independently and enforce a deadline.”

source.section: 26.13 Scenario 13 — A firmware update task stays “Running” forever

scenarios.title: Sensor reading differs between Redfish and IPMI
scenarios.prompt: Sensor reading differs between Redfish and IPMI. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: Inlet temperature: Redfish 24.0 °C, IPMI 31.0 °C.

steps.label: Plausible causes
steps.text: Different sensors with similar names; SDR conversion factors wrong (M/B); Redfish scaling bug; different sampling times; stale cached value. **Investigation sequence.** Identify the D-Bus source for each; read D- 3. Bus directly; decode the IPMI raw reading with SDR factors; compare at the same moment.

steps.label: Commands/code
steps.text:
```code
# busctl tree xyz.openbmc_project.HwmonTempSensor     (service names vary)
$ ipmitool ... sdr get "Inlet Temp"
```

steps.label: Expected observations
steps.text: D-Bus matches one side; the other side’s conversion or mapping is wrong.

steps.label: Distinguishing causes
steps.text: D-Bus = Redfish → IPMI SDR/conversion; D- Bus = IPMI → Redfish mapping; D-Bus differs from both → stale/different sensors.

steps.label: Corrective actions
steps.text: Bug to the faulty layer; cross-interface consistency test with tolerance.

steps.label: Interview-ready explanation
steps.text: “On OpenBMC both interfaces read D-Bus, so D-Bus is the referee. Whichever interface disagrees with D- Bus has the bug — SDR conversion on the IPMI side or mapping and scaling in bmcweb.”

source.section: 26.14 Scenario 14 — Sensor reading differs between Redfish and IPMI

scenarios.title: TLS errors start after a firmware update
scenarios.prompt: TLS errors start after a firmware update. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: SSLError: CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED from every Redfish test.

steps.label: Plausible causes
steps.text: BMC regenerated its self-signed certificate; installed lab certificate lost; clock reset (certificate “not yet valid”); new firmware changed TLS versions/ciphers.

steps.label: Investigation sequence
steps.text: Inspect presented certificate and dates; check BMC time.

steps.label: Commands/code
steps.text:
```code
$ openssl s_client -connect bmc.example.test:443 -servername
bmc.example.test </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
    | openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer -dates
# date -u
```

steps.label: Expected observations
steps.text: Issuer changed to self-signed; or notBefore in the “future” relative to the client; or handshake failure messages.

steps.label: Distinguishing causes
steps.text: New issuer → certificate replaced; date problem → clock; handshake alert → protocol/cipher change.

steps.label: Corrective actions
steps.text: Reinstall lab cert (and test persistence across updates as a requirement); fix NTP; never switch to verify=False.

steps.label: Interview-ready explanation
steps.text: “I look at what certificate the BMC presents now. If the issuer changed, the update replaced our lab certificate — which is itself a persistence bug to report. If dates look wrong, the BMC clock reset. Disabling verification would hide both.”

source.section: 26.15 Scenario 15 — TLS errors start after a firmware update

scenarios.title: Host does not power on although the command succeeded
scenarios.prompt: Host does not power on although the command succeeded. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: Redfish Reset On returns 204; PowerState stays Off.

steps.label: Plausible causes
steps.text: Power sequencing fault; PSU absent/failed; chassis intrusion or interlock; power-control service error after accepting; power restore/lock policies; command applied asynchronously and failed later.

steps.label: Investigation sequence
steps.text: Check event logs/SEL around the time; power-control service journal; PSU sensors; chassis state via IPMI; GPIO/power-good signals (lab).

steps.label: Commands/code
steps.text:
```code
$ ipmitool ... chassis status
$ ipmitool ... sel elist | tail
# journalctl -u xyz.openbmc_project.State.Chassis* -b    (unit names vary)
```

steps.label: Expected observations
steps.text: Power fault flag set; PSU errors; or a timeout waiting for power-good in logs.

steps.label: Distinguishing causes
steps.text: Fault flags/PSU errors → hardware/sequencing; service error without fault → software; nothing logged → command not propagated (bug).

steps.label: Corrective actions
steps.text: Hardware investigation or software bug; test must verify state change with deadline, not just the 2xx.

steps.label: Interview-ready explanation
steps.text: “A 2xx means the request was accepted, not that the host powered on. My tests always verify the effect with a deadline, and when it doesn’t happen I check fault indicators, PSU sensors and the power-control service logs.”

source.section: 26.16 Scenario 16 — Host does not power on although the command succeeded

scenarios.title: Redfish event subscription receives no events
scenarios.prompt: Redfish event subscription receives no events. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: Subscription created (201); SubmitTestEvent returns 204; listener sees nothing.

steps.label: Plausible causes
steps.text: Listener unreachable from the BMC (routing/firewall/DNS); TLS trust from BMC to listener; listener binding to localhost; event filtering (RegistryPrefixes/ResourceTypes) excluding the test event; delivery retries delayed.

steps.label: Investigation sequence
steps.text: From the BMC, test connectivity to the listener; check listener bind address; examine subscription properties; BMC journal for delivery errors.

steps.label: Commands/code
steps.text:
```code
# curl -v https://listener.lab.example.test:8443/events    (from BMC
shell, if curl exists)
$ ss -ltnp | grep 8443                                      (listener
host)
```

steps.label: Expected observations
steps.text: Connection failure from BMC; listener bound to 127.0.0.1; TLS error in BMC logs.

steps.label: Distinguishing causes
steps.text: Network failure → reachability; TLS error → certificate trust on BMC side; delivered but filtered → subscription filters.

steps.label: Corrective actions
steps.text: Bind listener to the lab interface; open firewall; install CA on BMC if needed; adjust filters; test also SSE as an alternative path.

steps.label: Interview-ready explanation
steps.text: “Push events reverse the usual direction: the BMC is the client. So I test reachability and TLS trust from the BMC to my listener, and check filters, before suspecting the event service.”

source.section: 26.17 Scenario 17 — Redfish event subscription receives no events

scenarios.title: IPMI works with cipher suite 3 but not 17
scenarios.prompt: IPMI works with cipher suite 3 but not 17. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: -C 3 sessions succeed; -C 17 fail with “Unable to establish IPMI v2 / RMCP+ session”.

steps.label: Plausible causes
steps.text: BMC doesn’t offer suite 17; suite 17 disabled in config; privilege max for suite 17 lower than requested; old ipmitool lacking 17 support.

steps.label: Investigation sequence
steps.text: lan print suites and privilege maxima; ipmitool version; try -C 17 -L USER.

steps.label: Commands/code
steps.text:
```code
$ ipmitool ... -C 3 lan print 1 | grep -i cipher
$ ipmitool -V
```

steps.label: Expected observations
steps.text: 17 missing from the suite list or with lower privilege max.

steps.label: Distinguishing causes
steps.text: Absent → BMC config/capability; present with low priv → privilege; tool version old → client.

steps.label: Corrective actions
steps.text: Enable 17 if required (security requirement), upgrade tool, adjust privilege; add a configuration test for offered suites.

steps.label: Interview-ready explanation
steps.text: “Cipher suites are negotiated at Open Session; if the BMC doesn’t offer 17 or caps its privilege, the session fails generically. lan print shows what’s offered, which turns a vague error into a specific configuration finding.”

source.section: 26.18 Scenario 18 — IPMI works with cipher suite 3 but not 17

scenarios.title: Console shows garbage after a firmware update
scenarios.prompt: Console shows garbage after a firmware update. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: Readable U-Boot output, then garbage once Linux starts.

steps.label: Plausible causes
steps.text: Kernel console baud different from U-Boot’s; wrong UART assignment; flow control change.

steps.label: Investigation sequence
steps.text: Try common baud rates for the kernel phase; check bootargs via SSH.

steps.label: Commands/code
steps.text:
```code
$ python -m serial.tools.miniterm /dev/serial/by-id/usb-... 57600
# cat /proc/cmdline
```

steps.label: Expected observations
steps.text: Clean text at another rate; bootargs show it.

steps.label: Distinguishing causes
steps.text: Readable at different rate → baud mismatch; garbage at all → electrical/level issue; silence → console moved.

steps.label: Corrective actions
steps.text: Report unintended change; update capture config per firmware line if intended.

steps.label: Interview-ready explanation
steps.text: “Readable boot loader output followed by garbage is the classic signature of a baud change between U-Boot and the kernel. Bootargs confirm it.”

source.section: 26.19 Scenario 19 — Console shows garbage after a firmware update

scenarios.title: A Jenkins job hangs forever
scenarios.prompt: A Jenkins job hangs forever. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: Job stuck for hours; last log line is a test name. 1.

steps.label: Plausible causes
steps.text: Missing timeout in a network/serial/subprocess call; waiting for an interactive prompt; deadlock reading SSH streams; lock never released.

steps.label: Investigation sequence
steps.text: Thread dump of the Python process (py-spy dump), check the last operation; review timeouts in that path.

steps.label: Commands/code
steps.text:
```code
$ py-spy dump --pid <pytest-pid>      # where is it stuck?
# pytest.ini safety net (pytest-timeout)
timeout = 900
```

steps.label: Expected observations
steps.text: Stack in socket.recv, serial.read with no timeout, or channel.recv in a stdout-then-stderr read.

steps.label: Distinguishing causes
steps.text: recv without timeout → missing timeout; SSH read pattern → window deadlock; input() or prompt → interactive.

steps.label: Corrective actions
steps.text: Explicit timeouts everywhere; drain SSH streams together; BatchMode; pipeline-level timeout(); pytest-timeout.

steps.label: Interview-ready explanation
steps.text: “A hang is always a missing timeout somewhere. I take a stack dump to find the blocking call, fix that call’s timeout, and add defence in depth: pytest-timeout and a pipeline timeout, so one bug can’t block the lab for a night.”

source.section: 26.20 Scenario 20 — A Jenkins job hangs forever

scenarios.title: A PATCH is accepted but the value reverts after reboot
scenarios.prompt: A PATCH is accepted but the value reverts after reboot. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: AssetTag set, reads back correctly, lost after BMC reboot.

steps.label: Plausible causes
steps.text: Setting stored only in volatile memory; persistence service failure; configuration restored from defaults by an update or factory-reset flag; two sources of truth (e.g. FRU vs settings DB).

steps.label: Investigation sequence
steps.text: Repeat with logs; inspect where the setting persists; check journal at shutdown/startup for persistence errors.

steps.label: Commands/code
steps.text:
```code
# journalctl -b -1 | grep -i -E "persist|save|settings"   (previous boot)
# df -h                                                   (writable
partition full?)
```

steps.label: Expected observations
steps.text: Write errors, full partition, or the property not implemented as persistent.

steps.label: Distinguishing causes
steps.text: Errors in log → persistence failure; no errors → design issue/defaults restored.

steps.label: Corrective actions
steps.text: Bug report with reproduction; persistence tests across reboot, AC cycle and update.

steps.label: Interview-ready explanation
steps.text: “Read-after-write proves the API, not persistence. I always add a reboot step to settings tests; when values revert, I check the previous boot’s logs and storage health to find whether saving failed or the value was never meant to persist.”

source.section: 26.21 Scenario 21 — A PATCH is accepted but the value reverts after reboot

scenarios.title: BMC reboots randomly during a long soak test
scenarios.prompt: BMC reboots randomly during a long soak test. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: Every few hours BMC uptime resets; tests see connection resets.

steps.label: Plausible causes
steps.text: Watchdog timeout due to CPU starvation; out-of-memory kills of critical services; kernel panic; hardware reset (power/ brown-out).

steps.label: Investigation sequence
steps.text: Console capture across the event; journal from previous boot (if persistent); watchdog/OOM messages; correlate with test load; memory trend.

steps.label: Commands/code
steps.text:
```code
# journalctl -b -1 -p warning | tail -100
# dmesg | grep -i -E "watchdog|oom|panic"
# cat /proc/meminfo
```

steps.label: Expected observations
steps.text: OOM killer messages and rising memory, 5. watchdog pre-timeout, or a panic trace on the console.

steps.label: Distinguishing causes
steps.text: OOM + growth → leak; watchdog + load → starvation; panic → kernel/driver; nothing logged + console shows sudden U-Boot → hardware reset.

steps.label: Corrective actions
steps.text: Bug with evidence; memory trend monitoring in soak tests; evidence collection hooks.

steps.label: Interview-ready explanation
steps.text: “Unexplained reboots during soak are usually memory leaks, watchdog starvation or crashes. Console capture plus previous-boot logs and memory trends tell them apart, and the soak test becomes the reproducer.”

source.section: 26.22 Scenario 22 — BMC reboots randomly during a long soak test

scenarios.title: Logging stops / SEL full
scenarios.prompt: Logging stops / SEL full. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: No new event log entries; SEL shows “full” or oldest entries remain.

steps.label: Plausible causes
steps.text: Log capacity reached with no-overwrite policy; logging service crashed; storage full.

steps.label: Investigation sequence
steps.text: Check log service capacity/policy (Redfish LogService MaxNumberOfRecords, OverWritePolicy), service status, storage.

steps.label: Commands/code
steps.text: `$ ipmitool ... sel info # systemctl status xyz.openbmc_project.Logging*     (unit names vary)`

steps.label: Expected observations
steps.text: Entries = max with policy NeverOver‐ Writes; or logging service failed.

steps.label: Distinguishing causes
steps.text: Policy-based → configuration/test hygiene; crashed service → defect.

steps.label: Corrective actions
steps.text: Save and clear logs in test setup (on dedicated systems); verify overwrite policy behaviour as a test.

steps.label: Interview-ready explanation
steps.text: “When events vanish, I first check whether the log is simply full under a no-overwrite policy — a test-environment issue — before chasing a logging-service defect.”

scenarios.title: pldmtool works manually but pldmd shows sensors unavailable
scenarios.prompt: pldmtool works manually but pldmd shows sensors unavailable. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: pldmtool platform GetSensorReading returns values; Redfish shows the sensor as unavailable.

steps.label: Plausible causes
steps.text: pldmd failed PDR parsing for that sensor; sensor association wrong; pldmd polling disabled/backed off after errors; D- Bus publication failure.

steps.label: Investigation sequence
steps.text: pldmd journal; D-Bus sensor objects; compare PDR data via pldmtool with what pldmd published.

steps.label: Commands/code
steps.text:
```code
# journalctl -u pldmd -b | grep -i -E "sensor|pdr|error"
# busctl tree xyz.openbmc_project.PLDM
```

steps.label: Expected observations
steps.text: Parse errors, missing D-Bus object, or Available=false with errors logged.

steps.label: Distinguishing causes
steps.text: No D-Bus object → discovery/PDR parsing; object but stale → polling; object fine but Redfish wrong → bmcweb.

steps.label: Corrective actions
steps.text: Bug to the right component with PDR dump; test comparing pldmtool readings to D-Bus/Redfish.

steps.label: Interview-ready explanation
steps.text: “pldmtool proves the device and transport work, which isolates the problem to pldmd’s processing or publication. D-Bus tells me which.”

source.section: 26.24 Scenario 24 — pldmtool works manually but pldmd shows sensors unavailable

scenarios.title: SSH host-key verification fails in CI after a factory reset
scenarios.prompt: SSH host-key verification fails in CI after a factory reset. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Context
steps.text: Symptoms. REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED in CI.

steps.label: Plausible causes
steps.text: Expected regeneration after reset; unexpected change (possible interception, or a different device answering on that IP).

steps.label: Investigation sequence
steps.text: Confirm reset occurred; verify new fingerprint via console (ssh-keygen -lf /etc/ssh/ssh_host_*.pub or Dropbear equivalent); confirm MAC/IP mapping.

steps.label: Commands/code
steps.text:
```code
$ ssh-keyscan -t ed25519 bmc.example.test | ssh-keygen -lf -
```

steps.label: Expected observations
steps.text: Fingerprint matches the console-reported key → legitimate.

steps.label: Distinguishing causes
steps.text: Matches → update known_hosts; doesn’t → investigate network.

steps.label: Corrective actions
steps.text: Update managed known_hosts through a reviewed change; never disable checking.

steps.label: Interview-ready explanation
steps.text: “A changed host key is either expected after a reset or a red flag. I verify the new fingerprint out-of-band on the console before updating the managed known_hosts.”

source.section: 26.25 Scenario 25 — SSH host-key verification fails in CI after a factory reset

scenarios.title: Redfish sensor collection takes seconds per request
scenarios.prompt: Redfish sensor collection takes seconds per request. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: GET Chassis/<id>/Sensors?$expand=. takes 8 s; tests time out.

steps.label: Plausible causes
steps.text: Expansion of many members each requiring D-Bus calls; slow sensor daemons; BMC CPU load; TLS renegotiation per request (no keep-alive).

steps.label: Investigation sequence
steps.text: Time with and without $expand; check connection reuse; BMC CPU during request.

steps.label: Commands/code
steps.text:
```code
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{time_total}\n" --cacert lab-ca.pem -H "X-
Auth-Token: $T" https://bmc.example.test/redfish/v1/Chassis/chassis/
Sensors
```

steps.label: Expected observations
steps.text: Expansion dominating; or new TLS handshake each call.

steps.label: Distinguishing causes
steps.text: Expand-only slowness → server-side aggregation; all calls slow → load/connection reuse.

steps.label: Corrective actions
steps.text: Use Session keep-alive; avoid expand or raise 7. read timeout; report performance against requirements.

steps.label: Interview-ready explanation
steps.text: “I separate client overhead — connection reuse — from server work — expansion and D-Bus fan-out — by timing variants. Then it’s either a test configuration fix or a performance finding against a requirement.”

source.section: 26.26 Scenario 26 — Redfish sensor collection takes seconds per request

scenarios.title: A test fails only on the first run after BMC boot
scenarios.prompt: A test fails only on the first run after BMC boot. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: First run fails (e.g. sensors missing), reruns pass. 1.

steps.label: Plausible causes
steps.text: Services still initialising (sensor discovery, PLDM discovery); caches cold; readiness gate too weak (only checks Redfish root).

steps.label: Investigation sequence
steps.text: Timestamp failure relative to boot; check service readiness states; measure time until sensors populate.

steps.label: Commands/code
steps.text:
```code
# cat /proc/uptime ; obmcutil state ; systemctl list-jobs
```

steps.label: Expected observations
steps.text: Failures within N minutes of boot; pending systemd jobs.

steps.label: Distinguishing causes
steps.text: Time-correlated with boot → readiness; random → other.

steps.label: Corrective actions
steps.text: Stronger readiness criteria (BMC Ready + no pending jobs + expected sensor count); requirement test for time-to-full-inventory.

steps.label: Interview-ready explanation
steps.text: “If only the first run fails, the system wasn’t fully ready. Redfish answering isn’t enough; I gate on BMC state, pending startup jobs and expected inventory, and measure time-to-ready as a requirement.”

source.section: 26.27 Scenario 27 — A test fails only on the first run after BMC boot

scenarios.title: An NVMe drive is missing from inventory
scenarios.prompt: An NVMe drive is missing from inventory. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: Drive visible to host OS; missing in BMC Redfish Storage/Drives.

steps.label: Plausible causes
steps.text: NVMe-MI over MCTP (or basic SMBus management) not discovered; drive slot’s SMBus path/mux not configured; drive doesn’t support NVMe-MI over the available binding; BMC daemon not polling that slot.

steps.label: Investigation sequence
steps.text: Check presence signals, bus path, MCTP discovery (message type 0x04 support), relevant daemon logs.

steps.label: Commands/code
steps.text: `# mctp link ; journalctl -b | grep -i nvme # i2cdetect -l                       (bus/mux layout for drive slots)`

steps.label: Expected observations
steps.text: Endpoint absent or lacking NVMe-MI type; mux/bus config missing for that slot.

steps.label: Distinguishing causes
steps.text: No bus response → physical/config; endpoint without NVMe-MI → drive capability; endpoint present, daemon silent → software.

steps.label: Corrective actions
steps.text: Fix platform configuration; document unsupported drives; inventory test comparing host-visible drives with BMC inventory.

steps.label: Interview-ready explanation
steps.text: “The host sees drives over PCIe data paths; the BMC sees them over management paths like SMBus with NVMe-MI over MCTP. A gap means the management path or its configuration is missing, so I trace that path layer by layer.”

source.section: 26.28 Scenario 28 — An NVMe drive is missing from inventory

scenarios.title: Logs from BMC and test runner appear out of order
scenarios.prompt: Logs from BMC and test runner appear out of order. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: BMC error appears “after” the test failure it caused.

steps.label: Plausible causes
steps.text: BMC clock drift/offset; time zone differences; buffered logging.

steps.label: Investigation sequence
steps.text: Measure offset (BMC date -u +%s.%N vs runner); check NTP on BMC; normalise all logs to UTC.

steps.label: Commands/code
steps.text:
```code
# date -u +%s.%N ; timedatectl
$ date -u +%s.%N
```

steps.label: Expected observations
steps.text: Offset of seconds; NTP unsynchronised.

steps.label: Distinguishing causes
steps.text: Constant offset → clock; varying → drift or buffering.

steps.label: Corrective actions
steps.text: Enable NTP; record offset at test start; correlation tooling that applies it (Chapter 20).

steps.label: Interview-ready explanation
steps.text: “Causality inverted in logs is a clock problem until proven otherwise. I measure the BMC-to-runner offset and normalise everything to UTC before drawing conclusions.”

source.section: 26.29 Scenario 29 — Logs from BMC and test runner appear out of order

scenarios.title: The automation account is locked out
scenarios.prompt: The automation account is locked out. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: All jobs fail with 401; admin sees account locked.

steps.label: Plausible causes
steps.text: A negative test used the real account with wrong passwords; a job with a stale password retried; lockout threshold low.

steps.label: Investigation sequence
steps.text: Check AccountService lockout settings and audit logs; identify job/time of failed attempts.

steps.label: Commands/code
steps.text:
```code
$ curl -s --cacert lab-ca.pem -u "$ADMIN" https://bmc.example.test/
redfish/v1/AccountService | python -m json.tool | grep -i lockout
```

steps.label: Expected observations
steps.text: Failed attempts from one job, matching threshold.

steps.label: Distinguishing causes
steps.text: Negative test → test design; stale credential → secret rotation process.

steps.label: Corrective actions
steps.text: Negative-auth tests use throwaway accounts; no retries on 401; credential rotation propagated to CI; alert on lockouts.

steps.label: Interview-ready explanation
steps.text: “Lockouts are usually self-inflicted: a negative test or a retry loop hammering with bad credentials. Authentication-failure tests must use disposable accounts, and clients must never retry 401s blindly.”

source.section: 26.30 Scenario 30 — The automation account is locked out

scenarios.title: The BMC doesn’t respond to ping.
scenarios.prompt: The BMC doesn’t respond to ping.. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Interpret
steps.text: No ICMP reply — host down, path broken, or ICMP blocked. Not yet a BMC fault.

steps.label: First command
steps.text: ip route get <bmc> then a TCP probe to 443 — confirms the path and tests a real service (ICMP may be filtered).

steps.label: Output meaning
steps.text: route OK + port open → ping is merely blocked; port timeout → path or host down.

steps.label: Next
steps.text: serial console; ARP ( ip neigh); try from another host on the same subnet.

steps.label: Hypotheses left
steps.text: BMC down/rebooting, network path/VLAN, IP changed.

steps.label: Confirming evidence
steps.text: console shows boot state; ARP resolves or not.

steps.label: Say
steps.text: “I don’t trust ping alone; I check the route and a real service port, then go to the serial console to see if the BMC itself is alive.”

source.section: 30.1 Scenario 1 — “The BMC doesn’t respond to ping.”

scenarios.title: Redfish returns 401 for every request, even with correct credentials.
scenarios.prompt: Redfish returns 401 for every request, even with correct credentials.. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Interpret
steps.text:
Service is up; authentication rejected.
First command: curl -sk -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' https://<bmc>/redfish/v1/ (expect 200, unauthenticated) — proves bmcweb works.

steps.label: Output meaning
steps.text: 200 → only auth path affected.

steps.label: Next
steps.text: account state (locked?), recent updates/factory reset, user manager service status and logs, LDAP config if used.

steps.label: Hypotheses
steps.text: account locked; password changed by reset; user-manager service failure; time skew breaking session tokens.

steps.label: Confirming
steps.text: journal of user-management/bmcweb shows lockout or PAM failure.

steps.label: Say
steps.text: “Separate service health from authentication, then check account and auth-service state.”

source.section: 30.2 Scenario 2 — “Redfish returns 401 for every request, even with correct credentials.”

scenarios.title: systemctl shows the service active, but its API returns stale data.
scenarios.prompt: systemctl shows the service active, but its API returns stale data.. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Interpret
steps.text: Process alive; functionality degraded.

steps.label: First command
steps.text: journalctl -u <svc> -b --since -30min — what has it been doing?

steps.label: Output meaning
steps.text: repeated read errors or silence since a timestamp.

steps.label: Next
steps.text: process state ( ps -o stat), D-Bus property timestamps/values, underlying device reads (sysfs).

steps.label: Hypotheses
steps.text: hung thread, cached values after errors, device failure.

steps.label: Confirming
steps.text: sysfs read fails while D-Bus value never changes.

steps.label: Say
steps.text: “‘Active’ means a process exists; I check whether it’s doing work by logs, process state and the layer below.”

source.section: 30.3 Scenario 3 — “systemctl shows the service active, but its API returns stale data.”

scenarios.title: Root filesystem is full on a test VM.
scenarios.prompt: Root filesystem is full on a test VM.. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Interpret
steps.text: ENOSPC impacts everything; find growth.

steps.label: First command
steps.text: df -h; df -i — bytes or inodes?

steps.label: Output meaning
steps.text: bytes 100% → large files; inodes 100% → many small files.

steps.label: Next
steps.text: du -xh / | sort -h | tail, deleted-open files, growth rate.

steps.label: Hypotheses
steps.text: logs, cores, artifacts, deleted-open file.

steps.label: Confirming
steps.text: growth rate of a file equals free-space decline.

steps.label: Say
steps.text: “I check bytes and inodes, find the biggest consumers, and identify the writer before cleaning — after saving evidence.”

source.section: 30.4 Scenario 4 — “Root filesystem is full on a test VM.”

scenarios.title: A test fails with ‘Connection refused’ to port 443 right after reboot.
scenarios.prompt: A test fails with ‘Connection refused’ to port 443 right after reboot.. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Interpret
steps.text: Host up, nothing listening yet or service failed.

steps.label: First command
