steps.text: console/SSH: systemctl is-system-running — still starting?

steps.label: Output meaning
steps.text: starting → timing; degraded → failure.

steps.label: Next
steps.text: systemctl status bmcweb.socket bmcweb; test waits with bounded polling.

steps.label: Hypotheses
steps.text: test doesn’t wait long enough; bmcweb failed.

steps.label: Confirming
steps.text: time-to-ready measurements vs test timeout.

steps.label: Say
steps.text: “Refused means the host is up; I check whether the system finished booting before blaming the service.”

source.section: 30.5 Scenario 5 — “A test fails with ‘Connection refused’ to port 443 right after reboot.”

scenarios.title: A firmware update test fails intermittently at the verify step.
scenarios.prompt: A firmware update test fails intermittently at the verify step.. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Interpret
steps.text: Version mismatch after reboot sometimes.

steps.label: First command
steps.text: compare boot IDs before/after for failing runs — did it reboot?

steps.label: Output meaning
steps.text: unchanged → reboot didn’t happen; changed → image booted something else.

steps.label: Next
steps.text: serial captures of failing runs (fallback?), activation logs.

steps.label: Hypotheses
steps.text: reboot not triggered; new image fails boot → fallback; verify step reads cached version too early.

steps.label: Confirming
steps.text: serial shows new kernel panic then old image boot.

steps.label: Say
steps.text: “I prove whether a reboot occurred via boot ID, then use serial logs to see which image booted.”

source.section: 30.6 Scenario 6 — “A firmware update test fails intermittently at the verify step.”

scenarios.title: dmesg shows I²C timeouts on bus 5.
scenarios.prompt: dmesg shows I²C timeouts on bus 5.. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Interpret
steps.text: Bus/device communication problem.

steps.label: First command
steps.text: dmesg -T | grep 'i2c-5' — which addresses, how often, since when.

steps.label: Output meaning
steps.text: all addresses → bus-level; one → device.

steps.label: Next
steps.text: correlate with host power, physical changes, temperature.

steps.label: Hypotheses
steps.text: device absent/unpowered, bus held low, mux, driver.

steps.label: Confirming
steps.text: controlled change (remove card, power state) toggles failures.

steps.label: Say
steps.text: “First I scope it: one device or the whole bus, then correlate with power and hardware changes.”

source.section: 30.7 Scenario 7 — “dmesg shows I²C timeouts on bus 5.”

scenarios.title: Journal shows nothing from before the last reboot.
scenarios.prompt: Journal shows nothing from before the last reboot.. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Interpret
steps.text: Volatile journal or lost.

steps.label: First command
steps.text: journalctl --list-boots and check /var/log/journal existence.

steps.label: Output meaning
steps.text: single boot listed → volatile.

steps.label: Next
steps.text: use serial capture, pstore, remote logs; enable persistent logs in lab.

steps.label: Hypotheses
steps.text: volatile by design; storage full prevented writing.

steps.label: Confirming
steps.text: Storage= config / no directory.

steps.label: Say
steps.text: “Missing evidence is information too: I check whether persistence was possible.”

source.section: 30.8 Scenario 8 — “Journal shows nothing from before the last reboot.”

scenarios.title: A Python test hangs forever in CI.
scenarios.prompt: A Python test hangs forever in CI.. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Interpret
steps.text: An unbounded wait.

steps.label: First command
steps.text: on the agent, ps -ef --forest (or pstree -p) for the job — which child is running?

steps.label: Output meaning
steps.text: e.g. an ssh child waiting → prompt or network hang.

steps.label: Next
steps.text: add timeout= to subprocess, ConnectTimeout, BatchMode=yes; stage timeouts.

steps.label: Hypotheses
steps.text: password prompt, network blackhole, serial read without timeout.

steps.label: Confirming
steps.text: py-spy dump or traceback on SIGTERM shows the blocking call.

steps.label: Say
steps.text: “I look at the process tree to find what it waits on, then make every external call bounded.”

source.section: 30.9 Scenario 9 — “A Python test hangs forever in CI.”

scenarios.title: After update, Redfish works but one PSU is missing.
scenarios.prompt: After update, Redfish works but one PSU is missing.. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Interpret
steps.text: Device visibility gap at some layer.

steps.label: First command
steps.text: ls /sys/bus/i2c/devices/ for the PSU address — is it instantiated?

steps.label: Output meaning
steps.text: present → kernel ok, look higher; absent → config/probe.

steps.label: Next
steps.text: D-Bus objects, entity-manager/PSU daemon logs, associations.

steps.label: Hypotheses
steps.text: config change for board rev, daemon failure, association.

steps.label: Confirming
steps.text: first layer where it disappears + log line.

steps.label: Say
steps.text: “I walk the layers until the device disappears.”

source.section: 30.10 Scenario 10 — “After update, Redfish works but one PSU is missing.”

scenarios.title: SSH to the BMC is slow (10 s to log in).
scenarios.prompt: SSH to the BMC is slow (10 s to log in).. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Interpret
steps.text: Delay in handshake or auth.

steps.label: First command
steps.text: ssh -vvv with timestamps ( ssh -vvv ... 2>&1 | ts if available) — where’s the pause?

steps.label: Output meaning
steps.text: pause after “Authenticated” → login shell/PAM; before → DNS reverse lookup or key exchange.

steps.label: Next
steps.text: server DNS config, CPU load, entropy at early boot.

steps.label: Hypotheses
steps.text: reverse DNS timeout, heavy load, slow crypto on small CPU.

steps.label: Confirming
steps.text: pause disappears when DNS fixed.

steps.label: Say
steps.text: “Verbose SSH tells me which phase is slow.”

source.section: 30.11 Scenario 11 — “SSH to the BMC is slow (10 s to log in).”

scenarios.title: A daemon restarts every 2 minutes.
scenarios.prompt: A daemon restarts every 2 minutes.. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Interpret
steps.text:
Crash loop.
First command: systemctl show <svc> -p Result,ExecMainStatus,NRestarts.

steps.label: Output meaning
steps.text: signal SEGV → crash; KILL → OOM/watchdog; exit code → config/ error.

steps.label: Next
steps.text: journal around first crash; dmesg; core dump.

steps.label: Hypotheses
steps.text: bug, config, memory, dependency.

steps.label: Confirming
steps.text: core backtrace / reproduction.

steps.label: Say
steps.text: “The exit reason tells me which family of causes to pursue.”

scenarios.title: Load average is 8 on a 2-core BMC, CPU idle 70%.
scenarios.prompt: Load average is 8 on a 2-core BMC, CPU idle 70%.. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Interpret
steps.text: Tasks in D state, not CPU.

steps.label: First command
steps.text: ps -eo pid,stat,wchan:20,cmd | awk '$2 ~ /D/' (BusyBox: inspect / `proc/*/stat).`

steps.label: Output meaning
steps.text: daemons blocked in I/O wait functions.

steps.label: Next
steps.text: dmesg storage/I²C errors; which resource they wait on.

steps.label: Hypotheses
steps.text: flash I/O stalls, I²C bus hang, NFS.

steps.label: Confirming
steps.text: errors in dmesg at same time; tasks unblock when resolved.

steps.label: Say
steps.text: “High load with idle CPU means waiting, not computing.”

source.section: 30.13 Scenario 13 — “Load average is 8 on a 2-core BMC, CPU idle 70%.”

scenarios.title: A test reads the wrong temperature:
scenarios.prompt: A test reads the wrong temperature:. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Interpret
steps.text: Scaling issue (millidegrees).

steps.label: First command
steps.text: cat /sys/class/hwmon/hwmonN/temp1_input → 24500 raw.

steps.label: Output meaning
steps.text: raw is correct millidegrees; scaling missing above.

steps.label: Next
steps.text: D-Bus value vs Redfish; config scale factor; test parsing.

steps.label: Hypotheses
steps.text: daemon config, API mapping, test bug.

steps.label: Confirming
steps.text: layer where value becomes wrong.

steps.label: Say
steps.text: “Compare layers to find where the conversion is lost.”

source.section: 30.14 Scenario 14 — “A test reads the wrong temperature:

scenarios.title: Jenkins says ‘Host key verification failed’ after nightly reflash.
scenarios.prompt: Jenkins says ‘Host key verification failed’ after nightly reflash.. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Interpret
steps.text: Expected after reflash (new keys), but must be handled safely.

steps.label: First command
steps.text: verify identity out-of-band (console: ssh-keygen -lf /etc/ssh/... or dropbear key fingerprint).

steps.label: Output meaning
steps.text: fingerprint matches new key → legitimate change.

steps.label: Next
steps.text: test framework updates a lab-scoped known_hosts after reflash, logging the change.

steps.label: Hypotheses
steps.text: legitimate reflash vs wrong device at the IP.

steps.label: Confirming
steps.text: fingerprint check.

steps.label: Say
steps.text: “I don’t disable host-key checking; I automate verified updates of a lab known_hosts.”

source.section: 30.15 Scenario 15 — “Jenkins says ‘Host key verification failed’ after nightly reflash.”

scenarios.title: Clock on BMC is 3 hours off.
scenarios.prompt: Clock on BMC is 3 hours off.. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Interpret
steps.text: Time sync issue or time zone confusion.

steps.label: First command
steps.text: date -u on BMC and test host.

steps.label: Output meaning
steps.text: UTC differs → clock wrong; same → display time zone only.

steps.label: Next
steps.text: NTP config/status, host-time sync settings, RTC.

steps.label: Hypotheses
steps.text: NTP unreachable, RTC battery, wrong mode.

steps.label: Confirming
steps.text: NTP logs, after-reboot drift pattern.

steps.label: Say
steps.text: “First separate wrong clock from wrong time zone using UTC.”

source.section: 30.16 Scenario 16 — “Clock on BMC is 3 hours off.”

scenarios.title: IPMI sensor list works, Redfish sensor collection is empty.
scenarios.prompt: IPMI sensor list works, Redfish sensor collection is empty.. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Interpret
steps.text: Different paths to similar data.

steps.label: First command
steps.text: busctl tree of sensor services — objects exist?

steps.label: Output meaning
steps.text: yes → Redfish mapping/associations; no → IPMI uses a different source (e.g. its own config).

steps.label: Next
steps.text: ObjectMapper associations to chassis; bmcweb logs.

steps.label: Hypotheses
steps.text: chassis association missing, bmcweb config, wrong chassis ID in test.

steps.label: Confirming
steps.text: GetSubTree / association objects.

steps.label: Say
steps.text: “Two APIs, two code paths — I compare at D-Bus.”

source.section: 30.17 Scenario 17 — “IPMI sensor list works, Redfish sensor collection is empty.”

scenarios.title: A Bash collector produced an empty report but exit 0.
scenarios.prompt: A Bash collector produced an empty report but exit 0.. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Interpret
steps.text: Failure hidden.

steps.label: First command
steps.text: bash -x collector.sh — see what ran.

steps.label: Output meaning
steps.text: a failing command inside $(...) or a pipeline; errors swallowed.

steps.label: Next
steps.text: add set -uo pipefail, explicit checks, a test for the failure path.

steps.label: Hypotheses
steps.text: pipeline masking, || true, wrong variable.

steps.label: Confirming
steps.text: trace shows the failing command.

steps.label: Say
steps.text: “Exit codes are a contract; I trace and then add tests for the failure path.”

source.section: 30.18 Scenario 18 — “A Bash collector produced an empty report but exit 0.”

scenarios.title: The host won’t power on via Redfish; the API returns 204.
scenarios.prompt: The host won’t power on via Redfish; the API returns 204.. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Interpret
steps.text: Request accepted; sequencing failed later.

steps.label: First command
steps.text: BMC journalctl -b --since -10min for power-on target units.

steps.label: Output meaning
steps.text: a power sequencing unit failed (e.g. waiting on a GPIO/PGOOD).

steps.label: Next
steps.text: chassis/host state objects, POST codes, PSU status.

steps.label: Hypotheses
steps.text: PSU/hardware, sequencing service, host firmware.

steps.label: Confirming
steps.text: unit failure + hardware signal evidence.

steps.label: Say
steps.text: “204 only means the request was accepted; I follow the power-on target on the BMC.”

source.section: 30.19 Scenario 19 — “The host won’t power on via Redfish; the API returns 204.”

scenarios.title: Test passes on board A, fails on board B, same firmware.
scenarios.prompt: Test passes on board A, fails on board B, same firmware.. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Interpret
steps.text: Hardware or board-config difference.

steps.label: First command
steps.text: collect board revision/FRU data from both.

steps.label: Output meaning
steps.text: different revisions → config mismatch candidate.

steps.label: Next
steps.text: swap components between boards; compare dmesg.

steps.label: Hypotheses
steps.text: hardware defect, revision-specific config.

steps.label: Confirming
steps.text: failure follows the swapped part or the revision.

steps.label: Say
steps.text: “Same firmware, different result: I diff the hardware.”

source.section: 30.20 Scenario 20 — “Test passes on board A, fails on board B, same firmware.”

scenarios.title: Serial console shows garbage.
scenarios.prompt: Serial console shows garbage.. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Interpret
steps.text: Baud/format mismatch or electrical issue.

steps.label: First command
steps.text: check /proc/cmdline on a known-good unit ( console=...,115200) and your terminal settings.

steps.label: Output meaning
steps.text: mismatch → fix settings.

steps.label: Next
steps.text: ground connection, adapter voltage, try another adapter.

steps.label: Hypotheses
steps.text: baud, ground, wrong UART.

steps.label: Confirming
steps.text: clean output at correct settings.

steps.label: Say
steps.text: “Garbage is almost always configuration or grounding.”

scenarios.title: Memory available on BMC drops after each Redfish test suite run.
scenarios.prompt: Memory available on BMC drops after each Redfish test suite run.. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Interpret
steps.text: Leak correlated with requests, or tmpfs growth.

steps.label: First command
steps.text: df -h /tmp /run and per-process RSS before/after.

steps.label: Output meaning
steps.text: tmpfs growing → files left; RSS growing → process leak.

steps.label: Next
steps.text: identify files/process; repeat runs to measure slope.

steps.label: Hypotheses
steps.text: session leak, temp files, cache.

steps.label: Confirming
steps.text: linear growth vs request count.

steps.label: Say
steps.text: “I attribute memory before blaming a process.”

source.section: 30.22 Scenario 22 — “Memory available on BMC drops after each Redfish test suite run.”

scenarios.title: A test sometimes reads a sensor as 0 RPM.
scenarios.prompt: A test sometimes reads a sensor as 0 RPM.. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Interpret
steps.text: Fan stopped, read error returning 0, or sampling at spin-up.

steps.label: First command
steps.text: sample sysfs fanN_input rapidly over time.

steps.label: Output meaning
steps.text: brief zeros → spin-up/PWM; long zeros → fan/tach issue.

steps.label: Next
steps.text: correlate with PWM changes and power events.

steps.label: Hypotheses
steps.text: tach glitch, test timing, hardware.

steps.label: Confirming
steps.text: zeros coincide with PWM transitions.

steps.label: Say
steps.text: “Is it the fan or the measurement? I sample and correlate.”

source.section: 30.23 Scenario 23 — “A test sometimes reads a sensor as 0 RPM.”

scenarios.title: Redfish task for update shows ‘Exception’ state.
scenarios.prompt: Redfish task for update shows ‘Exception’ state.. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Interpret
steps.text: Update failed; reason in task messages/logs.

steps.label: First command
steps.text: GET the task resource, read Messages.

steps.label: Output meaning
steps.text: e.g. image verification failure.

steps.label: Next
steps.text: updater journal, image MANIFEST/signature, compatibility.

steps.label: Hypotheses
steps.text: wrong image, corrupt upload, signature/key mismatch.

steps.label: Confirming
steps.text: checksum mismatch or verification log line.

steps.label: Say
steps.text: “The task tells me which stage failed; logs say why.”

source.section: 30.24 Scenario 24 — “Redfish task for update shows ‘Exception’ state.”

scenarios.title: A cron health check sends 50 alerts per day.
scenarios.prompt: A cron health check sends 50 alerts per day.. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Interpret
steps.text: Noisy alerting; maybe flapping or overlap. •

steps.label: First command
steps.text: grep -c FAIL per hour in the check’s log; check for overlapping runs.

steps.label: Output meaning
steps.text: flapping state; or overlapping runs causing false failures.

steps.label: Next
steps.text: add flock, alert on state change, tune thresholds with data.

steps.label: Hypotheses
steps.text: real intermittent problem vs check design.

steps.label: Confirming
steps.text: failures correlate with overlap or not.

steps.label: Say
steps.text: “Fix the alert design and investigate the flapping separately.”

source.section: 30.25 Scenario 25 — “A cron health check sends 50 alerts per day.”

scenarios.title: After reboot, bmcweb fails: ‘address already in use’.
scenarios.prompt: After reboot, bmcweb fails: ‘address already in use’.. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Interpret
steps.text: Port conflict.

steps.label: First command
steps.text: ss -tlnp | grep ':443' — who owns it?

steps.label: Output meaning
steps.text: socket unit or another process holds it.

steps.label: Next
steps.text: unit configuration (socket activation + service both binding), recent changes.

steps.label: Hypotheses
steps.text: duplicate listener, leftover process.

steps.label: Confirming
steps.text: owner PID/unit.

steps.label: Say
steps.text: “Find the owner of the port, then why two things bind it.”

source.section: 30.26 Scenario 26 — “After reboot, bmcweb fails: ‘address already in use’.”

scenarios.title: D-Bus calls succeed manually but fail from your test script.
scenarios.prompt: D-Bus calls succeed manually but fail from your test script.. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Interpret
steps.text: Environment/permissions difference.

steps.label: First command
steps.text: run the script’s exact command with the same user; compare id and environment ( DBUS_SYSTEM_BUS_ADDRESS).

steps.label: Output meaning
steps.text: AccessDenied → policy/user; ServiceUnknown → different bus/ environment.

steps.label: Next
steps.text: fix user/policy; ensure system bus used.

steps.label: Hypotheses
steps.text: user, bus address, quoting of arguments.

steps.label: Confirming
steps.text: identical command as same user works/fails.

steps.label: Say
steps.text: “Reproduce exactly as the automation runs.”

source.section: 30.27 Scenario 27 — “D-Bus calls succeed manually but fail from your test script.”

scenarios.title: A long soak test stops logging after 18 hours.
scenarios.prompt: A long soak test stops logging after 18 hours.. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Interpret
steps.text: Logging failure or capture failure.

steps.label: First command
steps.text: df -h on log destination; check capture process is alive.

steps.label: Output meaning
steps.text: disk full or capture process died.

steps.label: Next
steps.text: rotation, resource limits, process exit reason.

steps.label: Hypotheses
steps.text: disk full, fd exhaustion, process killed.

steps.label: Confirming
steps.text: time of stop matches disk-full or kill.

steps.label: Say
steps.text: “Silence is a symptom — I check the logger’s health and storage.”

source.section: 30.28 Scenario 28 — “A long soak test stops logging after 18 hours.”

scenarios.title: Host OS reports BMC USB NIC missing intermittently.
scenarios.prompt: Host OS reports BMC USB NIC missing intermittently.. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Interpret
steps.text: Host-BMC interface (USB gadget) issue.

steps.label: First command
steps.text: BMC dmesg for USB gadget events; host dmesg for USB disconnects.

steps.label: Output meaning
steps.text: disconnects coincide with BMC service restarts or resets.

steps.label: Next
steps.text: correlate with BMC events; check gadget configuration service.

steps.label: Hypotheses
steps.text: BMC-side service restart, cable/hub, host driver.

steps.label: Confirming
steps.text: timestamps align with a BMC event.

steps.label: Say
steps.text: “Correlate both sides’ logs on one UTC timeline.”

source.section: 30.29 Scenario 29 — “Host OS reports BMC USB NIC missing intermittently.”

scenarios.title: Your diagnosis turned out wrong. What do you do?
scenarios.prompt: Your diagnosis turned out wrong. What do you do?

steps.label: Interpret
steps.text: Normal in engineering; process matters.

steps.label: First step
steps.text: state clearly what changed (new evidence), retract the conclusion, and re-open hypotheses.

steps.label: Next
steps.text: review which evidence misled you and why (correlation, missing logs).

steps.label: Prevention
steps.text: improve evidence collection, add discriminating tests earlier.

steps.label: Say
steps.text: “I correct the record quickly, explain what evidence changed, and update the method so it’s less likely next time.”

source.section: 30.30 Scenario 30 — “Your diagnosis turned out wrong. What do you do?”

scenarios.title: Jenkins job works on one agent, fails on another
scenarios.prompt: Jenkins job works on one agent, fails on another. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: Same commit passes on linux-01, fails on linux-02 with ModuleNotFoundError or different results.

steps.label: Likely causes
steps.text: different Python versions/system packages; dependencies leaking from system site-packages; missing tools; permissions.

steps.label: Investigation
steps.text:
compare python --version, pip freeze artifacts, agent labels, environment dumps.
Commands: sh 'python3 --version; which python3; python3 -m pip --version; env |
```code
sort'
```

steps.label: Expected
steps.text: version or package differences.

steps.label: Corrective
steps.text: fresh venv from pinned requirements; or container agent.

steps.label: Prevention
steps.text: agent provisioning as code; env-check stage; archive pip freeze.

steps.label: Answer
steps.text: “I compared the archived environments of both builds, found the agents had different Python and packages, and made the pipeline build its own pinned venv so agents can’t differ silently.”

source.section: 33.1 Scenario 1 — Jenkins job works on one agent, fails on another

scenarios.title: Git checkout fails with authentication error
scenarios.prompt: Git checkout fails with authentication error. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Context
steps.text: Symptoms: Permission denied (publickey) or Authentication failed in the checkout stage.

steps.label: Likely causes
steps.text: wrong credential ID; deploy key removed; token expired; SSO not authorised.

steps.label: Investigation
steps.text:
job’s credential; repository deploy keys; test as the agent user.
Commands: GIT_SSH_COMMAND="ssh -v" git ls-remote git@host:org/repo.git (as jenkins on the agent).

steps.label: Expected
steps.text: “Offering public key … Authentication refused” or no key offered.

steps.label: Corrective
steps.text: fix/rotate the credential, re-add the deploy key. **Prevention:** documented service credentials with expiry monitoring; read-only • deploy keys.

steps.label: Answer
steps.text: “Checkout runs Git on the agent with the job’s credential, so I reproduced it as the agent user with verbose SSH and found the deploy key had been removed during a repo migration.”

source.section: 33.2 Scenario 2 — Git checkout fails with authentication error

scenarios.title: Tests pass locally but fail in CI
scenarios.prompt: Tests pass locally but fail in CI. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: green on laptop, red in Jenkins.

steps.label: Likely causes
steps.text: unpinned dependency, different Python, local files not in Git, environment variables set locally, time zone/locale, test order, network access.

steps.label: Investigation
steps.text:
reproduce with CI’s commit, pip-freeze.txt, parameters and command.
Commands: git checkout <GIT_COMMIT>; python -m venv /tmp/v; /tmp/v/bin/pip install
```code
-r pip-freeze.txt; <copied pytest command>
```

steps.label: Expected
steps.text: failure reproduces once environment matches.

steps.label: Corrective
steps.text: pin/add missing dependency; commit missing file; make tests independent of local env.

steps.label: Prevention
steps.text: run_local.sh mirroring CI; fresh venvs.

steps.label: Answer
steps.text: “I rebuilt the exact CI environment from the archived freeze file; the failure reproduced: a transitive dependency had a new release. I pinned it and added a constraints file.”

source.section: 33.3 Scenario 3 — Tests pass locally but fail in CI

scenarios.title: JUnit reports are missing
scenarios.prompt: JUnit reports are missing. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: No test report files were found; build FAILURE.

steps.label: Likely causes
steps.text: pytest never ran (earlier failure), wrong path, different working directory (dir()), report deleted by cleanup before publishing, pytest killed.

steps.label: Investigation
steps.text:
console order of steps; ls -R reports before junit.
Commands: sh 'ls -la reports || true' in post { always } before junit.

steps.label: Expected
steps.text: directory absent or file in a different path.

steps.label: Corrective
steps.text: fix path; publish before cleanWs(); ensure pytest runs with --junitxml.

steps.label: Prevention
steps.text: allowEmptyResults: false; standard REPORT_DIR variable.

steps.label: Answer
steps.text: “The report path was relative to a dir() block, so junit looked in the wrong folder. I standardised REPORT_DIR and kept missing reports as a hard failure.”

scenarios.title: A firmware test hangs until the pipeline timeout
scenarios.prompt: A firmware test hangs until the pipeline timeout. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: build ABORTED after 90 minutes; last line is in a firmware test.

steps.label: Likely causes
steps.text:
request without timeout; infinite wait loop; device hung; serial read blocking. **Investigation:** last log lines, which operation, device console at that time. •
Commands: add pytest-timeout (timeout = 120), requests.get(..., timeout=10), `timeout(time: 15, unit: 'MINUTES', activity: true).`

steps.label: Expected
steps.text: a per-test timeout now fails just that test with a stack trace showing the blocking call.

steps.label: Corrective
steps.text: bounded polling with deadline; timeouts on every call.

steps.label: Prevention
steps.text: code review rule “every wait has a deadline”; per-test timeouts.

steps.label: Answer
steps.text: “The pipeline timeout gave no useful evidence. I added per-test and per-call timeouts, so the next hang failed the single test with the stack trace pointing at an unbounded poll loop.”

source.section: 33.5 Scenario 5 — A firmware test hangs until the pipeline timeout

scenarios.title: Two jobs try to use the same BMC
scenarios.prompt: Two jobs try to use the same BMC. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: random reboots during sensor tests; both jobs fail inconsistently.

steps.label: Likely causes
steps.text: no locking; two jobs pointing at the same config.

steps.label: Investigation
steps.text:
overlapping build timelines; BMC event log shows unexpected resets.
Commands: lock(resource: 'bmc-lab-01') { ... }

steps.label: Expected
steps.text: second job waits “Waiting for lock on bmc-lab-01”.

steps.label: Corrective
steps.text: add locks to every job that touches the device.

steps.label: Prevention
steps.text: framework refuses to run lab tests without a lock (e.g. checks `LOCKED_RESOURCE env or holds DeviceLock).`

steps.label: Answer
steps.text: “Timelines overlapped and the BMC log showed a reset from the other job. I added Lockable Resources locks and made the framework take a local lock too.”

source.section: 33.6 Scenario 6 — Two jobs try to use the same BMC

scenarios.title: BMC unreachable after reboot
scenarios.prompt: BMC unreachable after reboot. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: tests after a reboot error with connection refused/timeouts.

steps.label: Likely causes
steps.text: boot slower than fixed sleep; network config lost after reboot; boot failure; IP changed (DHCP).

steps.label: Investigation
steps.text:
console log of the boot; time-to-ready history; ping vs Redfish vs SSH.
Commands: device.wait_until_ready(timeout_s=600, poll_s=5); UART capture during reboot.

steps.label: Expected
steps.text: either ready later than expected or boot stops with an error on console.

steps.label: Corrective
steps.text: replace sleep with polling; if boot fails, file defect / recover device.

steps.label: Prevention
steps.text: record boot time each run; alert on growth.

steps.label: Answer
steps.text: “A fixed sleep was shorter than boot after the new firmware. Polling with a deadline fixed the test, and the recorded boot time showed a 60-second increase that we reported as a firmware regression.”

scenarios.title: Jenkins agent disconnects during regression
scenarios.prompt: Jenkins agent disconnects during regression. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: ChannelClosedException, build FAILURE/ABORTED mid-suite.

steps.label: Likely causes
steps.text: agent host reboot, network blip, OOM, disk full.

steps.label: Investigation
steps.text:
agent log, system journal on agent, memory/disk graphs.
Commands: journalctl --since "2 hours ago" on agent; df -h; dmesg | grep -i oom.

steps.label: Expected
steps.text: OOM kill of the agent JVM or network events.

steps.label: Corrective
steps.text: fix resource issue; health-check device before reuse; rerun.

steps.label: Prevention
steps.text: monitoring, retry(conditions: [agent()]) around node allocation for idempotent stages, classify as infra.

steps.label: Answer
steps.text: “The agent JVM was OOM-killed. I fixed memory, treated the device as suspect until a health check passed, and classified the run as infrastructure so nobody chased a firmware bug.”

source.section: 33.8 Scenario 8 — Jenkins agent disconnects during regression

scenarios.title: Test fails because dependencies differ between environments
scenarios.prompt: Test fails because dependencies differ between environments. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: TypeError from a library API change.

steps.label: Likely causes
steps.text: unpinned dependency.

steps.label: Investigation
steps.text:
compare pip freeze of good vs bad builds.
Commands: diff <(curl -s .../good/artifact/pip-freeze.txt) <(curl -s .../bad/ `artifact/pip-freeze.txt)`

steps.label: Expected
steps.text: one package version changed.

steps.label: Corrective
steps.text: pin; adapt code deliberately later.

steps.label: Prevention
steps.text: lock files, scheduled dependency-update PRs.

steps.label: Answer
steps.text: “Diffing archived freeze files between builds showed a new library release; I pinned it and scheduled the upgrade as a reviewed change.”

source.section: 33.9 Scenario 9 — Test fails because dependencies differ between environments

scenarios.title: A failed test is reported as successful
scenarios.prompt: A failed test is reported as successful. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: console shows FAILED, build is green.

steps.label: Likely causes
steps.text: exit code lost (| tee without pipefail, || true, wrapper ignoring code), skipMarkingBuildUnstable, wrong report published (old file).

steps.label: Investigation
steps.text:
read the sh step; check exit-code handling and published file timestamps.
Commands: def rc = sh(returnStatus: true, script: '''#!/bin/bash ... exit $ `{PIPESTATUS[0]}''')`

steps.label: Expected
steps.text: rc 1 now visible; build UNSTABLE.

steps.label: Corrective
steps.text: propagate exit codes; clean reports/ at start.

steps.label: Prevention
steps.text: a “canary” failing test in a pipeline self-test job to prove failures turn red.

steps.label: Answer
steps.text: “pytest’s output was piped through tee under /bin/sh, so the step saw tee’s exit code. I switched to bash with PIPESTATUS and added a self-test that proves a failing test turns the build unstable.”

source.section: 33.10 Scenario 10 — A failed test is reported as successful

scenarios.title: A retry hides an intermittent firmware defect
scenarios.prompt: A retry hides an intermittent firmware defect. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: nightly green, but console shows reruns (R); field reports of the same symptom.

steps.label: Likely causes
steps.text: --reruns enabled globally.

steps.label: Investigation
steps.text: rerun counts per test across builds; first-attempt failure messages.

steps.label: Commands
steps.text: grep consoles for rerun; remove --reruns; run the test 50× on hardware.

steps.label: Expected
steps.text: reproducible intermittent failure (e.g. 1 in 10).

steps.label: Corrective
steps.text: file the defect with evidence; remove blanket reruns.

steps.label: Prevention
steps.text: reruns only for listed tests with tickets; report rerun count as a separate signal.

steps.label: Answer
steps.text: “Reruns turned an intermittent firmware race into a green build: the JUnit file showed zero failures. I removed blanket reruns, reproduced 1 in 10 failures, and the firmware team fixed a race in the fan service.”

source.section: 33.11 Scenario 11 — A retry hides an intermittent firmware defect

scenarios.title: Secrets appear in build logs
scenarios.prompt: Secrets appear in build logs. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: a password visible in console or archived log.

steps.label: Likely causes
steps.text: Groovy interpolation, set -x, debug print, transformed secret not masked.

steps.label: Investigation
steps.text: find the step; check how the secret reached the output.

steps.label: Commands
steps.text: use sh 'cmd "$BMC_PASSWORD"' (single quotes), set +x, Python logging mask.

steps.label: Expected
steps.text: or no mention at all.

steps.label: Corrective
steps.text: rotate the secret; delete affected logs; fix code.

steps.label: Prevention
steps.text: review checklist, masking in framework logs, least privilege.

steps.label: Answer
steps.text: “First I rotated the password and deleted the builds’ logs, then fixed a debug print in a helper; now logs are masked and the review checklist forbids printing request objects.”

source.section: 33.12 Scenario 12 — Secrets appear in build logs

scenarios.title: Health check fails with HTTP 401 after a weekend
scenarios.prompt: Health check fails with HTTP 401 after a weekend. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: health exit 11; all lab jobs failing.

steps.label: Likely causes
steps.text: password rotated on BMC but not in Jenkins; account locked after failed logins; BMC reflashed to defaults.

steps.label: Investigation
steps.text:
try the credential manually (securely); check BMC account status/ logs.
Commands: curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' -u "$BMC_USER:$BMC_PASSWORD" `https://$DUT/redfish/v1/Managers inside withCredentials.`

steps.label: Corrective
steps.text: update the Jenkins credential (same ID); unlock account.

steps.label: Prevention
steps.text: rotation procedure updating Jenkins in the same change; lockout-aware retries (do not retry auth).

steps.label: Answer
steps.text: “The health gate correctly reported AUTH; the BMC had been reflashed to defaults. We updated provisioning so reflashing re-creates the CI account.”

source.section: 33.13 Scenario 13 — Health check fails with HTTP 401 after a weekend

scenarios.title: pytest exits 5 in nightly
scenarios.prompt: pytest exits 5 in nightly. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: “no tests ran”, FAILURE.

steps.label: Likely causes
steps.text:
marker renamed; SUITE parameter value changed; tests moved out `of testpaths.`
Investigation: --collect-only -m <marker>.
Commands: python -m pytest --collect-only -q -m regression

steps.label: Expected
steps.text: 0 selected.

steps.label: Corrective
steps.text: fix marker mapping.

steps.label: Prevention
steps.text: --strict-markers; self-test that each suite selects ≥ N tests.

steps.label: Answer
steps.text: “A refactor renamed the marker; exit 5 failed the build as designed. I added a self-test that asserts each suite selects a minimum number of tests.”

scenarios.title: Collection error after a merge
scenarios.prompt: Collection error after a merge. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: exit 2, ERROR collecting tests/....

steps.label: Likely causes
steps.text: syntax/import error; plugin declared in non-root conftest; missing dependency.

steps.label: Investigation
steps.text:
first error in output.
Commands: python -m pytest --collect-only -q

steps.label: Expected
steps.text: traceback pointing at the file.

steps.label: Corrective
steps.text: fix code; move pytest_plugins to root conftest.

steps.label: Prevention
steps.text: PR checks run collection; pre-commit compileall.

steps.label: Answer
steps.text: “Collection errors stop everything, so we treat exit 2 as a pipeline failure and run a fast collect-only check on every PR.”

source.section: 33.15 Scenario 15 — Collection error after a merge

scenarios.title: Lock never released / jobs queue forever
scenarios.prompt: Lock never released / jobs queue forever. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: “Waiting for lock on bmc-lab-01” for hours.

steps.label: Likely causes
steps.text: a job holding the lock is stuck (no timeout); manual reservation forgotten.

steps.label: Investigation
steps.text: Lockable Resources page shows the holder. **Commands:** stage timeout around locked work; lock(..., timeoutForAllocateResource: • `60, timeoutUnit: 'MINUTES').`

steps.label: Expected
steps.text: stuck job identified.

steps.label: Corrective
steps.text: abort the holder; release.

steps.label: Prevention
steps.text: timeouts inside locks; minimal lock scope; alerts on long waits.

steps.label: Answer
steps.text: “A hung job held the lock without a timeout. I added stage timeouts inside lock blocks and a bounded wait for acquiring the lock.”

source.section: 33.16 Scenario 16 — Lock never released / jobs queue forever

scenarios.title: Serial port busy
scenarios.prompt: Serial port busy. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Context
steps.text: Symptoms: SerialException: could not open port /dev/ttyUSB0: [Errno 16] Device or `resource busy.`

steps.label: Likely causes
steps.text: a human’s picocom session; previous job’s process still running; two jobs.

steps.label: Investigation
steps.text:
find which process holds the port on the agent; check for a human console session or an orphaned process from an aborted build.
Commands: fuser -v /dev/ttyUSB0 or lsof /dev/ttyUSB0; ps -fp <pid>.

steps.label: Expected
steps.text: a PID holding the port (picocom, or a python capture process).

steps.label: Corrective
steps.text: stop it; ensure close in finally.

steps.label: Prevention
steps.text: lock serial ports as resources; background capture processes owned by the pipeline and killed in post.

steps.label: Answer
steps.text: “An orphaned capture process from an aborted build held the port; now captures are started and stopped by the pipeline and the port is part of the device lock.”

scenarios.title: Firmware update task stuck at a percentage
scenarios.prompt: Firmware update task stuck at a percentage. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: update test fails after update_timeout_s with “still Running”.

steps.label: Likely causes
steps.text: flash write hang; image incompatible; BMC service crash.

steps.label: Investigation
steps.text:
recorded status history; console; journal of the software manager.
Commands: Project 3 UpdateReport steps; journalctl -u <software manager service> over SSH if reachable.

steps.label: Expected
steps.text: stalled progress, maybe errors in journal.

steps.label: Corrective
steps.text: classify FIRMWARE_REGRESSION; recover device per lab procedure.

steps.label: Prevention
steps.text: bounded waits; evidence capture in finally.

steps.label: Answer
steps.text: “Because the orchestrator records every poll and the console tail even on failure, the report showed progress stalled at 75 % with a flash driver error, which went straight into the defect.”

source.section: 33.18 Scenario 18 — Firmware update task stuck at a percentage

scenarios.title: Wrong firmware tested
scenarios.prompt: Wrong firmware tested. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: results don’t match the release; version check fails or nobody checked.

steps.label: Likely causes
steps.text: flash step skipped; “latest” resolved differently; wrong device.

steps.label: Investigation
steps.text:
device-reported version vs parameter; build metadata.
Commands: smoke test_firmware_version_matches_expected.

steps.label: Expected
steps.text: mismatch.

steps.label: Corrective
steps.text: reflash; rerun.

steps.label: Prevention
steps.text: exact versions only; version assertion in smoke.

steps.label: Answer
steps.text: “The smoke suite asserts the device-reported version equals the requested one, so testing the wrong image fails in seconds.”

scenarios.title: Intermittent HTTP 503 from the BMC
scenarios.prompt: Intermittent HTTP 503 from the BMC. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: random tests fail with 503.

steps.label: Likely causes
steps.text: BMC web server overloaded/restarting; too many sessions; real defect.

steps.label: Investigation
steps.text: timing correlation; BMC journal for web service restarts; session count.

steps.label: Commands
steps.text: log each request’s status/latency; count 5xx per run.

steps.label: Expected
steps.text: bursts after specific operations.

steps.label: Corrective
steps.text: if service crashes → product defect; if test overload → reduce concurrency.

steps.label: Prevention
steps.text: classify 5xx separately; trend it.

steps.label: Answer
steps.text: “5xx is the BMC telling us it’s unhealthy, so we treat it as a product signal, not something to retry away; the journal showed the web service restarting after a large log request.”

source.section: 33.20 Scenario 20 — Intermittent HTTP 503 from the BMC

scenarios.title: Tests depend on order
scenarios.prompt: Tests depend on order. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: pass in full run, fail alone (or vice versa).

steps.label: Likely causes
steps.text: earlier test sets state later ones rely on.

steps.label: Investigation
steps.text:
run the failing test alone; random order on unit tests.
Commands: python -m pytest tests/x.py::test_y; -p randomly (pytest-randomly).

steps.label: Expected
steps.text: failure depends on a missing precondition.

steps.label: Corrective
steps.text: fixtures establish preconditions.

steps.label: Prevention
steps.text: isolation reviews; random order in CI for unit tests.

steps.label: Answer
steps.text: “The test assumed the host was powered on by a previous test; a fixture now ensures the precondition and restores it.”

scenarios.title: Build queue very long
scenarios.prompt: Build queue very long. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: builds wait an hour before starting.

steps.label: Likely causes
steps.text: too few lab agents/devices; long lock scopes; jobs on the wrong labels.

steps.label: Investigation
steps.text: queue reasons; lock holders; stage durations.

steps.label: Commands
steps.text: move setup/analysis outside lock; beforeAgent true.

steps.label: Expected
steps.text: locks held only during device stages.

steps.label: Corrective
steps.text: restructure; add capacity where justified.

steps.label: Prevention
steps.text: monitor queue time per label.

steps.label: Answer
steps.text: “Jobs held the device lock during venv creation and report generation; narrowing the lock cut device occupancy by 30 %.”

scenarios.title: Disk full on agent
scenarios.prompt: Disk full on agent. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: No space left on device at random steps (pip install, git checkout, report writing).

steps.label: Likely causes
steps.text: workspaces never cleaned; large logs or firmware images in workspaces; growing pip/docker caches.

steps.label: Investigation
steps.text:
which directories grow; which jobs leave large workspaces.
Commands: df -h /home/jenkins; du -sh /home/jenkins/agent/workspace/* | sort -h | `tail.`

steps.label: Expected
steps.text: a few job workspaces holding GBs (images, old reports, venvs).

steps.label: Corrective
steps.text: clean the workspaces; add post { cleanup { cleanWs() } }; move images to an artifact store.

steps.label: Prevention
steps.text: buildDiscarder; disk monitoring; the environment-check stage fails early below a free-space threshold (Project 2’s env_check.sh requires 500 MB).

steps.label: Answer
steps.text: “Old workspaces with firmware images filled the disk; we now clean workspaces after archiving, and the environment check fails fast with a clear message when space is low.”

scenarios.title: Pipeline green but HTML report empty or unstyled
scenarios.prompt: Pipeline green but HTML report empty or unstyled. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: JUnit results fine, but the HTML report page is blank or has no styling in Jenkins.

steps.label: Likely causes
steps.text: Jenkins’ Content Security Policy blocking the report’s scripts/styles; report not self-contained.

steps.label: Investigation
steps.text: open the browser developer console on the report page; download the file and open it locally.

steps.label: Commands
steps.text: regenerate with --self-contained-html; browser console → look for CSP violation messages.

steps.label: Expected
steps.text: CSP violation messages in the console; the downloaded file renders correctly.

steps.label: Corrective
steps.text: view downloaded copies, or configure a resource root URL (Manage Jenkins → Security) so user content is served from a separate origin.

steps.label: Prevention
steps.text: treat JUnit as the verdict source; HTML is a convenience view; avoid relaxing CSP globally.

steps.label: Answer
steps.text: “Jenkins’ CSP blocked the report’s inline content; the results themselves were fine. We configured a resource root URL so reports render safely instead of weakening CSP.”

source.section: 33.24 Scenario 24 — Pipeline green but HTML report empty or unstyled

scenarios.title: PR from a fork tries to print credentials
scenarios.prompt: PR from a fork tries to print credentials. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: a reviewer notices a PR adding env dumps or network calls to a helper script.

steps.label: Likely causes
steps.text: malicious or careless contribution.

steps.label: Investigation
steps.text: did any build with credentials run this PR? Which agents and which credentials were bound?

steps.label: Commands
steps.text: check the PR’s build console and the job’s branch-source trust settings; search the console for the injected output.

steps.label: Expected
steps.text: the PR build ran in the simulation pool with no credentials bound, so nothing sensitive was printed.

steps.label: Corrective
steps.text: if a credential was exposed, rotate it immediately; close the PR; delete affected logs.

steps.label: Prevention
steps.text: untrusted PRs run without credentials and without lab access; Jenkinsfile taken from the target branch for untrusted authors; maintainer approval before hardware runs.

steps.label: Answer
steps.text: “Fork PRs only run simulation on isolated agents with no secrets, so the attempt exposed nothing; we still reviewed trust settings and added the case to our security checklist.”

source.section: 33.25 Scenario 25 — PR from a fork tries to print credentials

scenarios.title: Duplicate builds for each push
scenarios.prompt: Duplicate builds for each push. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: two identical builds start for every commit.

steps.label: Likely causes
steps.text: both webhook and pollSCM configured; branch and PR both discovered for the same commit; two jobs watching the same repository.

steps.label: Investigation
steps.text: read “Started by …” at the top of each build’s console; check the job’s triggers and branch-source behaviours.

steps.label: Commands
steps.text: compare consoles: Started by GitHub push by … vs Started by an SCM change (polling).

steps.label: Expected
steps.text: two different trigger causes for the same commit.

steps.label: Corrective
steps.text: keep one trigger path (webhook), exclude branches that are also filed as PRs, remove the duplicate job.

steps.label: Prevention
steps.text: a documented trigger policy; disableConcurrentBuilds(abortPrevious: true) for rapid pushes; periodic indexing only as a safety net.

steps.label: Answer
steps.text: “The consoles showed two causes: webhook and polling. I kept the webhook with daily indexing as a fallback, and builds halved.”

source.section: 33.26 Scenario 26 — Duplicate builds for each push

scenarios.title: Agent can’t access /dev/ttyUSB0
scenarios.prompt: Agent can’t access /dev/ttyUSB0. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Context
steps.text: Symptoms: PermissionError: [Errno 13] Permission denied: '/dev/ttyUSB0' on one lab agent only.

steps.label: Likely causes
steps.text: agent user not in the dialout group; container started without --device; device enumerated under a different name.

steps.label: Investigation
steps.text:
compare user groups and device ownership with a working agent.
Commands: groups jenkins; ls -l /dev/ttyUSB0 /dev/serial/by-id/; fix with sudo usermod -aG dialout jenkins and restart the agent service.

steps.label: Expected
steps.text: device owned by group dialout, agent user not a member.

steps.label: Corrective
steps.text: add the group, restart the agent (group changes need a new login session).

steps.label: Prevention
steps.text: agent provisioning adds the group; env check verifies the port is readable; use stable /dev/serial/by-id names in config.

steps.label: Answer
steps.text: “The new agent’s user lacked the dialout group; provisioning now adds it and the environment check verifies the port before tests start.”

scenarios.title: Test passes against the simulator, fails on hardware
scenarios.prompt: Test passes against the simulator, fails on hardware. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: simulator run green; lab run red on the same test commit.

steps.label: Likely causes
steps.text: simulator model differs from the platform (resource IDs, units, schema details, timing); or a real product defect.

steps.label: Investigation
steps.text:
compare the real response (collected snapshot) with the simulator’s response for the failing resource.
Commands: python scripts/collect_logs.py in lab mode; diff <(jq -S . artifacts/ `bmc_snapshot/manager.json) <(jq -S . sim_manager.json).`

steps.label: Expected
steps.text: a structural difference (e.g. chassis ID, threshold format) or a genuinely wrong value.

steps.label: Corrective
steps.text: fix configuration/adapter mapping and improve the simulator; or file a product defect if the value is wrong.

steps.label: Prevention
steps.text: keep sanitised real response samples to update the simulator; contract tests that run the adapter against recorded responses.

steps.label: Answer
steps.text: “The real platform used a different chassis ID and threshold format; the adapter now reads IDs from config, and the simulator was updated from sanitised real responses.”

source.section: 33.28 Scenario 28 — Test passes against the simulator, fails on hardware

scenarios.title: Upstream firmware build triggers the test job with empty parameters
scenarios.prompt: Upstream firmware build triggers the test job with empty parameters. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: downstream regression runs with empty EXPECTED_FW and tests whatever is on the board.

steps.label: Likely causes
steps.text: upstream build job: call omits parameters; new job’s first run has no registered parameters.

steps.label: Investigation
steps.text:
downstream build’s Parameters page and “Started by upstream project” cause; upstream Jenkinsfile.
Commands: upstream: build job: 'bmc-regression', parameters: [string(name:
```code
'EXPECTED_FW', value: env.FW_VERSION)]; downstream: if (!params.EXPECTED_FW)
{ error('EXPECTED_FW is required') }.
```

steps.label: Expected
steps.text: parameters page shows an empty value.

steps.label: Corrective
steps.text: pass parameters explicitly; validate them at the start of the downstream pipeline.

steps.label: Prevention
steps.text: fail fast on missing required parameters; never fall back to “whatever is installed”.

steps.label: Answer
steps.text: “The downstream job now validates its parameters and fails with ‘EXPECTED_FW is required’ instead of silently testing the wrong firmware.”

source.section: 33.29 Scenario 29 — Upstream firmware build triggers the test job with empty parameters

scenarios.title: Evidence for an old failure is gone
scenarios.prompt: Evidence for an old failure is gone. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: a defect needs logs from a run two weeks ago; workspace cleaned, device reflashed, build discarded.

steps.label: Likely causes
steps.text: evidence kept only in workspaces; short buildDiscarder retention; no long-term export.

steps.label: Investigation
steps.text: what was archived for that build, and what the retention policy is.

steps.label: Commands
steps.text:
check the build’s Build Artifacts list;
```code
buildDiscarder(logRotator(numToKeepStr: '…', artifactNumToKeepStr: '…')) in the
```
Jenkinsfile.

steps.label: Expected
steps.text: only the console log survived, or the build itself was rotated away.

steps.label: Corrective
steps.text: reproduce if possible; for the future, archive evidence in `post { always }.`

steps.label: Prevention
steps.text: archive reports and device evidence for every run; longer retention (or “keep forever”) for release qualification; export summaries to long-term storage.

steps.label: Answer
steps.text: “Evidence lives in archived artifacts, not workspaces or devices; release-qualification builds are kept permanently and summaries exported.”

source.section: 33.30 Scenario 30 — Evidence for an old failure is gone

scenarios.title: Time-dependent failures right after BMC reboot
scenarios.prompt: Time-dependent failures right after BMC reboot. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: TLS certificate or session-token checks fail only in the first minutes after a reboot.

steps.label: Likely causes
steps.text: BMC clock not yet synchronised (NTP/RTC), so certificates look “not yet valid”; framework timers based on wall-clock time jump.

steps.label: Investigation
steps.text: compare BMC time with agent time in the evidence; check NTP status on the BMC.

steps.label: Commands
steps.text: Redfish GET /redfish/v1/Managers/{id} → DateTime; over SSH date -u and timedatectl (if available).

steps.label: Expected
steps.text: BMC time far off agent time until sync completes.

steps.label: Corrective
steps.text: include “time synchronised” in readiness; use time.monotonic() for all framework timers (Project 3 does).

steps.label: Prevention
steps.text: readiness checks that cover clock state; record BMC time in evidence.

steps.label: Answer
steps.text: “After reboot the BMC clock was hours off until NTP synced; readiness now waits for time sync and our timers use monotonic time.”

source.section: 33.31 Scenario 31 — Time-dependent failures right after BMC reboot

scenarios.title: Regression duration creeps up over months
scenarios.prompt: Regression duration creeps up over months. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: nightly regression grew from 4 h to 5.6 h without many new tests.

steps.label: Likely causes
steps.text: fixed sleeps added; slower BMC responses or boot (firmware); more retries.

steps.label: Investigation
steps.text: compare per-test durations and stage times between old and new builds; boot-time trend.

steps.label: Commands
steps.text: python -m pytest --durations=30; compare JUnit time attributes across builds; read waited_s from readiness logs.

steps.label: Expected
steps.text: a few tests or operations (e.g. Redfish latency, boot) account for most of the growth.

steps.label: Corrective
steps.text: remove sleeps; report firmware latency/boot regressions with data.

steps.label: Prevention
steps.text: track duration metrics per test and per operation; alert on budget overruns.

steps.label: Answer
steps.text: “Trend data showed Redfish latency doubling across firmware builds, a product regression we reported with timing evidence, and we removed two fixed sleeps that hid it.”

source.section: 33.32 Scenario 32 — Regression duration creeps up over months

scenarios.title: Case 1: BMC unreachable after reboot
scenarios.prompt: Case 1: BMC unreachable after reboot. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: After a scheduled Redfish Manager.Reset, the BMC doesn’t answer SSH or HTTPS for 15 minutes (normally back in 3).

steps.label: Environment
steps.text: Lab BMC, static IP 192.0.2.50, serial console server available.

steps.label: Commands
steps.text: Test host [RO]: ping -c3 192.0.2.50, ip neigh show 192.0.2.50, TCP probes 22/443. Serial console [RO]: observe boot; at login: ip -br addr, ip route, `systemctl is-system-running, systemctl --failed, journalctl -b -u systemd-networkd.`

steps.label: Expected observations
steps.text: Serial shows complete boot to login prompt; ip -br addr shows eth0 UP with **no IPv4 address**; networkd journal: “DHCP lease lost”/no static config.

steps.label: Possible causes
steps.text: Boot hang; network config lost (reset to DHCP); link down; IP conflict; services failing; switch port/VLAN.

steps.label: Investigation sequence
steps.text: Decision tree (Chapter 10): console output? → yes, login reached → network configured? → no IPv4 → check config files/D-Bus network objects and whether the update/reset touched persistent settings.

steps.label: Evidence to confirm
steps.text: Network configuration file missing/defaulted after reboot; persistent partition errors in dmesg or the overlay not mounted ( findmnt /etc).

steps.label: Corrective options
steps.text: Restore config from backup (lab), investigate why persistence failed (storage, overlay mount), fix and add persistence check to reboot tests.

steps.label: Verification
steps.text: 50 reboots with IP persistence verified each cycle; persistent storage mounted RW every boot.

steps.label: Interview explanation
steps.text: “Ping failed, so I went to the serial console: the BMC had booted fully but had no IPv4 address. The networkd logs showed DHCP mode instead of the static config, and findmnt showed the writable overlay wasn’t mounted because of flash errors in dmesg. So the root cause was persistent storage failing to mount, not the network itself.”

scenarios.title: Case 2: systemd service repeatedly restarting
scenarios.prompt: Case 2: systemd service repeatedly restarting. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: NRestarts for fake-sensord grows by ~30/hour; sensors flicker in Redfish.

steps.label: Environment
steps.text:
Lab BMC, SSH available.
Commands [RO]. systemctl status fake-sensord, systemctl show fake-sensord -p
```code
NRestarts,Result,ExecMainStatus,ExecMainCode, journalctl -u fake-sensord -b | grep -E
'Started|exited|Failed' | tail, dmesg | grep -iE 'segfault|oom', coredumpctl list (if
```
systemd-coredump is present). **Expected observations.** Result: core-dump, status=11/SEGV; journal shows crash 2 • minutes after each start; kernel segfault at 0 ip ... in fake-sensord.

steps.label: Possible causes
steps.text: Software bug (crash on specific data), corrupt config, memory corruption due to hardware, OOM kill (would show SIGKILL, not SEGV).

steps.label: Investigation sequence
steps.text: Capture status before restart; correlate crash times with sensor events; check if crash follows a specific sensor (config entry) by bisecting configuration in the lab.

steps.label: Evidence to confirm
steps.text: Core dump backtrace in the parsing function for a sensor with an empty threshold field; removing that entry stops crashes (controlled reproduction).

steps.label: Corrective options
steps.text: Fix the parsing bug; validate config; meanwhile, track as known issue.

steps.label: Verification
steps.text: NRestarts constant over 24 h; unit test added for empty threshold field.

steps.label: Interview explanation
steps.text: “Restart loops are a symptom. I looked at the exit reason: SIGSEGV, so a crash, not OOM. The crash interval matched a specific sensor’s polling, and the core dump pointed into config parsing — confirmed by removing and re-adding the entry.”

scenarios.title: Case 3: Root filesystem / persistent partition full
scenarios.prompt: Case 3: Root filesystem / persistent partition full. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text:
Settings changes don’t persist; services log “No space left on device”.
Commands [RO]. df -h, df -i, du -xh /var 2>/dev/null | sort -h | tail (BusyBox:
```code
du -x /var | sort -n | tail), ls -l /proc/[0-9]*/fd 2>/dev/null | grep deleted,
journalctl --disk-usage.
```

steps.label: Expected observations
steps.text: /var/persist 100%; a debug log /var/persist/debug/ trace.log of 3 MB growing; or deleted log held open.

steps.label: Possible causes
steps.text: Debug logging left enabled; core dumps; journal persistent with high limit; deleted-open file; inode exhaustion.

steps.label: Investigation
steps.text: Identify the largest consumers and growth rate (measure twice, 10 min apart); identify which process writes ( lsof if present, or /proc/*/fd links).

steps.label: Evidence to confirm
steps.text: Growth rate of the trace file matches the rate of free-space decrease.

steps.label: Corrective options
steps.text: Copy evidence off; disable debug logging (configuration change, [MOD]); clean up through the owning service; long-term: size limits/ rotation.

steps.label: Verification
steps.text: Free space stable over 24 h; settings persist across reboot.

steps.label: Interview explanation
steps.text: “ENOSPC is a symptom. I checked bytes and inodes, found the partition at 100%, measured which file grew, and tied the growth rate to a debug trace option left enabled by a previous test.”

source.section: 27.3 Case 3: Root filesystem / persistent partition full

scenarios.title: Case 4: Kernel log shows device communication failure
scenarios.prompt: Case 4: Kernel log shows device communication failure. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Context
steps.text:
Symptoms. dmesg: nvme nvme0: I/O 12 QID 3 timeout, reset controller (host-side) — or on BMC: i2c i2c-5: transfer timed out repeatedly.
Commands [RO]. dmesg -T | grep -E 'i2c-5|timeout', ls /sys/bus/i2c/devices/ | grep '^5-', per-device driver links, hwmon readings for devices on bus 5.

steps.label: Expected observations
steps.text: All devices on bus 5 fail at the same timestamps → bus-level; or only one address fails → device-level.

steps.label: Possible causes
steps.text: Device not responding; bus held low; mux channel stuck; controller driver issue; device powered off with host.

steps.label: Investigation
steps.text: Correlate with host power state; check other devices on the bus; check whether failures follow the board/riser.

steps.label: Evidence to confirm
steps.text: E.g. all bus-5 failures begin when a hot-plug card is inserted; removing it stops them (controlled) → card holds bus.

steps.label: Corrective options
steps.text: Replace/repair card; firmware workaround; isolate via mux configuration.

steps.label: Verification
steps.text: Bus error count zero over N hours with the replacement.

steps.label: Interview explanation
steps.text: “I first asked whether it was one device or the whole bus by comparing addresses at the same timestamps, then correlated with physical changes.”

source.section: 27.4 Case 4: Kernel log shows device communication failure

scenarios.title: Case 5: Redfish API unavailable while SSH works
scenarios.prompt: Case 5: Redfish API unavailable while SSH works. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text:
curl https://bmc/redfish/v1/ → connection refused; SSH fine.
Commands [RO]. On BMC: ss -tlnp | grep ':443', systemctl status bmcweb.socket `bmcweb.service, journalctl -u bmcweb -b | tail -50, df -h, free.`

steps.label: Expected observations
steps.text: Nothing listening on 443; bmcweb.service failed with exit code; journal: certificate file parse error.

steps.label: Possible causes
steps.text: bmcweb crashed; socket unit stopped; TLS certificate corrupt; port conflict; resource exhaustion.

steps.label: Investigation
steps.text: First error in bmcweb journal; check certificate file integrity and storage health.

steps.label: Evidence to confirm
steps.text: Journal shows failure loading the certificate; certificate file is zero-length after an interrupted write (storage full at the time).

steps.label: Corrective options
steps.text: Regenerate/restore certificate (lab procedure); fix storage issue; ensure atomic writes.

steps.label: Verification
steps.text: bmcweb active through 20 reboots; certificate valid.

steps.label: Interview explanation
steps.text: “SSH working proves the network and kernel are fine, so I moved straight to the service: not listening, unit failed, and the journal pointed to a corrupted certificate.”

source.section: 27.5 Case 5: Redfish API unavailable while SSH works

scenarios.title: Case 6: SSH works manually but fails in automation
scenarios.prompt: Case 6: SSH works manually but fails in automation. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: Jenkins job: Permission denied (publickey,password) / or hangs; manual SSH from your laptop works.

steps.label: Commands
steps.text: On agent [RO]: id, ls -l ~/.ssh, ssh -v -o BatchMode=yes -o `ConnectTimeout=10 root@192.0.2.50 true, echo "$SSH_AUTH_SOCK".`

steps.label: Expected observations
steps.text: Agent user lacks the key (works for you via your SSH agent); or prompt for host key acceptance blocks ( BatchMode=yes turns this into “Host key verification failed”).

steps.label: Possible causes
steps.text: Different user/HOME on agent; key not loaded; known_hosts missing/changed; password auth used manually but BatchMode disables prompts; network path differs from agent.

steps.label: Investigation
steps.text: Reproduce as the agent user, from the agent, with -v.

steps.label: Evidence to confirm
steps.text: ssh -v shows “Offering public key: …” none accepted, or “No ED25519 host key is known”.

steps.label: Corrective options
steps.text: Provision key via Jenkins credentials; manage lab known_hosts; never disable host key checking globally.

steps.label: Verification
steps.text: Job passes repeatedly from all agents with the label.

steps.label: Interview explanation
steps.text: “‘Works for me’ means the environment differs. I reproduced as the agent user with verbose SSH and saw it had no usable key and no known host entry.”

source.section: 27.6 Case 6: SSH works manually but fails in automation

scenarios.title: Case 7: Firmware update remains in a pending state
scenarios.prompt: Case 7: Firmware update remains in a pending state. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text:
Redfish task stays Running at 40% for 20 minutes.
**Commands [RO].** Redfish task GET; on BMC: journalctl -u '*code*' -b / update
```code
service unit(s) (names vary), busctl tree xyz.openbmc_project.Software.BMC.Updater
(name varies), get-property ... Activation, free, df -h /tmp, dmesg | grep -iE 'mtd|
```
spi|ubi|error', ps state of the updater.

steps.label: Expected observations
steps.text: Activation Activating, Progress 40 unchanged; updater in D state; dmesg shows SPI flash erase timeouts.

steps.label: Possible causes
steps.text: Flash write errors; lack of memory/space; updater hang; lock by another update; slow flash (normal but long).

steps.label: Investigation
steps.text: Baseline: how long does activation take normally? Then progress history + process state + kernel flash messages. **Evidence to confirm.** Flash driver errors at the same time progress stopped; • reproduces on this board only.

steps.label: Corrective options
steps.text: Hardware investigation of flash; recovery via alternate image (lab procedure).

steps.label: Verification
steps.text: Updates succeed on replacement flash/board 10/10.

steps.label: Interview explanation
steps.text: “A stuck update is a symptom; I compared with the normal activation time, then looked at the updater’s process state and kernel flash messages, which pointed to flash write timeouts.”

source.section: 27.7 Case 7: Firmware update remains in a pending state

scenarios.title: Case 8: UART log capture stops midway
scenarios.prompt: Case 8: UART log capture stops midway. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: Serial capture ends at kernel boot; device continues booting fine.

steps.label: Commands
steps.text: Host [RO]: dmesg | grep -i usb (adapter reset?), fuser /dev/ttyUSB0 or `lsof /dev/ttyUSB0; on BMC [RO]: cat /proc/cmdline.`

steps.label: Expected observations
steps.text: /proc/cmdline shows console=ttyS4,115200 while capture is on the UART that U-Boot uses (different), or a second process (another job) opened the port.

steps.label: Possible causes
steps.text: Console moved to another UART by kernel parameters; concurrent reader; adapter disconnect; device hang.

steps.label: Investigation
steps.text: Check capture gap markers; check host USB logs; check console configuration.

steps.label: Evidence to confirm
steps.text: Kernel console UART ≠ bootloader UART; or fuser shows second PID.

steps.label: Corrective options
steps.text: Capture the correct UART; enforce single reader via locks/ console server.

steps.label: Verification
steps.text: Full captures in 20 consecutive boots.

steps.label: Interview explanation
steps.text: “A stop at the same point every time suggests configuration, not random disconnects — the kernel’s console parameter pointed to a different UART.”

source.section: 27.8 Case 8: UART log capture stops midway

scenarios.title: Case 9: Service fails because of a missing configuration file
scenarios.prompt: Case 9: Service fails because of a missing configuration file. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text:
After updating, lab-sensord fails at boot: status=78/CONFIG.
Commands [RO]. systemctl status lab-sensord, systemctl cat lab-sensord, journalctl `-u lab-sensord -b, ls -l /etc/lab-sensord.conf, findmnt -T /etc.`

steps.label: Expected observations
steps.text: Journal: “cannot read config /etc/lab-sensord.conf”; file missing.

steps.label: Possible causes
steps.text: File not in new image; overlay hides it; migration deleted it; wrong path in new unit.

steps.label: Investigation
steps.text: Compare unit file and paths between versions; check whether file exists in the image’s lower layer.

steps.label: Evidence to confirm
steps.text: New unit file references a new path; old file never migrated.

steps.label: Corrective options
steps.text: Ship default config or migration; make unit fail clearly with a message (it did).

steps.label: Verification
steps.text: Clean update from previous version passes; unit active.

steps.label: Interview explanation
steps.text: “The exit code and the first log line said exactly what was missing; the deeper question was why — the new version changed the path without migration.”

source.section: 27.9 Case 9: Service fails because of a missing configuration file

scenarios.title: Case 10: A device appears in one diagnostic interface but not another
scenarios.prompt: Case 10: A device appears in one diagnostic interface but not another. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text:
PSU visible in sysfs ( /sys/bus/i2c/devices/7-0058 with hwmon) but missing in Redfish.
**Commands [RO].** hwmon readings; busctl tree of the PSU sensor daemon; ObjectMapper GetSubTree for sensors; journalctl -u <psu sensor unit>.

steps.label: Expected observations
steps.text: D-Bus object missing; daemon log: “No configuration found for PSU at 7-0058” or association failure.

steps.label: Possible causes
steps.text: Configuration (entity-manager) mismatch; daemon not started; association missing; bmcweb filter.

steps.label: Investigation
steps.text: Stage by stage (Chapter 22): described → probed → exposed → published → associated.

steps.label: Evidence to confirm
steps.text: Configuration expects address 0x59 on this board revision.

steps.label: Corrective options
steps.text: Fix configuration for board revision.

steps.label: Verification
steps.text: PSU appears in D-Bus and Redfish on both revisions.

steps.label: Interview explanation
steps.text: “I walked the layers and found the first one where the device disappeared — D-Bus publication — then the daemon log showed a config address mismatch.”

source.section: 27.10 Case 10: A device appears in one diagnostic interface but not another

scenarios.title: Case 11: Jenkins cannot access a test device
scenarios.prompt: Case 11: Jenkins cannot access a test device. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text:
All jobs on agent-3 fail at pre-flight with timeouts; other agents fine.
**Commands [RO].** On agent-3: ip route get 192.0.2.50, ping, TCP probe, ip -br addr; compare with agent-1.

steps.label: Expected observations
steps.text: agent-3 routes via a different interface (no lab VLAN), or DNS resolves the device name to an old IP.

steps.label: Possible causes
steps.text: Agent network config; DNS; firewall; lab VLAN membership; device moved.

steps.label: Investigation
steps.text: Compare route and resolution between agents; check recent infra changes.

steps.label: Evidence to confirm
steps.text: agent-3 lost its lab-network interface after a reboot (interface DOWN).

steps.label: Corrective options
steps.text: Fix agent network; add agent self-check stage.

steps.label: Verification
steps.text: Pre-flight passes from all agents.

steps.label: Interview explanation
steps.text: “Failing on one agent only is an infra signature; I compared routing between agents.”

source.section: 27.11 Case 11: Jenkins cannot access a test device

scenarios.title: Case 12: Test fails only after repeated reboots
scenarios.prompt: Case 12: Test fails only after repeated reboots. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text:
Reboot stress: cycles 1–37 pass, cycle 38 fails (sensor count lower), repeatable around 35–40.
**Commands [RO].** Per-cycle health JSON; df -h, df -i, free per cycle; journal size; NRestarts trends.

steps.label: Expected observations
steps.text: Persistent partition usage grows by ~100 KB per boot; failure when full.

steps.label: Possible causes
steps.text: Accumulating state per boot (logs, dumps, counters); flash wear; leaking resource persisted across boots. **Investigation.** Trend every resource across cycles; find the one that crosses a limit • at the failure cycle.

steps.label: Evidence to confirm
steps.text: A per-boot log file never rotated; removing it resets the failure point.

steps.label: Corrective options
steps.text: Rotation/cleanup; stress tests must track resource trends.

steps.label: Verification
steps.text: 500 cycles pass with stable usage.

steps.label: Interview explanation
steps.text: “A failure at a consistent cycle count suggests accumulation; I trended resources per cycle and found storage growth.”

source.section: 27.12 Case 12: Test fails only after repeated reboots

scenarios.title: Case 13: A diagnostic script exits with the wrong status
scenarios.prompt: Case 13: A diagnostic script exits with the wrong status. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: CI reports PASS though the log contains “FAIL svc_bmcweb”.

steps.label: Commands
steps.text: bash -x script.sh, check last commands; review pipelines.

steps.label: Expected observations
steps.text: Final line ... | tee report.txt — pipeline status is tee’s (0); or exit $failures with failures > 255 wrapping; or a cmd | while subshell losing the counter.

steps.label: Possible causes
steps.text: Pipeline status, subshell variable loss, exit with value ≥ 256 (wraps modulo 256), set -e interactions.

steps.label: Investigation
steps.text: Trace; inspect PIPESTATUS; check where the counter is incremented.

steps.label: Evidence to confirm
steps.text:
Counter incremented inside ... | while read (subshell); outer value stays 0.
Corrective options. done < <(cmd), set -o pipefail, exit $(( failures > 0 ? 1 : 0 )); add a test that asserts the exit code on a failing fixture.

steps.label: Verification
steps.text: Test with failing fixture returns 1.

steps.label: Interview explanation
steps.text: “The exit code is the script’s contract with CI; I traced it and found the counter was updated in a subshell.”

source.section: 27.13 Case 13: A diagnostic script exits with the wrong status

scenarios.title: Case 14: Log timestamps do not align
scenarios.prompt: Case 14: Log timestamps do not align. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text:
BMC journal says error at 09:40:02; test host says request at 09:39:58 got the error response at 09:40:01 — before the error?
**Commands [RO].** date -u on both; Redfish DateTime; timedatectl on BMC (if present); NTP status.

steps.label: Expected observations
steps.text: BMC clock 4.3 s ahead; or BMC in local time zone vs UTC on host.

steps.label: Possible causes
steps.text: Clock skew; time zone; NTP not synchronised; clock jump during test.

steps.label: Investigation
steps.text: Measure offset at test start/end; check for jumps (journal “Time has been changed”).

steps.label: Evidence to confirm
steps.text: Measured offset explains the misalignment.

steps.label: Corrective options
steps.text: NTP on BMC and agents; record offsets in reports; convert to UTC.

steps.label: Verification
steps.text: Aligned timeline after correction.

steps.label: Interview explanation
steps.text: “Effects before causes means clocks disagree — I measured the offset and corrected the timeline.”

source.section: 27.14 Case 14: Log timestamps do not align

scenarios.title: Case 15: A process consumes excessive memory
scenarios.prompt: Case 15: A process consumes excessive memory. How would you investigate?

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text:
BMC memory available drops from 40% to 5% over 3 days.
